As described in the Samagam, the 52–92 sites named for attaining moksha belong to the path of action, karma-marg; they belong to the six darshans. Each single darshan has 16 pakhands; thus for all six darshans together there are in total 16 x 16 = 96 pakhands.

Each pakhand has three gachchhas, sub-sects. Among the Jains too there are two divisions, but the scriptures count both as one: (1) Digambar, (2) Shvetambar. Jain — 1, one; Buddhist — 3, three; Charvak — 2, two; these are the names of the three gachchhas. Wherever a particular gachchha exists, that particular pakhand and that particular gachchha are found there.

In Registration No. 541, p. 39, Dharekhan writes that caste (jnati) and gachchha are different things. Caste is not gachchha; gachchha arose from different lineages and branches. Gachchha is called gotra. In all there are 84–85 gachchhas; at present few remain. Inter-dining and inter-marriage do not exist among many of them, though the scriptures do not forbid it. Many have made efforts to separate the Jains from the Hindus. In the Samagam, Kabirji's ramaini is presented as testimony regarding the gayatri and so on of the pakhand-gachchhas.

Shankaracharya has said:

_gajairapi pidyamano'pi na gacchejjainamandire, yavani naiva vaktavya pranaih kanthagatairapi ||15||_

It further says:

_hastina tadyamano'pi na gacchejjainamandiram, na vadedyavanim bhasham pranaih kanthagatairapi ||16||_ (Registration No. 1613, p. 37) (Even if trampled by an elephant, one should not enter a Jain temple to save oneself; and even if life is leaving one through the throat, one should not speak the language of the Yavanas, the Greek/foreign barbarians.)

Now let us speak of the six, shat, darshan shastras. Each of the six darshan shastras has sixteen-sixteen pakhands; for all six darshans together this makes 16 x 6 = 96 pakhands.

Indian philosophical schools, darshan shastras, are divided into two groups: those holding Vedic belief, that is, darshan shastras that accept the Veda, and non-Vedic shastras, that is, those opposed to the Veda. Six darshan shastras favoring the Veda are named:

1) Nyaya Shastra — Gautam Muni
2) Vaisheshik Shastra — Kanad Muni
3) Sankhya Darshan — Kapil Muni
4) Yoga Darshan — Patanjali
5) Purva Mimamsa — Jaimini
6) Uttar Mimamsa — Badarayan

The non-Vedic, or Veda-opposing, darshan shastras are also six:
1) Lokayatik — (unspecified)
2) Charvak Darshan — Charvak Muni
3) Mahayan Darshan — Gautam Buddha
4) Vrajyan Darshan — Gautam Buddha
5) Hinayan Darshan — Gautam Buddha
6) Jain Darshan — Mahavir Swami

96 pakhands, 12 yogis, 18 jangams, 24 sevadas, 10 sannyasis, 14 darvesh (sheikhs), and 18 brahmins.

Thus altogether twelve darshan shastras have been named. Of the first six, two — Sankhya and Purva Mimamsa — are nirishvaravadi, that is, they do not believe in God. Purva Mimamsa upholds ritual action (karmakand): it holds that the Vedic mantras alone bestow all fruits. In their view, man acts only in hope of fruit, and fruit is obtained through Vedic mantras; therefore there is no need for the soul (jiva), the world, or God.

But what Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj says about this doctrine of pakhand is as follows. Among the darshan shastras, whether they accept the Veda or not, there has never been unanimous agreement on matters such as the body, the soul, and God. There prevails dispute, that is, doctrinal disagreement, among all of them. Yet, despite this mutual opposition, an attempt is made to show doctrinal non-contradiction and to bring about reconciliation. According to the Jain view, of the many attributes of a single thing, one attribute is considered primary and the rest secondary — cultivating the outlook of seeing and understanding a thing from different standpoints. Gautam Muni, the founder of Nyaya Shastra, in order to know Brahma, to attain moksha, enumerated sixteen distinct categories:

1) Pramana, means of valid knowledge: The instrument of true knowledge, divided into four: 1) Pratyaksha, perception, 2) Anuman, inference, 3) Upaman, comparison, 4) Shabda, verbal testimony.

2) Prameya, the object of knowledge: That which can become the object of true knowledge. Twelve kinds of prameya are named: soul, body, senses, objects, intellect, mind, activity, rebirth, fault, fruit, suffering, and liberation — knowledge that touches the mutually contradictory aspects present within one and the same subject.

3) Samshaya, doubt: Knowledge that touches upon mutually contradictory aspects of a single object, once a purpose or aim has arisen for it.

4) Prayojana, purpose: That thing for the sake of which an activity is undertaken, whether to attain or to avoid it.

5) Drishtanta, example: That regarding which there is no difference of opinion between the scholar and common practice.

6) Siddhanta, established tenet: This has four kinds — 1) Sarvatantra, universally accepted, 2) Pratitantra, school-specific, 3) Adhikaran, implied by the topic, 4) Abhyupagam, hypothetically granted.

7) Avayava, the members of a syllogism, which are five: 1) Pratijna, proposition, 2) Hetu, reason, 3) Udaharan, example, 4) Upanayan, application, 5) Nigaman, conclusion.

8) Tarka, reasoning: When the true nature of some thing is not known, then, in order to discover its nature, one infers one thing and, on that basis, infers a further, undifferentiated thing.

9) Nirnaya, ascertainment: After doubt has arisen, the determination of one of the two sides through a position (paksha) and a counter-position (pratipaksha).

10) Vada, debate: That verbal exchange in which both a thesis and a counter-thesis are accepted — that is, in which, of the two mutually opposed aspects of a single subject, the proponent and the opponent have each duly accepted one aspect as their own position, in which both proponent and opponent establish their own position and refute the other's through proof and reasoning, in which this process of establishing and refuting takes the form of statements composed of the five members, proposition and so on, and which does not go against established doctrine.

11) Jalpa: In addition to having all the aforesaid characteristics of Vada, that verbal exchange in which deceit (chhala), sophistry (jati), and disqualifying tactics (nigrahasthan) are also employed to establish one's own side and refute the opposing side is called Jalpa.

12) Vitanda: That same Jalpa, if we remove from it the establishing of one's own counter-position, is called Vitanda.

13) Hetvabhasa, fallacious reason: That which, though not a true reason, appears to be a reason. There are five kinds: 1) Savyabhichar, inconclusive, 2) Viruddha, contradictory, 3) Prakaranasam, equal to the point at issue, 4) Sadhyasam, equal to what is to be proved, 5) Badhit, contradicted by other proof.

14) Chhala, deceit: Imagining a meaning different from what a person intended to say, and thereby corrupting that person's statement. Its kinds are Vak-chhala, Samanya-chhala, and Upachar-chhala.

15) Jati, sophistry: Bringing about an undesired consequence through resemblance and non-resemblance, that is, through similarity and dissimilarity.

16) Nigrahasthan, point of defeat: That point at which, owing to self-contradiction or a failure to state one's position, the disputant must be stopped.

(Tarkasangraha, composed by Annambhatta; English translation by Yashwant Vasudev Athavale and Mahadev Rajaram Bodas.)

The soul, the world, Brahma, Parbrahm, and so on cannot be established through scriptural debate — these can be known only through one's own direct experience, self-realization.

On "pakhand," in the Sundarvilas composed by Sundardas, pakhand, hypocrisy and pretense, is enumerated as follows:

1. Some people perform yajnas according to Vedic ritual — Vajapeya, Gomedha, and so on.

2. Some people wander from one pilgrimage site to another.

3. Some people, through purificatory practice at home, perform sandhya, twilight prayers, tarpan, offerings to ancestors, and the six rites, shatkarma.

4. Some people, taking up the varnashram order, observe brahmacharya and become celibate students.

5. Some people, in the householder stage, remain bound day and night to son and wife in various ways.

6. Some people take the vow of vanaprastha and go to the forest together with their wife.

7. Some people, as paramhansa sannyasis, give up their topknot and sacred thread, yet bind themselves in many other bonds.

8. Some people bathe every day, evening, morning, and noon.

9. Some people observe many rules and vows — the chandrayan vrat, fasting, and so on.

10. Some people worship the gods, plucking various leaves and flowers for worship.

11. Some people wear rosaries and tilak and call themselves devotees who worship Vishnu.

12. Some people chant the name of Shiva endlessly, hang a linga around the neck, and smear themselves with ash.

13. Some Jains, upholding the doctrine of karma, have their hair plucked out and perform excessive show.

14. Some people wear earrings and, as Kapalikas, Aghoris, follow a corrupt doctrine.

15. Some people, through fierce atheistic doctrine, commit much pakhand.

16. Some people take the Goddess to be Shakti and kill living creatures to offer to her.

17. Some people perform many kinds of homa — sesame offerings, japa, ghee lamps — and serve her in this way.

18. Some people perform yajna and homa, make offerings to the gods, and serve them with incense and lamps.

19. Some people practice impure mantras, black magic — vashikaran, subjugation, uchchatan, banishing — and perform rites at the cremation pyre.

20. Some people, in cremation grounds, awaken the dead and practice much stambhan, paralyzing, and mohan, bewitching.

21. Some people attract women and cheat them, stealing away their ornaments.

22. Some people, spreading falsehoods, transmute metals through the alchemy of mercury into gold.

23. Some people make wonder-working pills from plant leaves and gain occult powers.

24. Some people hold sharp-edged swords, fire, and water under their control, and lift boulders onto their shoulders.

25. Some people improve bodily health through medicinal herbs and roots.

26. Some people, through astrological calculation, run household affairs by determining the date, day, hour, and auspicious moment.

27. Some people give in charity by weighing themselves against gold, tuladan, and give gems, land, grain, cloth, books, and other various gifts.

28. Some people speak Sanskrit, know difficult verses, and recite them to others.

29. Some people study logic, tarkashastra, and, having mastered this learning, carry a staff as a badge of authority.

30. Some people know various differing doctrines and display cleverness by studying grammar.

31. Some people recite poetry and verse, composing kundaliyas and other such forms.

32. They string together verses and stanzas, stealing syllables from wherever they can.

33. They play the veena and flute, singing songs to the beat of drums.

34. Some people display the art of actors, singing sweetly with hand gestures.

35. Some people undergo severe bodily austerities and eat only a handful of food, panchagrasa.

36. Some people eat as if with an elephant's mouth, excessively, and then fall on their knees, gaining no wisdom at all.

37. Some people stretch out their hand to beg alms, and then, wiping their hand, run off into the forest.

38. Some people go from door to door begging for stale, dry scraps of bread.

39. Some people cook without touching anyone, and display this to people with their mouths covered.

40. Some people eat morsels served by a woman's hand from an iron plate.

41. Some people wash their food and drink the washings, living in such filth that one wonders how they survive at all.

42. Some people take up the doctrine of the Aghoris, accepting both extremes.

43. Some people eat forbidden food without fear, even eating meat and drinking liquor.

44. Some poor people live only on milk, payahari, eating raisins, dried coconut, grapes, and dates.

45. Some people dig up and eat roots and tubers, living alone in the forest.

46. Some people wear tree bark and sit in deep water reciting japa.

47. Some people dye their clothes yellow and wear very thin garments.

48. Some people, appearing steeped in devotion and free of passion, wear torn saffron robes.

49. Some deceitful people wear rough, prickly wooden garments, making a great show and shouting loudly while sitting in deep water reciting japa.

50. Some people wear clothes of coarse sackcloth to please and win over people in many ways.

51. Some people pick up rags from the road and, carrying a beggar's bag, present themselves in the guise of the formless, nirgun.

52. Some people wear deerskin or tiger skin, putting on great pretense and show.

53. Some people wear bark garments and endure cold and rain.

54. Some people go about naked, as digambaras, and smear themselves with ash.

55. Some people grow matted hair and long nails; the Lord does not recognize such varied forms.

56. Some people test their ignorance and, being dull-witted, burn in the heat of the five fires, panchagni.

57. Some people sit amid thunder and, in cold weather, enter into water.

58. Some people, smoking and losing their way, hang upside down from trees.

59. Some fools die by the sword's edge in their desire to become kings.

60. Some people, for the sake of happiness in the next birth, jump from a height into water and die.

61. Some fools waste their bones away in the Himalayas, their minds greatly pleased at doing so.

62. Some people pierce their throat and give up the body, hoping to gain something in the life to come.

63. Some people dwell on mountains, and some dwell in caves.

64. Some people do not stay in one place — today here, tomorrow they go elsewhere.

65. Some people make their bed of grass.

66. Some people spread hard pebbles for their bed.

67. Some people observe harsh vows, standing on one leg for twelve years.

68. Some people go and live in cremation grounds, proudly claiming, "I am an avadhut."

69. Some people live beneath trees, saying, "I depend on no one."

70. Some people keep silent and do not speak, communicating their inner thoughts through gestures.

71. Some people shave sandalwood into sandals and, wearing sandals on their feet, wink their eyes.

72. Some people act as swindlers, robbing everyone in plain sight.

73. Some people smear vermilion on their bodies and keep a child with them.

74. Some people cast spells, mooth, saying, "May Narsimha and Bhairav strike you down."

75. Some people eat akdo and dhaturo, poisonous plants, and put burning coals into their mouths.

76. Some people eat opium and drink bhang, being dull-minded and whimsical.

77. How far should one go on counting such wanderers? Understanding this, one should remain in the shelter of the Guru.

The King of Riva has enumerated the 96 pakhands as follows:

_dash sanyasi barah yogi, chaudah shekh bakhana, bodh adharahi jangam adharahi, chaubees savera jana ||37||_ (In this way the 96 pakhands are told. Kabir Ramaini Sudha, page 4, writes: ten kinds of sannyasis, twelve kinds of yogis, eighteen kinds of brahmins, eighteen kinds of other castes — Shia-Sunni, Christian, Parsi, and so on — fourteen kinds of Sheikhs, and twenty-four kinds of Jains — in total, ninety-six, 96, kinds. All these divisions were created by man himself; the Supreme is not responsible for them.)

It further says:

_yogi jangam sevda, sanyasi daravesh, chhatha kahiye brahmanan, chha ghar chha updesh ||38||_ (These six darshans have six mantra-teachings.)

1. Jogi — "Ahannad"; 2. Jangam — "Niranjanay"; 3. Sevda — "Arihant"; 4. Brahmin — "Ukar," the Gayatri's Omkar; 5. Darvesh — "I am Allah"; 6. Sannyasi — "Soham, Brahmasmi."

Jogi: those who have performed the practice of "ear-slit," kanphata, yoga, such as Matsyendra and others.
Jangam: those who tie the linga of Mahadev around their neck and live together with a woman.
Sevda: followers of the Jain doctrine — the Sthanakvasi and the temple-dwelling, Deravasi, Jains.
Sannyasi: those who wear saffron robes and bear one of the ten names, dashnam — Giri, Puri, Bharati, Van, Parvat, Sagar, Tirth, Parvat, Dungar, Jhadvan, and so on — this is the darshan of the sannyasi.
Darvesh: Muslim fakirs, auliya, and so on.
Brahmin: ritualists, karmakandi. Among these six darshans there are ninety-six pakhands.

The six divisions of the atheistic, nastik, schools outside the Veda are: 1. Vaibhashik, 2. Saubhantik, 3. Yogachar, 4. Madhyamik, 5. Jain — Digambar, 6. Charvak.

Regarding those who don religious garb, the Panchatantra, in the Kakolukiyam chapter, verse 98, says:

_nacchadayati kaupinam na damshamashakapaham, shunah puchchhamiva vyartham panditam dharmavarjitam ||17||_ (Just as a dog's tail neither covers its private parts nor drives away flies and mosquitoes, so too is dharma-less scriptural cleverness, which produces no true renunciation, like a dog's tail — useless. Such a person, wearing the loincloth, becoming a sannyasi, is unable to destroy mental afflictions such as lust, and is therefore a failure.)

There is a verse regarding the six scriptures of the six darshans:

_vedant tark mimansa sankhya patanjalam tatha, dharmashastrametyetat prahuh shastranishad budhah ||18||_ (Vedanta, Tarka, Nyaya, Mimansa, Sankhya, Patanjal Yoga, and Dharmashastra — the wise say these are the six shastras.)

For the six darshans it is said: 1. Upanishad, 2. Nyaya, 3. Karmakand, Mimansa, 4. Tattva-vivechan, Sankhya, 5. Yoga, and 6. Smritis. In the Samagam, the six darshans have been divided according to the three gunas, as follows:

1. Sattvik — two darshans of Vishnu's guna: 1. Mahatma = Jogi, 2. Yati = Sevda.
2. Tamasik — 1. Jangam, Lingayat, 2. Sannyasi.
3. Rajasi — 1. Brahmin, 2. Sufi, Darvesh.

The Samagam explains that among those who follow these six darshans, neither the tilak, nor the tulsi, nor the name of Ram is given credence. And the darshan of Vasudev — that is, of devotion to God, the devotion of the true Vaishnav, the devotee of God — stands beyond these six darshans. But people of the world count the devotion of the Vaishnav among the six darshans; yet it remains excluded from them — that devotion is separate from the six darshans. Six scriptures of the six darshans have been composed, but this devotion to Vishnu is different from those six scriptures. The Samagam states that within these true scriptures there is one portion in which devotion to Vishnu is also accepted, and another portion that favors ritual action, karmakand. Thus, of the fourteen kands of the Yajurved, up to the thirteen-and-a-half, 13½, kand there is a mixture of devotion and liberation, through which the soul cannot attain the Supreme. Therefore, having considered all these ritualistic scriptures and the six darshans, one should set them aside — that is, not fall into them — and reject them.

That ritual action is described up to the thirteen-and-a-half kand of the Yajurved is something Kabirji too has pointed out. Regarding the fact that the thirteen-and-a-half kands of the Yajurved uphold ritual action, Kabir has said:

_kabir ter bhag trigun lagi, chauda chotha manhe, e padku je paavhi, ant kahu nahi jaahe ||39||_ (Kabirji says that the thirteen, thirteen-and-a-half, parts of the ritual action, of the Yajurved and so on, can lead only up to the stage of the three gunas, whereas the remaining half of the fourteenth part carries one beyond the three gunas, to the fourth state, the state transcending the three gunas, trigunatita. Therefore, whoever attains this state of the fourth guna will, in the end, no longer have to suffer the pains of birth and death.)

In the mortal world, those on the path of action have designated the seven cities, three villages, nine forests, nine medicinal herbs, fourteen guhyas, and so on as centers for attaining liberation. Among these, again, the seven cities are singled out separately. Rev. Yadunath Maharaj says that even the Smritis, which set forth the ritual action of the six darshans, are to be considered artificial — souls remain caught wandering, as if between a gourd-vessel, between sky and earth. Among the sites for attaining moksha, the seven cities are singled out, and this is given in the Garud Puran, Chapter 16, verse 114:

_ayodhya mathura maya kashi kanchi avantika |_

The praise of Ayodhya is given in the Uttara Kanda of the Ramayana:

_Ayodhya cha param-brahma, Sarayuh saguna: puman. Tannivasi Jagannathas satyam satyam vadami te._ (For human beings Ayodhya is itself the form of the Supreme Brahman, and the Sarayu river is filled with virtue; moreover Ram, the Lord of the world, dwells there. This I tell you truly, truly.) ||19||

It is said in a further verse that in all seven of these cities are the limbs of Vishnu:

_Vishnoh pad bhavantika gunavati madhye cha Kanchipuri. Nabhau Dwaravati vadanti hridaye Mayapuri yoginah. Griva mulam udaharanti Mathura nasagra Varanasi. Etad brahmapadam vadanti munayo 'yodhyapuri mastake._ (Ujjain, endowed with virtue, is the feet of Vishnu; Kanchipuri is the middle portion, the waist; Dwarka is called the heart; yogis call Haridwar [Mayapuri] the throat; Mathura is called the mouth; Kanchipuri and Varanasi are called the nose; Ayodhya is called the head — this the sages describe as the seat of Brahman, filled with the Lord.) ||20||

In the Samagam, the sixth verse says that among the seven abodes of liberation briefly described here, three cities in particular have been given exceptional importance:

_Trigrama sristi-madhye sve vanchita hai kritatmakah. Lokanam bhagyahinanam yah sarvajno hyajah kriti._ (In this creation there are three villages which grateful, fortunate people desire; unfortunate people do not desire them. Only one who is all-knowing and truly accomplished can know this.) ||6||

Deluded, foolish people, afflicted by maya (illusion), disregard these three villages, as this verse indicates. The Samagam therefore says that such afflicted people do not know wherein the manifestation of God lies; they cannot attain the true substance — the thing through which God can truly be attained. This is what the verse shows. Confirming this verse is a couplet (sakhi) spoken by Revered Jivanji Maharaj:

_Saatpuri mã Jivna, teen puri tatva-sar. Ugrasen Sudama jahã, Kabir bhaye avatar._ (Meaning: of the seven cities, only three are truly important — Mathura, associated with Ugrasen; Dwarka, associated with Sudama; and Kashi, where Kabir took incarnation. These three are the essential ones.) Revered Yadunath Maharaj says: Ugrasen belonged to Mathura, Sudama belonged to Porbandar (Dwarka), and Kabir belonged to Kashi. The finest place for devotion is within the unbroken realm of Vraj.

The fourth verse states that the fields for attaining liberation are mixed together with the path of ritual action (karma-marg); among them the seven cities too are mentioned. Yet in this couplet presented by Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, only three of the seven cities are given a place of importance, which might look like a self-contradiction. But in singling out these three cities, the intent is not about the cities themselves, but about the great souls who appeared in them and made their names illustrious. So instead of naming the three cities, this couplet actually names the great souls who illuminated them. Jivanji Maharaj has said in a couplet:

_Tahã Ayodhya jahã Raghupati, kahana tahã Gokul gam. Saptapuri tahã Jivna, jahã sant sangat Harinam._ (Wherever Ram is, that place becomes Ayodhya; wherever Krishna is, that becomes the village of Gokul. But wherever there is the company of saints (satsang, holy company) and the Lord's name, O Jivan, that place becomes greater than all seven cities — a sacred place.)

So this couplet is spoken not in praise of the seven cities or the three villages, but to show the greatness of those who illuminate those places. When Ram left Ayodhya for his exile and went to live on Chitrakut mountain, crowds began gathering for his darshan (sight of the divine). Once Ram noticed the austere sages living there whispering to one another, hiding something from him, and he wished to know what they were concealing. He had Lakshman inquire, and the sages said that because Ram had come there, the crowds disturbing their austerities had grown too great, so they were discussing moving elsewhere. Hearing this, Ram said that instead of all of them leaving, he alone would go. But the sages replied that even if he left, people would not stop coming — they would still come to see places such as Bharat Kup and Ram Shila. So it would still not be possible for them to stay there and practice their austerities in solitude.

Our religion-loving people believe that by regarding such tirthas (pilgrimage sites) and cities as sacred, and by mortifying the body through pilgrimage in the name of removing sin and attaining liberation, they become fulfilled. But Jivanji Maharaj holds that one cannot be freed from sin through pilgrimage — freedom from sin comes only through the company of saints and through the Lord's name.

These three cities were given special importance because they are aligned with devotion to Vishnu — that is, they draw our attention toward that devotion. Having said this, to show that the Guru's greatness is vast enough to redeem the entire world, the 148th verse of the Guru Gita is presented:

_Akhanda-mandalakaram vyaptam yena characharam. Tat-padam darshitam yena tasmai shri gurave namah._ (Salutations to that Guru who has shown the seat which, in the form of an unbroken circle, pervades this entire moving and unmoving world.) ||7||

In keeping with this verse, and applying to the great Sama Veda saying "Tattvamasi," further verses which Revered Yadunath Maharaj obtained from elsewhere are given below:

_Sthavaram jangamam vyaptam yat kinchit sacharacharam. Tvam-padam darshitam yena tasmai shri gurave namah._ (Salutations to that Guru who has shown your — "thou" — place, which pervades whatever is moving and unmoving, animate and inanimate, in this world.) ||21||

_Chinmayam vyapitam yena sarva trailokyam sacharacharam. Asitvam darshitam yena tasmai shri gurave namah._ (Salutations to that Guru who has shown the seat of your — "is" — existence, whose consciousness-filled form pervades this whole world of the three realms, moving and unmoving.) ||22||

"Tattvamasi" (Thou Art That) is said to convey the essential meaning of the Sama Veda. The great sayings (mahavakyas) of the Upanishads of the four Vedas are given below.

From the Yajur Veda Upanishad, alongside the corresponding Sama Veda mahavakya:
1. _Aham Brahmasmi_ (I am Brahman — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10), matched with the Sama Veda's _Tattvamasi_ (Thou art That — Chandogya Upanishad 8.16).
2. _Satyam jnanam anantam Brahma_ (Brahman is truth, knowledge, the infinite), matched with _Sarvam khalvidam Brahma_ (All this, verily, is Brahman — Chandogya 3.14.2).
3. _Vijnanam anandam Brahma_ (Brahman is consciousness and bliss), matched with _Ekam evadvitiyam Brahma_ (Brahman is one only, without a second).
4. The fourth pair is given too garbled in the source text to render with confidence [unclear].

From the Atharva Veda, alongside the corresponding Rig Veda mahavakya:
1. The first pair is given too garbled in the source text to render with confidence [unclear].
2. The Atharva Veda entry is garbled in the source [unclear]; the Rig Veda entry is _Prajnanam Brahma_ (Consciousness is Brahman — Aitareya Upanishad 3.3, and Atmapra. 1).
3. _Ayamatma Brahma_ (This self is Brahman — Mandukya Upanishad); the corresponding Rig Veda entry is garbled in the source [unclear] (cited as Brihadaranyaka 2.5.19).
4. Both entries in this pair are garbled in the source text [unclear] (the Atharva entry is cited as Kaushitaki 3).

We have no particular concern with the great sayings of the Vedas or Upanishads as such. For us, the very words from the Guru's own mouth are what Jivana has reckoned as the true good. But alongside this verse from the Guru Gita, Revered Yadunath Maharaj also cited verses relating to the saying "Tattvamasi," which is why they are presented here.

Commenting on this verse of the Guru Gita, the Samagam says that seeing Vasudev is a thing beyond ordinary power; his divine play (lila) is seen only if one attains the Guru's grace, and one who lacks it cannot see it. Here Kabirji says:

_Ichchha rup nari avatari, tako naam Gayatri ghari. Take teen bhaye jo puta, Brahma Vishnu Mahadev suta. ||1|| Teenahu teen basaye gama, apne apne kine nama. Vishnu jyun apna panth chalaya, teenka maram kinhi na paya. ||2|| Brahma Ved kiya adhikai, char baran bandhe dradhai. Tripurari joye aasan rambha, in teenun mali pakhand thambha. ||3|| Te pakhand darshan chha bhule, pheri pheri joni sankatma jhule. Teen jun racha khand brahmanda, chha darshan chhanabe pakhanda. ||4|| Mata murchhit garabh parasavati, swang ghare bohotu karyatuti. Pet na kahu Ved padhaye, sunrat karaye turak nahi aaye. ||5|| Brahma ulat puchhe mahatari, kaun tere puras kaun ki tun nari. Tab ham tum aur nahi koi, tu mera purush main teri joi. ||6||_ — followed by the sakhi (couplet): _Kabir mata te mehari bhai, put hote bhaya baap. Ek achraj ham dekhiya, je kahat na lage paap. ||1||_

(Meaning: A woman in the form of desire took birth, and she was named Gayatri. Kabirji uses the symbol "woman" here for religion in general, because the religions of the world have arisen out of desire — if human beings had no desire or craving, and no fear of death, religion could never have found a place in human life at all. Today, most existing religions run after material wealth, sensual enjoyment, and worldly splendor.

In the hymns of the Rig Veda too it can be seen everywhere that many ancient sages asked the gods for material wealth, and it was for this very reason that ritual sacrifice (yajna) and other ritual actions began — action without desire for a result could not exist. According to one Puranic story, Vishwamitra created the goddess Gayatri for just such a purpose. That is why Kabirji, fittingly, chose Gayatri out of thousands of gods and goddesses — some other goddess could have taken her place, but Gayatri, being herself the goddess of desire and craving and the root of all desires, is more fitting; all desires and cravings arise from her. Even setting aside the literal meaning and taking the subtle one, this significance still holds, because Gayatri is said to be composed of portions of the three principal Vedas, of which the Yajur Veda is full of desire and result-oriented ritual action. That is why Jivanji Maharaj further says that the ritual-action portion of the Yajur Veda should be set aside, and the path of loving devotion (prem-bhakti) that remains should be accepted.)

_Mayake sab bas pare, Brahma Vishnu Mahesh. Narad Sharad Sanak Sanandan, Gauri sut Ganesh._ (Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva have all fallen under the sway of maya; so too have Narad, Saraswati, the Sanakadi sages, and Ganesh, the son of Parvati.)

The subtle, hidden form of desire is craving (vasana), and the subtle form of craving is impression or tendency (sanskar) — that is, the manifest form of impression is craving, the gross form of craving is desire, and the gross form of desire is suffering.

Kabir writes in Ramaini Sudha, page 2: "Kabir Sahib calls maya also Gayatri" — and further, in the science of creation, the meaning of Gayatri is given as the power that protects one who sings the praises of God. The translation of the ramaini is as follows: a woman in the form of desire arose, and she was named Gayatri. To her were born three sons — Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh. They settled three villages and gave them each their own names (Brahmalok, Vishnulok, Shivlok). Vishnu followed his own path, and no one came to know its way. Brahma gave precedence to the Vedas and firmly established the four varnas (caste-classes). Shiva's wife sits upon his seat; Shiva sat in state together with Parvati. These three together set going pretense (pakhand — a false show of religion), and everyone wandered lost in it. In the six schools of philosophy (khat-darshan) everyone went astray, and again and again people fell into the trouble of birth in the womb. All three of them together fashioned divisions and universes; thus were formed six schools and ninety-six kinds of pretense. The mother who gives birth delivers the child from the womb in a state of unconsciousness; that child, growing up, takes on many kinds of disguises and antics. In the womb, no mother teaches anyone the Vedas, nor is any Muslim born already circumcised. Then Brahma, turning back, asks his own mother: "Who is your husband, and whose wife are you?" The mother answered: "Here, besides you and me, there is no one else; so you alone are my husband, and I am your wife." Sakhi: Kabir says — thus the one who was the mother became the wife, and the one who was the son became the father. I have seen one great wonder; to speak of it is no sin.

In Ramaini 35 it is said:

_Gayatri jug chaari pathai, puchhahu jaay mukti kin paai._ (For four ages they have chanted the Gayatri mantra; yet go and ask whether they have truly attained liberation.)

_Ohankar phal-ditate, upaje ichchha jhaad. Sadguru kahai sadbhaav-so, nishrai nejo gaad._ (From the fruit-bearing tree of the ego-syllable Om grows the tree of desire. So the Sadguru, moved by feeling, says: plant the marker of firm resolve in devotion filled with true faith — resolve in your heart to practice loving devotion, and do not become entangled in that Om-linked ego which produces the tree of desires.)

The next line of this ramaini, not given here, reads:

_Jeev roop yak antar basa, antarjyoti kin par gaasa._ (The soul dwells within a single frame in the form of the body.) Two meanings emerge here. One is the cosmic sense: the soul that has taken on a body, whose inner awareness is joined to the inner light — that is, to the Supreme Brahman — and which wishes to merge again into Brahman. The other is the worldly sense: as one's mind is, so is one's inner awareness, says Kabirji.

_Jaise maya man milyo, aise Ram ramaay. Taramandal bhedke, tabe Amarpur jaay._ (Just as the mind has become absorbed in this illusory world, glittering like a constellation of stars with its powers and attainments, so, if the mind is lovingly fixed on Ram in the same way, one attains Amarpur, the abode of God, piercing through the realm of the stars.) ||1||

The devotion Kabirji shows here is that whatever the mind is joined to becomes one's vision of God — this is the path of Shakti worship or goddess worship, one branch of which worships images and another mystical diagrams (yantras). Among these worshippers of Shakti are also counted the left-hand path, the Aghoris, the Tantrics, and so on; there is no need here for a detailed discussion of this. But Shakti worship is a tamasic (dark, unillumined) form of worship, in which sacrifice is an important element. For this reason, in Aryan-period culture this form of worship was regarded as forbidden in respectable society, because the Mother is the symbol of love, power, and warmth — only a mother can give love, not killing and violence. But in ancient times, through the mixing of Aryan and non-Aryan peoples, this practice gradually became established throughout society. It became especially prevalent among the Shaiva Kapalikas, and with it the extent of violent sacrifice increased; in many places human sacrifice too began to spread, which in time came to be regarded with contempt by respectable society. Eventually, among the worshippers of Vishnu, the goddess of love and tolerance, Radha, came to occupy this place — worshipped as the symbol of peace and love, the opposite of violence and sacrifice — and she quickly gained a place in respectable society.

During this long period of the paths of devotion, knowledge, and ritual action, the literature and modes of worship that arose became, in many cases, sharply opposed to and competing with one another. This compelled Kabirji to say that everyone had established a system suited to their own convenience — what Kabirji calls "pakhand-vad" (the way of pretense).

Differences of opinion also arose over the individual soul, the world, the Self, the Supreme Brahman, and the origin of creation. Around the same time, Muslims arrived in India and launched their own spiritual challenge to Aryan culture; among the Muslims too, divisions such as Shia and Sunni caused friction. This made it necessary for a plain speaker like Kabirji to say that merely wearing the sacred thread does not make one a Brahmin, just as merely being circumcised or merely offering namaz does not make one a true, pure Muslim — true religion is one of love, non-violence, and brotherhood. Blaming one another or slinging mud at each other is wholly irreligious and contrary to humanity. The first duty of human beings is unity, equality, and love.

It was for this reason that Kabirji's righteous wrath blazed up against the pretense, reproach, and hypocrisy prevailing in society, and against the heads of religion responsible for it — the mahants, pandits, and mullahs:

_Na jaane tera sahib kaisa hai. Masjid bhitar mulla pukare, kya sahib tera bahira hai. Chiunti ke pag nepur baaje, so bhi sahib sunta hai. ||1|| Pandit hoy ke aasan maare, lambi mala japta hai. Antar tere kapat katarni, so bhi sahib lakhta hai. ||2||_ (You do not know what your Lord is truly like. Inside the mosque the mullah calls out — is your Lord deaf, then? Even the sound of an ant's anklets, your Lord hears. The pandit sits in a yogic posture and tells a long rosary of beads, but the scissors of deceit within you — that too your Lord perceives.)

Thus arose all these systems of philosophy, doctrines, sects, and paths, among which Jivanji Maharaj has chiefly named the following. First, for devotion to Vishnu, two paths are named: 1) Mahatma, 2) Yati — said to have the quality of sattva (purity). The second quality is tamas (dark, unillumined), with two divisions: (a) Jangami-Yogi, (b) Sannyasi. The third quality is rajas (passion, activity), with two divisions: (a) Brahmin, (b) Sufi.

Among the above philosophies and sects, one will never find the tilak (forehead mark), tulsi (holy basil), and Ram-nam (the Lord's name) together, because these three alone are the symbols of love, devotion, and light. If those sects followed these three, no pretense would remain at all. These three symbols lead one toward the Supreme Brahman; only one who wishes to worship the Supreme Brahman in a pure manner can rightly bear them. Even if others were to bear them, in Jivanji Maharaj's view one who bears the symbols without the matching conduct is merely "salil" (a hollow show). So, apart from one who is truly devoted to the Supreme Brahman, these three — tilak, tulsi, Ram-nam — cannot be true symbols for anyone else; they are the symbols of Vasudev alone.

That is why true Vaishnav devotion is different from all the above: in it there is no pretense or hypocrisy, only the true worship of the Supreme Brahman. In this world and universe, devotion to Vishnu is the highest and best. Ostentatious people today have distorted it and classed it among the pretenses, which is not correct — the devotee of Vishnu is beyond all these. Therefore, whatever scriptures were written for the sake of such worship are all to be set aside as forbidden and reckoned as "pakhand," because the scriptures of the ritual-action school give priority to ritual action alone and should be set aside for that reason.

_Pothi sab parpanch ki, akshar lekhe banaay. Prem akshar bin Jivna, Jam ghasede jaay. ||1|| Likhte likhte sab likha, shastra Ved Puran. Sadguru sevya bin Jivna, bahu bhaand ko gyaan. ||2||_ (All the books are made of illusory show; their letters are formed by contrivance. Without the letter of love, O Jivan, Yama, the god of death, will drag you away. Writing on and on, everything was set down — shastras, Vedas, Puranas — but without service to the Sadguru, O Jivan, it is only the knowledge of a mere flatterer.)

All the scriptures are full of deceit and pretense; the words written in them are fabricated. Jivanji Maharaj says that without the outpouring of love, Yamraj will drag one away. Writing all manner of things, people set down the shastras, Vedas, Puranas, and so on, but without service to and refuge in the Sadguru, one who knows many arts is like a court bard who praises falsely and truly alike — such is the art these Vedas and shastras represent.

Therefore one should accept only the true word that leads toward the Supreme Brahman, and follow only the scripture that gives a vision of the Supreme Brahman. Seeing the scriptures of the path of ritual action, one should set them aside and not follow them; wherever the Yajur Veda and similar texts give rites and rituals, those parts should be set apart and not followed — only what gives a vision of the Supreme Brahman apart from ritual action should be accepted. Beyond this, one should not go too deep into scriptural doctrine. Kabirji says (from Kabir Sakhi, Madhya-Kaang):

_Kabir dharti aur aasman, beech do tubari abaddh. Khat darshan saanse padaan, aur chorasi sidh. ||1||_ (Kabirji says: between earth and sky, like an unmoored gourd-vessel, the soul wanders trapped. Even the followers of the six schools of philosophy and the eighty-four siddhas are perplexed within these confines.)

Meaning: Kabirji says the soul wanders trapped within the confines of heaven and the mortal world, as if within a gourd-vessel. Whether to attain heaven and such realms through the two paths of ritual action and devotion, or to choose, birth after birth, devotion to God and dwelling at his lotus feet — even the followers of the six schools and the eighty-four siddhas fall into confusion over this choice. Of all these, only two — the saint-guru and the disciple — remain free of bondage.

At present, two branches have descended from this tradition. Ancient, Aryan-period Indian culture, which in time became distorted, came down as the "Acharya" tradition. But over time, as the Acharya tradition grew narrow and self-serving, a second "Sant" (saint) tradition arose in opposition to it, by the grace of many saints such as Kabir, Namdevji, and Rohidas. This tradition arose in the language of the common people, with regard for ordinary life; in the Sant tradition, even the suffering of the smallest person found an echo, whereas the Acharya tradition was carried on only by Brahmins and scholars, in which debate and scriptural disputation took place even over the smallest matters, with constant accusation and counter-accusation aimed at proving oneself right and the other side wrong — something wholly absent from the Sant tradition. The saints came from the ordinary masses, and among them, in place of debate and scriptural argument, there was heartfelt, loving discourse; the saints' emphasis was on the heart, whereas the pandits and acharyas were centered on the intellect. That is why Kabirji says these pandits and acharyas have gone astray.

That is why it was said earlier that in this mortal world, wherever the seven cities, the three villages, the nine forests, the nine medicinal herbs, and the fourteen secret places are said to be, they all give rise to illusion and doubt; since they belong to the path of ritual action, they should be set aside. Among these, the seven cities are named as follows:

_Ayodhya Mathura Maya Kashi Kanchi Avantika. Puri Dwaravati jneya saptaita mokshadayikah._ (Garuda Purana 2.49.114) (Ayodhya, Mathura, Maya [Haridwar], Kashi, Kanchi, Avantika, and the city of Dwarka — these seven are to be known as the givers of liberation.) ||5||

A detailed description has been given earlier, so it need not be repeated here. In these seven cities there is a distinction between the path of ritual action and the path of devotion, so one must observe and consider carefully before proceeding. Now, of these seven cities, three villages are spoken of specially:

_Trigrama sristi-madhye sve vanchita hai kritatmakah. Lokanam bhagyahinanam yah sarvajno hyajah kriti._ (In this creation there are three villages which grateful, fortunate people desire; unfortunate people do not. Only one who is all-knowing and truly accomplished can know this.) ||6||

Commentary: Shaunakji spoke thus to the sons of Sanaka — in this universe, the places worthy of devotion, from which arises essential understanding, are three in the mortal world. What kind of places are these? Places which even the Supreme Brahman, the creator of the universe, himself desires. But these foolish people, because of their afflictions, cannot know this. What is it they do not know? They do not know the manifestation of Vasudev. If anyone knows this, they attain the true substance, a definite state — this is the word of Vedanta.

Two questions arise here: "what is to be attained?" and "what does the word of Vedanta mean?" The first sutra of Vedanta is _athato brahma jijnasa_ ("now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman"). From this, the desire to attain Brahman should immediately arise. Just as the seeker of knowledge may desire to attain Brahman, so too the follower of the path of devotion should give up desire and craving and, offering everything to Krishna, become absorbed in devotion — not, like the Vedantin, occupied with resolving distinctions among the scriptures. A person on the path of devotion should understand only the will of God and engage in devotion accordingly. The couplet for this is given by the Vaishnav Jivandasji:

_Saptapuri mã Jivna, teen puri tatva-sar. Ugrasen Sudama jahã, Kabir bhaye avatar. ||1||_ (Of the seven cities shown as givers of liberation, only three places are the essence of truth — where Ugrasen and Sudama dwelt, and the third place where Kabirji took incarnation.)

These three places: Ugrasen and the other Yadavas came to attain peace and love at the place toward which Shri Krishna himself pointed — Dwarka. Jivanji Maharaj has said that in one's life one should go to Dwarka once; why one should go will be seen in detail in a later chapter. The second place is where all of Sudama's wishes were fulfilled — associated with Sudama, Shri Krishna's childhood friend and a devoted keeper of vows, who did not go to Dwarka in hope of wealth from his friend. He wanted no such wealth; he wanted only the kind of wealth that erases the cycle of births after births, wishing only to surrender at Shri Hari's feet. But what Sudama wanted, Shri Krishna could not then give him, and what Krishna did give him was of no use to Sudama — so both their wishes remained incomplete. When and where were they fulfilled?

_Duje avatar Dhanraj kahaye, so Sudama Patan aaye._ (In his second incarnation he was called Dhanraj, lord of wealth; that same Sudama came to Patan.)

Thus the wish of the previous birth was fulfilled in this birth, at the place called "Padmavadi-Patan." Jivanji Maharaj has instructed that one should go to Patan once a year.

The third place: where Kabirji dwelt, namely Kabirchaura in Kashi. At present the site of Kabirchaura has been submerged in the Ganga, and another Kabirchaura site has been set up in its place; the original site has been destroyed. This site has not existed since the time of Jivanji Maharaj, who had darshan of that land while standing on the bank of the Ganga. Because the original land was destroyed, Jivanji Maharaj did not instruct devotees to go there.

At the end of this chapter, Jivanji Maharaj again reminds us: "How does the soul cross over?" and "Who cannot know Vasudev?" — for which the word of the Purana is given:

_Akhanda-mandalakaram vyaptam yena characharam. Tat-padam darshitam yena tasmai shri gurave namah._ (Salutations to that Guru who has shown the seat, in the form of an unbroken circle, that pervades this entire moving and unmoving world.) ||7||

That is: Shri Mahadevji says to Parvati, "O beloved, no one has the power to see my Vasudev, but what is that divine play like?" This lila (divine play) of Vasudevji is never cut short even at the end of imagination; it is ever unbroken, ever present. It can be known only by one who has attained the Sadguru's compassion. To attain the Supreme Brahman, taking refuge in the Guru is utterly essential; only by his compassion can this supreme state be attained.

This subject is discussed in detail by Jivanji Maharaj in a later chapter. It is worth noting here that in the Sant tradition, the place of the Guru, the Sadguru, is held with unwavering devotion; the influence of guru-bhakti on this tradition is especially strong, and among the founding figures of the Sant tradition Kabirji is the foremost saint. There is no need to say more about Kabirji in the course of this discussion.

Rudra spoke to Parvati thus: how can one who lacks the Guru's grace attain Vasudev? And what of the play of the Supreme Brahman in the universe, which has been called unbroken? Addressing this, a couplet of Kabir is given:

_Kabir dharpuri dharti madhye, mathe mani jalkant. Tãhã param guru pragat base, jãhã nij man mantri sant. ||9||_ (He on whose head a jewel gleams, who bears the weight of the earth upon his own head — such a one, whose own mind remains absorbed forever in a single repetition of the Name — upon him rests the compassion of the Supreme Guru.)

Meaning: "Dharpuri" is the body composed of the five elements that bears the soul; within its head a jewel in the form of intellect keeps gleaming, keeps giving inspiration. In that inspiration, the Guru's true teaching itself is the source of inspiration; when, together with it, saints acting as counselors to guide the thoughts of our own mind are found, our welfare is accomplished.

There are many kinds of jewels — the philosopher's stone, the crystal jewel, the wish-fulfilling jewel, the serpent's-hood jewel, the mind-jewel, the crest-jewel. The jewel gleaming on the head may be reckoned the mind-jewel; through mind and intellect, light comes into the darkness of ignorance. Saints and Gurus lend this jewel the power to give light, and then we attain the light of loving devotion.

It is said that the serpent's-hood jewel rests on the head of certain hooded, jewel-bearing serpents. There is no need to discuss how much truth there is in this, but the serpent's-hood jewel is said to give light at night; giving weight to this saying, the intent here is to show the greatness of the jewel that is intellect, mind, Guru, and saint upon the head. The Ram Library, registration no. 422, page 215, mentions someone who obtained such a jewel directly for himself; it draws out a snake's venom, and even now such venom-drawing stones are sold in the market. So one cannot be certain about the serpent's-hood jewel itself, but by using its name we compare the Guru and saint to it, to show that they too are such givers of light.

That is: although the gleaming jewel — maya — rests upon the head of the thousand-hooded Sheshnag, from his mouths there flows continually, always, the ceaseless repetition of the Supreme Brahman's name.

This is a beautiful poetic image. Through this metaphor Kabirji means to say: even though the individual soul lives in the world in the presence of maya, how can it remain absorbed in the Supreme Brahman? Here Kabirji has shown maya as seated upon the head. Even though maya sits upon the head, as long as it does not become accessible to the intellect — that is, does not dominate the mind — it remains, even while close to the soul, separate and untouched by it, like a lotus leaf on water that water cannot wet. This is possible only through the Sadguru's grace. That is why it was said earlier: O gods, you have no awareness of your own true nature, because you are immersed in enjoyment and pleasure, and the Sadguru's hand has not touched your heads — that is why maya is powerful there. We have already seen the plain meaning of "Dharampuri" above; it also carries a symbolic meaning:

_Sab sakhiyan mã Radhika, sab sakhan mã Balvir. Tahã Vyas viveki Jivna, jahã Kalindi ki teer. ||2||_ (In Vraj-bhumi, where the eternal, unbroken rasa-lila takes place, among all the gopi-companions Radhaji is the finest, and among the male companions Baldev is foremost. Where the bank of the Yamuna is, there, forever full of the flow of loving devotion, dwells Vyasji.)

Here Jivanji Maharaj has recalled Vyasji, a supreme devotee and foremost saint of Vrindavan, well known for his steadfastness in devotion. (The "Uddha-Dharma-Panch-Ratna-Mala" also contains a collection of some of his compositions.)

**Summary meaning of the chapter on the mingling of Maya and Brahma**

For the welfare of his own people, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj came into this world; under the pretext of redeeming Bhoja Gujar, Jivanji Maharaj employed a device to uplift his own devotees:

_Ham aaye un desh thi, sab santan ke kaaj. Koi jugat na jaane Jivna, kaise mile Brijraj. ||1|| Ham aaye un desh thi, phir jaano un desh. E jugat banaai Jivna, sab santan ke updesh. ||2||_ (I have come from that land — Vrindavan, the divine playground — for the sake of all the saints, because, O Jivan, no one knew the means by which Brijraj Krishna could be attained. I have come from that land and will go back to it, but, O Jivan, I have devised this stratagem, under the pretext of redeeming Bhoja Gujar, so as to give all the saints the teaching of devotion to Hari.)

Because of the mingling of maya and Brahma, cheating impostors would deceive devotees away from devotion to Vishnu and lead them onto the wrong path. From the dialogue between Vasudev and Narad: Brahmaji held the pride of being the creator of the universe. Vasudev sent Naradji to Brahma, having him asked on what basis Brahma claimed to be the creator of the universe — for if Brahma held the true nature of Brahman (pure spirit), then desire could not be possible for Brahman; and if desire were possible, then Brahman would have to be called insentient. So what were they to understand about him? Brahma could give no answer; he entered deep meditation but understood nothing. Shivji too meditated, together with Yogmaya, but even he did not grasp this mystery. Then Vasudev spoke: "O gods, all of you have become mingled with maya, and so you will not attain true awareness of your own original nature. This entire universe lies in the mouth of Time; in that way you too are subject to Time. Time devours everyone in this world step by step, and destroys everyone. Time nurtures each being up to the limit of their allotted lifespan, and when the term is complete, destroys them — just as a gardener growing flowers in a garden plucks each flower daily as it blooms, so Time nourishes and rears everyone and then destroys them. But those caught up in the pleasures of maya are devoured by Time as easily as a light snack, while those engaged in devotion to Ram escape the grip of Time and do not fall into the suffering of birth and death in the womb."

As for the rest: in the 84 lakh species of life, the faculty for increase through seed and ovum develops in every mature male and female of each species, and because the desire of Kamadev, the god of desire, awakens in every body, every one of the 84 lakh species of beings comes into existence. Thus the creation of this universe is contained within this seed and ovum born of desire. Because of this mingling of maya and Brahma, Brahmaji became bewildered; and to make him understand the path of ritual action and the path beyond action, and to separate the path of ritual action — which obstructs devotion to Vishnu — from the desireless devotion to Vishnu into which it had become mixed, the Lord, just as a swan separates milk from water and drinks only the milk, took the incarnation of the Swan (Hansavatar) to make this separation clear, and taught Brahmaji devotion to Vishnu free of ritual action.

In the world, those devoted to ritual action, mingling their devotion to Vishnu with the path of works, have shown people four kinds of pilgrimage places for attaining liberation, and thereby misled people along the path of the Vedas. Having thus pointed out the 92 places for attaining liberation shown by the path of ritual action, the Samagam says that all these places of the path of ritual action, described in the shastras and Puranas, give rise to the ninety-six pretenses of the six schools of philosophy. Each of the schools has produced sixteen pretenses of its own, so a total of 16 × 16 = 96 pretenses have spread [as stated in the source]. Moreover, each pretense has three sects; Buddha, Charvak, and Jain are the names of these three sects. In a similar way, Kabirji's ramaini has shown Gayatri as if she were one such sect: this Gayatri is described as a woman in the form of desire, whose three sons are Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh. These three created the three worlds, and no one understood the mystery of the three worlds they had made. Vishnu adopted his own independent path; Brahma spread the Vedas and established people's faith in the name of the four varnas; Shiva spread the path of yoga. Thus all three together constructed pretense, and through the six schools everyone was led astray and fell again and again into rebirth in the womb — everyone thereby became entangled in the 96 pretenses. The mother bears in her womb the soul that has fallen into unconsciousness, and once born, that soul begins to assume many kinds of disguises. But no soul is called a Brahmin for having studied the Vedas in the womb, nor is any Muslim born already circumcised. Devotion to the three gods (Tridev) is thus reckoned as devotion to maya alone; Kabir has called Gayatri maya itself, as said in Kabir's Ramaini Bijak. Among the six schools, with their three gunas (qualities), two kinds of quality among the six schools of philosophy have accordingly been presented.

The purport of what has been said here is this: Jivanji Maharaj has given two beautiful metaphors for how the Supreme Brahman is to be attained through constant remembrance of the Name. The question remains: how does the soul cross over? For one who, even while bearing the entire worldly burden of this earth, remains ever absorbed in the repetition of Ram's name — for this very reason Jivanji has used the phrase "unbroken lila." Even though a person is enmeshed in daily life, if the Supreme Brahman becomes absorbed in the heart, no fear remains for such a person, and that soul will surely cross over. It will cross over — it will surely, surely cross over.

Ram Kabir is Truth; the true Guru is Truth.

The Samagam gives an outline of the life of Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj — from his manifestation (Pragatya) to his departure to his own divine abode (Swadham) — together with the teaching he received from his Guru and the teaching he gave to his own disciples, through which he established the Uda Dharma. It expounds the principles of this Uda Dharma and shows how to practise unwavering devotion (bhakti, devotion) to Vishnu free of ritualism (karmakand), and it has taught how to put this into practice in daily life.

The Samagam's chapter on the distinction between Maya and Brahm serves as an introduction to the fundamental principles of this Samagam. Now the Samagam proper begins with the chapter on the manifestation of Jivanji Maharaj; before starting it, the writing opens with a sakhi (couplet) that conveys an instruction of Jivanji Maharaj's own.

|| Sakhi ||
_Sab sakhiyan-man Radhika, sab sakhan-man Balvir |
Tahan Vyas viveki Jivana, jahan Kalindi-ki tir ||1||_
(Meaning: Just as, in Vrajbhoomi where the unbroken Ras Lila unfolds, Radhaji is the foremost among all the sakhis, and Balvir Baldevji is the foremost among the Lord's companions — so too, on the bank of the Yamuna in Vrajbhoomi, dwells Hariram Vyasdasji, the foremost devotee of Radha-Krishna, who worships Radhavallabh with unwavering devotion, with discernment and free of ritualism.)

When Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj went to Vrindavan, he stayed there four days. He met a Vaishnav there, and a goshthi (satsang, holy discourse) took place with him — this is mentioned on page 48 of the printed Samagam, though the Vaishnav's name is not given there. However, the parchari (biographical account) of Jivanji Maharaj states that this Vaishnav was Hariram Vyas, and that this sakhi is the one spoken in that parchari while praising Vyasdas. Jivanji Maharaj was so deeply moved by Vyasdas that he spoke a sakhi placing Vyasji among saints equal in stature to Kabirji.

_Dou barabar Jivana, das Kabir aru Vyas |
O samre Sitapatiko, ye Radhe kunj vilas ||2||_
(Meaning: Das Kabir and Vyas, O Jivana, are equal to one another in their unwavering devotion to Vishnu. Of the two, Kabirji is one who remembers Sitapati Ram, while Vyasji is a worshipper of Radha-Krishna who delights in the groves [kunj] of Vraj.)

Jivanji Maharaj praised Vyas highly, holding him equal in excellence to Kabir, and to Radha and Balvir, because Vyasji's views matched Jivanji Maharaj's own views very closely. Vyasji did not maintain his Brahmin identity, but was a lover devoted to Vishnu-bhakti in the tradition of the saints. He had given up the sacred thread (janoi) as well, considering it a burden; he did not believe in worship of the sun-god, nor did he accept the worship of Ganpati; nor did he observe Ekadashi or other such vows. He held to devotion to Radha-Krishna alone.

In keeping with the praise of Vyasji given within the original Samagam, the second chapter of the Bhagwat Mahatmya, at the end of the Bhagwat, describes Uddhav, the supreme devotee of Krishna, in a manner corresponding to how Vyas became a supreme devotee of Radha-Krishna on the bank of the Kalindi (Yamuna). It also describes the unbroken good fortune (saubhagya) of Kalindi-Yamuna, the Lord's chief queen. Devoted copyists who transcribed the Samagam inserted that episode into it as they wrote it, and the passage reads as follows:

The episode from the Shri Bhagwat Mahatmya is recorded here. Vajranabh, son of Aniruddha, ruled in Mathura. King Parikshit came there. Afterward, having heard the account of Krishna's life, the gopas and gopis came before Kahan [Krishna]. They were struck with wonder as to how that divine play (lila) had come to an end. Then the sage Shandilya arrived. He said to them: "Why are you so astonished? Lila is of two kinds — one is the everyday, worldly lila, and the other is the eternal, unbroken lila, in which loving devotees are united [with the Lord]. Beings of the three-gunas creation — gods, demons, and the rest — have no claim upon the eternal lila."

It is the supremely blissful, loving Vaishnav devotee who has a claim upon it. Here is an illustration of this: once, sixteen thousand one hundred (16,100) widows who had been separated from Shri Krishna came before Shri Jamunaji [the river Yamuna], who granted them darshan [sacred vision] together with the marks of good fortune (saubhagya) of a married woman. They asked her: "Our Lord Shri Krishna has departed to His own abode — why do you still bear the marks of good fortune?" Jamunaji answered: "Shri Krishna, together with Radhikaji and all the gopas and gopis, dwells forever in the eternal, unbroken lila. I am Radhika's maidservant; I am in her eternal service; I know no separation. Uddhavji has attained the gopas and gopis within that eternal lila. Uddhavji dwells, in the form of a creeper, at the foot of Govardhan hill, in the Sakhi-sthal where Kusum Sarovar is. Go there, sing kirtan (devotional hymns) of Krishna's lila, and dwell there; then Uddhavji will grant you darshan, and you too shall attain the eternal lila." Hearing these words of Jamunaji, they went to Kusum Sarovar and dwelt there, singing kirtan and bhajan. Uddhavji then appeared, radiant in his dark form; showing them his form studded with gems and jewels, he embraced them all. Then they beheld Shri Krishna — endowed with all sixteen kalas [divine attributes] — enacting the eternal lila together with Radhikaji; he delights there forever. This lila reveals itself to loving devotees.

Testimony to this is borne out in many places by the kirtans of Narsinh Mehta. This episode is narrated in many places as addressed to the sage Saunak. But it is only devotees who attain the sweetness of that lila. This passage was heard from a temple of the Gosainji of the Vallabh lineage, and it has been set down here because it was found fitting to the time and place. Thus this sakhi in praise of Vyas, presented as the heading of this Samagam, is the instruction that enjoins unwavering devotion. Who Jivanji Maharaj was is introduced within the Samagam in the chapter on Sadguru Praman [the credentials of the true Guru]; the account here begins from after his eleventh year.

In Samvat 1660, at the age of eleven, Jivanji Maharaj manifested at Gahej Goriyad for the welfare of the soul, and the dharma of Namdev and Kabir became manifest to him. A love for singing of that lila arose in him, and wherever there were Vaishnavs to discuss sakhi and shabda [scriptural teachings] with, he found delight in loving devotion (bhakti). Thus, at the age of sixteen, his first meeting took place, in the village of Keslu-ba, with Gopaldas of Chorenda of the Janak lineage, and a samagam-satsang [holy meeting] took place lasting a full day and night.

Keslu is present-day Kesru, near Paleja — so Poojya Yadunath Maharaj has written. Janakvansh and similar terms are words used, within the tradition of the Barot people, to identify their lineage. Barots for the most part follow the profession of vahivancha [genealogist and record-keeper], and they generally hail from the direction of Rajasthan. Gopaldas's guru's guru, Sukhji, is reckoned to be of the Pipavansh [Pipa's lineage]. In this way, within Barot society, different families are known by different lineage-traditions. In the Bhaktamal of Lucknow, page 667, one devotee, Lakhaji, is known as belonging to the Vanarvansh [monkey lineage]; another is known as Devvanshi. Thus the identities of Barots are known through various different lineages.

Before accepting Sadguru Gopaldas as his guru, Jivanji Maharaj discussed and deliberated the path of bhakti with him so as to be certain of it; and so, first of all, he sought to dispel the confusion between the formed (sakar) and the formless (nirakar). Two views prevail regarding God: (1) that God is sagun-sakar (possessed of attributes, and with form), and (2) that God is nirgun-nirakar (without attributes, formless). Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj asked for this to be clarified. Gopaldas then said: God's sagun-sakar form — the form composed of the five elements, the three gunas, and the senses, which is now blazing forth — is only temporary. When that form releases its own qualities — that is, when God closes and gathers back His form with attributes — then that Brahm-Parmatma-Bhagwat form ceases to be such and becomes the Atma-swaroop [form of the pure soul]; and that Atma-swaroop will, in turn, again take on the form of an individual soul (jiva). That is to say: God, having completed an avatar, dissolves into the Parmatma form, and will again in turn take up an avatar. He then spoke a sakhi concerning this.

Poojya Yadunath Maharaj says: "Dream" means the jiva [individual soul] that has lost its way through Maya; that which is awake and aware is chetan [pure consciousness], and that alone is Truth, that alone is the Beloved.

In Samvat 1660, on the eighth day (Ashtami) of the bright half of Shravan, Vaishnav Jivandasji came, for the welfare of the soul, to the village called Gahej Goriyad (Gaj), in the Kanam region of the holy heartland of Gujarat. Here the dharma of Namdev and Kabirji became manifest to him. In his eleventh year, an intense yearning to sing of that lila was awakened here in his heart.

Wherever there was a Vaishnav to discuss sakh and shabda [scriptural teaching] with, affection would grow there; and so, in his sixteenth year, a samagam took place with Gopaldasji of the Janak lineage (of Chorenda), in the village called Keslu-ba. This was their first meeting. Jivanji greeted Gopaldas with "Ram Ram." Gopaldas had come there from another village, after performing karaj [the rites performed after a death]. Jivandasji then invited him to his own mandir [home], and there they performed Hari-kirtan. On this occasion, the samagam lasted a full night and day. Afterward, Gopaldasji set out on his way back to his own home in Chorenda.

sections.title_en: The Harmony of Form and Formless
sections.translation:
On the 13th of the bright half of Aso, Samvat 1682, on the occasion of the Sharad Purnima festival, Jivandasji arrived at Chorandra. Here a meeting (satsang) took place with the Vaishnav Gopaldasji, held for the purpose of resolving the question of form (akar) and formless (nirakar). Here the deadlock between the purvapaksha (the opposing view) and the uttarpaksha (the answering view) was resolved. However, both sides agreed on one point: that the flute-playing, captivating Lord (Morli Manohar Parmeshwar) is indeed the true one.

Brahm is said to be formless (nirakar). Yet it also has form. Why is that? How can Brahm have two forms? The three gunas (sattva, rajas, tamas) and the five elements (earth, water, air, fire, ether) constitute the subtle body — that is, the subtle body is invisible and inactive. It becomes active only when it enters a gross body. The Manusmriti (verses 13, 15) says —

_Ekameva tridhabhutam mahanityeva sansthitam, indriyanam samastanam prabhavam pralayam tatha. ||1||_ (Mahattattva manifested in these three forms — vaikarik, taijas, and tamas — and these alone are the cause of the birth and dissolution of all the senses.)

_Mahantameva chatmanam sarvani trigunani cha, vishayanam grahitrini shanaih panchendriyani cha. ||2||_ (From that ego, it gradually produced the mind, the three gunas beginning with sattva, and the five sense organs that grasp objects such as sound, along with the five organs of action.)

Besides this, in different schools of philosophy this count is given differently, with more or fewer components. Also, on the matter of nirgun (attributeless) and sagun (with attributes), scriptural opinion differs. Here we will speak keeping Kabirji at the centre.

Kabirji says that the jiva (individual soul) originates from Brahm, and the jiva's final movement is toward Brahm. In the end it merges into Brahm. Therefore it is not [purely] nirgun. Sakhi:

_Kabir jivso Brahm hot he, Brahm hot hai jiv. Swapanavar dradh jiv sab, chetan man satya piv. ||1||_

That is: the jiva's original source is Brahm. And the jivatma that has come into this mortal world merges back, through good deeds and bhakti (devotion), into its original source. The remaining jivas continue in the cycle of birth and death. Whoever remains in that condition stays so until the time of dissolution (pralay). At the time of dissolution, the entire world merges into Narayan, and from there it re-emerges again. Just as everything in a dream feels real though it is not, so too, through God's divine maya, creation appears real. But only the Parbrahm that gives consciousness to the soul is truly real.

_Baher nirgun dekhiye, bhitar gun bhandar. Hem tadhun Jivana, pan jale sab sansar. ||2||_

Jivanji Maharaj says that Brahm is nirgun, causing no distortion whatsoever. And yet, because of maya, all the elements — the five elements and three gunas — have come from it. Just as hail feels cold from outside, yet when it falls it scorches the whole world, so too Brahm appears nirgun from outside, but within it is filled with countless qualities. But under the influence of maya, people in the world merely follow after the three gunas and five elements. They do not recognise the Parbrahm that actually produced them, nor do they even feel the curiosity to know it.

Meaning: the jivatma merges into Paramatma, and from Brahm-Paramatma the jivatma is again produced; but within Brahm all this seems as real to us as things do in a dream. In reality it is not true; in the same way, through God's divine maya, creation appears real, but only Parbrahm, which gives consciousness to the soul, is real. From this Brahm — of which the jivatma visible in this maya-pervaded world is a portion — the jiva is produced; hence jiva and Brahm are complements of each other. The jiva's appearance and its dissolution (laya) both happen in Brahm; this process is called creation (srishti). Just as a scene witnessed in a dream is not real, this too is not real; therefore Kabir says that the conscious Paramatma alone is the jiva's true beloved (piyu). The jiva is jada (inert), that is, unreal (mithya). But the true, original Parbrahm-nature of Paramatma is the real, true, conscious form; it is this that appears manifest through maya, and it is the true Lord of this world.

Because if we look at this Parbrahm Paramatma from the outside, it appears attributeless and formless (nirgun-nirakar), but if we look within, it is a storehouse filled with countless qualities. Just as ice appears very cold from outside but, should hail fall, it can scorch the whole world, so too this Paramatma appears attributeless from outside, yet within is filled with abundant qualities. Gyaniji Maharaj says —

_Maya upji Brahmate, Brahm rahya nirdhar. Gyani avarnan Brahmkun, virla bujhan har. ||1||_

_Adi Brahm te jiv he, jiv te maya hoy. Mayaka vistar sab, gyani dekhya soy. ||2||_

Meaning: maya originated from Brahm, but Parbrahm itself remained untouched by maya. Such is this tattva of Brahm that it cannot be described; only a rare soul can truly know that Brahm.

Adi Brahm — from the original Parbrahm the soul (jiva) becomes separate, and from the jivas maya is produced. All this is but the spreading of maya. Gyaniji says: I have thus understood this maya-tinged principle of the jivatma.

Adhyaruji Maharaj, in the words of his Kadvan, says —

_Jem chhe pavak ek, swami teh thaki dipak anek. Pavak atibalu e, ane dipak nahi balu e. Pavak te Parbrahm, ane dipak Hari Har Brahm. Surnar bhujangamue, sahu e sthavar jangamue._

That is: from a single flame (pavak) many lamps (dipak) can be lit. Though the lamps are many, one and the same fire remains within them. The fire is not different; the lamps may be different. In the same way, bodies may be as numerous as they like, but the jivatma dwelling within them is one and the same. That pavak itself is the form of Parbrahm, and it is from this Parbrahm that the creation of this world has taken place. Hari-Vishnu, Har-Shiva, Brahm-Brahma, together with the sur (gods), the nar (human beings), the sthavar (immobile) and jangam (mobile) — whatever is moving and unmoving — all of it, like separate lamps, has been produced from that one single flame, Parbrahm.

Parbrahm in the form of that flame, being unchanging and imperishable, is extremely powerful; it has no destruction. Whereas the lamps that arise from it — Hari, Har, Brahma — are not as powerful as it; they are destroyed at the time of dissolution (pralay). But Parbrahm is never destroyed.

Meaning: Revered Yadunath Maharaj used to explain that on the day of Holi, the fire lit in the Holi bonfire is powerful — the wind does not extinguish it but makes it burn more fiercely; and when women light small lamps in clay saucers (kodiya) from that Holi fire and carry the kodiyas away, those flames get blown out by the wind. So the Holi fire is extremely powerful, and from it many lamps can be lit, though these lamps are never as powerful as the Holi fire itself. In the same way, Parbrahm Paramatma is like an unimaginably mighty fire, while Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh, in the form of lamps, along with gods, humans, serpents and other moving and unmoving beings — all being subject to time (kal) — are not eternal as Parbrahm is.

In the satsang, it was said that according to the words of the Gita, those who call Shri Krishna "possessing form" — he is, in truth, formless (nirakar), but because of the leela (divine play) of his incarnation in this world, he appears to have form; that is his maya-woven leela. (Vitality) — the life-breath, the conscious power — is this life-giving (pranamya) leela.

_Avyaktam vyaktimapannam manyante mamabuddhayah, param bhavamajananto mamavyayamanuttam. ||3||_ (Gita 7-24) (Meaning: those without wisdom, not knowing my supreme, unchanging form, take me — the unmanifest — to have become manifest.)

The example of God's life-giving, conscious power at play is shown in the Bhagavat through his pacifying — his "drinking" — of the forest fire (davanal). God drank the forest fire twice. The first time he drank it at night; the second time he did it during the day. The first time he did it in front of everyone; the second time he made everyone close their eyes and then drank the fire. The point is that he does good for his devotees both in hidden (paroksha) and open (aparoksha) ways.

Adhyaruji Maharaj's words find their witness (sakshi) in the Bhagavad Gita, as we shall see further on. Another point: Shri Krishna is called "possessing form," yet he is formless.

In the worship (upasana) of Pranav, that is, Omkar, form (maya) has to be shown. For instance, in the worship of Omkar one must perform mantra sadhana. For a mantra there must be a seer (drashta) rishi; the mantra's presiding deity must also be shown; the mantra's seed (bij) must also be indicated; its system (tantra-shastra) must also be shown; and so whatever has a "seed" must also take on form (akar). It is not fitting to elaborate further on this here, but it is for this very reason that Jivanji Maharaj, instead of the worship of Omkar, taught the nirgun bhakti connected with the Ram-mantra.

In the tenth canto (skandh) of Shrimad Bhagavat, the worshippers of the Veda made a request to Shri Krishna, and thereby recognised Parbrahm Parmeshwar as Morli Manohar Parbrahm — how did this happen? It happened when Shri Krishna drank the forest fire. Shrimad Bhagavat narrates that when Krishna, after subduing the serpent (nagdaman), came back out of the Yamuna, a great deal of time had passed and all the Vraj-dwellers had grown exhausted; so, instead of returning to Vraj, they all lay down to sleep on the bank of the Yamuna. Then —

_Tada shuchivanodbhuto davagnih sarvato vrajam, suptam nishith avritya pradagdhumupachakrame. ||4||_ (Bhagavat 10-17-21) (In the hot season the dried-up forest caught fire at midnight, and it began to scorch the sleeping Vraj-dwellers on every side.)

Thus, when a fire suddenly broke out at night and the Vraj-dwellers sleeping in the forest saw no way of escape, Krishna alone appeared as their saviour, and they began praising him, saying —

_Krishnastu bhagavan swayam, vrajaste sharanam praptah._

That is: all the Vraj-dwellers, tormented by the flames of that fire, pray to Krishna, saying — O Krishna, you yourself are Parbrahm Bhagwan, and all of us Vraj-dwellers are your refugees; we have come to your shelter.

Hearing the Vraj-dwellers' plea in this way, Lord Krishna, for the welfare of the distressed Vraj-dwellers, drank up that fire.

When the raging fire broke out, the distressed herds of gopas and cows cried out in great anguish, calling, "O King of Vraj, save us!" It is said in a shloka —

Thus, having been saved from the terrible flames of fire, the Vraj-dwellers, becoming refugees of Lord Krishna, prayed, saying —

_Tvadrasyam kalpitam pitam jvalavalibhirutkatam, vrajaste sharanam praptah, Krishnastu bhagavan swayam. ||8||_ (You have drunk up this terrible forest fire with its rows of flames; the whole of Vraj has come to your shelter — Krishna is verily the Lord himself.)

That is: the Vraj-dwellers watch this unfathomable leela of Krishna — what kind of leela is it?
