He has saved the lives of all the Vraj-dwellers who took refuge in him, and he drank up the terrible flames of fire as easily as a child gulps milk from a bowl. Revered Yadunath Maharaj writes that this is what it means to be humble — to become a refugee (sharanagat) and perform bhakti. Praising the Lord, the gopa people say —

_Ittham svajanavaiklavyam nirikshya jagadishwarah, tamagnimapibattivramananto'nantashaktidhrik. ||5||_ (Bhagavat 10-17-25) (Jagadishwar Lord Shri Krishna, seeing his own people thus distressed, drank up that terrible fire.)

Further, in the nineteenth chapter, the author of the Bhagavat writes that once, when the cows had wandered far into the forest, a fire appeared before the Vraj-dwellers and the cows like death itself, as though it would destroy all creation; then he drank the fire with his mouth.

_Tatheti militakshesu bhagavanagnimulbanam, pitva mukhena tan krichchhrad yogadhisho vyamochayat. ||6||_ (Bhagavat 10-19-12) (Then Yogeshwar Shri Krishna, with their eyes closed, drank this terrible fire through his mouth and delivered everyone from that difficulty.)

_Davanal lagi prabal, vikal gop go vrind. Terat ati atur vachan, rakhi lehu Vraj Chandra. ||1||_

That is: Jivanji Maharaj explains that the Vraj-dwellers pleaded — O Shri Krishna, you yourself are Bhagwan, and the people of Vraj have taken refuge in you. Hearing this, he at once began drinking the fire. How? Just as a small child gulps milk from a vessel, he gulped down the fire in the same way.

There is a shloka for Ram, in which it is declared that "Ramastu bhagavansvayam" (Ram alone is verily the Lord himself) —

_Aishwaryenaya dharmena yashasancha shriyaiva cha, vairagya moksha shatkonaih sanjato bhagavan Harih. Poshanam bharanadharam sharanyam sarva vyapakam, karunyam shatbhih purno Ramastu bhagavansvayam. ||7||_ Iti Maharamayane. (Fully complete in six qualities — majesty, righteousness, fame and glory, renunciation, and liberation — and complete in six more — nourishing, sustaining, giving refuge, all-pervading, and compassion — such is Bhagwan Hari; Ram alone is verily the Lord himself. Thus it is said in the Maharamayan.)

Also, there are other shlokas as well, in which Krishna too is called "Krishnastu bhagavansvayam" —

_Avatara hyasankhyeya Hareh sattvanidherdvijah, yatha vidasinah kulyah sarasah syuh sahasrashah. ||8||_

_Rishayo manavo deva manuputra mahaujasah, kalah sarve Harereva saprajapatayastatha. ||9||_

_Ete chanshakalah pumsah, Krishnastu bhagavansvayam. Indrarivyakulam lokam mridyanti yuge yuge. ||10||_

_Vanajau vanajau kharvo, Ramau Krishnah kripo'kripah, avatara dashaite syuh, Krishnastu bhagavansvayam. ||11||_

(Meaning: the incarnations of Hari, the treasury of all being, are innumerable, O brahmins, like the thousands of streams flowing out of an inexhaustible lake. The rishis, the Manus, the gods, the mighty sons of Manu — all of them, together with the Prajapatis, are but partial (kala) manifestations of Hari. These are all portions and parts of the Supreme Person, but Krishna alone is Bhagwan himself; in every age he removes the distress of a world afflicted by the enemies of Indra. The two fish-and-tortoise forms, the dwarf, the two Rams, and Krishna — merciful and fierce — these ten are reckoned as incarnations, but Krishna alone is Bhagwan himself.)

The four great statements (mahavakyas) of bhakti are listed as follows:

1. _Krishnastu bhagavansvayam_ (Krishna alone is verily the Lord himself).
2. _Matah parataram nanyat_ (There is nothing higher than me).
3. _Brahmano hi pratishthaham_ (I am the foundation of Brahm).
4. _Mam ekam sharanam vraja_ (Take refuge in me alone).

Lord Krishna, [unclear] — that is, with nurturing tenderness — drank the forest fire for the welfare of the surrendered gopas. Dava means a claim, an entitlement born of desire (sakamvritti); if we perform bhakti out of such desire for reward, it turns into something like fire itself. Jivanji Maharaj calls one who presses such claims a poor wretch (garibdo).

_Davo kare so daladri, rude nahi vishwas. Ek nardave Narhar bhaje, so kahiye nij das. ||49||_

Meaning: the sense of "I and mine, and yours," held with the hope of reward, is itself utterly poor and wretched; such a person has no true trust in God. Whoever performs bhakti to God without any craving or expectation is alone called God's beloved devotee.

_Kabir dave dajhan hot hai, nardave nihshank. Nardave je jan rahe, so gane Indrakun rank. ||_

Meaning: making claims of entitlement keeps one burning with jealousy and envy; but whoever presses no claim at all has no fear of ever being burned. Hence those who live selflessly regard even Indra as a poor, insignificant wretch.

If a kite drops the piece of flesh it is carrying, it need no longer fear the birds circling after it. The davanal is understood in this way in the language of samadhi (meditative symbolism). The davanal, taken literally, cannot be drunk — a body (akar) would simply burn in such fire. So God cannot be called "possessing form"; yet if we call him formless, then without a body the davanal could not have been drunk at all. It is for this reason that the following sakhi is given —

_Bhagavan nirakar nijnam adhara. Mayabrahm the Hari he nyara._ (God, the Formless, rests on the support of his own Name; he stands apart from maya-Brahm.)

Shri Nana Parekh's testimony (guhai) offers confirmation of this, saying —

_Anjan rahit niranjan, so Vrajki juthan khaay. Andhe so anjan kare, Jivan kahi samjhaay. ||1||_

_Asht ghatki deh nahi, esa avigat rup. So khele Nandke angane, puran Brahm swarup. ||2||_

Meaning: he who is niranjan — free of any blemish — eats the leftover food of the Vraj-people, yet remains free from any fault whatsoever. Such a niranjan God can grant vision even to the blind. It is people who have themselves become blind who go searching for this unknowable God in idols and symbols and the like — so Jivanji explains. God has no body made of the eight metals; such is his unknowable form. This same Purna-Brahm-formed God plays in Nanda's courtyard. Adhyaruji too says —

_Khele khele so rang Gopal niranjan, anjanvan swarupo._

Meaning: Gopal Shri Krishna, who is niranjan, plays in visible, colourful form in the land of Vraj, seen there with the eyes. This same Krishna, whom the fortunate gopis behold, is described in one shloka —

_Dhanya Gokul kanya, vayamiha manyamahe jagati, yasam nayan saroje, anjanbhuto niranjan vasati. ||12||_ (Blessed are the daughters of Gokul — so do we, living in this world, judge them, for the one called niranjan, that Brahm, dwells like anjan in the lotus-eyes of these girls.)

Tulsidas has written a rekhto (verse) on the theme of anjan —

_Manjan so jo kate mel jyun, sajan so jo dukhe sukh bujhe. Nari so jo jare piya sang, shura so jo sanmukh jhujhe. Raja so jo praja pratipalan, sevak so jo raatdin laje. Tulsi jiv jaan japo Raghunandan, anjan so jo niranjan sujhe._

Meaning: Tulsidas says — true bathing is that which washes away impurity; a true kinsman is one who gives up his own comfort for one who suffers; a true wife is one who becomes one with her husband; a true hero is one who fights facing the enemy; a true king is one who nurtures and protects his subjects; a true servant is one who remains devoted to service day and night. Tulsidas says: O souls, understand this and worship Raghunandan (Ram) with true faith. Only when one truly understands that God is free of maya can it be said that one has truly beheld him; only then can it be called a true darshan. Only one who has true light can truly see.

In the Garga Samhita, in the Goloka Khand, chapter 1, Krishna is described as the Purna Purushottam (complete supreme person). Regarding the incarnations of Lord Hari, sages such as Vyas have described six distinctions: 1. akshansh, 2. ansh, 3. avesh, 4. kala, 5. purna, and 6. paripurnatam. On this subject, sages such as Marichi are akshansh; Brahma and others are ansh; incarnations such as Kapildev and the Tortoise are kala; sages such as Bhargava are avesh; Nrisinhavatar, Ramavatar, the Lord of Shwetdwip, Vaikunthbhagwan, Yajnanarayan, and Narnarayan are purna (complete); and Shri Krishna Bhagwan himself, directly, is paripurnatam — the most utterly complete. This most complete supreme person, Shri Krishna Bhagwan, is the ruler of countless millions of universes.

_Akar kahun to ang nahi, ang bin kaiso updesh. Varpar nahi Jivana, Hari dharyo Gopko bhes. ||1||_

Meaning: if we call Hari "possessing form," then he has no body at all — and without a body, how can there be any teaching? God, who has no beginning and no end, has taken on the guise of a gopa (cowherd). Gopa means one who is hidden, secret (gupta). What, then, is God truly like?

Now the question arises: if we call this Parbrahm formless, then he has no hands, no feet, no mouth, no head, no eyes — no form whatsoever. If we call him formless, then how did he drink the davanal? Without a body, the davanal cannot be drunk. And if we call Brahm "possessing form," then in that fire his limbs would burn; in fire, everything is reduced to ashes — nothing at all would remain. So how, then, can he be called formed Brahm, and how can he be called formless?

That is: do not fall into the dispute of form versus formless. Parbrahm himself has taken on the guise of a gopa-cowherd; that is, Parbrahm himself removes suffering.

_Nirakar akar the, adbhut ek arup. So sai hamare Jivana, je Sitapati ko rup. ||1||_

Meaning: God, beyond both attributeless-formless and with-attributes-formed, is the one wondrous, all-powerful being with no fixed form — such a God is our object of worship, he who takes the form of Sitapati, Ram.

That is: the formless itself is the form, and that which has form is itself the formless. Just as the jivatma dwelling within the body is itself formless and bodiless — it cannot be killed, burned, or seized by anyone; no place or time binds it — but when it takes on a body, that body experiences pleasure, pain, delusion, love, attachment, aversion, and so on. The point being made is this: what is the true nature of Parbrahm? We cannot see it by casting it into any fixed mould. Parbrahm is itself self-luminous, of the nature of light. Hence it is natural for the effect to dissolve back into its cause. It is said, _mukhad agnirajayata_ ("fire arose from the mouth") — the mouth itself is the birthplace of fire. That is why anger too is called agni — krodhagni, the fire of anger.

Pacifying the fire with the mouth — drinking the davanal — is shown for the reason that "mukh," the mouth, is itself the cause of both peace and unrest. We know of Duryodhan, who was humiliated because of Draupadi's harsh words. Just as God drinks the sweet nectar (sudharas) of his devotees' love, so he can drink all rasas; he can even drink the rasa of fire. He who is himself of the nature of self-luminous fire is all-powerful. The author of the Bhagavat has shown that the davanal was drunk twice — the first time at night, in front of everyone; the second time in the morning, with eyes closed — meaning that Parbrahm protects the welfare of his own devotees both in hidden and in open ways.

_Akar kahu to ant pare, nirakar niranjan Hari. Ayodhya taji Gokul aviya, Prabhu pragat leela kari._

Meaning: if I call God "possessing form," then God would be confined within that form — meaning one would have to say God has no other form — so within that form God would come to an end (ant); therefore God is [truly] formless. This same formless Lord, Ram, left Ayodhya and came to Gokul, and performed his leela there.

In the fourteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, called Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga (the yoga of the division of the three gunas), the distinction of the gunas is shown. Arjuna asks: the five elements and the three gunas are present in me, and they are present in you as well; yet I am sagun (possessing qualities) while you are nirgun (without qualities) — how can this be? Resolve my doubt. Then Lord Shri Krishna said: the five elements and the three gunas act according to my command, whereas you act according to the command of the five elements and the three gunas. This is the crucial difference. Therefore, though I bear a body, I remain beyond all of them, whereas the five elements and the three gunas, working through your body, carry out their own worldly business, and you are the one directing it [i.e., you are subject to it]. I am nirgun; you are sagun.

_Nanyam gunebhyah kartaram yada drashtanupashyati, gunebhyashcha param vetti madbhavam so'dhigachchhati. ||1||_ (Gita 14-19) (When the seer perceives no doer other than the gunas, and knows himself as beyond the gunas, he attains my state.)

That is: the sense of cause-and-effect arises from the gunas. But when the doer, going beyond his own gunas, does not take the effect to be caused by himself but sees another as its cause, he can remain free of the grip of cause-and-effect. The original world-teacher Shankaracharyaji explains that this is merely an ordinary, social, transactional way of seeing things; but by giving up the sense of "I"-ness, one attains Parmeshwar. What Shri Krishna means is: apart from me there is no other doer of the three gunas — I alone am the doer. When the doer takes me as the cause, the action does not become a bondage for him. Three gunas have been named: sattva, rajas, tamas. One should know Parbrahm to be beyond all three, and perform bhakti in that understanding. Whoever performs bhakti in this spirit, treating the world's dealings as mere transaction, attains Shri Krishna.

_Gunanetanatitya trindehi dehasamudbhavan, janmamrityujaraduhkhairvimukto'mritamashnute. ||10||_ (Gita 14-20) (Having gone beyond these three body-born gunas, the embodied soul, freed from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, attains liberation.)

That is: in all beings, these three gunas are joined through maya, and the three gunas are also the cause of the very origin of the body. The question, then, is how one becomes free from identification with the body. Those beings who go beyond these three gunas and worship Parbrahm are his "nij jano," his own people. They are free from the fear of time. Time is described as threefold — birth, death, and jara (old age) — that is, the three stages of human life: childhood, youth, and old age. These are the three cycles of time. In every stage one should remember him. In childhood, elders fulfil their duty by giving the child religious upbringing and guiding him onto the path of dharma. In youth, that duty becomes one's own. And in old age, one's very life should become an example for others; if it does not, that life has been in vain. This same life is the path to liberation, and there is no room for doubt in this, because —

_Urdhvam gachchhanti sattvastha madhye tishthanti rajasah, jaghanyagunavrittastha adho gachchhanti tamasah. ||11||_ (Gita 14-18) (Those established in sattva rise upward; those in rajas remain in the middle; and those of the lowest guna, established in tamas, go downward.)

That is: Jivanji Maharaj explains that whoever, true to the name, performs devotion to Vishnu through the sattvik guna attains the upward path. Whoever performs devotion to Vishnu through the rajasik guna attains Brahmalok. And through the tamasik guna, one attains the lower state, the abode of Kailas. But when one goes beyond the three gunas and worships me, one attains the gunaless Shri Krishna. Only that soul crosses over who performs bhakti free of the three gunas.

That is: Jivanji Maharaj explains that urdhva-gachchhanti — the upward movement — means the realm of the gods; madhye tishthanti means Brahmalok, that is, the earthly realm created by Brahma; and jaghanya guna, that is, the state of Kailas — meaning, those who, in the name of the God of gods, Shankar, practise base rites and spread among society the addictions of bhang, dhatura, ganja, charas, and the like, under the delusion of thereby attaining the state of Kailas, thereby degrade both Shankar and Kailas. Jivanji Maharaj has classed this group as the "base, irreligious class" (jaghanya adharma varg). Shankar (Shiva), the worshipper of the supreme name "Ram," should never be depicted as one who consumes bhang and dhatura and the like, because —

_Mam cha yo'vyabhicharena bhaktiyogena sevate, sa gunansamatityaitan brahmabhuyaya kalpate. ||12||_ (Gita 14-26) (Whoever serves me through unswerving devotion transcends these gunas and becomes fit to attain the state of Brahm.)

He dwells sheltered in the heart; his devotion should be performed only through pure, unswerving bhakti-yoga. That is, in bhakti there should be no place for outward show — costumes, ornaments, or pretension.

_Evam sarveshu bhuteshu bhaktiravyabhicharini, kartavya panditaih gyatva sarvabhutamayam Harim. ||13||_ (It is the duty of the wise to perform unswerving devotion to all beings, knowing that Hari pervades every being.)

_Na krodho na cha matsaryam na lobho nashubha matih, bhavanti kritapunyanam bhaktanam Purushottame. ||14||_ (Mahabharat, Anushasan Parva 140-135) (In the hearts of the meritorious devotees of Purushottam Parbrahm, no anger, envy, greed, or ill intent ever arises.)

_Kabir sikh hoye Narad sarikha, guru he machhimar. Va guruku jo parhare, taka var na paar. ||3||_

Kabirji says: even were the disciple like Narad himself, and the guru like a fisherman (as was Narad's own guru), if the disciple abandons such a guru, his liberation never comes. If a disciple abandons his guru upon learning that the guru is of a lowly caste, that disciple's liberation does not come about.

_Guru ghela guru bavara, guru devanka dev. Jo tun chela khara sayana, to karle gurki sev._

If you are a truly wise disciple, then even should your guru seem mad or foolish, know that he is greater than even the gods, and serve him accordingly.

Therefore Jivanji Maharaj says that avyabhichar — performing devotion to God with firm, one-pointed faith — enables one to attain him. This soul's mind may waver, and many wrong thoughts may arise, but if, setting those thoughts aside, one worships me with faith, one attains the state of being "myself the very form of Brahm." When does the jiva attain this? When the jiva, abandoning the very notion of jiva-hood, worships me — that is, when the jiva performs devotion having abandoned its desires — it attains my state. Here Sadguru Gopaldas has used a profound expression: that the jiva must abandon the notion of jiva.

The jiva must abandon the notion — the imagining — of jiva, of mind, and must follow the path of Vasudevji; only then is the supreme state attained, because — before writing shloka 13, the devotees who copied out the samagam wrote two dohas from the Gitavali corresponding to it —

_Moku ati dridh bhagatisu, seve chitke aay. Gunatit soi janiye, rahe param pad paay. ||26||_

Meaning: whoever worships me with intense, firm devotion, bringing loving devotion into the heart, is to be understood as gunatit, beyond the gunas; such a devotee attains my supreme state.

_Brahm amrit avyay jyun, nit sukh ekant jyun aai. Parath inki sarvada, dharo pratistha taahi. ||27||_

Brahm-Parbrahm, immortal and unchanging, remains eternally alone in constant, everlasting happiness. O Arjuna, hold reverence and devotion for that Paramatma Parbrahm always.

_Brahmano hi pratishthahamamritasyavyayasya cha, shashvatasya cha dharmasya sukhasyaikantikasya cha. ||13||_ (Gita 14-27) (I am the foundation of the immortal, unchanging Brahman, and of eternal dharma, and of unending happiness.)

That is: Shri Krishna said — Arjuna, you know me as gunmayi (composed of qualities). The reason for this, I have understood, is that devotees who are nirgun-nirakar, that is, beyond the gunas, do not turn their gaze toward the gunas at all; hence such nirguni devotees know me as nirgun-nirakar. And those who are drawn by the gunas know me as sagun-sakar, possessing qualities. That is why you, Arjuna, know me as gunmayi. You are gunmayi, but I am nirgun, for, as said before, I am the foundation (an amsha, a portion) of Brahm. Why is it called "an amsha of Brahm"? Because it is immortal, imperishable, unchanging, unmodifiable, eternal, and permanent. Further, as the next shloka says —

— _brahma bhuyaya kalpate_ — that is, that essence, Parbrahm, that is, Shri Krishna, is of the very nature of Brahm itself. He too is immortal; he too is the cause of moksha, the abode of refuge in Shri Hari; he too is supreme dharma; he too is the lord of supreme happiness. That is why Shri Krishna says: I am nirgun, and you, Arjuna, still carry gunas and faults, and that is precisely why I am reckoned nirgun, because —

_Je bhagatai rajya rup Janardanak._ (For my devotees, I am Janardan.)

In the Vishnu Sahasranama, the 126th name of Vishnu is Janardan. Shankaracharya, defining Janardan in his own words, has said —

_Janan durjananardayati hinasti, narakadin gamayatiti va Janardanah. Janaih purushartamabhyudayanihshreyasalakshanam yachyate iti Janardanah._ (He is called Janardan because he afflicts and destroys wicked people, or sends them to hell and the like; or he is called Janardan because people ask of him the supreme goal marked by both worldly well-being and ultimate liberation.)

That is: Parbrahm Shri Krishna is Janardan — the destroyer of maya — for his devotees. He is also their protector. Hence Shri Krishna says: Arjuna, I sing the glory of the qualities of my own people — that is why I am known as Janardan, for devotees are my own people, and I belong to my devotees. And for that reason I am nirgun — without inherent form or quality. The sakhi of Baba Kabirji is given in support —

_Kabir main nij man nirvan hun, aur sab jag vanye. Main ek duja jagat hun, bolun teh praman. ||1||_

_Kabir hun sakal agochar ek man, arun bolu sab ghat manhe. Muj bin duja ko nahi, sadguruye satya kahaay. ||2||_

Meaning: Baba Kabirji says that the jiva must abandon its own mind's imaginings, but God says: it is I alone who can restrain my own mind from making imaginings within this world; nothing else in the world can restrain the mind from its imaginings. I myself have turned, through another form, into the very form of the world. Therefore whatever I speak, or will, that alone comes to pass in the world. _Sa aikshata eko'ham bahusyam prajayeya_ — Parbrahm willed: "I am alone; now let me become many."

Baba Kabir says that God is saying: I dwell within the entire moving and unmoving creation, unseen, beyond the reach of the senses. According to my own mind's will alone, I speak within all bodies; I think within all bodies. Besides me, there is nothing else in the world. This is entirely true — the Ultimate Truth — and it is what the Sadguru has said, speaking as God's own voice.

Kabirji explains that Parbrahm alone is the cause of the world's creation and dissolution. He pervades the whole universe; the universe itself is contained within him. Just as the universe was contained within Shri Krishna's mouth, and Shri Krishna was also present within the universe as a child, he is one and the same, all-pervading and beyond the reach of the senses. Besides him there is nothing else at all in the universe. And this truth my Guru has explained to me.

For this reason, O Arjuna, I am nirgun — thus Shri Krishna has said in the Bhagavad Gita, and Kabirji too has declared this through his sakhi.

Further, in the fifty-first chapter of the tenth canto of Shrimad Bhagavat, the story of King Muchkund is told. King Muchkund was the son of Mandhata, of the Ikshvaku lineage. In Shrimad Bhagavat, Shukdevji narrates the story thus: Muchkund was a supreme devotee, true to his word, victorious in battle, and a great soul. Once, when Indra and the other gods grew fearful of the demons, they prayed to King Muchkund for protection, and he protected the gods for many days. After many days had passed in this way, and the danger had subsided, the gods, pleased, took leave of the king and blessed him, asking him to request a boon.

_Varam vrinishva bhadram te rite kaivalyamadya nah, eka eveshvarastasya bhagavan Vishnuravyayah. ||16||_ (Bhagavat 10-51-20) (O great one, choose whatever boon you wish; may good come to you. Except for moksha alone, we can grant you anything — the power to grant liberation belongs to Lord Vishnu alone.)

Hearing these words, the king asked for sleep. Here the samagam records that he had served the gods extensively, even performing base (adham) sacrifices to worship Indra and the other gods; but meanwhile some saints of Vasudev Krishna arrived and told him that, rather than worshipping the gods through such base rites, he should perform devotion to Krishna instead. Then, by his guru's grace, he renounced worldly pleasure and prosperity and devoted himself solely to Krishna's bhakti. He wished to behold only the Lord's mysterious, secret leela — something beyond the reach even of the gods' own authority. Pleased with his devotion, Lord Krishna gave him darshan and asked him to request a boon. Then, expressing his wish to see Krishna's secret leela, he said — I wish only to see your secret leela; what use have I for this wretched world without your ras-leela? The Lord then said — when the ras-leela takes place, I shall show it to you; until then, go and sleep in the cave of Mount Girnar; I shall come when the time is right — this promise he gave. Having experienced this world in every way and grown weary of it, and having seen its worthlessness, he finally resolved to give up everything. It is stated in the Narad Bhakti Sutra that —

_Yat labdhva puman siddho bhavati, amrito bhavati, tripto bhavati._ (Narad Bhakti Sutra 4) (Having attained it — bhakti — a person becomes accomplished, becomes immortal, and becomes fulfilled.)

That is: on attaining bhakti, all the disturbances within a person are removed; he grows ever more devoted to God. Then everything changes, as —

_Yat prapya na kinchidvanchhati na shochati, na dveshti na ramate notsahi bhavati._ (Narad Bhakti Sutra 5) (On its natural attainment — loving devotion to God — longing, grief, aversion, and attachment all subside.)

It is also stated in the Bhagavad Gita that —

_Yo na hrishyati na dveshti na shochati na kankshati, shubhashubhaparityagi bhaktimanyah sa me priyah. ||1||_ (Gita 12-17) (He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both good and evil — such a devoted one is dear to me.)

He feels no joy, no aversion, no grief, and no craving to obtain anything else. He renounces even the fruit of good and bad deeds, and desires only devotion (bhakti).

Thinking in this way, he chose to leave this material world behind and go into solitude to sleep. Narad Bhakti Sutra 67 states:

_Bhakta ekantino mukhyah ||_ (The single-minded devotee is foremost.)

That is, among all who practice devotion, the one who is God's own exclusive devotee, with no other object of worship, is the greatest of all.

That is to say: for a person who has come to know everything and has tasted it, and who is moving toward the stream of the nectar of devotion, identification with the body has died away — he has become set apart from the world, unattached to it. That is why Jivanji Maharaj says:

_Sab taj man nyaro rahe | taje kulki kaan ||
Jivan jugat ehi bin | Hari na paiye nirvaan ||_

(Meaning: without the skill by which the mind lets go of everything and remains detached, and abandons the bounds of family custom, one can never attain God, who alone bestows eternal peace.)

That is why Muchukundji has lain down to sleep. Here there is a distinction between the path of devotion (bhakti-marg) and Vedanta. The Vedantins call sleep "avidya" (ignorance); they also call it the state of deep sleep (sushupti). But there is a great difference between one sleep and another. King Muchukundji's sleep is free of the three gunas. His sleep leads to the Supreme Being (Purushottam). His sleep is not avidya, because even while asleep his mind and heart remain forever surrendered to God. The devotee's sleep means the continuous repetition of God's name goes on within him always. The devotee waits for God; he is certain, he is assured, that one day God will come and take him by the hand and raise him up. The man of knowledge (gyani), on the other hand, must remain forever awake — he must keep watching everywhere for where God is, and if he should see God somewhere, he must go forward himself to recognize Him; so he must always stay ready. If somewhere a doze of sleep (a lapse of love) should come over him and God should slip away, he would have to begin again from the very beginning. That is why the devotee king's sleep stands even beyond the waking state. Jivanji Maharaj says:

_Jaisi maya Jivana | taisi nidra jaan ||
In dono mil aatma | bhatkayo chare khaan ||1||_

_Oongh apradhan Jivana | Hari shu paade virodh ||
Gyan dhyan sab visre | taki khabar na shodh ||2||_

_Oongh nafat ke aatma | jo jo man vichaar ||
Deval deepak nahi Jivana | to kyo kar mite andhkaar ||3||_

_Ek nidra suto Jivana | Kumbhkarna nishchant ||
Ek nidra Ahilya sui rahi | hrude dhari Kamla kant ||4||_

_Jaiso melo karmko | esi nidra jaan ||
Inthe Jivan aatma | bhatkayo chare khaan ||5||_

(Meaning: Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj says — just as delusion (maya) is bad, so too is sleep bad; understand this well, for maya and sleep together have made the soul wander through the four wombs of creation [1]. Sleep is such a sinner that it breeds enmity with God; sleep makes us forget all remembrance and awareness of God, without even letting us know how it happened [2]. Who is it that shamelessly forgets God — is it sleep, or is it the soul? Reflect on this, and you will see: just as a temple without a lamp cannot have its darkness dispelled, so too, without vigilance, how can you behold or remember God? Here it is not the soul but sleep (drowsiness) that is shameless — the soul is not at fault, you will realize; but where the lamp of vigilance is absent, then it is the soul itself that is shameless [3]. Kumbhakarna, possessed of the tamasic quality, sleeps without any care whatsoever; Ahalya, too, was lying asleep, but she slept holding God within her heart — such is the difference between the two [4]. Just as a mass of many evil deeds gathered together brings a wretched state, understand sleep in the same way — for it is this sleep of forgetting God that makes the soul wander through the four wombs of creation [5].)

That is to say: there is a difference between one sleep and another. Kumbhakarna is one who is asleep in lust, anger, greed, delusion, and envy — this is a fine illustration: even while in a waking state, he had not emerged from these vices, and so the scripture-writers have depicted him as one who sleeps. Ravana, by contrast, was learned and wise, so the scriptures do not depict him as asleep — but the knowledge Ravana possessed had become stupefied and infatuated, and so he could not let go of maya.

_Yat karoshi yad ashnasi yaj juhoshi dadasi yat ||
Yat tapasyasi Kaunteya tat kurushva mad-arpanam ||18||_ (Gita 9.27)

(O son of Kunti! Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give away, whatever austerity you perform — offer all of it to Me.)

King Muchukundji went into a cave on Mount Gomatachal and lay down to sleep. When his yajna came to a halt, Yajna Devi, the goddess of the sacrifice, grew distressed, for she was no longer receiving the offerings of the havan. She petitioned God, who then gave her the charge of guarding the king: whoever disturbed him, she was to burn to ashes — that would be her food. So the king lay sleeping there. Krishna arrived, with Kalayavan following behind him. Krishna, who had come wearing a yellow silk garment (pitambar), covered the king with it and went and sat in a corner. Kalayavan, mistaking the king for Krishna, struck at his feet in disrespect; at that, the king woke from sleep, and the instant his gaze fell upon Kalayavan, Kalayavan was burnt to ashes. The king could not understand what had happened. Wondering "no one is in sight, so who woke me?", the king fell deep in thought — and then Shri Krishna appeared before him. Seeing him, the king asked:

_Ko bhavan iha sampraso vipine giri-gahvare ||
Padbhyam padma-palashabhyam vicharasy uru-kantake ||14||_

(Who are you, who have come here into this cave in the mountains, wandering through this thorn-covered world on feet as tender as lotus petals?)

The king asks: "O Maharaj, who are you? You are the one who long ago gave me the promise by which I came here and fell asleep. What is your purpose in coming onto this thorny ground on feet as tender as the lotus?" He further says:

_Kim svit tejasvinam tejo bhagavan va Vibhavasuh ||
Suryah Somo Mahendro va lokapalo'paro'pi va ||15||_

(Are you the very radiance of the radiant, or the god of fire? Or are you the sun, the moon, Mahendra, or some other guardian of the world?)

Commentary: Muchukund says, "Maharaj, the radiant splendor that pervades this universe — that itself is this very form of Parbrahm before me! This radiance of yours is the form of Parbrahm. That is, Parbrahm is of the nature of light: you shine more brightly than a thousand suns, you exceed millions of suns and moons; nectar rains from your gaze; you blaze with a radiance greater than millions of Indras; you are more fearsome than millions of Maharudras, gods like Kritant [the god of death and time]." (In the Yoga Vashishtha, the goddess Kalika destroys all beings and, rejoicing, cries out "ad, ad" — in just this way she devours beings, wears a garland of their skulls about her neck, and dances. Who can stand before such a Bhairav? In an instant she turns a settled place to wasteland, and a wasteland to a settled place; that is why she too is called a deva — the reason being, whoever brings forth great things and also destroys them, letting nothing remain permanent, is called Kritant. Muchukund is saying that Lord Krishna is even mightier than such a Maharudra, the god Kritant.) "Your form is more radiant than millions of Dikpals [guardians of the directions]; that is within your very power. It seems to me that your body itself is the manifest form of Parbrahm, and again and again love for you wells up within me."

_Manye tvam devadevanam trayanam purusharshabham ||
Yad badhase guha-dhvantam pradipah prabhaya yatha ||16||_

(O Lord! I regard you, Shri Krishna, as foremost among men and as the God of the three gods. For just as the gods dispel darkness with their own radiance, so you dispel the darkness of this cave.)

That is to say: Muchukundji says, "You have come to dwell within my pure heart. You are the God of the three gods — the three being Vishnu, Rudra, and Brahma; you are the maker of all three. Therefore you are the ancient Purushottam [the primeval Supreme Person], and since you are the maker of these three — Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh — you are the Lord of lords, and the master of the whole universe besides. _Yad badhase guha-dhvantam_ — that is, you came rushing in, breathing hard, in this astonishing manner. For whose sake? By your coming alone, light has blazed forth here — 'pradipah prabhaya', like a lamp's own radiance. Why have you come, shining like this? You have even placed your own yellow garment (pitambar) over me. O flute-bearer, your breath is heaving — with whom have you fought such a fierce enmity?"

_Shushrushatam avyalikam asmakam narapungava ||
Sva-janma karma gotram va kathyatam yadi rochate ||17||_

(O best of men! Let us serve you without pretense. If it pleases you, tell me of your birth, your deeds, and your lineage.)

That is to say: the king has offered this praise and expressed his wish that Parbrahm reveal to him the particulars of his birth, deeds, and gotra. Here the question arises — why should he ask such a thing? Because for the descendants born of Manu, the mind-born son of Brahma the creator, birth, deeds, and gotra have all been fixed. Birth means the species one is born into — human, yaksha, kinnar, gandharva, and so on. Deeds, too, are apportioned: the Brahmin's is to acquire spiritual knowledge and impart it to others; the Kshatriya's is to protect; the Vaishya's is trade and agriculture; the Shudra's is service alone. Gotra means the lineage into which one is born, and so on — and if anyone were to falsify these, he would be found out. That is why the king put this question. But this matter of birth, deeds, and gotra does not apply to the Harijan — that is, to Parbrahm's own people — nor does it apply to God himself; a matter we shall take up further ahead.

_Janma-karmabhidhanani santi me'nga sahasrashah ||
Na shakyante'nusankhyatum anantatvan mayapi hi ||18||_

(My births, deeds, and names are in the thousands; being infinite, even I am unable to number them.)

That is to say: no one is capable of knowing the births and deeds of God. To describe (abhidhan) the very nature of the Supreme is not possible — even the Supreme, God himself, is unable to do it; the number of his births and deeds cannot be counted. Why is this so:

_Bahuni me vyatitani janmani tava charjuna ||
Tany aham veda sarvani na tvam vettha Parantapa ||19||_ (Gita 4.5)

(O Arjuna! Many births of Mine and of yours have already passed. I know all of them, but you, O scorcher of foes, do not know them.)

Adhyaruji Maharaj further states, in the hymn named "Sant Sohago":

_Jire kali kaale Krishna anant roope ||
Prithvi parnaya Parbrahm swaroope ||2||_

(In this Kali age, Krishna comes in infinite forms, uniting with the earth in the very form of Parbrahm.)

That is to say: Parbrahm has many forms; the Supreme comes into this world in various forms and partial manifestations. Because God is the remover of others' sorrow, he must always come to take away the suffering and distress of his devotees, and to attain him one must rise beyond the three gunas. It is for the sake of his devotees alone that God always bears hardship, and that is why he has come here today, into this cave. It is said that he is easily attainable only for the one who worships him having set aside maya.

_Kvachid rajamsi vimame parthivany uru-janmabhih |
Guna-karmabhidhanani na me janmani karhichit ||19||_

(Someone might, over the course of many lifetimes, manage to count the specks of dust of the earth — but no one can ever count My qualities, deeds, names, and births.)

That is to say: there are indeed men who could count all the plants growing on the earth and state their total number; who could count the falling drops of rain; who, through great labor, could even count the grains of sand spread along the vast sea-shore — yet of the nature of Parbrahm, they can know nothing at all.

Adhyaruji Maharaj states, in the Ahar-Nish Ras, that those who give gold by tula-dan, who give cows in charity, who donate land, who give food and water in charity, who study the Vedas and Puranas, who perform yajnas, who keep vows, who practice austerities, who renounce their homes, who attain spiritual knowledge, who give up the highest pleasures and enjoyments of the flesh, who practice forgiveness and compassion, who serve their mother and father — and so on, and so forth — even after doing all these deeds, even after enjoying the pleasures of heaven, have remained unhappy, because they are unable to take refuge in Shri Hari. They have remained deprived of Parbrahm.

_Gaine vaine kai nav jaanu | Ramji vakhanu re swami ek chante ||1||
Govind gaata laagi re khaant | bhrant bhaagi bhav kod-tani ||2||_

(Meaning: Adhyaruji Maharaj says, "I do not know how to worship you through singing and the like — kirtan, bhajan, and so on; I choose only to remember Ram with a single, one-pointed mind. In singing the praises of Govind I have caught a fervent longing for devotion, and now the illusion, the fear, of the ocean of worldly existence has fled.")

That is to say: Parbrahm is exceedingly difficult to attain, yet he is just as effortlessly, easily attained by his devotees. Where there is the grace of the true Guru, he is found quite naturally. At the end of this chapter we shall see that:

_Sa gunan samatityaitan brahma-bhuyaya kalpate ||20||_

(Having gone beyond these three gunas, one becomes capable of attaining the state of Brahman.)

That is to say: "sa gunan" — if one wishes to become free of this world, this universe, which has arisen through the aid of the three gunas — sattva, rajas, and tamas — one must let go of the three gunas; only then does "brahma-bhuyaya kalpate" hold true — that is, by knowing and recognizing Brahman, the Supreme who lies beyond the world's imagining, one can attain oneness with him. When a person's mind (chit) separates itself from Parbrahm and becomes attached to the world, for what reason does this happen? That is, the mind ought to remain fixed in Parbrahm alone; if it turns away from him, a human birth is wasted. It is said in the Garbha Upanishad that when the soul dwells in the womb, it remembers all its past deeds, and, knowing it is about to be parted from Parbrahm and come into this world, it becomes exceedingly distressed. It entreats God: "Having taken birth in this world, I shall never forget you; I shall forever keep chanting your name alone; never again shall I fall into the wheel of karma." But the moment the soul enters this world — that is, the moment it is born — merely by the touch of this world's air, its understanding changes, and the knowledge of its past deeds and births is lost; and it sets about enjoying the world. That is why Jivanji Maharaj asks: for what reason does the mind separate itself from Parbrahm and become attached to the world?

These are that person's words — that indeed is what must be said. The sense of this line is that "that person" means one who knows Parbrahma, or who is near to Parbrahma, and the words spoken directly from his own mouth — here a more detailed and clear discussion is being carried on about Parbrahma. Let us begin with the form that Mahadevji himself described, in the raga Malini.

_asitagirisamam syat kajjalam sindhupatre_
_suratatuvarashakhalekhini patramurvim_
_likhati yadi grihitva sharada sarvakalam_
_tadapi tava gunanamisha param na yati_ ||21||
(Mahimnastotra – 32)

(If the ocean were the inkpot, holding collyrium as black as a mountain, if a branch of the wish-granting tree were the pen and the whole earth the paper, and if, taking up all this, the goddess Sharada were to keep writing through every age — even then, O Lord, she could never reach the far shore of Your virtues.)

If the ocean's basin were the inkpot, holding collyrium as black as mountains, and the branches of the wish-fulfilling trees were the pens, and the whole earth were paper, and with all these means Sharada were to go on writing through every age — even then, O God, she would not reach the limit of Your virtues.

Baba Kabirji has a sakhi (couplet):

_kabir kagad thoda gun ghana. kis bidh likhu banay ||_
_sayarmein pani ghana. vo gagri kaise samay ||1||_

(Meaning: Baba Kabirji says the paper is little and God's virtues are many, so how can he write them down briefly? Just as the sea holds so much water that it cannot fit into a small pot, so too God's virtues cannot be written down on so little paper.)

Meaning: Baba Kabirji says paper is scarce and God's virtues are many, so how is he to write them down in brief? Just as the ocean holds so much water that it could never fit into a small pitcher, so the virtues of God cannot be written down on so little paper.

The purport is that a full description of Parbrahma is not merely extremely difficult but impossible — for who could be capable of knowing His complete works and form? On this matter there is a related sakhi of Baba Kabirji.

_kabir dharatika kagad karu. lekhan karu banaray ||_
_saat samudraki mas karu. to hari gun likha na jaay ||1||_
(Samarath Ras – 61-5)

(Kabirji says: even if I were to make the earth into paper, turn all the vegetation upon it into a pen, and make ink out of the waters of the seven seas, still I could not write a full description of Parbrahma.)

Kabirji says that were he to make the earth into paper, and make a pen from all the vegetation upon the earth, and make ink as much as the water of the seven oceans, even then he could not write a description of Parbrahma. This same point is made in the Bhagavad Gita as well; it also appears in the Bhagavat. Further, Mahadevji too has described this Parbrahma, who is beyond the three gunas. He said to Parvatiji: listen to a description of my Vasudev.

_niranjano niralambo nirlepyo nirvinigrahah ||_
_nirguno nirvikalpo'thaabhayo'nanto'chalo'chyutah ||22||_

(The Lord is Niranjan — stainless; Niralamb — without support; Nirlep — unattached; without any restraint (nigrah); without gunas (vikalp); and He is Abhay — fearless; Anant — infinite; Achal — unmoving; and Achyut — imperishable.)

That is to say: Anjan-bhag (maya) is the name given to a body — the condition (upadhi), that is, the body upon which the smear (lep) of maya's collyrium (anjan) has not fallen, is called Niranjan; here "body" itself is spoken of as maya. One who, though embodied, remains videha — detached from the body — who has not fallen into maya, who is not entangled in it, is Niranjan. Niralamba — (nir + a + lamba) — one who has never taken the support (alamban, prop) of anyone else. One who has never, not even once, anywhere, accepted the support, prop, or refuge of another — that is the meaning here. In the gross sense it is not meant that one soul (jiva) helps another jiva; rather, the sole shelterer of the jiva is Parbrahma. In worldly dealings, support or help carries this gross meaning, but after coming into human birth, a person has not gone off into dependence on anyone else — worshipping other gods and goddesses (anadev), getting entangled in tantra-mantra, threads and charms. It is in this sense that the matter is to be understood here, as it has been explained in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad —

_atha yo'nyam devatamupaste'nyo'savanyo'hamasmiti_
_na sa veda yatha pashurevamsa devanam. yatha ha vai_
_bahavah pashavo manushyam bhunjyuyurevamekaikah purusho devanbhu_
_naktyekasminnaiva pashavadiyamane'priyam bhavati kimu_
_bahushu tasmadeshaan tanna priyam yadetanmanushya vidyuh ||1||_
(Brihadaranyaka – 1-4-10)

(One who worships another deity, thinking "he is other and I am other," does not know the truth. His state is like that of an animal belonging to the gods. Just as many animals together sustain one man, so each person sustains the gods through his worship of them. If even one animal is taken from its owner it displeases him — how much more so if many are taken. So this too [men abandoning their worship] does not please the gods.)

The person who worships another god, holding that "I am one and the gods are another," does not know the true matter. Such people's condition is like animals belonging to the gods. Just as many animals together sustain a man, so each person, by worshipping the gods, sustains the gods. If someone takes away even one animal it does not please its owner — how much less would it please him if many animals were taken? In the same way the gods too do not like this happening (men giving up their worship of them).

The meaning is that the lesser gods (anadev) can live only on the offerings (tarpan) of human beings. They too must enter the cycle of birth and death; when their merit is exhausted they too must take birth again. What is said here about niralamb is meant in this sense — one who has never, in worship or service, taken the shelter of anyone but Parbrahma — that alone is Niralamb.

Sin, merit, joy, sorrow, elation, grief, delusion, envy, greed, ego, lust, and anger do not touch him; all the senses, the five elements, the three gunas, and this whole creation and universe cannot obstruct him, cannot hinder him, cannot raise any difficulty for him — know this to be Nirvigraha, one beyond restraint or opposition. Rajas, Tamas and Sattva are the three gunas; where their maya does not touch, and the doer-person of these three gunas (Parbrahma) is Nirgun, without gunas. Where, even for time itself, this body of limbs (of flesh) does not become sustenance — meaning: hands, feet, mouth, head, eyes, and all of it — where He takes on no part or limb of a body at all — that should be known as Nirvikalpa, one without alternative form.

The purport meant here is that the limbs or senses by which the presence of a body is perceived are perishable, but it is not fitting to imagine such a thing of Parbrahma. "The Lord of all the worlds alone reigns and plays, without a body" — from the kadvu (a devotional verse-canto). He is one who is bodiless; hence He has been called Nirvikalp, for there is none other like Him. Parbrahma alone is all-powerful. Here Adhyaruji Maharaj says —

_rup arupe janiye. ane naam vade de par ||_
_narayan naam ocharo. joi lejo saar ||1||_
(Kirtan 13-15)

(Do not seek to know Him through debating form and formlessness; only by the Name can you cross over. Utter the Name "Narayan," and see — take in its essence.)

There is no need to fall into the dispute of form versus formlessness in order to know the Supreme. Only through the Name should you know Him — and Adhyaruji Maharaj says: utter the name "Narayan," and then see what fruit, what essence, comes of it.

One who has no fear of anyone is Abhay. The Supreme has been called Abhay. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says —

_so'bibhettasmat ekaki bibheti sahayamikshaam_
_chakre yanmadanyannnasti kasmanu vibhemiti tat evasya_
_bhayam viyaaya kasmadvyabheshyad dvitiyadvai bhayam bhavati ||2||_
(1-4-2)

(He became afraid; that is why one who is alone feels afraid. But he reflected: since there is nothing apart from Me, of whom should I be afraid? — and at that his fear departed. But why was he afraid at all? For fear indeed arises only from something other than oneself.)

That Brahma became afraid; therefore a person who is alone feels afraid. But he reflected: apart from Me there is nothing else, so of whom should I be afraid? — and then his fear left him. But why was he afraid in the first place? Fear indeed arises from another. Jivanji Maharaj has not accepted this independent capability of Brahma. He has not upheld the Vedantic teaching of worshipping Brahma; rather, Jivanji Maharaj explains the worship of Parbrahma, who is beyond even Brahma — that is why He alone is called Abhay, one who fears nothing.

That very Being can be Arup, formless, who, without form, performs crores and thousands of works in the universe — His, the formless Parbrahma's, contemplation and worship never go in vain. That is: though He is without colour or form, He remains ever ready to help in His devotees' undertakings — that is why He is also called Bhakta Vatsal, affectionate toward devotees.

_bhakt vatsal biru taharu. tuhaj garuo raay ||_
_lila sabli taahari. te varanan kehi pere thaay ||3||_

(Bhakta Vatsal is Your very title; You alone, O King, are great. Your play is so mighty — how could it ever be described?)

Further, another name of His is Achal, unmoving, for even at the end of the ages (kalpas) He remains unchanged, unshifting, unaltered — He is Achal. These are the very words of the great Rudra. As the testimony of the Vishnu scriptures bears witness, Shri Krishna, free of the three gunas, is truly this very Morli Manohar Parmeshwar — the flute-charming Supreme Lord. Kabirji bears witness to this —

_kabir ekahi akhar alakhse. maatra mile chhatris ||_
_rajas uthe sat likhe. sankele tam ish ||2||_

_kabir mor mugat pankaj nayan. kundal makaraakar ||_
_so murat mere nayana baso. chitmein karo vihaar ||3||_

Meaning: from that one undying syllable (akshar) of the Supreme — which cannot be known through vowels and consonants, nor written in words — thirty-six matras (measures) come forth. Within it, creation comes about in the world through God's rajasik disposition; through the satvik disposition its sustenance takes place; and the tamasik disposition of that Lord gathers the creation back into Himself, draws it back within Himself.

In the three gunas, each of the three gunas has twelve aspects (ang), and so 12 × 3 = 36 — the total aspects of the gunas come to thirty-six. Hence Kabirji says —

_kabir baar ang saakarka, baar ang niraakar ||_
_baaro ang niranjani, aur avastha chaar ||2||_

Meaning: the Supreme God's Sakar, embodied, form has twelve aspects, and the Nirakar, formless, form likewise has twelve aspects. All these twelve-and-twelve aspects belong to the God who is beyond maya, and in His creation there are four states — childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age. In keeping with this sakhi, Kabir says in another sakhi —

_kabir panch tatvako vraksh hai, trigunaka vistaar ||_
_rajas uthai tam khapai, saatvik samdhaar ||3||_

Meaning: the five elements form a tree, which has spread and expanded through the three gunas; that tree rises and grows through the rajas guna, dissolves through the tamas guna, while through the sattva guna it endures evenly from its rise to its end. If the Supreme's one syllable is reckoned as Om, it has eight matra-portions, and all eight together make one matra. Further, there are six ragas, each of which has six raginis (its consorts) —

Bindu — 1/2 matra
Ardhachandra — 1/4 matra
Nirodhini — 1/8 matra
Nad — 1/16 matra
Nadant — 1/32 matra
Shakti — 1/64 matra
Vyapini — 1/128 matra
Samana — 1/128 matra
Jod — 1 matra

— thus, in this way too, the matras of a single syllable can be counted as thirty-six. But for us, Kabirji, addressing the worldly conduct that runs by the rule of the three gunas, speaks of these thirty-six matras for those attached and coloured in the love of maya, given over to lust. But Kabirji's own devotion is toward Shri Krishna. Hence, in a sakhi, Kabirji says: he whose crown is a peacock feather, whose eyes are like lotuses, whose earrings sway like fish — may that form of Shri Krishna dwell within my sight, and may contemplation of it go on continually within my mind — this is what he wishes.

In the three pranayamas — Rechak, Kumbhak and Purak — Purak (inhalation) is filled with 4, 8 and 16 matras; then Kumbhak (retention) is filled with 16, 64 and 32 matras; and Rechak (exhalation) is carried out with 8, 32 and 16 matras. But pointing to such matras and to the three gunas and so forth, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, through Kabir's sakhi, counsels only the contemplation and meditation of Shri Krishna alone.

The revered Yadunath Maharaj, in his exposition of this Kabir sakhi of the "one undying syllable," has written: in life, when the rajasik disposition arises, it should be suppressed with the sattvik, and in the same way the tamas guna too should be gathered in and suppressed — the unknowable Alakh cannot be known, and it is from that very Alakh that all the languages of the world have come into being.

Meaning: the three great gods together made this creation by means of the three gunas, and the three of them divided the work among themselves — Brahma for creation, Vishnu for sustenance, Shiva for destruction. But the Parbrahma, crowned with a peacock's feathers, wearing golden earrings, may He dwell within the very pupils of my eyes. Vyasji, the foremost worshipper of Parbrahma Shri Krishna and eternal resident of Vrindavan, says —

_vyas jake kie tin gun. tatva aur chobis ||_
_ta mohanku govalani. phul chugave sis ||4||_

Meaning: He who has made the three gunas and the five elements, and who has also fashioned the five elements and the twenty-four qualities — that same all-capable Morli Manohar Parmeshwar, Shri Krishna, that Mohan — upon his head the cowherdesses lovingly offer flowers. There Kabirji says — there is a sakhi about how Shri Krishna remains under the sway of the innocent Gopis.

_bed bhed jaane nahi, neti neti kahai bain ||_
_ta mohanso raadhika, kahai mahaavaru dain ||4||_

Meaning: to that Shri Krishna, whose mystery even the Vedas do not know, and whom even the Vedas, unable to grasp His secret, can only describe as "not this, not this" (neti neti), Radhikaji says: apply mahavar to my feet — mahavar being the red dye that fortunate, married women apply to their feet.

_jaahi raaha pandit gaye, taahi gai baahar ||_
_uchi ghati naamki, taha chadh raha kabir ||5||_

Meaning: the path of knowledge, action, yoga, the Vedas, and ritual observance — that path the pandits took, but that road lay outside the true attainment of God. The road to the attainment of God is the road of the high mountain pass — the mountain path of "Ram Nam," the Name of Ram. Kabirji, for his part, is climbing that very path.

_jagat nachaayo baandhke, tin gunke dor ||_
_toku gokul govaalani, pakar nachave por ||6||_

Meaning: He who has bound and made the whole world dance with the thread of the three gunas — that same Shri Krishna is seized by the Gopis of Gokul and made to dance and play in the lanes of Gokul.

_kabir je van pavan na sanchare. pankhi koe na jaay ||_
_so van kabire dhundhiya jahaan. krishna charave gaay ||5||_
(Kasoti – 10-26)

In the forest so dense that even the wind cannot pass through its countless trees, where not even a single bird can dwell, Kabirji says that in such an inaccessible forest, Krishna grazes his cows. That is, Kabirji has discovered a forest which is supreme devotion (bhakti) itself, where no other worshippers can enter. Only he can come there who, having renounced everything else, every other form of worship, has attained supreme devotion alone — only he can reach this state.

This is the abode of the Lord's play, His forest. The wind stands for the individual souls (jivatmas). The bird stands for the mind. The cows He grazes stand for the senses — this sakhi is presented as such an allegory.

_kabir agam agochar gam nahi. jahaan jhalmal jyot ||_
_taha das kabira bandagi. jahaan paap pun nahi chhot ||6||_

Kabirji says: to know the form of Parbrahma, even the agam (the inaccessible — the Vedic scriptures and the like) and the agochar (the imperceptible — the senses and the like) find no understanding. Where the flame-like form of Parbrahma continually flickers and shimmers, none can grasp the way to that agam-agochar light. There, having himself reached such an exalted seat, he performs devotion to that form of Parbrahma, radiant with light, where neither sin nor merit can even enter. This sakhi appears in the Parchari (hagiographic account) of Rankaji in this manner —

_agam agochar gam nahi, taanhaa param sukh bhog ||_
_tiha bhakt jan ram rahya, jaanhaa paap pun nahi chhot ||7||_

Further, in the Sarvang Lila the closing line runs as follows —

_ras ramaadi gopika, hari ade abhade naahi ||_

In this line it is said: though the Lord performed the ras-lila with the Gopis, He remained free of any impurity — He is beyond sin and merit.

There Jivandasji spoke —

_nirgun brahmthe jivana. trigun bhayo vistaar ||_
_sakal gun seva kare. so aap raha niradhaar ||7||_

_trigun rahit gunmaan base. so sadguru diyo bataay ||_
_nirgun brahm vede kahyo. so vraj kul chaare gaay ||8||_

_to nirgun sagun jivana. so vraj kul chaare gaay ||_
_sagun vrikhabhanki daavadi. nirgun jadupati raay ||9||_

Meaning: Nirgun Brahma, that is, Shri Krishna, from whom the three gunas — rajas, tamas, sattva — arose, and all the gunas serve Him: this refers to Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesh, and the like, as well as the Vaishnavas who worship through the three gunas. "He Himself remains niradhar (without any support)" means that Shri Krishna, though He is the one who manifests the three gunas, remains untouched by them.

Jivanji Maharaj says that from Ishwar in His maya-conditioned aspect arose the three gunas — rajas, tamas, sattva — and these gunas serve that maya-conditioned Ishwar; that is his support. But He, Brahma, Parbrahma, is Himself niradhar, without support.

Parmeshwar, who is free of the three gunas, dwells also within the very substance of the three gunas. The existence of the three gunas has no separate existence apart from Parmeshwar — this the Sadguru has explained. The three gunas are subject to Parmeshwar. The Vedas call this Parbrahma Nirgun, beyond all gunas — yet that very God grazes cows in the abode of Vraj-kul, Vrindavan; He conducts the running of creation. There is no separate doer in Him — in that sense the Vaishnava who is gunatit, beyond the gunas, is a servant of Govind, gunatit like Krishna himself. That Supreme, who is both Nirgun and Sagun, that very Krishna grazes cows in Vraj-mandal. In this, God's Sagun form is Radhika, daughter of Vrishabhanu, and His Nirgun form is Shri Krishna, foremost of the Yadu clan.

That is: Brahma is Nirgun, unattached; Brahma does nothing at all, and yet the whole universe is wrapped around Him. Brahma Himself, though free of gunas, is that by whose influence alone everything else becomes active. The Sadguru has given us sight of such a Brahma. A lengthy discussion of the subject of Brahma will not be carried on here, but this very Nirgun Brahma grazes cows in Vraj-kul. Brahma's Sagun form is Radhaji, and His Nirgun form is Krishna.

_mayadhyakshena prakritih suyate sacharacharam ||_
_hetunanena kaunteya jagadviparivartate ||3||_
(Gita 9-10)

("O Kaunteya [Arjuna]! Under My — Krishna-Parbrahma's — superintendence Prakriti brings forth all that moves and does not move, and by this cause the universe undergoes its changes.")

"O Kaunteya (Arjuna)! Under My (Krishna-Parbrahma's) governance Prakriti conducts its manifold workings, and by that very means the world undergoes transformation."

_ek vishese jaaniye. ne dip vant akaar ||_
_ras paatra vrit paharaari. anjan saheja nivaar ||29||_
(Harsh Bhavan 29)

Prakriti has three gunas; though the three gunas are mutually opposed in nature to one another, worldly activity, creation, proceeds only through the union of all three. Just as oil, wick (cotton) and fire, though of opposite natures, give light only through the combination of all three — for oil alone does not burn, nor does cotton alone — yet where an unbroken lamp is burning, the cotton within the flame is not consumed even as the oil slowly burns away and gives light. In this way, though the three gunas are of opposing natures, the workings of the world could not proceed without even one of them.

_eko devah sarvabhuteshu gudhah sarvavyaapi sarvabhutantaraatma ||_
_karmaadhyaksah sarvabhutaadivaasah saakshi cheta kevalo nirgunashcha ||4||_
(Shvetashvatara Upanishad – 6-11)

(This one God dwells hidden in all beings; He is all-pervading, the inner self of all beings, the overseer of all works, the abode of all beings, the witness, the pure consciousness, and He alone is without gunas.)

This one, hidden Parbrahma dwells in all beings (humans and others), and this Brahma, dwelling within all beings, is the foremost witness of their actions, and He alone is entirely Nirgun.

That is: though dwelling together with Prakriti, who possesses the gunas, He is Nirgun — the gunas do not touch Him. Parbrahma is only the witness of it all; He is merely the doer, the maker of the whole world and so forth — nothing at all touches Him. Further, as was said earlier, that the Nirgun Brahma is spoken of in the Vedas — in the tenth mandala of the Rigveda, in speaking of the origin of creation, it is said —

_ko addhaavedakaihapravochatkuta aajaataakuta iyam visrishtih ||_
_arvaagdeva asyavisarjanenaathaakovedayata aabubhuva ||5||_
(Rigveda 10-129-6)

Who truly knows the elements of Prakriti? Who can describe them? By whose union — whose worship — did this creation come into being? For what cause did this manifold creation arise? The gods and the like too are themselves born as an inner part of this very creation — who then knows from where creation itself arose?

_iyam visrishtiryataabubhuvayadivaadadheyadivaanam ||_
_yo asyaadhyakshah paramevyoman tso adgavedayadivaanaveda ||6||_
(10-129-7)

"From where did this manifold creation arise? Who created it, and who did not create it? All this only he can know who dwells in the very own abode of Parbrahma-Parmeshwar. It may well be that even they — the gods and the like, Narad and others — do not know this."

In the Mahabharata there is a dialogue between Sanatkumar and Narad, in which Narad falls into delusion. But here one thing is worth noting: in the matter of the creation of the universe, the highest place has not been given to the gods Agni and Indra. The Brahma spoken of in Vedanta, Jivanji Maharaj has treated as secondary, and has shown Parbrahma's true form to be that which is even beyond Brahma. It is this form, beyond even Brahma, of which Jivanji Maharaj speaks — and Adhyaruji Maharaj too has expressed this very idea, most simply, in a verse of his kadvu. He has stated it so effortlessly that one would hardly realise what great, hidden mystery lies behind it.

_chidaanandam parabrahma dhyaanagamyam sanaatanam ||_
_aksharam nirmalam nityam niraakaram namaamyaham ||7||_

(I bow to that Parbrahma-Parmatma, who is of the nature of consciousness and bliss, attainable through meditation, eternal, imperishable (akshar), stainless, everlasting, and formless.)

I bow to the Parbrahma-Parmatma who is of the nature of knowledge and bliss, who can be experienced through meditation, who is sanatan (everlasting), akshar (imperishable), free of impurity, eternal, and formless.

_sur muni antariksh stave re gokul. hari te ati re akal ||_
_hari hari rame re govind aanand bharyo e ||1||_
_aapanape ramato pindaara ramaade. hari te rame ne ramaade ||_
_harite jame ne jamaade. harino gagan brahmaadik vichaar kare e ||2||_
_akal ramat maandi gokul maahen. ramat brahmaadik chaahe_
_hari te aapanape ade na abhade e. ||3||_

That is: Adhyaruji Maharaj clearly declares that this is the inconceivable play (lila) of Parbrahma, difficult to understand, bewildering even for Brahma and the other gods. The Vedantis (Shankaracharya and others), unable to grasp it, call this the "maya" of Brahma, while Vallabhacharya recognises it as the "lila" of Brahma. Further, Ramanujacharya sees this kind of form of Brahma as vishishtha — that is, as a wondrous form. But Jivanji Maharaj, Adhyaruji, and others mean by it that for Him anything at all in the world is possible; He holds every kind of power. Moreover, He remains pervading everywhere throughout the universe. What is spoken of as His cosmic (virat) form in the Puranas and in the Gita is this very form. And yet, more than the other acharyas, the saints of the Ramkabir tradition — from Gyaniji down to Jivanji, Padmanabh, and others — have not entered into the dispute over Parbrahma's form versus formlessness, but rather, having reconciled the two, have seen Parbrahma in both forms together. And yet no gross idol has been given a place or recognition in this tradition. Here a sakhi of Rankaji is given —

_ghareku dhijoon nahi. esa paaya naaka ||_
_aakaar niraakaar vivarjit. taaka sevak ranka ||10||_

_ghareku dhijoon sahi. rahoo adharke maahen ||_
_wanka taha vilambia. jaha dhoop nahi chhaay ||11||_

Meaning: this is a dialogue between the husband Ranka and the wife Vanka concerning God, given across these two sakhis. In it Ranka says: even were you to say that God takes on a Sakar, embodied, idol-form, still, however many attempts you make to persuade me that God dwells in this Sakar, embodying form, I will not accept what you say — I will not be swayed at all, because I have now obtained the most minute, subtle knowledge of exactly where the Supreme is to be found — that is, I have now come to full knowledge about God — so that I have now become this Ranka, the worshipper and devotee of that divine essence which is free of both Sagun-Sakar (embodied, qualified) and Nirgun-Nirakar (unembodied, unqualified).

Meaning: in answer, seemingly in contradiction and yet, in fact, supporting her husband's view by an inverse route, Ranka's devoted wife Vanka speaks. She says: O Ranka, though you may deny it, I for my part will indeed accept God's Sagun-Sakar form. But my loving devotion I will surely keep fixed upon the Nirgun-Nirakar — that is, though God can manifest as either the Sagun or the Nirgun principle, He Himself remains detached from both Sagun and Nirgun, and it is upon that divine essence that I shall fix my mind, says Vanka. I shall remain in the shelter and refuge of that very divine essence, where there is no such thing at all as sunshine or shade — that is, no such pair of opposites as joy and sorrow.

Ranka Bhagat says: material things are perishable; he places no trust in such things — this is the teaching, the guiding mark, that his Guru has shown him. He, Ranka Bhagat, is the servant of that Supreme who is the support of all, who has no fixed form, and for whom not even the notion of formlessness applies.

Vanka Bhagat says: today's perishable, material things — nothing can be accomplished without them, for performing devotion, receiving teaching, practising religious discipline, and carrying out activity cannot happen without the body. Therefore, for these purposes, she does hold the body as necessary — but her disposition (vritti) she keeps fixed on that support-less Supreme who is the support of all. In Him her disposition has become steady. What is that Supreme like? Where there is no shade, no sunshine, no joy or sorrow, but only the very nature of supreme bliss.

Rankaji, being extremely poor, his real name has been forgotten, and he came to be known by the name "Ranka" (meaning pauper). His wife too, though devoted to her husband, was, so to speak, positive-negative — the reverse-and-obverse of him — for Vanka would speak the opposite (vanku, crooked) of what Ranka said, yet her intention was always to lend support to Ranka himself, and for this crooked manner of speaking she became known by the name "Vanka." But the presentations of Ranka and Vanka are like two sides of a single coin, each true in its own way. When Rankaji refused to accept the Sakar, Vanka did not deny the Sakar but accepted it — yet did so in a roundabout way that ultimately lent support to Ranka's own position.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj's guru Gopaldas had four principal disciples, among whom was Anantdas of Borbar. He composed the Parcharis (hagiographic accounts) of nine saints in all. He held a line of thought that endorsed Jivanji Maharaj's own principles, and so he drew important sayings from the Parcharis of Namdevji and Pipaji into the Samagam. Here, then, let us look at a few verses from the Ranka-Vanka Parchari composed by Anantdas, in which there is material corresponding to these sakhis.

In this Parchari there is a small dialogue between Namdev and Ranka. Once, when Ranka's daughter had gone to the river to fetch water for worship and service, some drops fell on her water-vessel from Namdev's daughter nearby, upon which Ranka's daughter, quarrelling, said: "Your father practises a stubborn, insistent kind of devotion to God, but God helps His devotee without any need for such insistence — God is never unaware of His devotee's suffering. Therefore a true devotee does not speak out his suffering before God with his own mouth." Hearing this, Namdev came to Ranka and began to ask what fault there was in his own devotion. Then Ranka said: "You made God drink milk, you had God's temple moved, you brought a dead cow back to life — yet you have not attained the true understanding of devotion to God." And, pointing out his shortcoming, he said —

_pey piyo deval phiro, bhakti na aai tohe ||_
_sant puj re namdev, malia chaahe mohe ||8||_

Meaning: you made God drink milk, had His temple moved, yet true devotion to God has still not been attained by you. O Namdev, if you truly wish to attain God, then serve the saints instead. Let us now look at the discussion that follows.

_ta pichhe nirgun sagun katha chalaai, tehi ausar hari asht dve rup dhari aai ||_
_tab ranka kahe suno santajan bhaai, yame kahaakum bhajo so deho bataai ||9||_

Meaning: after that, discussion of Nirgun and Sagun began, in the course of which it was said that God, through His eightfold nature (ashtadha prakriti), the five elements and the three gunas, assumes both the Sagun and the Nirgun form. Then Rankaji asks: brother, listen — of these two, which form will you worship? (The Sagun of the ten avatars — the one who drank milk, who had the temple moved, who revived the dead cow — or the Nirgun?)

_dash kaho to hari dash naahi, ek kaho to nav kahaan samaai ||_
_tab namdevake man bhayo bicharu, yame kahaakum kahu kiratharu ||10||_

Meaning: if you say God has ten avatars, then He is not merely ten; and if you say God is only One, then where would the other nine be accommodated? At this, Namdev's mind fell to pondering which of these two alternatives he should call God.

_dekh charitra chit bhaari, kachu samajh na pare he harirai ||_
_tab ranke aad avinaashi diya jataai, naamarupki bhakti kahi samjhaai ||11||_

Meaning: seeing this bewildering conduct of God, Namdev's mind fell into great confusion, and he could make no sense at all of the matter of Hariraya. Then Ranka made known and explained to him the primordial, imperishable, complete Parbrahma-Parmatma, and explained to him how devotion to the Name-and-Form should be performed.

_rup naam shiv sanakaadik phunipati jaane, dhru prahlaad dhyaan man aane ||_
_vaanchhit bhakt kare chit laai, dini bhakt mukt vaikunth pad paai ||12||_

Meaning: Shiv, the Sanakadik sages, and Sheshnag with his thousand hoods all know how to perform devotion to the Name-and-Form. Dhruv and Prahlad too fix their minds in contemplation of Him. In this way devotees perform devotion with an eye toward the fruit they desire, and to such devotees God grants liberation and the state of Vaikunth.

_naam rupki bhakt kahi samjhaai, tab hari kala lai samaai ||_
_ek anek rup dhari aave, mool graha bina bharam na jaave ||13||_

Meaning: when devotion to the Name-and-Form had been explained, it was understood where God's kala (portion, aspect) finds its accommodation — that the one Supreme comes assuming many forms. Hence, without understanding God's true, original form, illusion cannot depart.

_daria lahera dve kachu naahin, upaje anek phuni tahanhi samaai ||_
_itani goshta bhai naamako man maanyo, ranakaku sadguru kahi pramaano ||14||_

Meaning: the ocean and its waves are not two separate things — many waves arise in the ocean and merge back into it again. In the same way there is no separateness between God and His avatars. Once this much discussion had taken place, Namdev's mind was satisfied, and he acknowledged Ranka as his Sadguru.

Meaning: he will not trust, will not be swayed by, will not give weight to the form the Supreme takes on — he cares nothing for form, he will not accept the Sagun principle as the ultimate God.

In the tradition, Rankaji and Vankaji are famed together as a couple of devotees. Their special quality is that they present every matter in an inverted manner — that is, speaking in terms of language, their statements are always couched in a figure of paronomasia (shlesh). Here too they explain, in the same beautiful language, that "Gharekoo" refers to the matter of Parbrahma — that is, for the sake of Parbrahma's Sagun-Sakar worship he cannot keep his patience; he does not waste time, nor allow any kind of delay — such is his resolve, that without falling into debates over form and formlessness he has never stopped or slowed the pace of his worship. Whereas Rankaji's wife says that she does not perform the worship of Parbrahma hastily, without knowing and understanding it — she chooses her path of worship and devotion with all seriousness; she remains within her worship of both the Sagun and the Nirgun, and of that which is beyond both — her Parmeshwar is beyond both sunshine (form) and shade (formlessness).

Thus, though expressed each in their own style, both are conveying the same single point — that in choosing one's path of worship one ought not to waste time. This is the inner intent conveyed here. And yet, to wander about anywhere at all, without knowing or understanding anything, is likewise sheer folly, tantamount to self-destruction — for time waits for no one, and the path of devotion must always remain free of dispute. Devotion alone should be the mantra of life; not the slightest scholarly pedantry has any place in devotion, and further, for the path of devotion one must become free of ego — ego is the greatest gateway to downfall on the path of devotion. Therefore one should worship the innocent, faultless Parbrahma rather than scriptures or abstruse learning, without leaning on any prop whatsoever, and devotees should never allow any delay in their devotion either.

(Rankaji was born in Pandharpur in Vikram Samvat 1347, Magshar Sud 2. Vankaji was born in Pandharpur in Vikram Samvat 1351, Vaishakh Vad 7.)

_niraakaar niradhaar hai. aakaare aanand ||_
_god khelaave jashomati. so puran parmaanand ||12||_

_e rup arupe shaamalo. khele nand dwaar ||_
_aadi omkaar upanyo jivana. koti brahmaand vistaar ||13||_

_niraakaar aakaarthe. adbhut ek arup ||_
_so saai hamaare jivana. je sitaapatiko rup ||14||_

Meaning: the Nirakar, formless, needs no support of form; hence in the worship of a Nirgun God, one cannot enjoy the flavour of love. But when devotion is performed to the Sagun form, one may take pleasure in the joy of love in relation to Him. Such is the Lord Krishna of Sagun-Sakar form, whom Jashodaji plays with in her lap as her son — the same Krishna who is Himself of the nature of supreme bliss. — 11

This dark-complexioned (shyamal) Krishna, who is of embodied form and yet, as formless, is also without any form, plays as a child in Nandji's palace. Jivanji Maharaj says that this very Krishna precedes even the Omkari, triguni creation itself — it was from this Parmatma Krishna that the crores of triguni universes first spread into expansion. — 12

Jivanji Maharaj says: the God who is astonishing beyond even Nirgun-Nirakar and Sagun-Sakar, who is without any form at all — such is our object of worship, who abides in the form of Sitapati Ram. — 13

In discussing the form of Parbrahma, Jivanji Maharaj, further ahead in this same section, explains the matter of Nirgun Brahma; now here he explains the matter of this Nirgun Brahma's Sakar form — the Nirakar Parbrahma has been called Niradhar, without support or foundation, for even Parbrahma, in order to act — that is, for the protection of His devotees — must come, out of the formless, into a form, into some definite mould or shape. Hence the Nirakar form too merges back into the complete Brahma; Brahma's Sakar form is but a portion of Parbrahma. For instance, Krishna's form was of the thirtieth part — a partial manifestation. Thus one must understand the complete form of Parbrahma, which not every soul (jiva) has the capacity to behold. Furthermore, since Parbrahma is present within all elements and within every kind of nature (prakriti), by what form is He to be recognised? Here, in the pad of Brahmaruli, Adhyaruji Maharaj says —

_vaayu gandh maahen sanchare. ture brahmaaruli || gandh muke nij rup ||35||_
_tem hari gunmaan sanchare || ture brahmaaruli || nirgun jape tuj naam ||36||_

Meaning: in every single thing — trees, leaves, fruit, flowers, the earth, and so on — there is a scent, and the wind enters into that scent and spreads it. In the same way, the scent that resides in a tree, its fruit, its flowers, leaves its own original source-form of tree, leaf and fruit, and diffuses into the wind — so too you make your own existence merge into Parbrahma, the ruler of the universe. In the very same way God too enters into the three gunas, and this Nirgun-Nirakar Parbrahma keeps repeating your Name and Form. So too you make your own existence merge into Parbrahma, the ruler of the universe.
