In the fifth incarnation, in the form of Vamana, He granted King Bali an unshakeable kingdom in the netherworld, and protected Indra's own throne. In the sixth incarnation He appeared as Parashuram and made the earth free of kshatriyas. In the seventh incarnation He appeared as Ram and slew Ravan, and put an end to the deeds of Kumbhakarna. In the eighth incarnation, in the form of Balram-Balabhadra, He bore the plough and destroyed the mlecchhas and the like. In the ninth incarnation, appearing as Buddha, He practised meditation and redeemed countless beings. In the tenth incarnation, as Kalki, He will destroy the yavanas and the like.

All these ten incarnations He Himself took on, in King Ambarish's place. What task of Ambarish's own was accomplished through all these incarnations? Did any fruit come to him from it? Neither was devotion to Vishnu practised through it, nor was any work for the welfare of the people accomplished through it. Whatever was done, the Lord Himself did it — that is, King Ambarish was deceived, and it was the Lord who had to take incarnation in his place. In this, the King himself remained free of action, and yet became burdened with the fault of action. And whose word, after all, was kept — Durvasa's? If we look at it plainly, King Ambarish did clearly refuse. The Lord gave assurance that He would keep His word — but Jivanji Maharaj explains that the Lord goes wherever there is the wish of the devotee, and takes whatever form suits whatever need arises for whoever is in distress. The Lord has been called bhakt-vatsal — ever tender toward His devotees. He is always present to protect His own devotees. Here, the Lord kept the word of both — of Durvasa and of Ambarish — and in doing so, deceived them both.

_bhakt manorath jivanaa. hari ghare dase avataar._
_nrip rishi dou chhetare. prabhu leela anant apaar._ ||27||

(Dasaka Ang – 59)

In this way, the Lord comes at a single call for help — and foremost among these are Ram and Krishna. The Lord's Leela, moreover, is unbroken. Through His incarnations the Lord has accomplished many tasks. What, then, is meant by His taking ten incarnations? These are simply the names given to His various forms. The Leela that belongs to Ram and to Krishna — these are, after all, only the names of the One who holds the Leela. In assuming this form, whose name was taken, and for what reason?

Wherever, and whatever distress a devotee faces, there the Lord has assumed a corresponding form. Wherever there is a particular form, there a corresponding name too has been given.

That is: there is no end to the Lord's Leela. Moreover, the various Puranic tales are also full of the Lord's incarnations, deeds, the relationships between gods and demons, and the relationships among the Lord's various gods and goddesses, vow-stories, the glories of pilgrimage sites, and so on. In such Puranic tales an ordinary person may often become confused; it also happens that many Puranic stories contradict one another. At such times it becomes exceedingly difficult to find and know the truth. So then, what is this matter of the ten incarnations spoken of here? The answer to that will be given further on.

Here, once again, the word of the all-pervading Leela:

_dhanpat swaroopi raam hai. laheri ve avataar._
_aage pichhe madhyas jal. taakaa e vistaar._ ||28||

Meaning: That Parbrahma-Parmatma who came to Ambarish's aid plays out many roles, as an actor (a performer of plays) does, and in this way He has played the roles of the ten incarnations and so on. But all the people of the world, seeing such various incarnations, keep taking the Lord to be many different beings in many different ways — yet this Lord is not really different from Himself; it is one and the same Lord who, like an actor, assumes different forms.

He who plays throughout all things is Parbrahma in the form of Ram — that is the master of "dhan" (rain-wealth), the ocean; and the waves are the ten incarnations. Before, behind, and in the middle of the waves is the water in the form of Brahma-consciousness — that is its extent. In the incarnation that came before, the one in the middle, and the one that will come after — in each, that same Parbrahma in the form of Ram alone abides.

Parbrahma is like the ocean; the ten incarnations are its waves. The water at the very centre of this ocean is in the form of Ram-Krishna — this is called Naam-roop (name as form). And what comes before and after — that is, the ten incarnations that come before and after Ram-Krishna — these are called Roop-naam (form as name). Further, at the time of the Ras-leela, there was one Krishna between each and every gopi — this was because, of the gopis who had adorned themselves with the sixteen ornaments, each one, like a mirror, reflected the form of Krishna in many different ways. But the original form of Krishna was that one true Krishna around whose neck Radhaji had placed her arms while performing the Ras-leela — that alone was the real Krishna. The rest — the Krishnas seen reflected in the gopis' adornments — were, like reflections in a mirror, mere appearances only. And the Lord who came to Ambarish's aid was this very same original Parbrahma-Parmatma. So the Krishna seen in such adornment-like reflections could not have given such help, because that is only an appearance (aabhaas) of Parbrahma; and since the ten incarnations, too, are of this same nature — mere appearances of the Lord — they are counted and reckoned only as names given to that form, names attached to the form of the incarnation, resembling the Krishna seen in the gopis' adornments — from these, it is useless to expect any real help.

The water in the midst of Radhaji's hands is the flute-charming Krishna — that is the very form of the Supreme Being. He alone is the doer and sustainer of the world. The Lord is formless (nirgun, niraakaar), and that is why He has been compared to water. Radhaji's hand rests around the neck of this very Lord Krishna, and that is why Radhaji is able to relish the joy of this Leela of the Lord. But when the shadow of the gods fell, the Lord became invisible — yet He went away taking Radhaji along with Him. That is why it is said, on page 77 of the Samagam, that Radhaji had become filled with pride — Radhaji felt that "the Lord is in the midst of my very hands" — and so the Lord, taking Radha along, became invisible. That is, it points us toward the truth that one should be free of pride — for even when Radhaji herself became proud, the Lord departed even from her presence.

Now, what is meant by this "water in the midst of Radhaji's hands"? For this, two kinds of statement have been made — Naam-roop and Roop-naam. In place of Ambarish, the Lord agreed to take ten incarnations; in those incarnations, whatever form the Lord assumed, a name accordingly arose — but that was not the Lord's original, permanent form; so in that incarnation, whatever form the Lord had, that very same was its name — hence that is "Roop-naam." But the Lord who assumes such incarnations — that original Parbrahma is called "Naam-roop." Hence that alone is the true Supreme Being of Naam-roop. In the palm of a hand, water can remain only in a very tiny quantity. On this there is a riddle:

"A shallow pond, a shallow bank — not even a paisa's worth of water stays" — the answer to which is: a palm. In a palm, only a negligible amount of water can remain — so in Radhaji's hands is the formless (nirgun) Krishna, who is not like such a shallow pond, but is of Naam-roop; so in this pond that is of Roop-naam, there is only the mere appearance of the formless Parbrahma. In the Bhagwat it is said:

_avataaraa hyasankhyeyaa hareh sattvanidhervijaah._
_yathaa'vinaashinah kulyaah sarasah syuh sahasrashah._ ||17||

(9-3-26)

(O Brahmins! Just as thousands of small, unfailing streams flow out from an inexhaustible lake, in that same way countless incarnations arise from Shri Hari, the ocean of the quality of sattva.)

O Brahmins! Just as thousands of little rivers flow out from an inexhaustible lake, in the same way countless incarnations arise from Shri Hari, the ocean of the quality of sattva.

Just as there is a cycle of transformation in the oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen cycles, so too a cycle of transformation runs its course here.

That is: "dhan" — meaning clouds and rain — has as its lord the ocean; from the ocean's own water, vapour forms and becomes clouds of wealth-rain, and these same clouds come back down again in the form of rain, and the water returns once more to the ocean. This process goes on continually. The tales told of the Ocean of Milk in the Puranas and other scriptures are of this very same kind — a Leela of Parbrahma — in which creation arises, and in the end is again absorbed back into that very same source. Whatever substance, thing, or object — moving or unmoving — exists in this world, all of it is but the various forms of that same complete Parbrahma. But these forms are not unchanging — form is subject to breaking; form keeps changing. Whereas the name is unchanging, and imperishable. But when we utter a name, the very first thing that appears before our sight is a vision of its form. For instance, if someone utters the word "snake," before our very eyes there appears a fearsome, long, rope-like creature — even though it may not actually be physically present. No form need be physically present — but on hearing the name, its form becomes vividly present before us, indirectly. The illustration that was discussed at the very start of this chapter is here explained once again, with a fitting example: from the middle part of the ocean a wave arises, and dashes against the rocks of the shore. This wave is the incarnation. The wave is momentary. On the ocean's water, by the force of the wind, a wave arises; but only as long as the wind's control persists over it does its life continue — after that it is destroyed, and again a new wave comes. This process goes on unceasingly. In this, we can give a name to each and every wave. Each and every wave that arises completes its own lifespan and is destroyed. But if it is given a definite name, that name is not destroyed along with it, nor will it ever be. Names remain preserved for endless time. If we try once more to understand this metaphor: the entire ocean, in its one single body, is spread out everywhere, and its water, too, remains the very same — there is no increase or decrease in it, no change occurs in it. Even for the forming of clouds, the ocean's water goes up into the sky, and yet no decrease is seen in its quantity because of that, nor any increase from the coming of the rains; nor is any change seen in the ocean becoming saltier or less salty.

That is: in this world, in this universe, whatever things — moving and unmoving — are visible, and the countless multitudes of stars — in these too, increase and decrease go on occurring. Just as, in the ocean, sometimes more waves come and sometimes fewer, without that causing any real change — in exactly the same way, in this universe too, what is visible today may perhaps not be visible tomorrow; changes keep occurring in form — one comes while another goes. In just the same way, this is the arithmetic that governs Parbrahma's incarnations as well. Just as the wave that arises in the middle of the ocean — the name given to such waves is Ram and Krishna. Form undergoes destruction, but the name is never destroyed. The name is unchanging and imperishable; moreover, no defect or alteration ever occurs in it.

Once a name has been given, it does not change; the form changes — just as we give a name to a small child, but that child's form keeps changing with time. The one who was a small child becomes a grown boy, then a young man, becomes middle-aged too, and at last becomes a frail old person and finally passes away. Yet through every one of these stages, the name does not change.

Thus, what we call Ram and Krishna are names of the Form — and the ten incarnations spoken of, that came before and after, are likewise names of that same form. Further — what should this Form and this Name be called?

Here Jivanji Maharaj has posed a very deep and knotty question. Just as, in the Ras-leela, there was one Krishna between each and every sakhi (gopi) — that is, if a young woman, adorned and ready in her gleaming sixteen ornaments, were to be set with countless tiny mirrors, then as many reflections of whoever stood facing her would appear in them. Though the young woman is one, countless reflections of her appear all around her. In just the same way, in the Ras-leela, Radhaji is Prakriti (Nature itself), and the other gopis are but various forms of that very same Prakriti. Krishna has joined Himself, in various ways, with these various forms — that is, He is united with every form of Prakriti. But to see His reflection, a mirror is needed. This mirror is Radhaji, who is the subtle form of Prakriti. Shri Krishna and Radhaji cannot be seen in their gross, physical form, for to do so would serve no purpose.

"The water in the middle — that is the flute-charming Shri Krishna, in the midst of Radhaji's hands. This is His name — He who came to Ambarish's call! By Name-and-Form, He is truly this very flute-charming Supreme Lord; and by Form-and-Name — for what reason does that come about? What fruit is produced by worshipping that? This world, this universe, is a bond, a binding factor — it is bound by this very universe. Why should one be bound by it?"

That is: this is a Samagam saying. The all-powerful Parbrahma alone is the cause of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world. In the midst of Radhaji's hands is water — that is, the subtle form of water is the very cause by which Parbrahma becomes perceptible. It is from this subtle element of water that we are able to obtain outward knowledge — form, taste, smell, and so on. At the front surface of the pupil of the eye there is a moist film of water, by which sight is possible; there is water upon the tongue, and that is why we can experience taste. Thus every element of Nature has two aspects — one its gross form, and the other its subtle form. Parbrahma dwells, in subtle form, within every element — but this Parbrahma is not something that can be perceived by the senses; He is beyond the organs of action and of knowledge. And yet, even so, in order to understand Him, the gross

A basis in physical form is also necessary. Only through the gross form can one reach the subtle form. For the protection of King Ambarish, He was continuously present in subtle form. But when He came together with Rishi Durvasa to remove the curse, that was in an embodied form. Thus, that entity called Parbrahma, which is subtle and beyond even that, can remain simultaneously in subtle form and in embodied form. And whatever is embodied is also formless (nirgun), and this very formless one can, whenever needed, take on an embodied form in any shape. In seeing, in experience, or even in direct perception, illusion or ignorance can arise, and this direct experience can be false, or it can be true — this is a profound subject. Just as a rope lying in a dark room creates the illusion of a snake — even though seen directly, that knowledge is false; it is not a snake, only a rope. In the same way, one who has not gone beyond the outer senses cannot know and recognize Parbrahma. To recognize Him, one needs not the gross senses but His subtle essence. In the Mahabharata war, the gross senses were useless for beholding Krishna's universal form (Vishwarupa), so a subtle sense was granted to Arjuna. This same is the nature of Radha and Krishna. Who came to Ambarish's rescue for his protection? The name and form of that essence which came there has been shown by Jivanji Maharaj to be the Flute-Charming Supreme Lord (Morli Manohar Parmeshwar).

Why did Parbrahma have to come there Himself? Because it was on account of a Brahmin that He had to come. The name "Brahmin" too gives rise to a kind of ego, which is an outer worldly attachment (vasana). And because of this outer attachment, Durvasa made a mistake in recognizing Him. And the king, too, was overcome with ego. Thus, because of two opposing egos, both went astray. Earlier it was said in a sakhi that both the king and the sage were deceived — thus both went astray and both were deceived. To show how they were deceived, a beautiful sakhi is given here.

_amarikh gohare aaviyo. hari dharyo natvar vesh ||_
_sab jug bhulyo jeevana. karat anek anek ||29||_

(Meaning: Hari came to Ambarish's rescue and took on the guise of an actor — various forms and incarnations such as Krishna and so on. In this He has confused the entire world, and people come to see God as many, in numerous forms, and so they try to recognize Him through many incarnations and elements, and wander about in various places trying to find Him.)

Just as an actor in a bhavai (folk drama) puts on a different costume every day — one day he becomes a king, another day he becomes a pauper — Parbrahma is just like that actor. According to need, He comes in whatever guise (birth) is required and departs again, and out of all this, only very few souls are able to recognize Him. The rest of the world wanders here and there trying to recognize Him, yet they cannot know Him. Thus Parbrahma is one and the same; only the guise changes. But if, letting go of Parbrahma, one clings only to the guise, the soul cannot be freed — that is, it falls into a lower state. Therefore, leaving aside the various guises, one should recognize only that original, root essence. Just as an actor may sometimes take on the guise of King Bhoj, but because of that he cannot actually remove anyone's suffering — because once the intoxication of the role wears off, he himself becomes poor again. This is why the names and forms Ram and Krishna alone are such that they can grant the soul a vision of Parbrahma's true form. What happens if the soul falls into doubt and confusion (dagdago)? The Bhagavat Mahatmya, chapter 2, verse 20, says:

_bhaktidrohakara ye cha te sidanti jagatraye ||_
_durvasa duhkham aapannah pura bhaktir vinindakah ||18||_

(Meaning: Those who commit treachery against devotion suffer in the three worlds, just as Durvasa suffered for once disparaging devotion.)

_aave aave re govaliyani sange ramato ||_
_sange ramato more man gamato ||1||_

In this malgodi song, Narsinh Mehta sings on seeing Shri Krishna approaching him. According to the story, once his son-in-law asked Narsinh Mehta: "Bhagat, you are a beloved devotee of God, and you have seen Krishna — will you not show Him to me?" The devotee said, "Certainly, I will grant you His vision." So one day both walked together, going far out into the wilderness, where, seeing God approaching from the opposite direction in the guise of a cowherd, Mehtaji burst into song, but the son-in-law could not recognize Him and began mocking Mehtaji, saying he had made an ordinary cowherd out to be the real Krishna. Thus, one who looks only at the outer guise remains confused and deceived, and the soul does not attain God.

_das avatarke dag dage. bhulya sab sansar ||_
_ko ek ugare jeevana. jine guru mukh kiyo vichar ||30||_

(Meaning: Because of confusion over which of God's ten incarnations to worship, all the people of the world fell into confusion and error. But those who received true understanding from a guru and, understanding the true essence of God, engaged in devotion to Him, were saved.)

For those who fall into confusion over which of these ten incarnations to worship, the Parchari (biography) of Krishnadas says:

_kaustubh mani mukh morli, sundar shyam sharir ||_
_so nanddware jeevana, je dashrath kul badvir ||29||_

(Meaning: He who wears the Kaustubh jewel and holds the flute at His mouth, whose body is beautifully dark-hued, that very One who became a great hero born in Dashrath's lineage, sports in Nanda's court as Krishna.)

_ehi roop hirdeme dharo, ehi naam rasana uchaaro ||_
_inki chhaya moorat karahi, sab koi moortakun anusarahi ||_
_mool chhand chhayakun dhyave, aad roop bisar hi jave ||_
_aad roop hirdemein dharo, taako naam rasana uchaaro ||_
_ese tokun kahi nishani, aur baat kahun man mani ||_
_kou machharoopku dhyave, koo kachhapkun batave ||_
_koo seetakun man lave, koo ram lakshman gun gave ||_
_koo radhe radhe karahi, koo girdhari chit dharahi ||_
_hamare ram krishna do nama, guru kripaye sarahi kaama ||_
(Krishnadas Parchari)

(Meaning: Hold this form of Ram-Krishna, adorned with the Kaustubh jewel and the flute, within your heart, and chant only His name with your tongue. But people make idols of His shadow-illusion form, and everyone follows these idols in devotion — leaving God's original form and worshipping His shadow-maya, the form of an incarnation, thereby forgetting God's original form. But we should keep only God's primal original form within our hearts and utter and worship His name with the tongue. Thus I have explained to you the sign of God's true form as against His maya-shadow form; but let me also speak of those who worship God according to their own mind's fancy, imagining various invented forms. In their minds some worship the form of the Fish incarnation, some regard the Tortoise incarnation as their object of worship, while others keep Sita in mind, and some sing the praises of Ram and Lakshman in devotion. Still others worship by chanting "Radhe Radhe," while others mentally worship the form of Girdhari Krishna, the lifter of Govardhan. But truly, for us, only these two names — Ram and Krishna — are worthy of worship; by the guru's grace, remembering and reciting this name will accomplish the work of crossing the ocean of worldly existence — not the worship of His various other forms.)

_avatar apradhi kahe jeevana. jaake nahi guru pir ||_
_aadi ant madhya shyamalo. nirgun brahma sharir ||31||_

Pir-Samarth — one who has not found a capable guru mistakes the incarnations for God and goes astray, taking the incarnation itself to be God. But before, during, and after any incarnation, the dark-complexioned Krishna Himself is present in every state. He, the Supreme Being, alone is real; but deluded, offending people take even this Ram-Krishna to be among these ten incarnations. Yet this Ram-Krishna, before these incarnations occur, during the incarnation, and after the incarnation, remains without any change whatsoever, exactly as He is, in His own original form. Therefore this Ram-Krishna must be counted apart from — excluded from — the Ram-Krishna figures found among these ten incarnations. They should be recognized not by form but by name.

The world, which is not guided by a guru, has fallen into confusion over talk of incarnations, and such a worldly soul does not cross over; only the one guided by a guru, who places faith in the guru's words, crosses over.

_nagara mil baatan kare. kahe ram krishna avatar ||_
_aur gaali kaha jeevana. dhik taako parivar ||32||_

(Meaning: Worthless, deceitful people gather and talk among themselves, saying that Ram and Krishna are also merely incarnations, and that they themselves are Brahm. They ask: then why should Ram-Krishna not likewise be regarded as Parbrahma? The answer is that this Ram-Krishna is not Brahm merely by body, but is indeed Parbrahma in consciousness; and if one says Ram-Krishna is not Parbrahma, then Jivanji Maharaj says: what greater curse could be given to such people — their entire family is to be condemned, because Ram-Krishna is verily Parbrahma manifest, and therefore should not be counted among the ten incarnations.)

Those who have not taken a guru are called "guru-less" (nugra). They cannot recognize the true Name and Form, and so they come to regard the names Ram and Krishna as false talk about mere incarnations. This is a very great curse upon them. What worse insult could there be for them? Such an entire family is to be condemned.

"If one worships Ram and Krishna, the soul crosses over; of what use is it to remember and chant the mantra of other incarnations? Worship of other incarnations does not serve the purpose."

Meaning: If one worships Ram and Krishna, the soul crosses over. Ram and Krishna are not merely incarnated great persons, but are the very name of the formless, unblemished Parbrahma. That is: the Puranic scriptures contain various kinds of stories, in which, along with many incarnations, various mantras, vows, fasts, the greatness of holy places, and also various stories about the lives and deeds of different gods and goddesses are given. Moreover, not all the Puranas together lead to one single, fixed goal, nor is there a single agreed opinion among them. The Vishnu-based Puranas hold Vishnu to be the Lord of all; the Shiva-based Puranas hold Shiva so; the Devi Puranas hold Shakti or Devi worship so; and so on — thus there is no single agreed view among these various stories. Furthermore, what is the point of confusing ordinary people and keeping them far from truth through various mantras, tantras, and modes of worship? Thus Jivanji Maharaj, setting aside the fascinating stories of the incarnations and without entering into any dispute, suggests only the remembrance of the one Name and pure worship of Parbrahma with body and mind.

Thus, without considering all the other paths, one should proceed by only the one path. Jivanji Maharaj does not wish to engage in any scriptural debate on this subject, nor does he wish to trouble anyone who holds an opposing view. Rather, he wishes to find his own path from among all these and proceed along it. Those who have faith in the words of the guru should keep that faith and follow accordingly. Here, the conclusion or summary of the dialogue that took place between Guru Gopaldas and Jivanji Maharaj has been presented. The part that consisted of debate and dispute has not been included anywhere here. Because once the truth has been found, there is no purpose in dwelling on falsehood. Jivanji Maharaj obtained what he needed, so only that essential matter has been presented here, and that too has been stated very concisely. Rather than wasting time on useless talk, he has conveyed only the essential matter — words whose very utterance changes the dignity of the atmosphere, brings a wave of loving devotion, and gladdens the mind. Useless matters have not been told to the devotees; in a single sentence he said what needed to be said: that other incarnations did not serve the purpose — that is, one need not get involved with other incarnations or their stories, nor is it worth recalling them here. Having said this, concluding this discussion, he states a sakhi:

_ram krishna je jeevana. do sagun avatar ||_
_andh dhandh kaha bhaju. je ved na pave paar ||33||_

Parbrahma's two names, Ram and Krishna, are also given in the Puranas as the story of two incarnations with attributes (sagun). But one should not blindly plunge, eyes closed, into the illusion-shadowed, disordered other incarnations, because even the Vedas know nothing about Parbrahma — even they are ignorant of Him. Therefore one should not fall into the worship of any deity without proper understanding and reflection.

Here is a sakhi of Baba Kabirji:

_kabir saayi hamara ramji. jaaka dashrath baap ||_
_duniyakun dojakh diya. hamkun apna jaap ||34||_

_kabir bavan akshar teen lokman. unka sab vistar ||_
_unthi je uparant hai. so niranjan nirakar ||35||_

Meaning: Kabirji says that many people argue at length over the name of Ram. Such learned people remain absorbed only in disputation and thereby suffer — that is, they fall into hell. But for us, it is one name of Parbrahma, which we recite in remembrance.

The maya of Brahma pervades the fifty-two letters and all three worlds, and deluded people worship this, thinking it to be Parbrahma. But beyond that — that is, beyond maya — is the formless, unblemished Parbrahma.

God's ten incarnations are counted, but among them we worship only Ram and Krishna. Moreover, if for some separate fancy one remembers, worships, or chants the mantra of another incarnation, it is of no use — other incarnations do not serve the purpose, that is, they are of no use in crossing the ocean of existence. In keeping with this, Jivanji Maharaj states this sakhi: that Ram and Krishna are the two manifest, embodied forms of God with attributes. All the other incarnations are disordered and illusory, through which one cannot gain a true realization of God as He really is; therefore Jivanji Maharaj declares those other incarnations to be avoided. But the two principal incarnations, Ram and Krishna, are the exact, fitting, complete Purushottam form of God. Therefore worship of them brings well-being. Moreover, these attribute-bearing incarnations should not be regarded as equal to the other incarnations, because even these incarnations of Ram and Krishna carry God's shadow (maya) — whereas the form of Ram and Krishna, though possessing attributes, is beyond maya. In support of this view, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj presents the 19th sakhi of Kabirji's Das Ang, saying:

_saayi hamaara raamji_ (a variant reading),

_thakur hamara ramji, jaaka dashrath baap_ — such statements might seem self-contradictory, but here Kabirji explains through the 14th sakhi of the Agadhko Ang that although the name of God taken in the three worlds is limited to the fifty-two letters of the alphabet, the name of Parbrahma is not bound by the limits of the letters of any alphabet. He is beyond even speech, unutterable by words — that formless, unblemished Supreme Being who is Ram-Krishna. Even though, in His attribute-bearing form, He may be called the son of a father like Dashrath, yet His true parentage, in the context of Ram, cannot actually be stated in words. The world knows Dashrath as the father of Ram; and this misleads worldly people about Ram. Because of this, taking Him to be merely the son of Dashrath, they go to hell.

Whether to count Ram and Krishna among the ten attribute-bearing, embodied incarnations, or to regard them as beyond these, is a point of confusion. Kabirji too, in his sakhis, has shown this very confusion and resolved it. This is worth understanding: Kabirji means to say that Ram has misled the world.

_nagar ayodhya rai tum, bhaye anek hi vaar ||_
_apni aadi bhulaviya, tum kaise keertaar ||30||_

Kabir says: You have become the king of Ayodhya city, called the Lord of Ayodhya, age after age, many times over, and you make the people of the world forget your true original form as the Supreme Being — what kind of Creator of the world are you, then?

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj says the same:

_guru kije vicharke, jehi batave ram ||_
_sarjutire jeevana, nagar ayodhya gaam ||31||_
_saayi hamaran ramji, jaake bharat shatrughna bhrat ||_
_shankarshan sang janaki, jeevan e jag taat ||32||_

Jivanji Maharaj says: You should choose as your guru, after careful consideration, one who shows you the true Ram — the Ram who lived on the banks of the river Saryu, in the town called Ayodhya.

Moreover, my object of worship is Ram, whose brothers are Bharat and Shatrughna, and who is accompanied by Lakshman and Sitaji — He is the father of the world.

_sadguru-e samjhaayo jeevana, tab bhayo man dheer ||_
_pay paayo deval phiro, tab yu kahi das kabir ||33||_

When the Sadguru explained the true understanding of devotion to such a Ram, my mind became assured that this is the same Ram who drank Namdev's milk and turned the temple around — so says Das Kabir. Meaning: this Ram directly drinks milk for His devotee and even turns the direction of a temple — such a capable ruler of the world is He. That very Ram, whom the people of the world regard as the Ram of Ayodhya on the banks of the Saryu, is the same Ram who, in Pandharpur, drank milk for a devotee like Namdev and turned the temple — showing that God can also take on a manifest, embodied form. This Ram possesses both name and form. That is why Kabir has said:

_kabir sagun to ek sant hai, nirgun naam aadhaar ||_
_nirgun sagunmein mil rahya, tab bhayo ek vichaar ||34||_

Kabirji says: God is with attributes (sagun) in the form of the saint, and without attributes (nirgun) on the basis of Name and Form. Thus, when the nirgun Name merges into the sagun saint whom the devotee worships, sagun and nirgun become one, and there is then no need to consider any distinction between nirgun and sagun.

Thus Kabir said that Ram, whose father is Dashrath, is his object of worship. Furthermore, Jivanji Maharaj firmly declared that Ram, on the banks of the Saryu, is together with Sita, and has Lakshman, Shatrughna, and Bharat as brothers. But the devotee can make the nirgun Ram into sagun and even make Him drink milk — so what is to be said of such a Ram? In this connection, Anantdas, in the Parchari of Ranka Vanka, has said:

_pay paayo deval phiro. bhakti na aayi tohe ||_
_sant poojare naamdev. jo miliya chaahe mohe ||35||_

You made Me drink milk, and for you I turned My temple, yet even so, you did not attain devotion to that God who is formless and without attributes. Therefore God says: if you wish to meet Me, serve the saints — do not seek Me in this idol. So He tells Namdev in the Ranka Vanka.

Kabirji has said that God is beyond the three gunas (qualities):

_kabir nugara nar sanse padya. suni nahi gurumukh baat ||_
_trigun ateet niradhaar hai. so dashrathsut raghuveer ||36||_

That Ram who is called the son of Dashrath is truly beyond the three gunas — this understanding, not having heard the guru's teaching, guru-less people failed to grasp; and so they fell into doubt, taking Him to merely be Dashrath's boy. Kabir says —

_raam naam sab kahat hai. so to naam ameer ||_
_ajar amar ek raam hai. vaaku jape kabir ||37||_

Everyone speaks the name of Ram as they please, in the ordinary way, but that name of Ram is filled with deep mystery. There is one Ram who is ageless and immortal — it is Him that Kabirji worships.

The Parchari of Krishnadas says:

_kabir saacha sadguru jab mile. to sat bataave raam ||_
_sarju teere khelke. aayo gokul gaam ||38||_

If one finds a Sadguru who explains the true Ram, he will show how to worship the true Ram — the Ram who sported on the banks of the Saryu at Ayodhya and who came as Krishna in Gokul. This means there is no distinction between Krishna and Ram. If one obtains a guru who has this correct understanding, he will make it clear to us that there is no difference between Ram and Krishna. Only a true Sadguru gives the understanding that Ram and Krishna are the manifest form of Parbrahma — not that he says they are merely incarnations. Jivanji Maharaj says —

_sadguru-e samjhaayo jeevana. gupt pragat je baat ||_
_ek roop ghat ghat base. ek seetapati raghunath ||39||_
(Gurudev 40)

The Sadguru has made clear the true reality of Ram — that Ram who exists manifest with attributes, or who remains hidden, formless. In one form Ram pervades every heart, and in one form Ram remains as the husband of Sita. In the Vicharak Ang, Kabir says:

_kabir raam raam sabko kahe. taame bohot vichaar ||_
_sohi raam sati saadhu kahe. sohi kautuk haar ||40||_

Everyone says "Ram, Ram," but there is a great deal to consider in how it is said. Behold — one, by uttering the name Ram, rises to sainthood, while another who merely watches this Ram as a spectacle calls it a mere show.

_kabir bhaand bhavaai dugaliya. sabko kahe raam ||_
_satnaam jaanya vina. kis vidh sare kaam ||41||_

Bards, minstrels, folk-actors, and jugglers — all of them say "Ram, Ram." But without knowing the true Name, how can their purpose be accomplished? How can they attain liberation?

_kabir ek raam dashrath ghar dole. ek raam sab ghatmein baale ||_
_ek raamka sakal pasaara. ek raam tinguNse nyaara ||42||_

One Ram wanders in Dashrath's house; a second speaks within every heart; a third Ram's expanse pervades everything; a fourth Ram is entirely apart from the three gunas.

_kabir kaun raam dashrath ghar dole. kaun raam ghatghatmein bole ||_
_kaun raamka saphal pasaara. kaun raam tinguNse nyaara ||43||_

Which Ram wanders in Dashrath's house? And which Ram speaks in every heart? And which Ram pervades everything? And which Ram is apart from the three gunas?

_aakaar raam dashrath ghar dole. niraakaar ghatghatmein bole ||_
_niranjan raamka sakal pasaara. niraalamb raam sabhise nyaara ||44||_

The embodied Ram wanders in Dashrath's house; the formless one, as the breath-form soul, speaks in every heart; the point-like unblemished Ram extends everywhere; and the unsupported, pure-consciousness Ram is apart from all.

Thus Ram is described in four ways, but in the end a single conclusion is given for all:

_kabir sohi raam sab ghatme bole. sohi raam dashrath ghar dole ||_
_sohi raamka sakal pasaara. sohi raam sabhise nyaara ||45||_

Though Ram is spoken of in four ways, it is this one and the same Ram who speaks in every heart, and it is this same Ram who wanders in Dashrath's house; likewise it is this same Ram who pervades everything, and this same Ram who is apart from all.

_kabir suno bhaai saadho. nij naamke e chaaro ||_
_chotha raam sada avinaashi. kahe kabir vichaar ||46||_

Listen, O saints — these four are the names of one's own self; among them, the fourth kind of Ram is eternally imperishable — so says Kabir, having reflected and understood.

_kabir saahab mera ek hai. dooja kaha na jaay ||_
_dooja saahab jo kahu. saahab khara risaay ||47||_

My Lord, my object of worship, is one alone; it cannot be said that there is a second Lord. And if I say there is a second Lord, the true Lord would be displeased, and I would lose His true devotion. Further, in the Bijak, in verse ("shabda") 30 — or 26 — it is said:

_bhai re dui jagdeesh kahaanse aaya, kahu kavne bauraaya ||_

Sadguru Kabir says: O brother, from where have two Lords of the universe come? Tell me — who has driven you into such delusion?

_kabir saahab sabka baap hai. beta kisika naahi ||_
_beta hokar avatare. so to saahab naahi ||48||_

God is the father of all; He is no one's son. If He were to be born incarnate as a son, then He would not be the true Lord.

In our lives we jokingly ask small children whose child they are — their father's or their mother's. In truth, a son does not belong exclusively to either the father or the mother. In the same way, then, how is it proper to call a God like Ram the son of Dashrath? In fact, the intent of saying "Dashrath" is that the one whom people take to be the son of Dashrath is actually the wondrous, playful Ram of God. Therefore, one should not fall into confusion, taking "whose father is Dashrath" to mean an ordinary incarnate Ram.

_nij karta avatar dharat nahi. mrityu lokke chole ||_
_jinka karta sakal kul hovat. so to kyu ghar ghar dole ||49||_

Meaning: God Himself, the Creator of the universe, having taken an incarnation in a body in the mortal world, is the Creator of the entire creation — why, then, should He wander from house to house, from birth to birth?

Now let us explain the qualities and pastimes (leela) of Ram and Krishna that have been spoken of. That is, let us here explain in detail the pastimes described in the great Bhagavat Purana.

_kab raghupati kab jadupati. bhagat het avatar ||_
_bemukh nav samjhe jeevana. e sab ekaakaar ||36||_
_dhanurvidya raghupati padhe. morli dhari jadunath ||_
_lankeshwar maarya jeevana. giri dharya ve haath ||37||_

Meaning: Sometimes as Raghupati King Ram, sometimes as Yadupati Shri Krishna — He took birth for the sake of His devotees. But those turned away from Him, the faithless, do not understand that both these forms belong to one and the same Supreme Being.

King Ram studied the art of archery and bore that weapon, while Shri Krishna bore the flute. With the very same hands with which Parbrahma slew Ravana, the lord of Lanka, He also lifted Mount Govardhan. That is, in terms of embodied form, these two incarnations are different, but for the devotee who sees the formless, attributeless reality, there is no difference or wonder in this — it is merely Parbrahma's action, His leela (divine play). This is merely Parbrahma's "play." Kabirji says —

In Raag Kalyan (Bhairav):

_raghupati jadupati ki bal jaau, de dhare payo hari naanu ||_
_raghupati vanme kino vaas, jadupati mathura nagar nivaas ||tek||_
_raghupati vaanar rinch milai, jadupati gopi gwal khelai ||_
_raghupati charne ahalya taari, jadupati kubja adhik sohai ||1||_
_raghupati shaayar paaj bandhai, jadupati govardhan kar dhaari ||_
_raghupati raavan maar liyo, jadupati kans nikandan kiyo ||2||_
_raghupati raaj bibhishan diyo, jadupati ugrasenkun raaj diyo ||_
_raghupati jadupati ek sharira, het kari gaave das kabira ||3||_

Kabirji says: I offer myself to Raghupati and Jadupati (Ram and Krishna); taking on a body, they bore these two names, Ram and Krishna, and through both forms they performed, in nearly the same way, the work of creation. Raghupati dwelt in the forest, Jadupati dwelt in the city of Mathura. Raghupati gathered together monkeys and bears, Jadupati sported with the gopis and cowherds. Raghupati redeemed Ahalya at His feet, Jadupati was greatly adorned with Kubja. Raghupati had a bridge built across the ocean, Jadupati lifted Govardhan in His hand. Raghupati slew Ravana, Jadupati destroyed Kansa. Raghupati gave the kingdom to Vibhishan, Jadupati gave the kingdom to Ugrasen. Raghupati and Jadupati are one and the same body — with love, Das Kabir sings of them.

Related to this pada of Kabirji, a pada of Parashuram expressing the oneness of Ram and Krishna has been given in the Samagam. In this pada, the non-difference between Krishna and Ram is shown. When Tulsidas went to the place named Gyan Gudri, at the temple of Madan Gopal, Shri Krishna was adorned — with the flute, with the staff, with the peacock-feather crown upon His head, with the garland worn on His chest, and standing close to Radhaji, the stealer of hearts — such was the threefold-bending (tribhangi) image that shone there. One day, as Tulsidasji was preparing to prostrate himself, a worshipper of Krishna recited to him this doha of Parashuram:

_apne apne ishtako naman karai sab koi ||_
_isht viheene parashuram namai so moorakh hoi ||50||_

Everyone bows to their own chosen deity. But Parashuram says: whoever bows to someone other than his chosen deity is a fool.

So Tulsidas grew alarmed, and in response he says:

_parashuraamke vachan suni maanat hiye hulaas ||_
_seetaravan samaarike bole tulsidas ||51||_

Hearing these words of Parashuram's sakhi, and bringing joy to his heart, Tulsidas, holding fast in his mind to Sita's Lord (Ram), spoke these words.

_kaha kahau chhabi aajki bhale bane ho naath ||_
_tulsi mastak jab navai dharo dhanush shar haath ||52||_

O Lord! What can I say of today's beauty — you look very handsome indeed. But Tulsidas will only bow his head to you when you take up the bow and arrow in your hand.

_mor mugat neeche dharo. kanakmugat dharo sees ||_
_dhanushbaan kar dharo. tab tulsi name sees ||53||_

Set aside the peacock-feather crown, wear the golden crown on your head, take up bow and arrow in your hand — then Tulsidas will bow his head to you.

_tulsi teri tekkun. dhan kahat raghunath ||_
_dhanush baan jab kare dharo. tab tulsi naayo maath ||54||_

The Lord says: Tulsidas, blessed be your steadfastness. When the Lord took up the bow and arrow, Tulsidas bowed his head.

_murli lakut duraaikai. dharyo dhanush shar haath ||_
_tulsi lakhi ruchi daaski. naath bhaye raghunath ||55||_

Setting aside the flute and the staff, He took up the bow and arrow in His hand. Thus, understanding and honoring the wish of His devotee Tulsidas, Lord Krishna took on the form of Ram.

_kit murli kit chandrika, kit gopiyanke saath ||_
_apne janke kaarane, krishna bhaye raghunath ||56||_

Where is Krishna's flute, where the peacock-crown's moonlight, where His sporting with the gopis — for the sake of His own devotee, Krishna became Raghunath (Ram). Writing Tulsidas's life story, Veni Madhavdas has written thus:

_vipra naabha sahit hari darshanke het._
_gaye gusaai mudit man mohanmadan niket ||1||_
_raam upaasak jaani prabhu turat dhare dhanu baan ||_
_darshan diye sanaath kiye, bhakt vachhal bhagvaan ||2||_

Tulsidas, along with the Brahmin Nabha, went joyfully with delight in his heart to have darshan of Hari at the beautiful abode of the enchanting Madan Gopal. Then, recognizing him as a worshipper of Ram, the Lord immediately took up the bow and arrow, gave him His darshan, made him feel cared for, and thus the Lord, who is affectionate to His devotees, fulfilled him.

About this incident of Tulsidas, Revered Yadunath Maharaj writes: devotion cannot happen without insistence (a steadfast, persistent devotion). Jivanji Maharaj has shown this kind of insistent devotion in the community of devotees. This insistence has another name — every name of God is good, but you have been given the guru-bestowed name Ramkabir. Just as, for a newborn child, whatever milk suits it from its own mother, no other milk suits it so well. There are shlokas concerning this Ram-Krishna:

_na nandasuno prithagasti raamo na raamato vaa vasudevasunuh ||_
_tathaapyayodhyapurpaalabaale, salakshmane dhaavati me manisha ||19||_

Krishna, the son of Nanda, is not separate from Ram, nor is Ram separate from Vasudev's son Krishna; and yet my mind runs also toward the child protector of the city of Ayodhya, together with Lakshman.

_tatha kaushalaakhye pure raamachandrastatha mathuraakhye yashodaakishorah ||_
_dvayoraikata naiva bhedo vidheyo madeeya manisha yashodaakishore ||20||_

In the same way, Ramchandra of the city called Kaushala, and Yashoda's youthful son of the city called Mathura — there is no distinction between the two, my mind holds; this is what my intellect says regarding Yashoda's son.

Agradas made this bow-bearing Krishna take up the flute again, and at that time the devotee fell at His feet — such is the tribhangi image. Kabirji has said an extraordinary thing —

_kabir kaha kahu chhabi aajki, mein dekhe nandkumaar ||_
_dadhisutaasut upare, saamvadani sang naar ||57||_

Meaning: If one looks at their forms, the two are indeed different, and their deeds are different, but the formless, unblemished Parbrahma is only one. There is no difference between the two, because for a devotee of Parbrahma, there is no distinction such as embodied versus formless — such a devotee does not enter into any dispute. One who is beyond all dispute is truly called a devotee. Furthermore, Kabirji says at the end that Das Kabir only sings Hari's virtues — the supreme duty of a devotee is only to sing the praises of Hari, not to engage in dispute.

_madan gopal hamare shreeraam._
_madan gopal hamare shree raam ||1||_
_itahi dhanush it bimal ben kar ||_
_peetbasan aru tan ghan shyaam ||teka||_
_apni bhuja jene jalnidhi baandhyo ||_
_raas nachaavyo kotik kaam ||_
_tab raghuvar ab jaduvar mohan ||_
_leela lalit bimal sukh dhaam ||_
_bhed rahit das premaanand ||_
_nij jan mali gaaye gun gaan ||_

Meaning: The composer of this pada is the devotee Shri Parmanand (Premanandji). He was a staunch Ramanandi Vaishnav. Once he went to Gokul, and there, early in the morning at the time of the mangal aarti, he came to the palace (temple) of Shri Krishna, the lord of Govardhan. There, the servants (priests) who were present called out and said, "Open the doors of Shri Ramji, it is the time for the mangal aarti."

Then the servants said: "O Parmanandji! Your Ramji lives in Ayodhya — here it is the palace of Madan Gopalji."

Hearing these words, Parmanandji sang the above pada — that to him, there is unity between Ramji and Madan Gopal; there is no distinction for him, no duality here — both are but two different names of the same non-dual form. In truth, both are two different forms of the one Parbrahma, who takes on whatever form is desired and grants darshan accordingly. Parmanand says: without distinction, we sing His virtues together with our own fellow devotees. Thus there is no difference between Ram and Krishna.

Further, Parmanandji says that Parbrahma's leela is truly infinite; it has no end, and moreover, His names too are without end. Thus, understanding Ram and Krishna to be without difference, one should sing the praises of the one Parbrahma alone.

Kabirji too has sung of this very union of Ram-Krishna as the Supreme Lord. Here, explaining the unity of the two forms, Jivanji Maharaj says:

_doi baraabar jeevana. bhagataraaj ranadheer ||_
_kaashi vaasi kabeerji. sarayu teer raghuveer ||38||_
_doi baraabar jeevana. bhagataraaj bhagat bheer ||_
_taat paavan kiyo raghupati. yahaan raamaanand kabeer ||39||_
_saraguN raghupati jeevana. nirguN daas kabeer ||_
_o vishvakun poshataa. o guN bhanjan shareer ||40||_
_prem roop kabeerji. aatam raghupati naam ||_
_jan taravekun jeevana. kali kiyo vishraam ||41||_
_raam svaroopi naam hai. naam svaroopi sant ||_
_kali kaalmaan jeevana. bhajavekun do meet ||42||_
_niravaasik je jeevana. harijan taaka naam ||_
_sarag narak vaikunth taj. je samare seetaraam ||43||_
_nihakaami niramal dasaa. pakade chaarau khoont ||_
_kahe kabeer taa daaski. aash kare vaikunth ||44||_
_sant darashankun jeevana. aas kare vaikunth ||_
_vaikunth baparekee kahaa chali. jo vaanchhe kamalaakanth ||45||_

Meaning: "Doi barabar" means one plus one equals two, and yet equals one: Kabir plus Ram equals one "Ramkabir." Kabirji of Kashi and Ram of the Saryu banks are one and the same. Between these two there is no difference.

Kabir and Ram share much in common. Both are among the foremost of devotees. Both remove the sufferings of their devotees. Through the second, Ram, Dashrath's name became illustrious; while through Kabirji, Ramanand gained even greater fame. Both Dashrath and Ramanand were already renowned through their own deeds, but through Ram and Kabir respectively they became worthy of even greater praise.

Through a son like Ram, a father like Dashrath was made sacred; and through a disciple like Kabir, a sannyasi guru like Ramanand was made illustrious.

Ram is the sustainer and nurturer of the world; therefore Ram fulfills the needs of the world, and so He is called sagun — Ram, being endowed with the three gunas beginning with sattva, is sagun. Kabirji, on the other hand, is beyond the three gunas; he is without any modification, and therefore beyond the gunas — hence Kabir is nirgun. And though dwelling in a body, he has no identification with the body. Thus Ram is sagun and Kabir is nirgun.

Revered Yadunath Maharaj writes that Kabirji is the very image of love, in whom shines the name of God. In the sakhis of Name and Form, Kabir is described as follows:

Baba Kabirji is the very image of love; he moves and acts through the power of the Merciful Lord. If the soul is present, the body rises and stands; and if there were no body, who would sustain the soul?

Therefore, "Vaishnavjan" is the form, and Shri Krishna is the name — thus Kabirji is the form of love, and the name of Ram is the soul that dwells within Kabir. Kabirji has come before us for the very purpose of ferrying across the devotees of this Kali Yuga.

The Name has the form of Ram, and the saint has the form of the Name. In this age of Kali, Jivanji Maharaj advises that taking refuge in this matter of Name and Form alone brings true well-being.

Baba Kabirji says: whichever devotee performs devotion with a desireless attitude, whose mind's state is pure, free from any kind of sin, and who, in every way, holds fast only to the support of God — then even the abode of Vaikunth longs for and waits for such a devotee, hoping that he will one day come to that abode.

Raghupati (Ram) is called sagun, while Kabirji is called nirgun — why? Both are the names of incarnate persons. Though the body, composed of the three gunas, is perishable, Kabirji's nirgun speech is immortal. Thus, holding the nirgun doctrine, Jivanji Maharaj has called Kabirji nirgun, while Ram, the ideal man (Maryada Purushottam), has been called sagun.

The essence of devotion that exists in this world is loving, and it pervades everywhere; this is Kabirji's own quality. Even in the sharpness of his words there is love and compassion for people. And the soul dwelling within the body is a portion separated from Parbrahma; therefore it has been called of the nature of Raghupati (Lord Ram). Because of Kabirji's influence, the deceitful goings-on that were current in Kashi slowed down, and an atmosphere of devotion spread everywhere.

The form of Parbrahma that the scriptures and Puranas describe under the Name "Ram" has, in this Kali Yuga, manifested in the form of Kabir. That is why, for remembrance of the Name in worship, the name "Ramkabir" has been given.

The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad speaks, in connection with the gods, of one who is "nirvasik" -- meaning one who, while dwelling in a place of shelter, drives away craving. The gods dwell dependent on human beings, living off what is given to them without earning it. One who, while dwelling in such shelter, drives away craving and worships only Parbrahma -- that one alone is a Harijan (a person of Hari). Such are those who give up every hope and craving and worship only the one Parbrahma, who do not even wish for heaven or hell.

Saints and holy ones (sadhu-sant) are always pure and unique; the influence of their love spreads to the four corners of the world. Naturally everyone longs for the darshan of such a saint, but even the darshan of their servants (das) is a matter of great fortune -- so much so that even Vaikunth desires the darshan of such servants.

Even Vaikunth longs for the darshan of a saint, and the Lord of Lakshmi Himself holds the very same longing -- so what then to say of poor, helpless Vaikunth? Jasvantji has told, in his kirtan (hymn), what this Kamalakanth Parbrahma (the Lord of Kamala, i.e. Vishnu) desires.

_Hamaro das basat hai jaanhi |_
_Lakshman sahit sameep Janki | me joon basatahun taanhi ||1||_
_Jab mero keval jan sove tab nikat nisa me jaagu ||_
_Jab mero jan uth chale | tab dor dor sang laagu ||2||_
_Jab mero jan uvate chale | tab kar grahi baat bataau ||_
_Apne pitambar-ki karu chhaanh | ham jab tab sang rahun ||3||_
_Mope ber kare me sahun | mere jan-ku sahyo nav jaai ||_
_Bal bal vaani shri mukh keri | jan Jasvante gaai ||4||_

(Wherever My devotee dwells, there I remain, together with Lakshman and Janki nearby. ||1|| When My true devotee is asleep, I stay awake close by him in the night; when he rises and sets out, I run along close beside him. ||2|| When My devotee strays from the path, I take his hand and show him the way; I hold the shade of My own yellow garment over him -- I remain with him at all times. ||3|| If someone bears enmity toward Me, I bear with it, but I cannot bear anyone wronging My devotee. Blessed, blessed is this speech from the Lord's own mouth, sung by devotee Jasvant. ||4||)

This is Jasvantji's testimony (sakhi) verse. Parbrahma says: wherever My devotee dwells, there I remain together with Lakshman and Sitaji; when he falls asleep, I stay awake near him; when he rises and sets about his work, I remain with him; and if he goes astray or does something wrong, I show him the way as well. And if someone bears enmity toward Me, I bear it, but I cannot bear any offense against My devotee. It is for this very reason that Parbrahma has been called Bhaktavatsal, one who loves his devotees dearly. This verse was sung by Jasvantji, and Jaydevji bears witness to it -- a saying from the Ashtapadi Gita Govinda.

_Patati patre vichalati patre shankita bhavad-upayaanam |_
_Rachayati shayanam sachakita-nayanam pashyati tava panthaanam ||_
_Dheer sameere Yamuna-teere vasati vane Vanamaali ||29||_
(Gita Govinda 5-11-3)

(When a leaf falls, when a leaf stirs, she suspects it is Your arrival; with startled eyes she prepares the bed and watches for Your path. By the calm-breezed banks of the Yamuna, Vanamali dwells in the grove.)

Purport (bhavarth): Shri Krishna, for the joy of union, has gone to the trysting place; His beauty is supreme, like that of ten million Kandarps (Cupids). Such is Shri Krishna, seated on the banks of the Yamuna, where a gentle, fragrant breeze is blowing.

Made eager at the very hint of Radha's name, He plays the flute in a sweet tone; He even loves the dust flying on the breeze that has touched your (Radha's) body. Krishna, so eager for Radha's arrival, watches your path on every side -- if a bird stirs on one side, or leaves fall from the trees, Krishna looks all around for your path, and prepares a bed of leaves for you. Just as eagerly as Shri Krishna waits for Radha, with that same eagerness the Lord remains eager to look after His devotee, wherever he may dwell. Finally...

In the Mahabharata there is an episode: once Durvasa, together with his community of disciples, became a guest of Duryodhan. After enjoying full hospitality there, when the pleased Durvasa told the king to ask for whatever boon he desired, Duryodhan -- seeing that everything had gone exactly according to plan -- said to the sage, as pre-arranged: just as you are pleased with me, show that same grace to my elder brother Yudhishthir also, and go to him at an inopportune time to receive his hospitality.

Duryodhan began to feel pleased at the thought that the Pandavas, living in poverty in the forest, would fail to honor the sage properly and would thus be cursed by Durvasa, and his own purpose would be accomplished. Hearing Duryodhan's words, Durvasa set out at once to meet the Pandavas; arriving at an inopportune time, he expressed a wish for a meal, and came to the riverbank together with his community of disciples to bathe.

Meanwhile Draupadi grew greatly distressed -- there was not a single grain of food left in the house -- and what if the sage were not pleased? What a disaster that would be! In this distress, Draupadi remembered Krishna, her companion in times of crisis. Hearing his sister's call, Krishna arrived at once. Learning of her distress, through His unfailing power He easily took away the hunger of Durvasa and his whole community of disciples, and they began to feel fully satisfied -- so much so that everyone felt not a single grain of food could enter their stomachs any longer. Durvasa began to lament that he had made Draupadi cook food for nothing; since no more food could now be eaten, her cooking would go to waste -- and if that happened, the Pandavas would burn them to ashes.

_Vritha paakena raajarsher-aparaadh: kritoo mahaan ||_
_Maa smaana-dhaakshur drishtaiva Paandavaah kroor-chakshushaa ||21||_
_Smritvaanu-bhaavam raajarsher-Ambarishasya dheemata: ||_
_Bibhemi sutaraam vipraa Hari-paadaashrayaaj-janaat ||22||_
_Kruddhaas-te nirdaheyur-vai toola-raashim-ivaanala: ||_
_Tata etaan prishtvaiva shishyaah shighram palaayata ||23||_

(Truly, by having food cooked needlessly, without hunger, we have committed a great offense against the royal sage Yudhishthir. Let it not happen that the Pandavas turn a fierce gaze on us and burn us to ashes! O brahmins, remembering the power of the supremely wise King Ambarish, I remain truly afraid of such devotees as have taken refuge at the feet of Lord Hari. If the Pandavas grow angry, they can burn us to ashes in the same way fire burns a heap of hay. So, O disciples, let us flee from here at once, without even asking the Pandavas.)

Truly, by having food cooked needlessly (without hunger), we have committed a great offense against the royal sage Yudhishthir; let it not happen that the Pandavas look on us with a fierce gaze and burn us to ashes! O brahmins, remembering the power of the supremely wise King Ambarish, I truly remain afraid of such devotees, who have taken refuge at the feet of Lord Shri Hari. If the Pandavas fall into anger, they can burn us to ashes in that very way -- as one might set fire to a heap of hay. So, O disciples, let us flee from here at once, without even asking the Pandavas.

In this way Durvasa, having grown frightened, left from there without meeting the Pandavas. Sahadev wandered far and wide searching for him, but could find no trace of him anywhere, until some ascetics related to him the account as told above. Then Krishna, consoling the Pandavas, says --

_Dharma-nityaastu ye kechin-na te seedanti karhichit ||24||_

(Those who are ever devoted to dharma, who remain righteous, never fall into distress.)

Looking at this chapter as a whole, Jivanji Maharaj has drawn our attention to many matters, and has also expounded some points at length. If we look at the main subject, it is this: "Morli Manohar Parmeshwar te khara" (He alone is truly the flute-charming Supreme Lord). On this subject Jivanji Maharaj has, in a very simple way, clearly stated whom to worship, how to worship, and whom to accept as Parbrahma, and why. Here he has shown the true identity of Parbrahma, and has also shown the unity of form between Ram and Krishna. At the same time, he has brought together Akar (form) and Nirakar (formlessness). This matter of Akar-Nirakar had already been discussed earlier in a separate chapter, but here it has been explained again, still more clearly. And he has given the clear instruction that, rising above the debates that go on over Sagun and Nirgun, we should recognize and worship our own Parmeshwar.

The second important point is avatarvad, the doctrine of incarnation. On this question Jivanji Maharaj's stance is entirely clear. Without being drawn by worldly thinking, and remaining above worldly or material desire, he speaks only of devotion to Parmeshwar -- and that too, pure devotion free of any expectation or aspiration, and free of any kind of bondage. He has also, indirectly, indicated in this chapter that devotees of God should not fall into any false debates, for the bond among devotees is one of love. Devotees are bound by the thread of love, not of argument; there can never be any difference of opinion among devotees -- devotees are joined heart to heart through feeling and love. He has shown this point in particular through the example of Rankaji and Vankaji. This is a beautiful illustration of what kind of thread of devotion should exist between two differing positions. Further, staying apart from the many avatars, gods and goddesses, and the various paths, mantras and vows of worship, and instead worshipping the one Parbrahma alone with pure body and mind, living the same simple life as the devotees who have gone before in this world -- this is how the task entrusted by God is to be carried through. On this point too Jivanji Maharaj has left no room for lengthy debate; he has further endorsed it through Kabirji's sakhis, explaining it in a still simpler way. The devotees of Jivanji Maharaj now have only to follow accordingly.

The third point -- small, but important -- is nitya-sada vasant, the ever-present, eternal spring. In very few words Jivanji Maharaj has said a great deal here. Vasant (spring) means joy and celebration, the exchange of love; for devotees, the season of shishir -- that is, autumn's decline -- never comes; it is ever joy and only joy, because there is no obstacle on the path of devotion; here there is no need for scriptural knowledge or great scholarship. A devotee may be without even literacy, while a learned pandit remains weighed down under the burden of his own knowledge, entangled in the web of the scriptures. The knowledgeable one must keep changing his knowledge with each season; and further, just as a sword must be kept clean so that it does not rust, knowledge too must be kept sharp -- whereas devotion gathers no such rust at all. Vasant is the symbol of devotion; it is also the very best time for worship (upasana).

With the example of King Ambarish, Jivanji Maharaj proves Parbrahma's tender love for his devotees. Devotees should worship Shri Hari without any fear. Parbrahma is always ready to protect his devotees -- this we have already seen earlier, so there is no need to speak of it again here.

Finally, Jivanji Maharaj speaks of the oneness between Kabirji and Parbrahma. Their two names are different, their forms are different, yet there is no difference at all between the two -- here he has spoken of this "difference that is without difference." He has shown Kabirji's identity with Parbrahma, presenting here the union of the soul with Parbrahma. In the end, he brings this to completion by showing the unbroken bond between Shri Krishna and Radhika -- she who has stolen his mind, whom he searches for restlessly, his eyes startled, looking about him on every side in doubt for her. Finally, let us take in one sakhi of Kabirji.

_Man mera nirmal bhaya | jaise chokha nir ||_
_Pichhe pichhe Hari phirat | kahat Kabir Kabir ||58||_

(My mind has become pure, like clear water; behind me, behind me, Hari wanders, calling out "Kabir, Kabir.")

That is, Kabirji says: I do not go about following behind God -- rather, God goes about behind me, calling out my own name, "Kabir, Kabir."

That is to say: for one whose mind has become wholly devoted to God, nothing like a separate self or a separate world remains any longer -- and God Himself takes care of such devotees of His.

That is why Kripanath had to go there — for the Word itself is God.

Now the question of who Kripanath is need not detain us here, for the two preceding chapters have already discussed this at length. This chapter opens with these very words. Looking at them, a question arises: where did Kripanath have to go, and why did he have to go? We have earlier called Kripanath one who loves His devotees (bhakta-vatsal). Such a devotee-loving Parbrahm must go to many places, because although He is free of all bondage, He allows Himself to be bound by His own devotees. He commands the five elements and the three gunas and yet is free of them; He acts, yet remains untouched by action; nothing at all touches Him; He has no birth, no old age, no death, no decay — imperishable (akshay), beyond the senses (agochar) is this Parbrahm, whom Jaidevji has sung of, whom Adhyaruji has sung of. But such a devotee-devoted Parbrahm — who can make Him known? We have already spoken of His form (swarup); it is only through that form that He can be recognised. Just as a traveller on an unfamiliar road repeatedly asks his way of a guide, and, led and inspired by such a guide, advances toward his true destination, so too does the one advancing on the path of spiritual devotion move forward with the support of the Sadguru, who is his guide. Only with the strength and support of the Guru — the Sadguru — can Parbrahm be known. On the soil of India the saints and great souls have shown the immense glory of the Guru-disciple bond. Devotees such as Kabir, Mira, and Narsinh, among others, have likewise described this Guru-disciple relationship at length. Since that subject is to be taken up in later chapters, it is not discussed further here.

But here, at the very outset, the question was raised: what does it mean that God "had to go"? If we answer it, this is simply Parbrahm's own natural, fundamental disposition — that is, His quality (lakshan). He pervades everywhere, and although present everywhere at once, He remains, in a special sense, closer to His devotees. Again the question arises: if He is near, then in what way is He near? He is not visible. What, then, is He? And if He is far, then how far is He? We answer: Parbrahm cannot be seen through the medium of the body and the like, for He does not become perceptible through the body or any other such component medium. Nor is He, like every embodied soul, bound up in worldly cause and action; and yet He appears bound by the condition of embodiment (upadhi), in the same way that the world is bound by the discriminating intellect (bheda-buddhi). And through the use of words, that very same single reality is separated out and seen as many different things by this discriminating intellect. Take an example: in a pot, a water-vessel (kamandal), a tunnel, and the like, there is space — that is, a hollow — present within each. Yet ordinary embodied souls commonly call it ghatakash, that is, "the space (the hollow, the air) contained within the pot." In just this way, differences regarding God have arisen even within such relations. The Shwetashvatara Upanishad says—

_Na tasya karyam karanam cha vidyate, na tatsamashchabhyadhikashcha drashyate |_
_Parasya shaktirvividhaiva shruyate, swabhaviki gyanabalakriya cha ||1||_
(Shweta-3-11)

(He, the Ishwar, has no action, that is, no body, and no instrument, that is, no organ of sense; nor is there anyone equal to Him or greater than Him. But His supreme power is heard of through His manifold and varied works, and His activity is known through the power of knowledge, that is, His inherent understanding.)

_Apanipado javano grahita, pashyatyachakshuh sa shrunotyakarnah |_
_Sa vetti vedyam na cha tasyaasti vetta, tamahuragryam purusham mahantam ||2||_
(Shweta-3-11)

(Though without hands or feet, He grasps and holds, and He moves with swiftness; though without eyes He sees, though without ears He hears. He knows all that is to be known, yet none can know Him as He is known — and for this they call Him the foremost, the great, primordial Being.)

That is why we say: the Word itself is the Supreme — for it is only through the Guru's words that He can be known, that He can be recognised. The words spoken of here are the words of Kabirji, of Gopaldasji, and of Jivanji Maharaj. Thus the devotees who have become gurumukh (turned toward the Guru) should listen to the Guru's words with faith, and should receive them. They should not view them with a worldly eye, but with the eye of ultimate truth (paramarthik drishti) — for when seen with a worldly eye, discriminating intellect (bheda-buddhi) arises and truth cannot be understood. This same matter, pointed to earlier in the scriptures, Adhyaruji has expounded in plain and simple Gujarati, in the words of his kadvu (devotional canto).

_Chidanandam parabrahma dhyanagamyam sanatanam |_
_Aksharam nirmalam nityam nirakaram namamyaham ||3||_

(I bow to that Parbrahm, of the very nature of consciousness and bliss, attainable through meditation — the eternal, imperishable, stainless, everlasting, formless Parbrahm.)

_Sur muni antariksh stave re gokul, hari te ati re akal |_
_Hari hari rame re govind, anand bharyo e ||1||_
_Aapanape ramato pindara ramade, hari te rame ne ramade |_
_Harite jame ne jamade, harino gagan brahmadik vichar kare e ||2||_
_Akal ramat mandi gokul mahen, ramat brahmadik chahe |_
_Hari te aapanape ade na abhade e ||3||_

(The sage-gods dwelling in the heavens sing this hymn of praise about Gokul — how utterly inconceivable Hari is! Hari, Hari — Govind sports, ever filled with bliss. Sporting in His own being, He makes the embodied souls sport with Him too; He Himself plays and makes others play, He Himself feeds and makes others feed; even Brahma and the other gods can only wonder at Hari's vast, sky-like being. Having set this ungraspable play in motion within Gokul, Brahma and the other gods long to share in it — yet Hari, sporting in His own being, is never sullied or touched by any of it.)

The sage-gods who dwell in the heavens sing the praises of such a Being — one so inconceivable that none can grasp or recognise Him — that blissful Govind who is enacting all this "play," this "lila." And He draws us too into it. His play, His lila, has no end or limit; even Brahma and the other gods behold it with wonder and astonishment.

That is, one who has become gurumukh should reflect upon such words with patient endurance (titiksha). This play of Parbrahm the original world-teacher Shankaracharya has called "maya." Vallabhacharya has called it "lila." Adhyaruji calls it Parbrahm's "ramat" (sport, play). For as soon as the word "maya" is used, a discriminating intellect readily arises between the soul (atma) and the Supreme Soul (paramatma). Once such a distinction arises, the individual soul (jivatma) becomes separated. In truth the jivatma is bound, without distinction, to every one of Parbrahm's works, and is a co-participant in them. Further, in the term "lila," used by the earlier school (purvapaksha), the jivatma is set apart from Parbrahm, and the jivatma's place in Parbrahm's works becomes secondary. Parbrahm alone pervades everywhere and thereby creates the distinction. Moreover, in this the identity (tadatmya) of atma and paramatma comes to be forgotten, for Parbrahm alone becomes the principal doer, and once such supremacy is asserted, the identity is destroyed.

Here a doubt arises: on the path of worship, where exactly do words such as "maya" and "lila" become an obstruction? The answer may be given thus: those who surrender everything as "Krishnarpan" (an offering to Krishna) and live their whole lives in pure, desireless devotion have no need to know anything further or to perform any special action, for one who offers everything to Parbrahm and lives merely to sustain the body has, for himself, no place left at all for "the world" — and for him words like "maya" and "lila" become useless. And yet, what of those who have not yet become wholly absorbed and merged in Parbrahm, or those seeking devotees still eager to know more of dharma? For them, more must be said. Unlettered women devotees such as Harmaba, Kunvarbai, and Panabai placed complete faith and trust in the Guru's words and offered everything as Krishnarpan, and so crossed the ocean of worldly existence with ease. But for knowledgeable and inquiring seekers such as Gopaldas and Krishnadas, it must be explained at length. If we look here according to the Vedantic view, first comes Shankaracharya. His doctrine is: Brahm satya, jagat mithya, jivo brahmaivanaparah — that is, Brahm-Ishwar is true (satya), and the world — that is, maya — is false (mithya); the individual soul (jiva) is Brahm itself and nothing else. But then the question arises: if everything whatsoever is Brahm and nothing else exists, then why should "maya" be called false? Why should it stand apart from Brahm? Here this discriminating thought arises: if the jivatma itself is Brahm, then why could maya too not be called a form of that very Brahm? For this reason this doctrine cannot be established as fully complete.

Vallabhacharya, on the other hand, in place of the word "maya," used the word "lila," and further stated his own doctrine thus—

_Sarve khalvidam brahma neha nanaasti kinchana |_
_Brahma satyam, jaganmithya jivo brahmaivanaparah ||4||_

(All this indeed is Brahm; here there is no plurality whatsoever. Brahm is true, the world is not false, the jiva is Brahm itself and nothing else.)

Brahm is true, the world is not false, the jiva is Brahm itself — in this way he attempted to show a unity. Yet in order to make clear the relation between jiva, world, and Brahm, he too had to say that all this is merely Parbrahm's "lila." And for self-liberation, for "moksha," Brahm's grace (kripa) is needed; without His grace the jivatma cannot be uplifted — that is, cannot attain the movement toward liberation.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has given no sanction at all to words such as "lila," "moksha," "mukti," and has not thought it right to cast the world into the snare of such words. We, he says, are simply His creatures; we live with Him, we eat with Him, we sleep with Him, and thus, going about our worldly work, we remain just as He keeps us — for Shri Krishna says in the Bhagavad Gita—

_Yad yad vibhutimat sattvam shrimad urjitam eva va |_
_Tat tad evavagaccha tvam mama tejo'nshasambhavam ||5||_
(Gita 10-41)

(Whatever being is possessed of glory, of splendour, or of vigour, know all of that to have sprung from a mere spark of My own radiance.)

Shri Krishna tells Arjuna: whatever being (jivatma) is endowed with lordly power, adorned with grace and fortune, or filled with vigorous, radiant strength — know all of them to be born from a mere fragment of My splendour; or know that it is by that very splendour that the world stands firm.

Thus, whatever disposition (bhava) a person sees Him with, in that same disposition he attains Him. Further, in this world some worship Him desiring heaven; some worship Him to gain release from the cycle of birth and death; some remember Him only to increase the fruits of their action (karma); and yet others worship Him with no expectation whatsoever.

_Antakale cha mameva smaran muktva kalevaram |_
_Yah prayati sa madbhavam yati nastyatra samshayah ||6||_
(Gita 8-5)

(Whatever soul departs at the time of death remembering Me alone, giving up the body, attains My very being — of this there is no doubt.)

The jivatma who, at the time of death, departs remembering none but Me, attains Me — of this, harbour no doubt.

_Yam yam vaapi smaran bhaavam tyajatyante kalevaram |_
_Tam tam eva iti kaunteya sada tadbhaavabhaavitah ||7||_
(Gita 8-6)

(O Kaunteya! Whatever state a man remembers when he finally quits the body, to that very state he goes, ever having been shaped by that same disposition.)

O Kaunteya! Whatever thing a person remembers as he leaves the body at the end, in that very disposition does the jivatma attain that thing.

The purport is this: as one's inner longing (vasana) has been, so is one's destiny. Thus those who become gurumukh and surrender everything to Him attain a good destiny — and this is why we say: the Word itself is the Supreme. That is, the Guru's word should be accepted with faith, and it is only in this way that Parbrahm can be attained — of this, hold no doubt or suspicion whatsoever.

Having looked at this preliminary groundwork, let us now come to our actual subject: what do the words of our Sadguru say?

That is why Kripanath had to go there, because of Ambarish's devotion to Ram, for his protection — for the Word itself is God — and Baba Kabirji bears witness to this. That is, God comes to fulfil His devotees' heartfelt wishes: trusting in such words of the Guru, Ambarish worshipped Him, and so the Lord had to come there. Thus the saying that the Word itself is the Supreme has proved true. That very Ishwar danced together with Chaitanya Mahaprabhu; He came swiftly at the sound of Narsinh's cymbals; and He became absorbed too in Mira's love. So what does Baba Kabir say?

_Ladha hai kachhu ladha hai hira, kamariye bandha hai ||1||_
_Avaran ek akal avinashi, ghatghat vyapi raha harate ||2||_
_Aho jhaako mool na tol map, kachhu nahi ganate gaan na hoi re |_
_Na kachhu halka na kachhu bhari, paar lakhe na koi re ||3||_
_Jaame ham soi ham maanhe, jal tarang jem ek bhaya |_
_Em jhaanat nar koi na marasi, van jaane nar bohot moova ||4||_
_Kahet kabir ram ras paaya, peevanhaar na paau re |_
_Bidhike vachan pahechaanat naahi, to kaadhi kaahaa dekhlaau re nar ||5||_

(Kabirji says: I have found something, I have found a diamond, and I have bound it tight to my waist. Formless, indescribable, unfathomable, imperishable, that Hari pervades every single vessel of being. Ah, He has no root, no weight, no measure — nothing about Him can be counted or sung. He is neither light nor heavy; none can fathom His limit. In Him I dwell, and I dwell in Him — we have become one, as a wave becomes one with water. Whoever truly knows this will never die; those who do not know it, many indeed have died. Kabir declares: I have obtained the taste of Ram's nectar, yet I find none to drink of it with me. Those who do not recognise the Creator's word — what, then, can I bring out and show them?)

That is: Kabirji tells us — "I have found something, I have found something as priceless as a diamond" — the word "Ram," obtained through the Guru, which he has taken firm hold of.
