It is beyond all reckoning of worth. So that this diamond, in the form of Hari, might never be lost or forgotten, he has bound it tight — that is, cinched it firmly — into his own inner being. That diamond is formless, beyond the measure of place or time, ungraspable by anyone, imperishable, and pervades every single vessel of existence. It has no weight, no measure; those who attempt to measure it possess no true knowledge — they are the ignorant, for the Supreme is beyond all measure. The Supreme is neither light nor heavy, nor can it be called this or that by anyone; none can reach its limit. He is in me, and I am in Him — the Supreme is the water of Brahm, and I am its ripple; that is, the soul and the Supreme Soul are one. Such is the name of "Ram" that has come to Kabirji. Thus the word obtained through the Guru is itself the word denoting Parbrahm; one should therefore place faith in such words and follow them. Here a doubt arises: why "Ram" alone — is there no other word? The word "Ram" is not the name of any particular individual but is the word denoting Parbrahm; it has not been applied here to signify any specific person, for this is the Sadguru's word. Then the question arises: what is the guarantee of that? Continuing, Kabirji explains that whoever truly knows this will never die — that is, those who have known the Supreme in His true essence have crossed the ocean of worldly existence and are freed from birth and death; those who do not know Him, many indeed have perished in ignorance. Baba Kabir says: I have obtained the taste of Ram's nectar, and I drink of it, and I long to give it to others too — but I find none willing to drink. So to whom shall I offer this Ram-rasa? And even when I offer it, they do not drink. The Creator's word — the utterance of Brahm, the eternal, ultimate truth — I explain as the name of Ram, yet they do not understand that word; what, then, can I bring out and show them — how, like Hanuman, could I tear open my own chest to show it?

In this pad, in Granth No. 8, page 21, a third verse appears as an addition, as follows:

_Puran brahm sakalmein ekai, ghat ghat bhitar aap rahai |_
_Bahar bhitar sakal nirantar, taaso dooja kaun kahe ||6||_

(The complete Brahm is one and the same in all; He Himself dwells within every single vessel of being. Outside and within, He remains constantly, unbrokenly one throughout; how, then, could anyone call another separate from Him?)

Meaning: the complete Brahm is one and the same, the very same, in every single being. Within every single body He Himself resides. Outside or within, He is present in the same unbroken way in everything; hence how can He be said to be anything separate from ourselves?

The names given to God, that is, His words, are indeed many, while God is one — so which of these words should be heeded? Hear now the source from which all these words arise — a sakhi:

_Sarkho saakshi sarvamein, jyun bhaajanmein bhaan |_
_Brahma keet patangalu, kahe kubera praan ||1||_

(The witness within every being is alike, as the sun is reflected alike in every vessel of water; whether in Brahma, in an insect, in a moth, or even, so to speak, in Kubera, the life-breath within is one and the same.)

Meaning: just as the sun appears the same in every vessel filled with water, so the Supreme is alike, one and the same, in every embodied being. Whether in Brahma or in an insect or a moth or even in Kubera, the life-breath — the jiva — is likewise one and the same.

_Sikhi saakhi laakh mile, kirtaniya paanch karod |_
_Koi brahm chine chinaave, te aage rahu kar jod ||2||_

(Those who have merely memorised sayings by rote number in the lakhs, and hired singers of kirtan number in the crores; but should I find even one who truly knows Brahm and can help others know Him, before that one I would stand with folded hands.)

Meaning: those who, like parrots, have simply memorised sayings and couplets about devotion to God — such people can be found in the lakhs; and those who sing kirtan for a fee, out of self-interest, may number as many as five crores. But should one find even a single person who truly and rightly knows God and could grant a true realisation of Him, one should submit oneself to him and, with folded hands, take refuge at his feet.

_Paanch pahar dhandha kiya, teen pahar rahya soy |_
_Ek pahar hari na bhajya, to mukti kaanse hoy ||3||_

(Five watches of the day were spent in worldly toil, three watches of the night in sleep; not even a single watch was given to remembering Hari — so from where, then, could liberation come?)

Meaning: five pahors (watches) were spent in household work, employment, and business; three pahors of the night were spent asleep; but not even a single pahor was given to the remembrance of God — so how, then, could liberation be attained?

_Kabir ja karan jag dhundhata, so to ghatahi maanhi |_
_Padda diya bharamka, taathe soojhat naahi ||4||_

(Kabir says: that which he was searching for throughout the world was, all along, within his own being; but a veil of delusion had been drawn over it, and so it could not be seen.)

Meaning: he who was searching throughout the world for God was, all the while, present within his own being — but a veil of illusion (bharam) had been cast over it, and so he could not see Him.

_Arab kharab vaani kathi, granth koti hazaar |_
_Karta purush kabir hai, naabhe kiyo vichaar ||5||_

(Utterances beyond count, arbs and kharabs, have been spoken, and thousands upon thousands, crores, of scriptures composed; yet Nabha, upon reflection, concluded that Kabir alone is the Creator-Person.)

Meaning: Nabha Swami, in composing the Bhaktamal, spoke words beyond counting — arbs and kharabs — and even composed thousands and crores of scriptures; yet Nabhaji became certain that it is Kabirji alone who is the form of the Creator, the Supreme Person, the Parmatma Himself. All other utterances pertain merely to the characters and deeds of His devotees.

Kabirji is eager to have all drink the nectar of divine love, and those who have drunk of this nectar he has briefly described in the Bijak, Shabda 12. In Kabirvani, issue 21, page 2, he has also discussed this at length, where it is stated: "Here a doubt arises — have there truly ever been such saints as have drunk the cup of the nectar of loving devotion?" Sadguru Kabirji answers this by saying that Gorakhnath, Dattatreya, Vashishtha, Vyas, Hanuman, Narad, and Shukdev Muni, and others, gathered together and sat in an assembly together with Shambhu and the Sanakadik sages — and upon the lips of every one of them rests the cup of the nectar of loving devotion. Ambarish, Yagyavalkya, King Janak, and Jad Bharat have drunk of this nectar of love, and Sheshnag has tasted this nectar of love through his thousand mouths — the count cannot be exhausted. In this way the devotees Dhruv, Prahlad, and Vibhishan too became intoxicated with love. Parvatiji, wife of Shivji, also drank of this nectar of devotional love and was filled with joy. In Shri Krishna's loving devotion, the entire company of the cowherds, cowherd-women, and cowherd children of Vraj drank this nectar of love and became overwhelmed with divine feeling.

(This was heard as a saying about the Word from the mouth of Bhagat Gokulbhai Dwarkadas, a poet, of Kudeda.)

_Vachan pakade so mard hai, maheri sab sansaar |_
_Pandya to randya bhaya, bhetya nahi bharathaar ||7||_

(He who firmly grasps the Word alone is truly brave; to him the whole world is like his own obedient wife. The scholars and pandits, by contrast, have become like wandering women who have never met their true husband.)

_Vachanna mahelmein vachan diya kare, ved katebathi vaat nyaari |_
_Brahmka mahalmein brahm bhadka kare, guruna naam par jaay vaari ||8||_

(In the palace of the Word, the Word alone bestows the Word — a matter altogether different from what the Vedas and the Quran declare. In the palace of Brahm-knowledge, Brahm flares up as a mere flash; I offer myself in sacrifice to the Guru's name alone.)

_Vachan aar hai vachan paar hai, vachan gam gheriyo |_
_Vachanse vachan neepaje, vohi sadguru ki deriyo ||9||_

(The Word is the support, the Word is the final goal; hold fast to the path, the understanding, of the Word. From the Word the true Word is born — and that alone is the dwelling place of the Sadguru.)

Meaning: he who recognises the Word is truly courageous and wise; for him, the world — maya — becomes obedient to him like a wife under his command. Pandits and scholars, by contrast, wander about like unfaithful women who have never truly met their rightful husband. In the domain of the Word, the words of the Guru and the saints act like a guiding lamp, dispelling ignorance through their teaching. The words they utter are unlike anything found in the Vedas or the Quran. In the atmosphere of Brahm-knowledge and philosophical learning, mere philosophy gives only a flicker of light before going out — flashing on and off like an inconstant devotee's resolve. But when the Guru's own instructive words are uttered, then even the flare of Brahm-knowledge is offered up in sacrifice before them; one abandons the mere flickering talk of Brahm-knowledge and surrenders oneself entirely to the Guru. Thus the Word is "aar" — that is, it has firm support — and the Word is "paar" — that is, it carries final, decisive certainty. One should hold fast to, that is, keep firmly encircled, the path of such a Word. Only from such words will the true Word be born, and that Word alone is the true dwelling place of the Sadguru.

Bhagat Trikambhai Gordhanbhai of Suyadhoda, in his diary of the year 1978, on page 193, has written the following concerning the Word:

1. The Word itself is God (Samagam).
2. For the sake of the Word, the Pandavas surrendered their kingdom and Draupadi to the Kauravas (Mahabharat).
4. For the sake of the Word, King Nal endured exile in the forest (Nalakhyan).
5. For the sake of the Word, King Harishchandra sold his own wife and son (Mahabharat).
6. For the sake of the Word, Lord Vaman became a doorkeeper in the house of King Bali (Mahabharat).
7. For the sake of the Word, Dhruv, at his stepmother's word, went into the forest and endured great hardship (Mahabharat).
8. For the sake of the Word, Sudhanva entered a cauldron of boiling oil.
9. For the sake of the Word, the descendants of Pratap Rana keep straw as their bed, in fulfilment of their vow (History).
10. For the sake of the Word, the Sikh people wear the bangle (kangan), the vermilion mark (kanku), and the comb (kaanchko).
11. For the sake of the Word, Edward the Eighth gave up the throne of Britain.
12. For the sake of the Word, Pratap Rao Gaekwad too gave up the throne of Vadodara.
13. For the sake of the Word, Narsinh Mehta left his home at his sister-in-law's word.
13/1. For the sake of the Word, Tulsidas left the household life at Ratnavali's word.
14. For the sake of the Word, Vitthaldas Maharaj, descendant of Jivanji Maharaj of Puniyad, stood holding a horse through an entire night.
15. For the sake of the Word, Jadunath gave up eating in company and lived until his final moment on fruit alone.

A chhappo (six-line verse):

He who did not keep his word lost the fruit of all his good deeds. He who did not keep his word died an unnatural death. He who did not keep his word was punished by God Himself. He who did not keep his word had his head and body marked with shame (mundan, the shaving of the head). Whoever became unfaithful to his word lost all his divine splendour (daivat = the oil of divine glory). Shamal says: he who does not keep his word — once the word is gone, what is left at all?

In the ledger of the Shasak Printing Press are further examples of keeping one's word:

1. For the sake of serving the saints, Ghana Bhagat fed the saints his entire stock of wheat-grain.
2. For the sake of serving the saints, Kelaiya offered up his own life as sacrifice.
3. For the sake of serving the saints, Baba Kabir dared to commit theft.
4. For the sake of serving the saints, Pipa Bhagat and Sita Mata pawned their own clothes.
5. Dama Bhagat used up all his grain, and Lord Damodar came to his aid.
6. King Shibi offered up the flesh of his own body for the protection of a refugee.

Even in this Kali Yuga, in an age piled high with deceit and treachery, such kings and rulers too have shown courage in keeping the rule of righteous conduct. Let us understand Kabirji's words further.

_Kahet kabir ram ras paayo, peevanhaar na paau re ||_

(Kabir says: I have obtained the nectar of Ram, yet I find no one to drink it with me.)

That is, the Guru has given Kabirji the nectar of Ram; this nectar is such that only once one has drunk it can one savour its true delight — but those who cannot recognise it, whose minds remain fixed on sensory objects and their disturbances, cannot recognise this nectar nor enjoy its delight. That is why Kabirji says: I myself have drunk it, and I offer it to others too, but even when I offer it, whoever does not drink it — how can I make him drink? Such wretched souls simply cannot understand it. Yet the further question arises: how, then, is this to be recognised? How is one to believe that this is indeed the Guru's word? Only through practice (abhyas) — that is, through sustained effort — should one strive to understand it. And it must be understood through the impressions (sanskaras) carried over from past lives. Moreover, we should come to know this word "Ram" by following those who, before us, have already known it. Jivanji Maharaj says—

_Ramanande je kahi, so suni das kabir |_
_So sadguru kahi jivana, bhaj sitapati raghuvir ||10||_

(What Ramanand spoke, that was heard by Das Kabir; and that same word the Sadguru speaks, O Jivana — worship the Lord of Sita, the hero of the Raghu line.)

That is, this Guru-word has come down even from before Jivanji Maharaj himself; it is this very word that Jivanji Maharaj has received and shown to us. Further—

_Sadgurukhe updeshka, aradh naam pravesh |_
_Bhavsagar mitke jivana, hum aavenge unadesh ||11||_

(Through the Sadguru's teaching, entry may be gained even through half the Name; and through it, O Jivana, once the ocean of worldly existence is crossed away, we shall arrive at that far shore.)

Meaning: through the name "Ram," which the Sadguru has given, if one grasps and practises even half that word — that is, the syllable "Ra" alone — with faith, that alone gives the power to cross the ocean of worldly existence and reach that far shore.

Jivanji Maharaj says: for this, we must now make the effort — for—

_Aagha mata saadhka, jahaan parbrahmaki aas |_
_Poora mata tahaan jivana, jahaan sadguru shabd vishwas ||12||_

(The seeker's understanding is but partial where there is only longing for Parbrahm; the understanding is complete, O Jivana, only where there is faith in the Sadguru's word.)

Meaning: even if one grasps, with faith, only half of the divine Name "Ram" given by the Sadguru — that is, the syllable "Ra" alone — one can still cross the ocean of worldly existence. But should someone, without ever having received the name Ram or any other divine name from the Sadguru, believe that by the divine name alone he can cross this ocean, or that through japa, austerity, vows and the like he may attain heaven and such, and so set the Guru aside and worship in his own self-willed manner — then, for such a devotee, whatever devotion he practises through the divine name, his understanding remains only half true. But one who, having received the divine name from the Sadguru, practises devotion with faith placed in it, attains the complete and entire fulfilment of God. Whereas without the Sadguru, one attains only an incomplete fulfilment of God. For—

_Aadha mata kaun kaamka, je paave vaikunthko dhaam |_
_Taathe jagat bhali jivana, kabahu sant sangat vishraam ||13||_
(Sant)

(Of what use is a half-true understanding, even if it should attain the abode of Vaikunth? Better than that, O Jivana, is this world itself, where at times one may find rest and repose in the company of saints.)

Meaning: whatever fruit is gained through the performance of ordinary religious duties, or through japa, austerity, vows, sacrifices, and the like — of what use is that, when it leads merely to Vaikunth or heaven? Far better than attaining such a place is to take birth in this very world — for at least, at times, in this world one gets the chance to dwell in the company of saints, an opportunity that is not possible in Vaikunth or the like.

The seeker can traverse half the road, for his yearning, his longing to attain Parbrahm, has reached its highest pitch of intensity; by the sheer force of that yearning he has already completed half the journey. But the remaining road must be travelled onward through practice, placing faith in the Sadguru's word.

_Pakh chhooti dohodish gai, rahyo sant samagam saar |_
_Sadguru shabde jivana, utariye peli paar ||14||_

(All partisan leanings, in every direction, have fallen away; what remains, as the very essence, is the company of saints. By the Sadguru's word, O Jivana, we shall cross over to that far shore.)

Meaning: there was once a clash of sects and differing doctrines, a confusion over which path — japa, austerity, vows, sacrifice, pilgrimage, and the other paths of religious duty — one ought to follow. From this confusion the seeker has now become free, and, from every direction, from every side, he has resolved to hold fast to one single support alone, and through that support to make the essence of all essences the company of saints (sant samagam). By walking in accordance with the Sadguru's teaching, one shall be able to cross to the far shore of the ocean of worldly existence.

The obstruction of factional leanings has now fallen away, because one has taken hold of the Sadguru's hand — hence every obstruction shall be removed, and the bondage of sectarian directions too has been removed. Only the essential words that come through the company of saints now remain, and by means of these one shall reach the far shore of the ocean of worldly existence with ease.

_Jahaan sadgurukaa dava nahi, tahaan jamka dava hoy |_
_Raam bharunse jivana, bharam pado mat koi ||15||_

(Where there is no claim of the Sadguru, there Death's claim holds sway; trust in Ram alone, O Jivana — let none fall into delusion.)

_Hari bhaje hari na paaiye, sab aap aapkun dhaay |_
_Guru samasa bin jivana, kaal jhapete jaay ||16||_

(One may worship Hari and still not attain Hari, for each runs merely after his own self-interest; without the Guru's true direction, O Jivana, one is snatched away by the grip of Death.)

Knowledge without a Guru is like an incomplete education, and the finest example of this is given by the story of Narad Muni in the Puranas. That is why Jivanji Maharaj explains: however learned a person may be, without the recognition of the Sadguru he remains unhappy and suffers. Whatever direction — whatever hint or gesture — the Guru points toward, if one fails to grasp it, one falls into the grip of death. Only through the Guru's words can one become gurumukh, for—

_Sadguru sabad bin jivana, jyun andho aarasi paay ||17||_

(Without the Sadguru's word, O Jivana, it is as if a blind man were handed a mirror.)

If a mirror is placed before a blind man, it is of no use whatsoever, for he cannot even see his own face in it. Kabirji, describing the glory of the Guru, likewise says that through the Guru's influence his own speech has been utterly transformed — what was once bitter has become sweet.

_Kabir vaani hamaari palti, ya mulak ya desh |_
_Khaari te meethi bhai, sadgurukhe updesh ||18||_

(Kabir says: my speech has been utterly transformed — in this land, in this country — that which was bitter has become sweet, through the teaching of the Sadguru.)

For Kabirji also says, reflecting on the Sadguru's word—

_Kabir shabd vichaari jo chale, guru mukh hoye nihaal |_
_Kaam krodh vyaape nahi, kabahu na graase kaal ||19||_

(Kabir says: whoever walks having reflected on the Word becomes gurumukh and is made joyful and fulfilled; lust and anger no longer take hold of him, and Death can never seize him.)

Without the Guru, the true path cannot be attained. This subject will be discussed further ahead in greater detail. Looking further here, Jivanji Maharaj says that, as Jaidevji's words spoken earlier had it — patati patatre — "when a leaf falls, when a leaf stirs" — for the joy of union, Lord Krishna once went to the appointed forest bower, and there, restless with longing for Radhaji's arrival, believed that at even the stirring of a single leaf Radhaji must be arriving, and so, filled with eager anticipation, began preparing a welcome for her. In just this way, should any devotee show even the slightest willingness to act according to the gurumukh's word and teaching, then just as the Lord holds such eagerness to welcome Radha, He holds the very same eagerness to meet such a devotee. While Jaidev's Geet Govind was being sung, the Lord followed after the daughter of a garland-maker who was gathering flowers — for such is the glory of these paramount words: they are themselves the very form of God made manifest. In the Adi Purana there is a verse.

_Madbhaktaa yatra gacchanti tatra gacchaami paarthiva |_
_Bhaktaanaamanugacchanti muktayah shrutibhih saha ||8||_

(O Partha, wherever My devotees go, there I go too; and liberation itself, together with the Vedas, follows after such devotees.)

Meaning: O Partha, wherever My devotees go, there I go too; and liberation too, together with the Vedas, follows after such devotees. Here, seeing the disposition (bhava) of King Ambarish, Krishna had withdrawn from sight and had to come back again — for when there is faith in the Guru's word, Kripanath must come. That is why we say the Word itself is the Supreme, and Kabirji, too, confirms this through the bhajan quoted above — as when he says, I have obtained the nectar of Ram, yet find none to drink it with me — I long to give it, yet why can I find no one to drink it? And if I do find someone, why do they still not drink?

This is indeed a difficult, knotty question — that the nectar of Ram is to be given, yet none is ready to drink it — how is this to be understood, and what does it mean? Kabirji explains: I have offered the taste of this nectar to many, yet some unwise people cannot understand its true savour — what, then, is to be said to such wretched souls? And further, some, though wise, cannot bring themselves to practise it — for them too, where is one to go even to shed tears? Kabirji says that for such people it is entirely useless even to speak of dharma, for—

_Is loknakun bahe jaan de — hansa, is loknakun bahe jaan de |_
_Hansa hans mili chalo re sarovar, bagahikun medak khaan de ||1||_

(Let these people go their own way, O swan — let these people go their own way. Come, O swan, let us go together to the lake; leave the frogs to be eaten by the herons.)

That is, those who, knowing full well, wish only to fall into the pit — how can such people be stopped? That is why Kabirji says: should you meet a true seeker of saintly company, give him to drink the elixir of Ram; but should you fall among the worldly-minded, they will only caw and croak like crows — words that carry no meaning at all. Wise souls, then, should not waste their time on such people but should press onward themselves — for the path of saints is one thing entirely, while the path of the worldly-minded is filled with quarrel and strife, and further, is steeped in maya, delusion, and attachment. The wise should abandon such company and themselves consider the path by which Parbrahm may be attained through devotion. Kabir says—

(Raga Godi)

_Hari ras saar santo, raam ras saar, je re peeve taako mite re vikaara ||Teka||_
_Hari ras amal saval sun bhaai, amaldaar koi peevega |_
_Je re peeve so hoy avinaasi, amar jugojug jeevega ||1||_
_E ras sanakaadik piya, or umiyaapati swaami |_
_Naaradse muni ketiek varanu, jogeshwar nij naami ||2||_
_Ya sun sharan tumhaare aayo, sitaapati raghunaatha |_
_Daas kabir aharnish peeve, hari ras santo saatha ||3||_

(O saints, the nectar of Hari, the nectar of Ram, is the very essence — whoever drinks it, all his disorders of desire are removed. Listen, brothers, to the true intoxication of Hari's nectar: only a true intoxicant will drink of it; whoever drinks it becomes imperishable, and lives on, immortal, through age after age. This nectar was drunk by the Sanakadik sages and by Umiyapati Shiva, the Lord Himself. How many renowned yogis, beginning with Narad, could I even name? Hearing of this, O Lord of Sita, Raghunath, I have come to Your refuge; Your servant Kabir drinks this nectar of Hari day and night, together with the saints.)

Meaning: O saints, the nectar of Hari alone is the highest essence; whoever drinks it, his disorders of desire are removed. Let me tell you of the effect of the intoxication that this nectar of Hari brings — listen: only one who is a true intoxicant will drink of it and savour its taste. Whoever drinks it becomes imperishable, indestructible, and lives on through age upon age. This nectar has been drunk by the Sanakadik sages and by Umapati Mahadev; how many could one even count among Narad and the other renowned yogis? Hearing the praises of this nectar, O Sitapati Ram, I have come to Your refuge. Your servant Kabir drinks this nectar day and night, together with the saints.

_Samajhe naraku hari kathaa, ana samajhekun haaji |_
_Sabad sabad aanti pade, jaise doodhmein kaanji ||20||_

(To the one who understands, the story of Hari is received as understanding; to the one who does not understand, only mindless agreement follows. Word tangles against word, as when vinegar is dropped into milk.)

Meaning: if something is told to a wise person, he receives the discourse on God with the love with which he would listen to it; but the unwise person, without understanding, simply keeps saying "yes, yes" — and further, whatever we say to him, he twists every word we speak and takes offence, just as milk curdles and splits when vinegar falls into it, so too does such an unwise person turn against us in resentment.

The name of this Ram-elixir should be given only where there is one who can understand it as it truly is — for only where there is one able to understand the name "Ram" should the "Name" be used at all. However precious a diamond may be, if the jeweller's power of discernment is weak, he cannot rightly appraise its true worth. So too, only before one who is a true connoisseur of the real diamond should the matter of the Ram-elixir be spoken — only then can its true worth be understood. If no one capable of recognising it is found, it will be treated with contempt. Thus, since the Guru's word is precious, it must be spread and propagated only in such a way that its importance is preserved — and it should never be given to anyone unworthy; that is, the name "Ram" should not even be uttered in front of them.

In society, there are many who never utter the name "Ramkabir." If one greets them first with the name "Ramkabir," they simply stand with folded hands in silence, or else, instead of "Ramkabir," they will utter the name of whatever other path or sect they are affiliated with or influenced by. Before such people the name "Ramkabir" should not be uttered, nor should they be urged to utter it — for neither side gains any benefit from it. For Jivanji Maharaj, through the words of Narsinh Mehta, says—

_Jire dhanyatun dhanyatun em kahe shri hari, narasaiya tun maaro bhakt saacho |_
_Meli purushaatan, sakhi re veshe thayo, taahera premthi hun re naachyo ||_
_Jire mujmaan tujmaan, bhed nahi naagaraa, maan tun maahyari ved vaani |_
_Haju tane pratit na upaje, me tane mokalyun taadhun paani |_
_Mosaalu kidhun te kem gayo visari, haar aapyo pratyaksh bhoop |_
_Chaud lokmaan mahaare tuj samo ko nahi, taaharu maaharu ek roop |_
_Taahara akshar gaayane saambhle, tehnaa kuntumb sahit paavan thaaye |_
_Bhane narasaiyo meethaan boli su rijavo, taare kar jodi krishnaji sam khaaye ||_

(Blessed, blessed indeed — thus Shri Hari says — Narsinh, you are My true devotee; you laid aside your manhood and took the guise of a sakhi, and I danced for love of you. There is no difference at all, O Nagar, between you and Me; accept this as My own true, Veda-like word. If you still do not believe it — I sent you cool water in your hour of need; I performed your mother-in-law's ritual gift for you — how could you have forgotten that? I gave you, in person, a garland with My own hand. In all the fourteen worlds there is none like you; yours and Mine are, in truth, a single form. Whoever hears your verses sung is purified, together with his whole family. Narsinh says: pleased by such sweet words, I fold my hands, and Krishnaji Himself swears an oath to it.)

"Blessed, blessed are you" — that is, here, beyond all identification with the body, an unbroken identity (tadatmya) has been forged between the jiva and Parbrahm — a bond not made through the outer senses. Free of the false distinction that says "this is the body, this is the soul," this is a non-dual oneness, free of every disorder belonging to the objects of the senses — a pure, conscious identity with Parbrahm. This is the very "Ram-rasa" of which Kabirji has spoken; and the drinker of that nectar he spoke of is none other than the devotee Narsinh Mehta, who has drunk of this Ram-rasa. Having tasted that nectar, he became wholly "Ram-formed" (Rammaya). Every kind of distinction and bondage has fallen away from him, for now there is no difference left at all between the man of Nagar, Narsaiya, and Parbrahm. Men are not granted entry into Lord Krishna's Ras. Narsinh Mehta abandoned his identity as a man and, showing the disposition of a woman, drank of the nectar of the Ras. Such is the state of one who becomes wholly immersed in the nectar of Hari's love — and in his pad on spring, Narsinh Mehta says:

_Je harine ojhalade aave, te purush panun vege visare |_

(Whoever comes into the very shadow of Hari's presence swiftly forgets his own manhood.)

Meaning: whoever comes within the shadow of Hari's loving devotion swiftly forgets his own manhood, his masculine identity. (Udadharma Panchratnamala, page 426, 4th edition.)

Such is the effect of the taste of divine love upon whoever drinks of that nectar of love, and this same effect befell Narsinh Mehta. Sundardas has sung of this in a savaiya:

_Jo man naariki or nihaarat, to man hot naarike roopaa |_
_Jo man kaahusu krodh bicharat, to man hai bahi tad roopaa ||1||_
_Jo man maayaa hi maayaa rate, to man padat hai maayake koopa |_
_Sundar jo man brahm bicharat, to man hot hai brahmamay tadroopaa ||2||_

(If the mind gazes toward a woman, the mind itself takes on the form of a woman. If the mind dwells in anger against someone, the mind itself flows into that very form of anger. If the mind only ever chants maya, maya, the mind falls into the very well of maya. Sundar says: if the mind contemplates Brahm, the mind itself becomes Brahm-formed, of that very same nature.)

Meaning: if the mind dwells on thoughts of a woman, the mind itself takes on the form of a woman; and if the mind dwells on anger toward someone, the mind itself becomes anger-formed. If the mind only chants "maya, maya," the mind falls into the very well of maya. Sundardas says: if the mind contemplates Brahm-Parbrahm, the mind itself becomes wholly Brahm-Parbrahm-formed.

In the Harmala it is said, "I drink in the whole of the crores of universes." In the pad of supplication it is said:

_Maahaare jahevi vraj sundari tehvo jan narasaiyo |_
_Ine niramal mane maaharo jas gaao |_
_Jire tunj leelaae madhukar kunj maadhavaa |_
_Purush naame koi paas na aave |_

(Narsaiya, this devotee, is to Me just like the beautiful women of Vraj; with a pure mind he has sung My glory. In Your bower-play, O Madhava, roaming like a bee, no one bearing the name of manhood may draw near.)

Meaning: Krishna says: for Me, this Narsinh Mehta is just like the beautiful women of Vraj. With a pure mind he has sung My praises. In the play of the bower in Vrindavan, where Krishna roamed like a bee, drinking the love-nectar of the cowherd-women, no one bearing the mark of manhood can even approach this play. Thus Narsinh Mehta too, setting aside his own manhood, drank of the nectar of the Ras-lila in the disposition of a gopi — for the Narad Bhakti Sutra says—

_Tanmayah_

(Becoming wholly absorbed, one with Him.)

That is, to become wholly absorbed and one with Him — the devotee becomes so immersed in God that he forgets his own separate form. Here no distinction remains at all. Shandilya Muni says—

_Ananya bhaktyaa tad buddhi bundaatyalayaantam |_

(Through single-minded, undivided devotion, the discriminating intellect dissolves entirely into That.)

Through undivided devotion, once that discriminating intellect (bheda-buddhi) is fully dissolved, the oneness of atma and Parbrahm is accomplished.

_Kabir main jaanu hari door hai, hari rahyaa sakal bharapoor |_
_Aap pechhaanaa baaheraa, teraa hi te door ||21||_

(Kabir says: I once thought Hari was far away, yet Hari is present, filling all things entirely. It is your own self that has strayed outward — it is that very straying that has kept you far from Him.)

_Kabir meraa saain mujhmein, bhamyo naanaa ne taas |_
_Kasturi kaa mrig jyaun, phir phir sudhe dhaas ||22||_

(Kabir says: my Lord is within me, yet I wandered about in every direction searching for Him — like the musk-deer who runs here and there, again and again, chasing after the scent of grass.)

_Kabir ja karan jag dhundhiya, so to ghatahi maanhi |_
_Pardaa diyaa bharmakaa, taaten soojhe naahi ||23||_

(Kabir says: that which he searched for throughout the world was, all along, within his own body — but a veil of delusion had been drawn, and so it could not be seen.)

_Kabir ham jaanaa hari door hai, lok vedki chhaanhi |_
_Giri gehvar dhoondhat phire, hari biraaje ghatmaanhi ||24||_

(Kabir says: we thought Hari was far away, under the shade of worldly custom and scripture; we wandered searching through mountains and caves, while Hari all along dwelt within our own being.)

_Kabir daudat daudat daudiyaa, jab lagi manki daud |_
_Daud thaki man thir bhaayaa, vast thaurki thaur ||25||_

(Kabir says: I ran and ran and kept on running, for as long as the mind's own restless running lasted; when the running wearied and the mind at last grew still, the sought-for thing was found right there, in its own place.)

That is: if, without understanding the Sadguru's word, one keeps running here and there like the musk-deer chasing after fragrance and flavour, one will only end up exhausted and, in the end, must come right back to where one began. One should not go wandering about anywhere in search of Parbrahm; rather, one should place faith in the Sadguru and live one's life accordingly. Jivanji Maharaj has truly taught the Udabhakta community how to live a true life — but how, then, should one live? We shall look at the answer to this question further ahead. There Jivandasji spoke — what did he speak?

_Dehi darshan sab ko kare, sabad darshan nav hoy,
sabad darshan bin jivana, paar na pahonchya koy ||1||_ (Everyone can behold a person's outward form, but the vision of the Word does not come this way. Without the vision of the Word, life reaches no one to the far shore.)

That is to say: in the path of devotion there should be no worship of a person as an individual. The Guru's position is important indeed, but if we take to worshipping only him as God, it becomes like discarding gold to buy iron. Today we see, in many places in society, how deeply people have sunk into worship of individuals; many have even lost their own power of discernment. To such blindly faithful devotees Maharaj Jivanji gives this warning: do not defile devotion by taking a mere person to be God Himself, the Manifest One, or a direct incarnation of Parbrahm. And if anyone gets himself called the Manifest One or God, he ought to be shunned. For it is of such men that Kabirji speaks:

_Kabir gadi baitha mahant kahave, baitha pooja khay,
kol hokare otare, khod khod mar jaye ||26||_ (One who sits upon the seat and calls himself mahant sits there and consumes the worship offered to him — he is like a burrowing mole that digs and digs and dies in its own digging.)

_Kabir dikhya leeni shikh bhaya, kari muktiki thaan,
sadguru to khoja nahi, thook bharaya kaan ||27||_ (Kabir says: he took initiation and became a disciple, and set his resolve on liberation, but he never truly sought out the true Sadguru — so only spit filled his ear.)

That is: one should not be led astray by someone's outward pomp and show. Otherwise, falling into the wrong hands is like a merchant who buys fake goods and later regrets it — so too, one who sets out to cross this ocean of worldly existence ends up drowning in it instead, and becomes an object of ridicule in society. Many people, going to buy gold cheap, lose both their real gold and their money, and afterward find themselves in a state that can neither be spoken of nor endured. It becomes, further, like the thief's mother weeping with her face buried in the grain-bin. Rather than fall into such a state, one should seek out a true Sadguru and receive devotion from him. From a guru who merely blows a mantra into the ear, only his spit will reach that ear — the true Name of Ram is never obtained from such a false guru. Such gurus are born taking the incarnation of a "kol", a large burrowing rat. So, to show what difference there is between a true Sadguru and a so-called guru, Kabirji says:

_Kabir sabad sabad kaha karo, sabad ko haath na paanv,
ek sabad okhad kare, ek sabad kare ghaav ||2||_ (Kabir says: keep speaking of the Word — the Word itself has neither hand nor foot, yet one Word acts as medicine while another Word inflicts a wound.)

"Aushadhi" (herb-medicine) removes disease. The Manusmriti, Chapter 1, verse 46, says that plants bearing abundant flowers and fruit, which die once the fruit has ripened, are called "aushadhi". Fruit that ripens and falls of itself — barley, chickpea, wheat and other such grains — belong to this class. Ten grains of the field together are called "sarvaushadhi", the all-herb group: these ten grains are — 1) dhanya (grain/rice), 2) jav (barley), 3) til (sesame), 4) adad (black gram), 5) sauva, 6) cheno (a millet), 7) ghau (wheat), 8) masur (lentil), 9) vatana (peas). [As printed, only nine grains are listed though the text says "ten".]

By speaking words that sound pleasant, people show sympathy; by uttering harsh, bitter, cutting words, people run to strike in anger. In the same way, taking God's Name brings well-being, while uttering impure incantations brings downfall. The Panchatantra, in the Kakolukiyam, verse 111, says:

_Rohate sayakair viddham chhinnam rohati chasina,
vacho durruktam bibhatsam na prarohati vaakshatam ||9||_ (A limb pierced by arrows heals; a wound from a sword also heals. But a heart pierced by speech never heals. Therefore harsh words should never be spoken.)

_Vakya baan nahi chhodiye, tikshanta yoon tu joy,
katu vachan Kuru kul hanyo, Bhim krodh vash hoy ||28||_ (The arrow of speech should not be loosed — see how sharp its force is: because of one bitter word, Bhim, overcome with anger, destroyed the whole Kaurava clan.)

_Dukh na hata sansarmen, hata na shok viyog,
sukh hi men dukh la diya, boli bole log ||29||_ (There was no sorrow in the world, nor grief, nor separation — but people, by speaking such words, brought the pain of grief and the separation of loved ones into what had been happiness.)

How great a difference there is between one word and another! The Guru's word is a form of graciousness, while the hypocrite's word is like a wound, exceedingly painful. To show whose words cause such a wound, Govinddas states in the Sarvangalila:

_Je sant sabad mane nahi, eh ohalanghe aap,
dasha bhulo daaladriyun bohotu kahego baap ||3||_ (Whoever, out of ego, does not follow the Saint's teaching but transgresses it — that poor soul, having lost the true direction, will, from suffering so much distress, cry out again and again, "Oh father, oh father!")

One who transgresses the Saint's words becomes directionless and greatly sorrowful, for a man intoxicated with his own conceit heeds not even the saintly precepts — such as the scriptural words "speak truth, practice righteousness, speak agreeably" — and the like. Such a man becomes very unhappy. Moreover, one who does not conduct himself according to dharma behaves as though wounding others: he himself becomes unhappy, and the person he faces becomes unhappy too. Here it has been shown how one who transgresses the Saint's words behaves like one dealing a wound. Now Maharaj Jivanji shows how the Saint's words are, by contrast, like medicine.

_Daarki chuki baandari, shabadka chukya hans,
sabhaka chukya pandita, teenoka nirvansh ||30||_ (If a female monkey misses her branch, if the soul forgets the Guru's spoken teaching, and if a scholar slips in an assembly or examination — all three meet complete ruin.)

_Tavad askhalitam yavat sukham yati same pathi,
skhalite cha samutpanne vishame cha pade pade ||10||_ (A man can walk on level ground without stumbling only as long as he walks with ease; but once he loses his footing and strays from the path, he stumbles at every single step.)

_Char mukti mide bhai, jahan prem bhakti prakash,
jivan mugat jan Jivana, jahan sadguru shabad vishwas ||4||_ (Maharaj Jivanji says: when I received the light of loving devotion, I set aside all four kinds of liberation. When faith is placed in the Sadguru's teaching, then even while living a devotee's life one becomes free from every kind of worldly bondage.)

Maharaj Jivanji says:

_Gyaan kathe so baavra, mukti mage so moodh,
prem bhakti bin Jivana, jamki phaansi praudh ||31||_ (Those who keep speaking of attaining divine and self-knowledge are all frantic and out of their minds; and those who beg for liberation are foolish and lacking understanding — for even attaining such knowledge or liberation without loving devotion, they will certainly fall into the terrible noose of death.)

Kabirji says: one who, for the sake of liberation, takes refuge in divine knowledge or ritual religious duty, only wanders lost in the darkness of Maya.

_Kabir deepak pragata premka, jahan sadguru shabad prakash,
andhiyara sab jagatkun, jahan karma dharmaki aash ||32||_ (Baba Kabirji says: when the light of the Sadguru's teaching is received, the lamp of loving devotion is lit; but where people, without love and devotion, merely walk the path of ritual duty — japa, tapa, vows and the like — hoping thereby to attain God, such worldly people only stumble about in the darkness of delusion and attachment.) Maharaj Gnaniji says:

_Sant sangat je janiye, jake dradh vrat Hari naam,
char mukti mage nahi, or vaikunthko dhaam ||33||_ (Maharaj Gnaniji says: know that whoever has taken a firm resolve to recite the divine Name has kept true company with saints. Such devotees ask for none of the four kinds of liberation, nor even for the abode of Vaikuntha.)

Kabirji says:

_Kabir mugat na maagun bhagati na chhandun, Hari gun sunat sunaun,
Ram Krishna avatar manorath, janam janam gun gaun ||34||_ (Baba Kabirji says: I do not ask even for liberation, nor will I ever give up devotion to God — I shall hear and recount the glories of Hari. May Ram and Krishna go on taking incarnation, and birth after birth may I sing their glories and perform their devotion — such is my longing.)

Vyasji says:

_Vyas char mugat bilakhat phire, Shri Vrindavanki khor,
mohe baas kyun na Vrajmen diyo, main neerkhun jugal kishor ||35||_ (All four kinds of liberation wander about, restless and distressed, in the narrow lanes of Vrindavan, saying: "Why did God not grant us the privilege of dwelling in Vraj? Had He granted it, we too would have enjoyed the bliss of beholding Shri Krishna.")

_Salokya-sarshti-samipya-sarupyaikatvam aayutam,
diyamanam na grihnanti vina matsevanam janah ||11||_ (Bhagavat, Skandh, Adhyaya 29, Shlok 13 — Even when offered the five kinds of liberation — salokya, sarshti, samipya, sarupya and sayujya, oneness — desireless devotees do not accept them by forsaking My service.) (Salokya = dwelling in the same realm as God; sarshti = attaining opulence equal to God's; samipya = staying near God; sarupya = attaining a four-armed form like God's; sayujya, oneness = merging with God as the Ganga's water merges with the ocean. This is stated in order to establish faith in the Sadguru's word:)

_Parkho guruka shabadko jo guru kahe vichar,
bina shabad kachhu na mile, dekho nayan nihaar ||36||_ (Understand well the teaching that the Guru gives after deep thought — without this teaching nothing at all is attained; open your eyes and see for yourself.) Hence it is said:

_Apne apne dharmame, dradh raho sab kaal,
nij dharma paale rahe, saheje bhaya nihaal ||37||_ (Always remain firmly established in your own dharma; one who continues to observe his own dharma easily attains fulfillment — his boat crosses over.)

In the treatise on Maya and Brahm, Maharaj Jivanji does not accept the four kinds of liberation, namely: 1) salokya, 2) sarupya, 3) sanidhya, 4) sayujya. In this sakhi he states that none of these four kinds of liberation have any real meaning, because a person who has not learned how to truly live his life in this world, whose living has become sheer poison, with what face can he speak of attaining happiness after death? This is nothing but hypocrisy. One whose life lacks love, devotion, and light is, though living, as good as dead.

Even many highly religious people are unable to truly live their lives. That one ought to live according to dharma is a hundred percent true statement. But what true dharma is — that is extremely difficult to understand. Those who, under the influence of religion, become blindly faithful and turn timid or cowardly have never truly lived; there is nothing more to them than a soft, mushy sheep. Just as we speak of karma-yoga, jnana-yoga and bhakti-yoga, so too a "life-yoga" — a discipline of living — should be recognised. If a religion makes a person cowardly or spineless, then no matter how widespread that religion is, and however good it may appear, it is not worthy of acceptance. So now we explain the nature of that love, devotion and light, and of the Sadguru's Word. The essence of the Supreme Being may be reckoned subtler even than the atom and the sub-atomic particle — so fine, so subtle, has it been known within life.

_Pushp vaaspe patla, aisa prem prakash,
roop rekh nahi Jivana, jahan darshan pave das ||5||_

_Kabir paani seti patla, dhunva seti jheen,
pavan beg utaavla, so dost Kabire keen ||6||_

The Sadguru has shown the vision of Parbrahm in the form of the Word: that He is finer even than the fragrance of a flower's scent, subtle, without shape or outline — and yet the devotee-servants of God do behold the vision of this loving light of Parbrahm. Kabirji says: that Supreme Being is thinner than water, finer than smoke, and swifter than the wind — such a Parbrahm is Kabirji's friend; that Supreme Truth I have attained.

_Kabir sant santoshi sarvada, sabad bhed suvichaar,
ta par sadgurukee daya, sahaj seel su mat saar ||7||_

_Kabir Ram baith vichariya, sevak tu shabash,
muj sarikha tuj paas hai, pan tu so nahin muj paas ||8||_

The devotee marked by loving devotion, reflecting on the secret of the Sadguru's teaching, remains ever content, always pleased with whatever he has received. Through the grace of the ever-watchful Sadguru, he attains the natural state and the finest of the finest, a devotion-filled understanding. Seeing such a devotee, God, praising him, says:

Seeing such a devotee of firm character and steadfast faith in the Guru, this thought came to Ram: "O devotee, you deserve praise, for even one such as I remain present and manifest before a devotee like you — but I have no other devotee as steadfast as you; scarcely one such may exist; your like I find nowhere else."

Kabirji says:

_Sajan ham na bisariya, jo tum bahut milaaye,
muj jaisa tere bahut hai, tuj jaisa mere naahi ||38||_

Kabirji says: I went searching for another like God, all the way to the ocean, but the Imperishable Supreme Being was one alone; whereas Kabirs like me existed on the earth, and yet, in the very waters of the ocean too, I saw crores of Kabirs like myself. This astonished me — what kind of Kabir dwells in the ocean, and what kind on its shore, is not something one can grasp; nor what the essence of the Kabir dwelling in a body might be. But then I understood: wherever there is one who receives the Sadguru's teaching, there too are souls who attain God.

In this sakhi, regarding the wondrous nature of God, Kabirji says it cannot truly be understood in what manner God, in His qualified aspect, dwells within the soul, and in what manner He, in His unqualified aspect, also dwells within the soul. Kabirji reflects deeply and repeatedly upon God; one incident is worth considering.

Dadu-ji's guru, Rajab-ji, was a Brahmin. He was on his way to be married; the wedding procession was passing. Someone asked Kabir Sahib, "What is this that is going?" He said, "A tanner is going." Hearing this, Rajab-ji got down from his horse and said, "I am a Brahmin — why do you call me a tanner?" Kabir replied: "Whatever trade a man follows, he is named accordingly — for example, a carpenter goes to fetch wood, but you are going to fetch skin, so you are a tanner" (since, through marriage, he was about to obtain a person of bone and flesh). At this, understanding dawned on him; he touched Kabir Sahib's feet and took his teaching.

Dadu-ji then thought: "Everywhere such special praise is given to Kabirji — are other saints then not gifted?" With this thought he resolved to go where Kabir's name would not be heard. Thinking so, he set out by boat upon the sea; there, in the middle of the ocean, a fish uttered a sound.

_Sant pariksha lenkun, gaye samudra teer,
gyani machhi mukh suni, ratat Kabir Kabir ||39||_ (A saint like Dadu-ji went all the way to the ocean to test Kabirji; but by his own understanding it became clear, on reflection, that even the fish living in the water could be heard chanting "Kabir, Kabir" — that is, everywhere in the world, in every single soul, devotion to God and God's own reflection are present.)

Dadu-ji says:

_Kaun Kabir jalmen base, kaun samudra teer,
sapt dweep nav khandmen, kete hai Kabir ||40||_ (What kind of Kabir-essence dwells in the water, the unqualified, formless aspect of God; and what kind resides on the ocean's shore, the qualified, embodied aspect? On the whole earth, of seven continents and nine divisions, how many such Kabir-forms of God are there?) — so Dadu-ji began to ask. The fish says:

_Sohi Kabir jalmen base, sohi samudra teer,
sapt dweep navkhandmen, ek hi Ram Kabir ||41||_ (The very God-essence present as Kabir in the unqualified aspect is present too in the qualified aspect. Therefore, in the whole created earth of seven continents and nine divisions, the God-essence — Ram-Kabir — is one and the same essence; for God, there is no difference between the qualified and the unqualified.)

When God, praising a devotee like Kabir, said, "One like Me is with you, but no other one like you is with Me," Kabirji said:

_Kabir dhundhat dhundhat main phira, sant samudra teer,
avinashi to ek hai, muse kot Kabir ||9||_ (O Lord! Searching for one like You, I went all the way to the ocean's shore, but You alone are the one Imperishable God like You; while of ones like me, crores were found — devotees like me who worship You with single-minded devotion.)

Saint Dadu has also written a similarly humble sakhi:

_Tumkun hamse bahut hai, hamkun tumse naahi,
Dadukun jani pariharai, tun rahu naina hun maahi ||42||_ (Dadu-ji says: O Lord, before You there are many like me, but before us there is no other merciful one like You. So never abandon a lowly devotee like me — I wish to keep You within my very eyes.)

Yet Kabirji, contrariwise, also says the opposite — it is his nature to speak both crosswise and straight.

_Dware tere Ramji, milahu Kabira mohi,
tain to sabme mili raha, main na milungaa tohi ||43||_ (O God! At Your door, devotees like me will indeed be found; but You pervade everywhere, present within everyone — yet I shall not be able to find You in that "everywhere".)

Thus Kabirji at one time says there is no other God like You in the world, and again says You dwell everywhere in the world — speaking, as it were, in reverse with God. Kabirji, moreover, sets at nought even the gods and other such beings.

_Indralok achraj bhaya, Brahma bada vichar,
Kabira chala Ram pai, kautuk kahar apaar ||44||_ (When such a soul, leaving behind attachment to sense-objects, set out to meet Ram, wonder arose in Indralok — the pleasure-loving gods fell into astonishment; and Brahmaji, absorbed in worldly activity, seeing this soul free of worldly entanglement, fell into deep thought, considering it more fortunate than himself; and a profound wonder occurred everywhere.)

It is said in a doha:

_Mere to tum ek ho, tumhare or anek,
sarovar hansa bohot hai, hansa sarovar ek ||45||_

The lake is one and the swans many, but whichever swan goes to the lake and takes refuge there, the lake surely grants it shelter. The king is one and the queens many, but whichever queen, through body, mind and wealth, conducts herself so as to please the king and truly becomes his — that queen gradually brings the king under her sway, so that gradually the king becomes hers.

_Kabir kaha Kabir jalman base, kaha jalki teer,
kaha Kabir ghatman base, jyun shabad tyun Kabir ||10||_ (My understanding tells me: the Supreme Reality in the form of Kabir dwells in the water, and dwells also on the ocean's shore — that is, there is no difference between the qualified and unqualified, embodied and formless aspects of the divine. So the unqualified God-essence in the form of Ram, and the qualified, embodied form of God as Kabir, are not different; this Ram and Kabir are one and the same.)

_Kabir herat herat heriya, sudh na rahi heraye,
boond samani samudrame, so ku heri jaaye ||11||_

_Kabir herat herat heriya, sudh na rahi heraye,
samudra samani boondmen, so ku hera jaaye ||12||_ (Kabirji says: searching, searching for the divine essence, I searched until, in that search, all awareness itself was lost — for how can it be understood that an ordinary soul became absorbed into a Parbrahm as vast as the ocean? Moreover, how can it be understood that the Supreme Reality, as vast as the ocean, has become contained in a small body like a mere drop — and yet has indeed become contained in that creature?)

For the person who has become free of the sense of duality, and who has offered his all into the Sadguru's words, his natural, virtuous character is now what is essential — that is, the qualities of the "sthitaprajna", the one of steady wisdom, that Krishna described to Arjuna: one whose every desire has, at all times, come to an end; whose mind, fixed upon a single object, need think of nothing else; who is unmoved by happiness or sorrow — upon such a one the Sadguru's mercy and compassion rain down, unceasing.

God says: "Kabir, I must go to devotees like you." For devotees, God is very easily accessible; but for God, obtaining a true devotee is very difficult. That is exactly why Kabirji says it is a matter of great wonder that in the whole ocean, drops of water become absorbed — but here, the entire ocean has become absorbed within a single drop. That is: if the soul, with the support of Parbrahm's Name, relinquishes the body, it attains Parbrahm, becomes absorbed into Him. But here the reverse has happened: Parbrahm, who pervades all moving and unmoving creation, has become absorbed into the tiny, subtle soul. Kabirji asks: what is this? He himself answers:

_Kabir boond samani samudrama, te jaane sab koy,
samudra samana boondmen, te chinhe virla koy ||13||_

_Kabir herat herat he sakhi, main gai samudra teer,
jeti boond samudramen, te te das Kabir ||14||_

_Kabir balihari us doodhki, jame nikase ghiu,
sabad ek Kabirka, so chaar bedka jeev ||15||_

_Kabir dil mila dayal so, tab kachhu antar naahi,
pala gali pani bhaya, yon Harijan Hari maahi ||16||_

_Kabir santka mata ek hai, doojaku ant na paar,
ek sabadmen sab kachhu, santan koti hazaar ||17||_

_Kabir adhar jalechu adhar dhar, adhar aash vishwas,
adhar Kabira hi mile, adhar nirantar baas ||18||_

_Kabir kartam karta na hota, na hota hat aur pat,
tabtha Kabir Ramjan, jine dekhayo ghat ghat ||19||_

_Kabir paani pavan ambar nahi, na hota Omkar,
tabka das Kabir hai, so kaha jane sansar ||20||_

_Kabir sabad teta boliya, je gaya jahan chal,
sabko aap aapne mukhse, jahar kari majal ||21||_

_Kabir vachan hu the paiye, chor sahuku ghaat,
jesi bast bhajanmen, so nikase mukhki vaat ||22||_

Kabirji says: that the soul, like a drop, can become absorbed into the Supreme Being, like the ocean — everyone can understand that. But that the Supreme Being, like the ocean, can also become absorbed into the soul, like a drop — only some rare one, like a Sadguru, can explain that.

That one drop of water is absorbed into the ocean is easy to understand, but that the whole ocean should be absorbed into a single drop is difficult to understand. Yet, for the meditating person, in the matter between soul and Supreme Being, precisely this happens. In the meditating person absorbed in devotion, the inner sky of the heart, the innermost self, is like a single drop — within it he is able to see the Supreme Being, or the whole universe. In a heart that has become pure and illumined, the reflection of the entire universe can be seen. This subject of yoga, or the wholly absorbed devotee, is extremely profound, and so only rare, true devotees can understand it. The supreme devotee says:

_Bartan chhota vast ghana, kaho guru ka kije,
champ dharun to bartan phoote, bahar dharun to chhije ||46||_ (O Guruji! The vessel that is my heart is small, and the substance that is the Supreme Being is abundant — if I press and fill it in, the vessel will burst; if I keep it outside, it spills over. What remedy is there for this? Please show me.)

The Guru says:

_Sejalna sejan deena, sej surat lolai,
sejanvar to Kabirji, bartan kare samai ||47||_

The little bed of the heart, prepared for the Supreme Being to lie upon, is one on which God is made to lie with total absorption. The one who spreads such a bed of absorption is the supreme, most excellent Sadguru, Kabirji — a Guru so capable that he can make the Supreme Being become contained within this vessel that is the heart. The all-pervading, formless Lord — a capable devotee causes Him, in His qualified embodied aspect, to become contained within the Name. The Name of Ram is greater even than Ram himself.

Kabirji says: my attention, searching for God and for others like Kabir, went all the way to the ocean's shore, to the very end — and there it was found that in every single drop of the ocean's water there is only Kabir, Kabir. That is, drop by drop, throughout the whole world, each devotee has been given such power that God must remain subject to them. I am not Kabir alone; every single thing in the world, just like Kabir, holds God in its sway.

Kabirji says: just as the milk from which ghee is obtained is greatly praiseworthy, so too, of the words formed from the fifty-two-lettered alphabet, bad words bring us harm while good words bring us great benefit. Such is the wondrous virtue of this milk that is the alphabet — that the words which come to us as teaching, through the Guru, in the form of God's Name, bring about our well-being. Not only that, but the single word "Ram" that a Sadguru like Kabir has given is so important that, because of it, even the honest-merchant-thief, the four Vedas, receive the gift of life in this world. If the Vedas were to remove a word like "Ram", they would become lifeless. The Vedas have stolen the word "Ram", yet, since they still possess this stolen good, they are able to remain relevant in the world.

Maharaj Jivanji says that the Vedas have stolen the word "Ram":

_Ola jhola Jivana, je sadguru diya bataay,
karma dharmaman Raghupati, je vede dharya chhapaay ||48||_ (Gurudevko Ank 13 — The Sadguru, having resolved the tangled mystery hidden behind the veil, showed us the true essence. That true essence was the Name of Ram, which the Vedas had concealed within the practice of ritual duty — recitations, austerities, vows, pilgrimages, sacrifices and the like — but he opened it up and showed it to us. Thus the Vedas, deceiving through ritual religion, are the "honest-thief".)

Kabirji says: when our inner self becomes united and blended with the merciful God, then no difference remains between the unqualified Supreme Being and the qualified soul — just as water becomes ice, there is no real difference between Hari and Hari's devotee. When the ice of the ego melts, it merges into the water.

Kabirji, on the union of heart with the Merciful One, says in a Holi hymn:

_|| Hori ||
Jab dil milyo dayal so, tab kachhu antar naahi sakhiri || teka ||
Sahaj bhav upaje sahi ho, kahe na koi patiaay,
aham vyadhi sanso hare, aur aavaagavan nasaay ||1||
Surati sarovar gyan jal, naana var tarang,
aapa mitai to mile saain, tujhe mile tero rang ||2||
Ankur birvan phool phal, sab dekhe ek thaanv,
chit chetan kare chete ho, tab kaha le dhariye naav ||3||
Het deep sadguru milai, prem preeti prakash,
jwar virah na paaiya, jako kahe Kabir vilaas ||4||_

O friend! When our inner self becomes united and blended with the merciful God, then no difference remains between us and the formless Supreme Being. Natural love truly arises — were we to speak of it, no one would believe it. The disease of the fault of ego is cured, and the cycle of coming and going departs. In the lake of longing, many beautiful waves of the water of self-realization arise, and one attains the joy of one's own love. The tree of love, its sprout, its flowers and its fruit are all seen in one and the same place. When the awakened soul stirs into consciousness, whose Name should be taken? — then the Sadguru comes to meet us, carrying the lamp that casts the light of loving devotion. But if the pain of the fever of separation is not felt, Kabirji calls that mere pleasure, not true love.

The Saint's teaching is solely for the worship of the one Parbrahm, the Supreme Being; whereas all the other teachings of the Vedas, Puranas and scriptures never come to an end — they are endless. But the saints have taught that the sum total of crores and thousands of kinds of instruction is contained within the single word "Ram-Naam" alone.

"Adhar" — beyond the gunas, transcending them; "duliya" — path; and "ghar", dwelling — the state beyond the body: in Parbrahm, in that state beyond all the gunas, where there is no need even to place trust in any particular quality, Kabir the devotee ever dwells; the devotee remains in a state transcending the three gunas.

When there was neither any kind of Maya in the universe, nor Brahma nor other creators, nor the traffic of coming-and-going and dwelling in the womb, nor even the path of ritual karma — even then, God's saintly ones had existed from time immemorial. Such saints have shown the true nature of this Supreme Being as pervading every body, in vessel after vessel, throughout creation.

Kabirji says: when there was neither wind nor water, nor even Om itself — when in this creation only Parbrahm existed and nothing else — even then, the devotee Kabir was present with Parbrahm; the whole world knows this.

Whatever desires and cravings, whatever feelings arose within a being's inner self, that being's inclinations began to run after those very feelings. In this way each and every soul, through its own inward face, manifested its journey of dwelling in the womb in this world, according to its own feelings.

"Sahukar", the honest merchant, here means one who separates people from the Sadguru's family; and "thief" means one who leads people astray, deceiving them within this three-gunas'd creation — the one who devises the schemes of ritual observance, recitations, austerities, vows, sacrifices and the like, to lead people toward the heavenly realms. Such a person, harbouring deceit, does not speak the truth; he utters scripturally-worded speech only to entice and deceive. From this alone it becomes evident whether he is a thief or a genuine person. But it is the Sadguru who reveals who is true and who is false — for whatever substance a vessel holds, that same substance comes out through its opening.

The Vedas too have practised the trade of "honest-thief". By saying that performing a certain sacrifice yields a certain fruit, and other such enticing, sweet-sounding words, they entangle people in ritual observance. Even the Gita condemns the scholars who take interest in the Vedic path, and the doctrine of the Vedas itself (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 2):

_Yamimam pushpitam vacham prapadyantyavipashchitah,
Vedavadaratah Partha nanyad astiti vadinah ||42||
Kamatmanah swargapara janmakarmaphalapradam,
kriyavishesha bahulam bhogaishwaryagatim prati ||43||_ (O Arjuna! Those absorbed in worldly desires, who consider heaven and heavenly pleasures the supreme, sole attainable good, become attached to the fruit-promising words of the Vedas and say there is nothing better than this. Such undiscerning people, in order to attain the enjoyment- and opulence-bearing states that yield the fruits of action across births, describe the many kinds of ritual actions set forth in the flowery, fruit-praising language of the Vedas — words that display abundant temptations of reward — and keep speaking such sweet, enticing words.)

Thus the Vedas too have practised the work of deceiving through sweet talk. But Sadguru Jivanji has exposed openly the theft and concealment that the Vedas have committed.

_Ola ola Jivana, jai sadguru diya bataay,
karma dharmaman Raghupati, je vede dharya chhapaay ||13||_ (Gurudevko Ang — what the Sadguru showed and revealed was the Lord Raghupati, whom the Vedas had kept hidden within the practice of ritual religion; that he brought to light.)

That deceit which confused us and cast us into wandering — the deceit by which the Vedas hid Raghupati within the rites of ritual duty — the Sadguru has revealed the Name of Ram that lay concealed within it.

The point is that a discerning person will immediately understand, from someone's manner of speech, whether that person intends to deceive. Sadguru Maharaj Jivanji has declared that no one should get entangled in the cleverness of the Vedas. It is through speech and conduct alone that a loyal person or a deceiver is recognised.

_Nari kahave piuki, rahai aur sang soi,
jaar purush hirde basai, khasam khushi kyon hoi ||49||_ (A woman calls herself her husband's wife, but if she keeps lying with another man and a paramour dwells in her heart, how can her husband remain pleased with her?)

One who worships his chosen deity with true faith, and one who secretly worships some other god, will each in time be recognised for what they are.

The Sadguru's words should be like milk, for from milk the finest thing, ghee, is obtained; likewise, if nothing is gained from the Guru's words, they are useless. So Kabirji says there is not much substance in the words of the Vedas — not all of the Vedas is acceptable. With each single word of Kabir's, as it were, the incomplete gurus, pandits and mullahs of the Vedic tradition are struck down. The devotee's heart and meditation are joined with Parbrahm; there is no gap between the devotee and God — just as ice melts and becomes water, there is no fundamental difference between ice and water, their inner composition being one and the same. Such is the relationship between Hari and Hari's devotee. Saints proceed solely on the basis of the Sadguru's words; there is no difference of opinion among them, however many thousands of saints there may be — whereas among scholars and pandits there is never unanimous agreement (the Narada Bhakti Sutra states that devotees of single-minded devotion are foremost, Sutra 67).

Kabirji says: when there was neither earth nor sky, I was present with Parbrahm, contained within Him — that is, at the time of dissolution the entire universe remains contained within Him, and creation is generated out of Him.

To those who hold faith in various scriptural doctrines, Kabirji says: when there was neither wind, water, nor sky, and not even Om — after that period of dissolution, creation came into being. Who then was there to witness it, or from where did creation arise? The various things we talk about today have no real meaning. Therefore, instead of delighting in false illusion, one should seek out the true Sadguru and take shelter in Hari.

Kabirji says: as is the mind, so is the word that is spoken — from the mouth of one with impure intent comes the denial of Parbrahm, while from the mouth of a saint no foul word ever comes. In this way every person is recognised by his manner of speech; it is through utterance alone that a thief and an honest merchant are recognised. As is a person's occupation and his deed, so is the word that comes from his mouth. Even if the word "Ram" comes from the mouth of a thief or a base person, it goes to waste, and in time he is recognised for what he is.

_Kabir bhaari kahun to bohu darun, halka kahun to jooth,
main kaha janun Ramkun, nayana kabahun na deeth ||23||_

_Kabir deetha hai to kis kahun, kaha kon patiyaaye,
Hari jaisa hai taisa hi hai, tun harkhi harkhi gun gaaye ||24||_

_Kabir aisa adbhoot jan katho, adbhoot rakhi lo koye,
Ved kateb na lakha, so kaha kon patiyaaye ||25||_

_Kabir hase na bole unmani, chanchal mahela maar,
kahe Kabir bheetar bheda, sadguru ke hathiyaar ||26||_

_Kabir Ram beth vichariya, sakhi kaho Kabir,
bhavsagarmen doobtan, ko ek paave teer ||27||_

Kabirji says: how can I say what Shri Hari is like? If I call Him heavy, mighty and weighty, I am greatly afraid; if I call Him light, simple and innocent, I would be speaking falsely, for these two eyes of mine have never seen Him. To behold Parbrahm one needs divine sight — without that, Hari cannot be seen.

And even if I had seen Him, to whom could I tell it, for who would believe me? Today is not an age for the truthful — it is the hypocrite and the false pretender who is worshipped. So, rather than asking what Hari is like, let Him be whatever He is — devotees should set aside all such disputes and simply sing His praises out of love for Shri Hari alone.

No one will be able to say that He is such-and-such a wondrous being — let everyone simply hold that He is wondrous, for such a Being has not even been described in the Vedas or in the Kateb (the other scriptures) — that is, they too do not know Him, so who then can explain Him? Of Parbrahm... [text continues onto the next part]

To know or understand it, no yogic technique of Aum nor any tantric knowledge is of any use — it is attained only when, through the Sadguru's word, the doors of the heart within are pierced open. ||25||

Baba Kabirji says: when the Sadguru's weapon-like instrument of love-imbued devotion pierces through the sense-vices lodged within a disciple, and he attains the unmani state, such a disciple no longer sets his heart on sense-pleasures and worldly enjoyment. He takes no delight in the objects of maya, because within his heart, owing to loving devotion, the restlessness, agitation and eagerness of the pain of separation are exceedingly intense. ||26||

Unmani is the state in which the soul and the mind become one, so that one is freed from maya and becomes wholly devoted to God. Yogis call it the fifth and final state — beyond waking, dream, deep sleep and turiya — the state beyond turiya, or the unmani state; in that same way the loving devotee too becomes free of maya. Thus the Sadguru's word is like the manifest form of God Himself. The definition of unmani is given in the Hathayoga Dipika:

_Shankh dundubhi nadam cha na shrunoti kadacha na, kashth vagyayate deh unmunyavasthaya dhruva ||12||_ (One does not hear even the sound of the conch or the war-drum; the body becomes like wood, firmly steadied in the unmani state.)

Meaning: [continuing the earlier passage] — When it occurred to God how, given maya's coverings, His devotees would be saved and would attain the far shore of the ocean of birth and death, God sat in peace, reflected, and commanded Sadguru Kabir: Kabir, go to this earth and, through sakhis (devotional couplets), shabdas and the like, give teaching and tell devotees about true devotion, so that some worthy souls, drowning in the ocean of existence, may be rescued from it and attain Me. ||27||

This sakhi appears in the Parcharee (hagiographic account) of Krishnadas. There, while explaining to Krishnadasji the meaning of Ramkabir, Jivanji Maharaj, speaking about Kabir, showed that this Sadguru was sent to this earth by the grace of the Guru to deliver devotees. It shows what feeling God has for His devotee. Just as, out of concern for the deliverance of devotees, Ram commanded Kabir to give teaching, in the same way one sakhi also pertains to Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj:

_Sainye shabad pukariya, tun sun re Jivandas, nij janaku parmodhake, lavo hamare pas ||50||_ (God called out and gave this command: O Jivandas, listen — teach My own worthy devotees and bring them to Me.)

In the Parcharee of Jivanji Maharaj it is said —

_Ek same Hari karuna kini, Jivandasaku agya dini, vege jao tum karo prabodhu, sab santanaki lijo sodhu._ (Once God showed grace and commanded Jivanji: go quickly, give teaching, and take care of all the sants.)

_Kabir tirath varat vakh veladi, rahe chohe jug chhahe, kabire mul nikandiya, so kon halahal khae ||28||
To kul kabiro pragata, tab vede kiya vichar, harijansu kari vinati, hamkun rahene do sansar ||29||_

(The poison-spreading creeper of pilgrimage-places and vows — which throws one into the hell of sense-desires — has spread its tendrils on every side across all four ages, casting its shade everywhere. But Sadguru Kabir has uprooted this pilgrimage-and-vow creeper entirely, root and all — that is, he made people give up pilgrimages and vows completely. So then, who would fall into the trap of this fierce poison laid down by a creeper whose very root has been destroyed? ||28|| In the community of sants who propagated devotion to Vishnu among the devotee lineage, when devotees were being caught in the trap of Vedic ritual karmakand — the trap of both the honest and the deceitful among the Vedic knowers — God, moved by concern for His devotees, manifested Sadguru Kabir on this earth. From the time Kabir began, in Kashi, to break the net of ritual karmakand, the Vedic ritualists who led people into ritual worship grew frightened and thought: our power will not prevail against these propagators of Vishnu-bhakti. So these Vedic followers pleaded and entreated the Harijans (devotees), begging: cast a little grace upon us too, so that we too may somehow get a lease of life and be allowed to remain in this world. ||29||)

When Kabirji manifested in Kashi and drove out the path of ritual karmakand, Jivanji Maharaj, as stated in the Parcharee of Krishnadas, records what Shyamdasji wrote —

_Tab kashime pragate ai, karma marag sab diyo bahai._ (When Ram commanded Kabir, he manifested in Kashi and swept away the entire path of ritual karmakand.)

In the Gyan Mahima of Shyamdasji Maharaj it is said —

_Tehi ausar Kabir pragat bhayeu, bharam karam aur sabhi gayeu._ (At that critical time when pilgrimage, vows and ritual karmakand held sway, Kabirji manifested and dispelled all the delusions of ritual religion.)

*(Kabir Ram beth vichariya: there is doubt as to whether this sakhi is truly Kabirji's own. It is an imagined story in which a dialogue takes place between Kabirji and Parbrahm Ram about how the soul can cross over — Kabirji gives the answer. Since Jivanji Maharaj is discussing this very subject here, this sakhi is quoted at this point.)

Ram, after deep reflection, said to Kabirji: O Kabir, tell the people trapped in worldly maya, with true proof, so that some genuine, worthy souls may cross this ocean of existence — and tell them how they may cross it — go into the world and explain it through the evidence of sakhis and shabdas.

Kabirji says: in the world, man wanders to many pilgrimage places, keeps vows and restraints, and wishes to live his life relying on poison — that is, on the poisonous plant of ritual karmakand — but I have utterly destroyed, root and all, this whole poisonous forest-plant of pilgrimage.

When Kabirji manifested in Kashi, the Veda (the Brahmins learned in the Veda) reflected on the path of ritual and thought that they would no longer be able to remain in Kashi. So the devotees of Shri Hari made this plea: allow us too to remain in the world. Because —

_Guru Kabir jyan vidit hai, bhakti mukti datar, jiv mulavan karane, aye jagat mojhar ||51||_ (It is known everywhere in the world that Sadguru Kabirji is the bestower of devotion and liberation; he has come into the midst of this world to grant souls liberation.)

_Riddhi siddhi hamma base, jahan mage tahan det, harijan Hari bhajo jivana, ham hi kahet he net.
Je je kar bhayo jivana, jab pragate das Kabir, karma dharma sab katke, pragat kiye Raghuvir.
Ola jhola jivana, je Sadguru diya batay, karma dharmame Raghupati, je vede dharya chhapay.
Tin lokamen tattvatha, so Sadguru diya batay, kund adavis jivana, je janke diya chhoday.
Shesh sahasra samukh je jape, so sala lakho Hanuman, so Sadguru kahyo jivana, je Gori patiko dhyan.
Kushal padi re jivana, jab Sadguru pakade hath, anek janam ramanam bin, baval dini bath ||35||_

_Chhelo janam bhayo jivana, jab Sadguru diyo updesh, sant samagamamam malyo, Ayodhya tano naresh ||36||
Asht sidh nav nidhi jivana, jahan Sadguru shabad vishvas, sol kalasu shamalo, jahan Hari ke nij das ||37||
Nabhi kamal Brahma hava, so Gokul mahi Goval, mor pichchh shir dhundhachi, so jivan vraj pratipal ||38||_

(Riddhi and siddhi — powers and treasures — dwell in us, and give wherever asked; O Harijan, worship Hari, Jivana — we ourselves only say "not that, not that." Whatever came to be, Jivana, when the servant Kabir manifested — having cut away all ritual and religion, he made Raghuvir manifest. Whatever shelter, Jivana, the Sadguru showed us, the Raghupati whom the Veda kept hidden within ritual and religion — the truth of the three worlds, that the Sadguru has shown; the twenty-eight sacred pools, Jivana, from which he freed his devotees. He who is meditated upon by the thousand-hooded Shesh with his thousand faces, whom Hanuman knows as friend — that is the one the Sadguru named, Jivana, on whom even Gauripati Shiva meditates. Good fortune has come, Jivana, now that the Sadguru has taken hold of my hand — for many births, without Ram's name, I clung to a thorny babul tree.

In this life, Jivana, since the Sadguru has given his teaching, this has become the last birth; meeting in the company of sants, I attained the king of Ayodhya. ||36||

Before the Sadguru's word, the eight siddhis and nine treasures are as nothing; the sixteen-arted dark-hued Lord is there, where Hari's own servants dwell. ||37||

He from whose lotus navel Brahma came, he himself, as the cowherd tending cows in Gokul; on whose head is the peacock-feather crown, and around whose neck shines the garland of gunja-berries — that one, Jivana, is Vraj's protector. ||38||)
