This is how Nazar has translated this hymn. Revered Yadunath Maharaj, in the Shubh Sangraha file, has recorded the following note about Gnaniji:

Ramkabir, 2-12-29:

Chi. Chatursinh (Gnaniji), son of Motisinh, king of Jaisalmer (Marwad), when the time came for his marriage, refused his father, saying, "I have not come to rule a kingdom, but to worship God and lead others to worship Him." When many kings sent marriage proposals and each was refused, people began to wonder: since he is refusing the daughters of all these kings, what can be on his mind — is he perhaps going to marry a girl from outside the caste? To settle this, all the kings gathered together at Udaipur in Mewad. At that time the Rana of Udaipur was Jasvantsinh; he sent a proposal to Jaisalmer for his own daughter, Gangabai. The king of Jaisalmer persuaded the prince that a proposal from such a good family could not be turned down. Chatursinh refused, but when his father would not agree, he asked that the wedding turmeric (pithi) be applied only to the thumb of his right hand. The wedding party (jaan) went to Udaipur for the marriage, but as soon as the fourth round of the wedding circumambulation was completed, Gnaniji fled and came to Jaipur.

The account of Jaipur:

The king of Jaipur had earlier been a disciple of a Kanphata ascetic (Kanphatas are of two kinds — those who keep rings in the ear; one kind keeps rings of glass in the ear. In this tradition, when the ear is completely split by a heavy ring, one is to take living samadhi — living samadhi is given). That king had a rule that he would not eat food without first having darshan of his Guru Maharaj or of his ring. The Maharaj's ashram was far outside the city, but at night he would not let any traveller stay there. Yet, if anyone did stay, at night he would take the form of a tiger and kill them. It happened that some old Vaishnav mahatma came there; but this Kanphata mahant told the saint to go back into the city at night. But the saint said, "I will stay here tonight and go in the morning." At night, the king's Kanphata Guru took the form of a tiger and came to kill the mahatma. But because of the radiance of the Vaishnav saint, he could not come near. When he began to make trouble from a distance, the saint sprinkled a handful of water and turned him into the form of a donkey; he also made the ring in his ear, and the ring kept in a box, disappear. In the morning, when the king came for darshan, though he searched for his Guru, the Maharaj could not be found, nor could the ring be found. He then asked the old mahatma, who told him, "Look in the ravines — something may be grazing there." The king saw his own Guru grazing in the form of a donkey and prostrated himself before the saint. He then brought the saint to his palace and asked to take discipleship. The saint agreed on the following conditions: that a temple of Ramji be built on this spot, that his people bring five bundles of firewood every day, and that the king become his disciple. This practice continues to this day. That mahatma had two disciples. Gnaniji Maharaj, having fled from the wedding pavilion, came to the chief disciple of that mahatma, Geshji (Khojiji) Maharaj, and asked to be given initiation (diksha). The Maharaj said, "Here, initiation is given to fakirs, not to the wealthy." Gnaniji took off his own ornaments and took initiation. Then he asked for service to perform; he was given oversight of the temple servants. Afterward he asked for another service, and was given the task of fanning Thakorji. At that time, a ship belonging to one of the Maharaj's disciples was sinking, and Gnaniji, perceiving the inclination of his Guru's mind, showed him the trick of, after placing the crown on the image, also placing the garland the right way. Because of this, the Guru named him Gnaniji. He was then given leave to go and see the world, and was given seven things: 1. the invisible cap — the quilt of knowledge (Gyan-godadi); 2. the boon of fearlessness (abhay-vadan); 3. the knowledge of reviving the dead (mrut sanjivani vidya); 4. the knowledge of restoring severed limbs (angabhang vidya); 5. the power to make one's word come true (vachan siddhi); 6. the Varun mantra; and seventh, that he should then go to Shuklatirth. There he was to meet Nirvan Sahib and Kabirji. Kabir Sahib was to show him that there was no solitary place for him to stay; so, by the Varun mantra, land was to be sought near the Narmada, and Dharmadas was to grant him the island. Nirvanji warned him about Surat. There, harassment by Muslims was to occur, and Gnaniji was to be saved; Gnaniji was to go to Manipur. He was to live between the slaughterhouse quarter and the courtesans' quarter, where he would be persecuted. Seven hundred and fifty were to be brought back to life, and the sugar of the caravan-trader (vanjara) was to be turned to salt. The Muslim soldiers were to seek him out, and among them the Sultan's soldier was to die. On this there is still to this day a dreadful shrine (dargah) built by hand. In Register No. 283, in the book on the pilgrimage of Hindustan, on page 55, it is written: "Here the king is a Yaduvanshi Rajput. King Rao Jesal founded this city in the year 1156 CE. The king has the honor of a 15-gun salute."

Natvarlal, the 15th successor of Gnaniji's lineage at Mota Sanja, writes on page 100 of a long letter that he wrote: "I am writing this from what is written in the hand of Bapuji Ramkishandasji.

Note taken from the vahivancha's ledger:

Birthplace: Prayagraj (Ramanandji), a Kanyakubja Brahmin, the founding figure (mool purush) of the Galta seat of Jaipur, a Jagadguru, born Samvat 1356, Magh Vad 6, Sunday. Disciple of Ramanandji was Anantanandji; disciple of Anantanandji was Gesji, also called Khojiji; and the disciple of Khojiji was Shri Maharaj Gnaniji, also called Gnanacharya, through the seat at Mota Sanja. (This birth date may be that of Khojiji; he may have been a Brahmin.)

Vahivancha Keshavray, in an inland letter dated 4-1-58 written to Ramkishandas, the Mahant of Mota Sanja, has recorded the genealogy of Gnaniji; in it he writes:

'The institution (sansthan), village Sanja, taluka Jhagadia, district Bharuch, via Ankleshwar, post Sanja. The founding figure, Shri Gnaniji Maharaj, first arrived there in Samvat 1968.'"

Natvarlal writes on page 99 of his long letter:

Having set out from Jaisalmer, Gehji Maharaj set out together with Gnaniji Maharaj. The king of that region followed the Jain faith. They were staying overnight in the forest of some kingdom. That king had gone out hunting, and as evening approached he lost his way. Gnaniji and Gehji Maharaj were in the forest at that time; the king came to Gnaniji and Gehji Maharaj and said, "I wish to stay here for the night — if you will let me, I shall stay." Gnaniji said, "If you wish to stay, then stay." So the king tied up his horse and got down. Gnaniji then told the king, "Come, please eat." But the king said, "I follow the Jain faith, and since the day is about to end, I shall not eat." Then Gnaniji lifted up the served plate and held it back, so that it seemed to the king that there were still two ghadis [about 48 minutes] of daylight left. The king said, "There are still two ghadis of daylight, so let me eat." The king then sat down to eat, and by the time he finished eating and rose, he realized that two ghadis of the night had already passed. The king then thought, "This must be some miraculous person." So the king said to Gnaniji, "Please stay here, and take whatever you need from us — only please stay here." But Gnaniji said, "It is good for a sadhu to keep moving on." So Gnaniji Maharaj set off from there and came to Jaipur. Since the king of Jaipur's Guru was a Kanphata, Gnaniji lay down in the outskirts of Jaipur, having lit a dhuni (sacred fire). The Kanphata then thought to himself, "This must be some miraculous person, and if any miracle of Gnaniji Maharaj becomes known, the king will remove me from the position of Guru." So the Kanphata sent someone to tell Gnaniji, "It would be better if you went elsewhere from here." Then Gnaniji Maharaj and Geshji Maharaj tied up the burning dhuni in a cloth, took it, and went far away, and set the burning dhuni down there and stayed. But the Kanphata thought to himself, "It would be good if I killed this holy man." So at night he sent, by means of a mantra, a stone weighing twelve maunds. Gnaniji realized that this stone had been sent to kill him, so Gnaniji raised his tongs (chipiyo), and the stone broke into pieces. Gnaniji then thought that he too should show some miracle. So, by mantra, Gnaniji brought under his own bedding the rings of all the Kanphatas, from the senior-most down to the junior-most; but he left in place the ring of the senior Kanphata, the king's own Guru, and instead turned him into a donkey. In the morning, when the king went for the darshan of his Guru, he could not find him. So he asked someone, and was told that some holy man had come to the edge of the village, and that his Guru might have gone to him. So the king, searching for Gnaniji, came to him and asked. Gnaniji Maharaj said, "Brother, your Guru must have turned into a donkey." The king then saw a donkey grazing, and recognized it by the ring in its ear. He then thought: "If my Guru cannot even save himself, how can he save me or grant me liberation?" And he said, "I do not want such a Guru — my Guru is Gnaniji." This much I know, and this much I write. — Written by J. U. Natvarlal, page 102 of his letter.

Excerpt from the newspaper "Pratap," dated 11-7-1974, Ashadh Vad 6, Thursday.

"Let us solve the historical puzzle of 'Bava Ghor' (While on personal work in Rajpipla, the enthusiastic researcher of the college there, Dr. Kantikumar Bhatt (M.A., Ph.D., Sahityaratna), spoke about the details he had gathered on 'Bava Ghor.' These have been presented here for reading. Researchers throughout Gujarat are especially invited to present a verified history on this subject. — Editor.

In Bharuch district, near Jhagadia, there is a village named Ratanpur. Up until the fourteenth century of the Vikram era, it was a large, prosperous town. Nearby there is a hill known as the 'Bava Ghor' hill. On that hill is the tomb (majar) of 'Bava Ghor.' Investigating who Bava Ghor was, various different accounts are found. These accounts differ so much from one another that no single common fact can be established from them.

Shri Ramanlal Shah of Ranipara village, near Jhagadia, in his account of Gnaniji, has identified Bava Ghor as Gnaniji's bodyguard. This Gnaniji was originally a prince of Jaisalmer. Moved by a spirit of renunciation, he fled from the wedding altar and came to the site of Kabirvad. There he took initiation from Kabir Sahib. His seat is at Mota Sanja, very close to Bava Ghor. The king of Jaisalmer had sent the bodyguard Bava Sahib to search for him. When he came here, he was practising yoga in the thicket of Shulpaneshwar. Despite his father's efforts, he did not return. Baba Sahib stayed here along with Gnaniji's betrothed wife, Gangakuvarba. It is said that the land that was given to this Baba Sahib in Jaisalmer still runs in the name of his descendants to this day. No other evidence is found to confirm this account.

The second account is entirely different from this one........"

Natvarlal's letter, on page 111, records:

Dictated by Prahladdasji, disciple of Kundandasji:

Four accomplished ones (siddha purush) came from Uttarkhand — Gnaniji Maharaj, Kabirji, Nirvan, and Tejanand. Kabirji remained on the island (bet) of Kabirvad in the Narmada. Before going to Mota Sanja, Gnaniji Maharaj stayed for a while where there was then forest. Tejanand went to Kharvasa, and Nirvan Sahib made his abode in Surat.

Gnaniji Maharaj began his devotional practice (bhajan) and, in order to bathe, built a well; water rose up from the ground of its own accord, over the parapet, and flowed out. Gnaniji Maharaj used to bathe every day from this well that he had built; the well still stands there.

(Note: This is written on page 37 of the letter.)

_Pani chhe amap patalka, nicha daman kup_
_Bhajanke pratapse, Varundev aaya up ||11||_
(Meaning: There is immeasurable water in the netherworld, lying deep below the well; but by the power of devotional practice, that water — Varun Dev, the deity of water — rose up to the top of the well.)

After cleaning his teeth with a neem twig, he planted it split into two; it is said to still be alive — that neem is sweet in taste, and the split into two branches can still be seen. By his power, a fair (melo) is held for a month; there, Udabhagats and sadhu-saints gather with great devotion. The fair is held from Posh Sud 11. Groups of devotees come to the fair from far away — from Surat, Charotar, Vadodara, and Bharuch districts — and there is great rejoicing and celebration. After Gnaniji Maharaj took samadhi, Rai Gnandevji Maharaj remained as successor. His wife also came here; though he had renounced married life after their marriage, being devoted to her husband (pativrata), she came here, and only when she met Rai Gnandev did she take food and water. Bava Ghor became a disciple.....

In a manuscript obtained from Gnaniji's seat at Mota Sanja, No. 5, page 276, it is written that in Samvat 1444, Shri Gnaniji Maharaj took samadhi here, during the reign of Rajjit Sigji of Nandod. (Note: There is an error in the Samvat date.)

In the third volume of the four large volumes of the Bhaktamal published by Ramanand Pustakalaya, Sudamapuri, Vrindavan, it is shown as though Khojiji himself were Gnaniji. But this institution evidently did not have information about Mota Sanja, and so, in the couplet about the "batak bij ki mand" (banyan-seed), instead of writing "Jan Gnanika sansa mita" (the devotee Gnani's doubt was resolved), they wrote "Khojika sanshay mita" (Khoji's doubt was resolved), and explained the Batak-bij couplet in this way, as follows:

_Batak bijmein vad base, mool daal phal phool_
_Gyani guru parsad te, pakda jab nij mool ||12||_
(from the Gyani Granthavali)
(Meaning: Within the seed of the banyan dwell the banyan tree, its roots, branches, fruit, and flower. Having understood all this by the grace of the Guru, I have taken refuge in the original Supreme Brahman who fashions both the tree and the seed.)

The doubt indeed belonged to both Gnaniji and his Guru Khojiji, but the author of this couplet is Gnaniji himself.

As for the earlier episode concerning the Kanphata written about in connection with Gnaniji, that same episode is shown, in the second volume of the Vrindavan Bhaktamal, in the life-account of Krishnadas Payahari — a Guru in Gnaniji's own Guru lineage — as one where it was Krishnadas who subdued the Kanphata. Thus, many kinds of differing variations are found in the Bhaktamal, but these episodes do belong to these great souls.

In the Bhaktamal, the names of 35 Gurus in total, in the Guru lineage of Jivanji Maharaj, are given. Among them, the life-accounts of 9 Gurus are not found in Nabha Swami's Bhaktamal; but since the Gurus of the lineage after Dwarkadasji belong to five generations later than Nabha Swami, we have already seen, among the information we have about the Gurus from Gnaniji down to Jivanji Maharaj, the accounts of Gnaniji and Dada Sukhji. Thus, of the nine generations of Gurus after Dwarkadas, no mention is found in the Bhaktamal; but let us look at a brief account of those about whom the Bhaktamal does have something written.

Narharidasji:

Once he went for the darshan of Jagannathji. There he thought that if he performed a full prostration (sashtang dandavat) before Thakorji, that much time of darshan would be lost; so instead he bowed with his feet toward the deity. Seeing this as improper conduct, the temple priests (pandas) seized him by the feet and dragged him out of the temple. But by Jagannathji's gracious command, everyone then honored him.

Sariramdasji:

Once, near Chitrakoot, in a village named Tvarra, [he went] to warn the people there...

...had gone. Because the people of that village were hostile to Vaishnavs. He came to the courtyard of one of them, but that wretched man did not even let him stand there, so he went and stayed by the riverbank instead. That day the king's son of that place had died, and they had brought him to the riverbank. He told them: if your king and the villagers pledge, from today, to serve the Vaishnavs, then by the Lord's grace I will bring this boy back to life. When the king, along with the villagers, made a firm pledge — persuaded by his wise ministers — the saint gave the boy the sacred foot-water [charanamrut] and brought him back to life. In this way he awakened that whole region and made its people devotees of Hari.

Krishnadas Payahari:

He lived his whole life on a diet of milk alone, so he came to be called Payahari [the milk-drinker]. Regarding him — just as we saw in the account of Gnaniji Maharaj, where Gnaniji subdued the ear-slit ascetic [kanphata guru] of the king of Jaipur — that same episode is described in the Bhaktamal as having been done by Krishnadas. So for every saint-devotee, different sources hold different views in different places; but here this episode has been attributed to the life of Krishnadasji.

Krishnadasji is said to have been born into the lineage of Dahima (Dadhichi). It is also said that he was an incarnation of Shatrughnaji. Every devotee holds his own guru to be an incarnation of God — such is the loving, reverent devotion of disciples toward their guru. In the same way, the followers of Ramanandji, the Ramanandis, regard him as an incarnation of Ram.

_Ramanand: svayam Ramah pradurbhuta mahi tale_ (Ramanand is Ram himself, who has become manifest upon the earth.)

Krishnadasji observed the vow of never begging [ajachak vrat]. He never held out his hand before those on whose head he had placed his hand [as guru]; hence it is said:

_Jaake shir kar dharyo, tasu kartar nahi adyo ||_ (Before whomever's head he placed his hand upon — that is, whomever he made his disciple — he never held out his own hand to them [to ask anything].)

Karmachandji:

In the village of Devasa in Rajasthan there lived a merchant named Dhanchand. He was miserly by nature, but his wife was generous. Their children did not survive; once, when a son died, he began pulling to have the wife burned along with the son [on the pyre]. At that time Anantanandji, the chief disciple of Ramanand, arrived there; with the sacred foot-water of the saints he brought the son back to life — that very [son] was this Karmachandji. Once, when ascetics were on their way on pilgrimage to Amarnath, Karmachand gave them blankets and woolen wraps; because of this Dhanchand stopped the pilgrims and demanded the wraps back. The sadhus told him: count however many are missing from your shop [and take that many] — but on counting, not a single blanket was missing.

He was devoted to the [Divine] Name, served sadhus, and was steadfast in devotion to his guru. [Footnote: Lucknow Bhaktamal p. 306, Vrindavan Bhaktamal p. 125.]

Gayeshji:

He used to wander about singing the names and glories of the Lord. Once, while meditating on the Lord beneath a dried-up tree, a certain accomplished Shvetambar Jain ascetic of that village began to say, mockingly, that this holy man would remain in samadhi only until this dry tamarind tree turned green. He said this as a taunt. But the Lord, to protect the honor of His saint, truly made the tamarind tree turn lush and green at once. Then that Jain ascetic, taking his own guru's permission, cast a black-magic spell [mooth] upon Gayeshji — but instead it was his own guru who died from it. At this the man fell at Gayeshji's feet; Gayeshji had mercy on him and brought him back to life. In this way he spread the Vaishnav faith. [Footnote: Lucknow Bhaktamal p. 306, Vrindavan p. 124.]

Yoganandji:

The great souls have held him to be an incarnation of Lord Kapil, the author of the Sankhya philosophy — hence he is known by the name Yoganandji. The Agastya Samhita says:

_Vaishakh krishna-saptamyam mule parigha-samyute || Budhe karke'atha Kapilo Yogando janishyati ||2||_ (On the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Vaishakh, in the Mool nakshatra joined with the Parigh yoga, on a Wednesday under the Karka ascendant, Kapil will be born as Yoganand.)

In Gujarat, the accomplished Brahmin Manishankar performed worship of the Sun in longing for a son. One day the Lord granted a [divine] fruit, which the husband and wife ate; and so, in V.S. 1457, on the seventh day of the dark half of Vaishakh, a Wednesday, under the Mool nakshatra, Parigh yoga, and Karka ascendant, Lord Kapil, the teacher of Sankhya-yoga, came to them as a son. Because of the practice of meditation carried over from his previous birth, at four years of age Yagnesh-Yoganand remained with his eyes half-closed. Once a group of saints arrived; he went with his parents to their darshan, and then, for the first time, opened both his eyes fully to behold them.

Anantanandji:

Shri Avadhoot Pandit worshipped the goddess Saraswati, and she granted him the boon that a son, a partial incarnation of Brahmaji, would be born to him. So in V.S. 1363, on the full-moon day of Kartik, a son was born to Shri Avadhoot Pandit — that very son was Anantanandji. The Agastya Samhita says:

_Ayushman kritikayukta purnimayam dhane shanau || Svayambhuh Karttikasyaddha Anantanando bhavishyati ||3||_ (Long-lived, joined with the Krittika nakshatra, on a full-moon day, with Saturn in the ninth [wealth] house, the self-manifest one shall indeed become Anantanand, in the month of Kartik.)

He appeared in the village of Maheshpur, on the bank of the river Ramrekha near Ayodhya. His father's name was Vishwanathmani Tripathi; they were Sanadhya Brahmins. On every holy festival they used to come to Ayodhya, and so he came to be called Shri Avadhoot Pandit.

His mother died giving birth to him, so the cowherds [gwalas] who were the patrons of Shri Avadhoot Pandit raised and nurtured the child. The cowherds called him Chhannu. Living among the cowherds, he came to think of himself as a cowherd boy [Gwal Lal], and he too grazed cows and calves. In the meditation of Pandit Shyamkishor, the Lord commanded him to raise and educate the boy as his own son; because of the persecution by the Muslims [yavans], Pandit Shyamkishor went to Kashi, where he passed away. Once Ramanandji sounded his conch-shell; hearing it, [the boy] went to Ramanandji and became his chief disciple. Janakiji [Sita], being pleased, placed her hand upon his head. Once, in the region of Sambhar, the king's gardener would not let him pluck guavas; the next day not a single guava remained there, so the king came and took refuge with him.

Ramanand:

He was born in V.S. 1356 and passed away in 1446. He used to study under a certain Dandi Swami. As he was passing by Raghavanand one day, Raghavanand said to him: your life-span is nearly at its end, yet you have not taken refuge in Hari. Hearing this, he took refuge with Raghavanand. Raghavanand, through pranayama, postponed the time of his death, so that he lived a long life. He is held to be an incarnation of Ram. Ramanand's father's name was Punyasadan and his mother's name was Sushiladevi. In matters of food and drink, Ramanandji's forward-looking [reformist] stance differed from that of Ramanuja; his heart's love reached even to the outcastes [chandals]. For this reason his guru gave his consent for him to establish a separate seat [gaddi]; he raised up, to the very sky of dharma, people from the lowest strata — the weaver Kabir, the farmer Dhana, the barber Sena, the Kshatriya Pipa, and the cobbler Rohidas. On his way to Dwarka he stayed at Girnar, where his footprints are worshipped even today. At Abu he established a temple to Raghunathji. In this way he spread devotion far and wide.

Raghavanandji:

Just as Ramanand was held to be an incarnation of Ram, Raghavanand is held to be an incarnation of Vashishthaji. He was Ramanandji's guru. Once a king called him to make his son a disciple; at that very moment, hearing the prayers of two other people [elsewhere], he took on three forms at once and went to all three places. The matter came to light the next day.

Hariyanandji:

He remained ever immersed in the bliss of Hari, so his guru (Shri Yanandacharya) gave him the name Haryanand. He had gone on the chariot-procession [rathayatra] at Jagannathji; when the chariot came to a stop, he told everyone to let go of the chariot [ropes], saying: by the grace of Jagadish the chariot will move by itself.

Devadhipacharya Swami (Devacharya):

While on pilgrimage to Kashi, he was narrating the story of the Yamalarjuna episode beside a tree along the way; the moment the telling was finished, that very tree fell down, and everyone saw a man and a celestial chariot [vimana]. That man bowed at his feet and said: I was a great sinner who had become a tree, having come from hell, and through hearing this tale of Hari I have become free of sin, and now I shall go to the supreme abode. [Footnote: Lucknow Bhaktamal p. 296.]

In the Bhaktamal it appears that Devacharya's guru was Ramanuj. It is likewise shown there that Lalacharya, the son-in-law of Ramanuj, also had Ramanuj as his guru. Therefore, regarding the guru-lineage after Devacharya, the 30th verse [chhappay] of the Bhaktamal gives the guru-lineage as it is stated in the Samagam. In it, the epithet used for Shathkopji is "munivarya supuni shathkop." This is how it appears in the Vrindavan Bhaktamal; the Lucknow Bhaktamal gives the same, but there a dash has been placed between "munivarya" and "sumuni" — which creates the illusion that these might be the names of two separate gurus. But Shathkop is counted right after Vishvaksen, who comes after Lakshmiji; so "munivraj" and "supina" (sumuni) are not names of gurus but epithets used for Shathkop himself. Thus there is some confusion in the guru-lineage after Devacharya. So, after Devacharya, we shall look next at Lalacharya, whose guru was his own father-in-law, Ramanuj. Further, after Devacharya, the Samagam gives Devacharya's guru's name as Ramanidh, his guru as Ramaanuj, his guru as Saraswati Bhatt, and his guru as Lalacharya — and it also separately states that his guru was Lalacharya. But Lalacharya and Devacharya are both disciples of Ramanuj alone; so now we shall look at Lalacharya. Our purpose here is only to gain a brief acquaintance, from what the Bhaktamal tells us, with devotees such as Lalacharya within this lineage.

Lalacharya:

For Lalacharya's father-in-law and guru, Ramanuj, verse 33 [chhand] of the Bhaktamal uses the word "acharaj-jamat" [the acharya's son-in-law]; this has been mistakenly understood as though Lalacharya's guru's name was "Acharya Jayamat." But that is not the name of a guru — Lalacharya is the son-in-law of Ramanujacharya.

Knowing that Lord Krishna is pleased with a Vaishnav who wears a garland of holy beads [maladhari], [Lalacharya] used to honor maladhari Vaishnavs greatly. Once the dead body of a maladhari was seen floating down the river Kaveri; Lalacharya's wife, who had gone there to fetch water, was mocked by her friends, who said: who is this — your younger or elder brother-in-law? The wife came home and expressed her distress before her husband. Lalacharya, recognizing him as a fellow disciple of his guru [guru-bhai], had him seated in a palanquin, performed his cremation, and invited Brahmins for a meal — but the Brahmins did not come. When they went to Ramanuj about this, Ramanuj summoned the attendants of Vaikunth, the Hari-jans, who came and began to partake of the offering [prasad]. Everyone saw them eating but no one saw them leave. After they had finished eating, the Brahmins wanted to mock them, but could not manage to; but when they learned that these had all been residents of Vaikunth, they repented, and, picking up grain by grain the leftover prasad that had fallen on the ground, they ate it, and became disciples of Lalacharya.

Ramanuj:

Ramanuj was an incarnation of Sheshnag. The word "sahasrasya" [thousand-faced], used in verse 31 [chhappay] of the Bhaktamal, means the thousand-faced Lord Shesha. Ramanuj was born to Mangalamayi, wife of the Asuri Keshavbhatt of Perumbar (Bhutpuri), on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra in V.S. 1074; he was named Lakshman (Lakshman too is held to be an incarnation of Shesha). His guru, Goshtipurnacharya, gave him a mantra with the instruction to keep it secret within his heart; repeating it, he had a vision of Ramchandraji. Seeing the power of this mantra, moved with compassion for all beings and wishing that everyone attain God, he climbed up onto the temple gate-tower [gopuram] and proclaimed the mantra aloud in a great voice — even those who were asleep [nearby] absorbed it. His first chief disciple was Kulatarak. Ramanuj, climbing the gopuram (gateway), cried out the mantra aloud even though it was meant to be kept secret, so that an unprecedented sound spread everywhere.

Since Sheshnag chants the name of Ram with a thousand mouths, the utterance of the words Ram-Ram produces the resounding echo known as "rankar." [Ramanuj] took upon his own head the weight of having transgressed his guru's command, and because of this his guru, deeply moved, and the Lord too, were exceedingly pleased with him. There is a verse regarding this very incarnation of Sheshnag:

_Prathamo'nantarupashcha tritiyo Lakshmanastatha || Dvitiyo Balaramashcha kalau Ramanujo munih ||4||_ (Meaning: the first form is Ananta [Shesha], the third is Lakshman, the second is Balaram, and the fourth, in the Kali age, is the sage Ramanuj — all of these are incarnations of Shesha.)

On page 117 of the Samagam, the guru-lineage from Ramanand's disciple Pipaji down to Ramanuj is given, and that is correct.

Yamunacharya (Jayamat Muni):

Ishwarmuni, son of Nathmuni, is Yamunacharya's father. He appeared in V.S. 1010 in Madra [Madura]. He is held to be an incarnation of the Lord's throne [simhasan].

When Nathmuni took sanyas, Yamunacharya was ten years old, and by that time his father too had already departed for the other world. So his upbringing, education, and so on took place under the care of his grandmother and mother. Around that time, at the court of the Pandya king, there lived a great scholar named Kolahal, who used to defeat everyone in debate. Hearing of Yamunacharya's fame, he sent him a challenge to a scriptural debate. As Yamunacharya was arriving in a palanquin, the queen, seeing his divine radiance, said that this scholar would defeat Kolahal. A wager was made between the king and queen: if the queen's word proved true, half the kingdom would have to be given away. Kolahal Pandit said: I will refute whatever you say. Yamunacharya made three statements: 1. Your mother is kaakvandhya [a mother of only one child]. 2. King Pandya is a great master of statecraft and a knower of dharma. 3. The queen is a supremely chaste and devoted wife [pativrata]. Kolahal Pandit lost the debate, and the king had to give half his kingdom to Yamunacharya. His grandfather Nathmuni, before dying, had entrusted his care to Rammishra. On beholding Shri Ranganathji, such deep devotion arose in him that he surrendered everything at Ranganath's feet and stayed on there, spreading devotion widely.

Rammishraji:

He was a disciple of Nathmuni. He was a great scholar, but he only ever noticed others' faults. Because of this, even after countless spiritual practices, his mind found no peace. Once he went to serve the great soul Pundarikakshaji and said: Lord, my mind stays unsteady, I have no firmness in my own dharma — please show me a remedy. Pundarikakshaji said: the remedy that would bring you firmness is one you are not practicing. Mishraji then said: tell me, and I will surely do it. He was given a period of six months; then the Acharya said: mental weakness is removed by hiding others' faults and revealing one's own. From that time Rammishraji's life changed completely. He began to see virtue in everyone, and held goodwill and compassion for all. Seeing the all-pervading Paramatma in everyone, Nabhaji used the phrase "Rammishra Rasrashi" [Rammishra, the abundance of divine essence] for Rammishra — that is, the Paramatma is of the nature of rasa [divine essence]; he was one whose daily experience was an abundance of the bliss born of direct realization.

Pundarikakshaji:

He was the son of Mahapurna Swamiji and a disciple of Shri Ramanujacharyaji.

Shri Nathmuniji:

He was Yamunacharyaji's grandfather. He resided in Madura city in South India.

He was a foremost scholar of the Vedas, the scriptures, the Puranas, and so on. He was a great siddha, that is, a jivanmukta [liberated while living]. "Mangalmuni" is an epithet used for Shri Nathmuni. So, in the Samagam, through a mix-up, this Mangalmuni has been mistakenly taken as the name of a separate person and given as Nathmuni's guru — that may be an error. According to our handwritten manuscript no. 37, p. 137, and handwritten manuscript no. 220, p. 177, Munivraj is a disciple of Vishvaksen, and Supin is a disciple of [Muni]vraj.

Bopdev (of the Bhagavat):

In childhood he was of dull intellect and could remember nothing. Even his teachers gave up trying to teach him and expelled him from school. Sorrowful, he was walking along and, growing tired, sat down to rest on the edge of a well. Some women had come there to draw water; the wear of their ropes had cut a groove into the stone. Seeing this, he took heart: surely, he thought, I too shall attain success. Thinking this, he returned to his studies. As a result, his intelligence grew immensely — whatever text he took up, he would commit to memory by mere repetition. Nabhaji writes that out of the eighteen Puranas, Bopdev extracted the essence of essences — the very butter, so to speak — in the form of the four verses [chatuh-shloki] of the Bhagavat. It is said that in the library of Kashmir, the Muslims burned so many texts that the fire did not go out for six months; among them the Bhagavat Purana too was lost, and its loss caused an uproar among the Vaishnavs. Bopdev had the entire text memorized from beginning to end. At the Vaishnavs' request he wrote it out again from memory. Nabhaswami says, in verse [chhand] 17, that this Bhagavat Purana is the butter — the essence — of the eighteen Puranas. He composed many works on the Bhagavat Purana, of which the Harilila and the Muktaphal are the best known. The Harilila contains the dialogues of the Bhagavat, and the Muktaphal is a collection of its teachings.

Shathkopji:

He is held to be an incarnation of Vishvaksen, the Lord's attendant [parshad]. Seeing devotion in decline in the Kali age, the Lord commanded Garud and his attendant Vishvaksen to take incarnation on earth; both were born in the Pandya country after thirteen years of the Kali age had passed. His father's name was Karimaran, who held a high office at the court of the king of Pandya. His wife Udayanange was also devoted. Seeing an image of the Lord, she became so entranced that she prayed for a son just like Him. The Lord gave her a dream that His own attendant, Vishvaksen, would be born as her son. He was named Shathkop because he had turned his wrath [kop] upon shath — that is, upon worldly illusion [maya]. His other name was Nimmalvar. Like Rohidas, for ten days he too refused to take his mother's milk, so they left him near a temple of the Lord.

There was an old tamarind tree there; in a hollow of it he remained in unbroken samadhi for sixteen years. The Lord gave him a mantra. Madhukavi asked him five questions; in answer he gave the teaching of the Sahasragita, a hymn of a thousand verses. He composed four works. He remained absorbed especially in the mood of devotion to Radha; in his verses one finds the graceful expression of the pathos of separation [viraha] and the ornamentation of love [shringar]. In separation he would wail, dance, sing, and fall into swoons; once, in the episode of Uluka-bandhan (Indra, the fool), he remained in a swoon for six months. Lalitaji revived him back to consciousness. He remained in this world for 35 years. He has been given the epithet "munivar supuni" (also, "munivar") — but through a misunderstanding, the Samagam takes "Supin" and "Munivar" as separate names and holds them to be his gurus, which is an error.

Vishvaksen:

The Lord's principal attendants [parshads] number sixteen; these attendants' form resembles that of the Lord. The only difference is that they do not bear the Shrivatsa mark or the Kaustubh jewel. Among these sixteen attendants, Vishvaksen holds the foremost place. Each of these attendants possesses the strength of ten thousand elephants. [Scripture] calls the children of demons Prahladaji [meaning: souls capable of the same devotion as Prahlad]. To please the Lord, it is not enough to become a Brahmin, a deity, or a sage, or to be of good conduct and manifold learning; nor is austerity, sacrifice, physical or mental valor, or the observance of great vows sufficient. Rather, the Lord is pleased only by loving devotion [prem-bhakti]. Everything else besides is mere mockery and deceit. Such is the selfless, love-natured devotion found in these attendants of the Lord. These attendants are eternally accomplished, that is, eternally liberated. They are ever engaged in the Lord's service, remain absorbed in meditation upon Him, and, out of loving affection, look after His devotees.

Lakshmiji:

In verse [chhand] 9 of the Bhaktamal, among those counted as "Harivallabh" — those most dear to the Lord — Lakshmiji and others are named. Among those who serve the Lord's feet, Lakshmiji is foremost. Jivanji Maharaj tells us to strive only to dwell at the Lord's lotus feet. Not everyone is granted the merit to dwell at these lotus feet.

_Hari bhagatkun Jivanaa, chaar mugat vishraam || sant bhagatki kaahaa kahu, charan kamal nij naam ||13||_ (To devotees of Hari, O Jivan[ji], the four kinds of liberation are but a resting place; what more shall I say of the devotion of saints — theirs is [dwelling in] the very name of [His] lotus feet.)

Sant [The Saint]:

It is only through service to saints that one attains to dwell at the Lord's lotus feet. When one merely performs devotion to the Lord alone, the Lord grants the four kinds of liberation, but does not grant rest at His lotus feet. Lakshmiji too enjoys the privilege of the Lord's lotus feet, and the reason for this too is that she remains a maidservant of the saints. Narsinh Mehta has sung of this — Panchratnamala, p. 704, in Raga Ashavari:

_Lakshmiji ardhaangana maari, te maaraa santni daasi re |_ (Lakshmiji is my consort — [yet] she is the maidservant of my saint.)

Narayan:

In the Mahabharata, in the Narayaniya episode of the Mokshadharma [section], there is a description of this. Narada, on a long journey to the north, went to the shore of the Ocean of Milk; on the way lay Shvetadvip [White Island], whose inhabitants worshipped Narayan, that is, Vishnu. It is also said that Narayan, that is, Vishnu, is Himself the infinite Brahman, from whom the twenty-five elements/principles of Sankhya arose. In the Narayana and Atmabodha Upanishads, "Om Namo Narayana" is given as the mantra — and it is also the initiation mantra of the Vaishnav tradition.

Adhyaruji Maharaj has said, in the Padam Ghol:

_Vaikunthnaath jahaan avatarya re, devataane sudh ||_ (Where the Lord of Vaikunth took incarnation — even the gods came to know of it.)

So Padmanabh is held to be an incarnation of Vishnu. And in the Harsh Bhavan he says:

_Govind Krishna Moraari tu re, ane Naaraayan ne Raam ||_ (You are Govind, Krishna, Morari — and you are Narayan and Ram.)

He says further as well. Thus, on the basis of our own guru-lineage, we hold Lord Padmanabhji to be an incarnation of Narayan — and also as that very Narayan shown within our guru-lineage, our original Sadguru, the Lord Parbrahm — the refuge of Parbrahm Paramatma that has come to us through the grace of sadgurus such as Namdev-Kabir.

The guru-lineage given in the Samagam is recorded, in doha form, in handwritten manuscript no. 37, page 137, and handwritten manuscript no. 220, page 277, listing all the gurus as follows:

Doha:

_Shri Ramanandi sampradaa, aacharaj Lakshmiji jaan || vaahi prataap bal, Vishvaksen balvaan ||1||_
_Vishvaksenke Munivraj, Supinke Shathgop bhaye || Bopdevke Bhagavat jun Mangalke, Nathmuni bhaye ||2||_
_Pundarikke Ramamisar, Jamatke Ramaanjat || Kulataarik Ramanujke, aacharaj jaamaat ||3||_
_Vaake Lalaacharaj ke Sarasvati Bhatke, Ramaanuke Ramaanidhke || Devaadaasanke Hariaanandji, taake Raadhavaanand ||4||_
_Swami Ramanandji taake Anantanand, unke Jogaanandke || Shri Gesji, teenke, bhaye Krishnachand ke ||5||_
_Pay-aahaari Krishnadasjike, Saariramke Narahardas bhaye || taake sheekh jan Dwarka, teenke jan Gnani bhaye ||6||_
_Sadguru mile Kabirji batak beejki maandme, dekh bhaya man dheer || jan Gnaanikaa sanshay mitya, jab sadguru mile Kabir ||7||_
_Gnaanike paramodhme sukhdaata, Jasvantji bhaye || taake sheekh Gopalji, jan Jivanji updesh diyo ||8||_
_Vidhi nishedh sarav taalke, pan pratit Hari naam vare ||_

(Meaning, in summary: Lakshmiji is the founding acharya of the Shri Ramanandi tradition; from him, by his glorious power, came the mighty Vishvaksen; from him Munivraj; from him Supin; from him Shathgop; from him the author of the Bhagavat, Bopdev; from him Mangalmuni; from him Nathmuni; from him Pundarik; from him Rammishra; from him Jamatmuni; from him Ramanuj; from him Kulatarak; the son-in-law of Acharya Ramanuj was Lalacharya; from him Saraswati Bhatt; from him Ramaanuj; from him Ramanidh; from him Devacharya (Devadas); from him Hariyanand; from him Raghavanand; from him Swami Ramanandji; from him Anantanand; from him Yoganand; from him Shri Gesji [Gayeshji]; from him Krishnachand; from him Payahari Krishnadasji; from him Saariram; from him Narahardasji, whose disciple was Jan Dwarkadas, whose disciple became Gnaniji; who — in the matter of the banyan fruit — won over Sadguru Kabirji, and, meeting him, gained steadiness of mind, and whose doubt was dispelled when he met Kabirji; in Gnaniji's tradition came the joy-giving Jasvantji, whose disciple Gopalji gave teaching to Jan Jivanji; who, setting aside all rules of injunction and prohibition, held fast, with faith, to devotion to the name of Hari.)

The founding acharya of the Ramanandi tradition is Lakshmiji; by his glory the mighty and powerful Vishvaksen became his disciple; his disciple was Munivraj; his disciple was Supin; his disciple became Shathkop; his disciple became the author of the Bhagavat, Bopdev; his disciple became Mangalmuni; his disciple became Nathmuni; his disciple was Pundarik; his disciple was Rammishra; his disciple was Jamatmuni; his disciple was Ramanuj; his disciple was Kulatarak. Acharya Ramanuj's son-in-law was Lalacharya; his disciple was Saraswati Bhatt; his disciple was Ramaanuj; his disciple was Ramanidh; his disciple was Devacharya (Devadas); his disciple was Hariyanand; his disciple was Raghavanand; his disciple was Swami Ramanandji; his disciple was Anantanand; his disciple was Yoganand; his disciple became Shri Gesji [Gayeshji]. His disciple was Krishnachand (Karmachand); his disciple was Payahari Krishnadasji; his disciple was Saariram; his disciple was Narahardasji; his disciple was Jan Dwarkadas; his disciple became Gnaniji. He it was who told the story of the banyan fruit and won over Sadguru Kabirji; meeting him gave Gnaniji's mind steadiness, and Jan Gnaniji's doubt was dispelled when he met Kabirji. In Gnaniji's tradition came the joy-giving Jasvantji; his disciple Gopaldasji gave teaching to Jan Jivanji, who, cutting away all the rites of injunction and prohibition, held fast, with steadfastness and faith, to devotion to the name of Hari.

Guru-Lineage [Guru Pranalika]:

Kavit verses, from the Samagam —

Kavit — 1:

_Kali khalu jiv nistaarvaa, chaturbhyo avataar pragatya || trigun rahit Bhagavaan, Ramaaniij Ramaa paddhat bhani ||_
_kiyo vishva udyot, pragat jot dinmani mani || satgun Sanakaadik muni, Limbaanand avataar liyo ||_
_rajgun Viranchi gungunit, Madhvaacharaj Hari jas piyo || tamasgun Tripurari Vishnusaam, seemaa subhat ||_
_kali khalu jiv nistaarvaa, chaturbhyo avataar pragat ||_

(Meaning: To truly liberate the souls of the Kali age, four incarnations appeared. Among them, the Lord free of the three gunas, Ramanuj, taught the discipline of Lakshmiji's Shri tradition, and, as though the light of the sun-jewel had shone forth, spread the light of devotion across the whole world. From among the Sanakadik sages, in sattva-guna, came the incarnation of Nimbarkacharya, who established the Nimbark tradition. Endowed with the qualities of rajas-guna Brahmaji, Madhvacharyaji established the Madhva tradition and took up the merit of spreading devotion to Hari. From tamas-guna Shiva, through Shri Vishnuswami, the Vishnuswami tradition arose. Thus indeed, to liberate the souls of the Kali age, four incarnations appeared.)

Kavit — 2:

_Sampradaay shiromani Naaraayan parnaalikaa || ichchhaa svaroop aanand, tahaan jan Keshi ujaar ||_
_Krishna Keshi Harijan bhaye, taa sheekh Sutaa Sindhu Saagar || tahaan Ujaasmuni Vishvaksen sheekh, pragat je sahasraphanaa gun gaaen ||_
_Paraankush Ujaas muni (Yaamun muni), tahaan Jot muni paraayan || Gambhir muni, Achal muni, Prakaashmuni taahaan Naarad ||_
_Fatak muni Krishna muni, Kripaal muni, Sukh Saarad || Vairaag muni, Tyaag muni, Jog muni sukhdaayak ||_
_Sampradaay shiromani, e Naaraayan parnaalikaa ||_

(Meaning: This is the guru-lineage of Narayan, the crown and foremost of the tradition — of him who, by the Lord's own will, is of the very nature of bliss. Among the lion-like, radiant devotees, Krishna became foremost among the Hari-jans; his disciple was Suta, daughter of the Ocean [Sagar], namely Lakshmiji; her disciple was Vishvaksen, who appeared singing the glories of Hari like the thousand-hooded Sheshnag. From him came Parankush muni; from him, Ujaasmuni (Yamun muni); from him, the loving Jyotmuni; from him, Gambhirmuni; from him, Achalmuni; from him, Prakashmuni; from him, Narad; from him, Fatakmuni; from him, Krishnamuni; from him, Kripalmuni; from him, Suk Sharad; from him, Vairagyamuni; from him, Tyagmuni; from him, the joy-giving Jogmuni. This is the guru-lineage of Narayan, foremost and crown of the tradition.

Note: this lineage matches the Bhaktamal only in part; the rest of it is not found in the Bhaktamal.)

Kavit — 3:

_Te Jogmuni updeshte rahit muni Videh || tahaan Dheeraj muni, Seel muni, Santosh muni sukhdaayak ||_
_Dayaamuni, Tulsi muni, tahaan Chandramuni paraayan || Varsh muni Finho muni, Siro muni, Jaaman muni ||_
_Harnaath muni sheekh pragatyaa, tahaan Pundarikaaksh, Hari bhagat jan || Paraankush deekshaa ju grahi, Pipaadev param sujaan ||_
_tahaan Raamaamishra Raamaa-anuj, pragat sheekh mahaapraan || Gangaal nidhi, Kaam nidhi, Vidyaadhar muni Choveh ||_
_Jog muni updeshthe, rahit muni Videh ||_

(Meaning: Yoganand — whom the great souls have held to be an incarnation of Lord Kapil, author of the Sankhya scripture — remained in a videh [bodiless, transcendent] state. From the teaching of that Jogmuni [Yoganand] came Dheerajmuni; from him, the joy-giving Santoshmuni; from him, Dayamuni; from him, Tulsimuni; from him, the devoted Chandramuni; from him, Varshmuni; from him, Finhomuni; from him, Siromuni; from him, Jaamanmuni; from him, Harnathmuni — his disciple appeared, Pundarikaksha; his servant, the Hari-devotee, took initiation from Parankush and became the supremely wise Pipadev; from him, Ramamishra; from him, Ramaanuj, his renowned and deeply devoted disciple; from him, Gangalnidhi; from him, Kaamnidhi; from him, Vidyadhar Muni Choveh. From the teaching of Jogmuni came this one who dwelt in the videh state.)

Kavit — 4:

_Vidyaadhar muni Choveh the, pragat sant Vasudev || tahaan Jagaasmuni, Suratmuni, Raamaaniij surat prakaash ||_
_tahaan Surat dev, Mangalmuni, Paataal muni Sarasgop || je Kul Taarak Padmaa Vilochan, Padmaachaarya anup ||_
_Devaachaarya sheekh pragat, Sukhaachaarya bhavpaar kar || Shridharaachaarya Hari jas punit, Kripaachaarya Hari bhagat vari ||_
_tahaan Vishnu Aachaarya poornakalaa, jyu bhav bohitmaan khev || Vidyaadhar muni Choveh the, pragat sant Vasudev ||_

(Meaning: From Vidyadhar Muni Choveh appeared his disciple, Sant Vasudev; from him, Jagaasmuni, Suratmuni, the manifestation of Ramanuj's inner light [surat prakash]; from him, Suratdev, and Mangalmuni, and Paatalmuni, and Sarasgop who was Kulatarak; from him, Padma Vilochan; from him, Padmacharya, an incomparable one to whom devotion to Hari came as his very inheritance; from him, Devacharya, whose disciple appeared as Sukhacharya, who ferried [souls] across the ocean of existence; from him, Shridharacharya, whose fame in Hari was pure and holy; from him, Kripacharya, who won devotees of Hari; from him, Vishnu Acharya, who, with full attainment, was the boatman ferrying the ship across the ocean of worldly existence. From Vidyadhar Muni Choveh appeared his disciple, Sant Vasudev.

Note: This guru-lineage matches the Bhaktamal only in some measure; of the remaining names nothing further can be understood. But it is in this form that the original Samagam records this lineage, in these kavit verses.)

Four Sampradays [Traditions]:

In the Samagam, verse [chhand] 29 of the Bhaktamal is given, presenting the acharyas of the four kinds of tradition. Of these four acharyas, the name of Ramanujacharya has already come within our own guru-lineage; a brief account of Ramanuj has been given above. Thus there are four sampradays:

The Four Vaishnav Sampradays: (1) Lakshmiji (2) Brahmaji (3) Sanakadik (4) Shivji — corresponding respectively to the traditions of Ramanuj, Madhva, Nimbark, and Vishnuswami.

The Shri Ramanuj tradition proceeded from Shri Lakshmiji; Ramanuj propagated the doctrine of Vishishtadvaita. Ramanujacharya arrives right up to, and stops short of full identity with, the form of Sheshshayi Narayan [Vishnu reclining upon the serpent Shesha]; this is called the Shri Sampraday.

The Madhva tradition proceeded from Brahmaji. It is a dualist [dvaitavadi] doctrine; according to the dualist view, the oneness of the individual soul and God is never possible, at any time.

The Shri Vishnuswami tradition proceeded from Shivji. He propagated the doctrine of Shuddhadvaita [pure non-dualism].

The Nimbark tradition proceeded from the Sanakadik sages. Nimbarkacharya holds the doctrine of Dvaitadvaita [dualistic non-dualism]. But to hold both positions at once becomes a matter of ambiguity — it cannot properly be called a settled doctrine; moreover, Nimbarkacharya did not compose a commentary [bhashya] on the Brahmasutra. For this reason it is not proper to count him among the [major] acharyas. All four of these propounded dualist doctrines and refuted the non-dualist [advaita] doctrine established by Shankaracharya.

This, then, is the guru-tradition as stated. Among these, the Vaishnav sampradays that have been named are chiefly of four kinds: (1) Ramanandacharyaji (2) Vishnuswami Tripurari (3) Nimbarkacharya Sanakadik (4) Madhavacharya.

Of these, the Vaishnav Gopaldasji, of the lineage of Janak, belonged to the tradition of Ramanandacharya.

Now, as for Baba Kabirji, who came within Ramanandji's tradition — we shall here speak of his particular path [partharo]; we shall also speak of his own dharma [nij dharma]. This is the partharo of Namdev-Kabir.

The word "partharo" is itself our true identity. It is an ornament of the community of devotees born of one womb [i.e., a spiritual family]. It is a social renewal, an awakening. It is a place where one becomes wholly absorbed in love for one another. If we were to call it the very life-breath of Jivanji Maharaj, that too would not be wrong to say. Partharo is our own distinct identity.

In the Bhakti Sutras, Naradji speaks of nirodh [restraint]:

_Nirodhastu lokavedavyaparanyasah ||8||_ (That is, restraint means the setting-aside of worldly and scriptural undertakings — in other words, in devotion, worldly dealings act as an obstruction.)

But for our devotees, where and when has anything ever become an obstruction to devotion? Partharo means a way of life [jivan pranalika]. We shall not give a long discourse on partharo here; but if its essence were to be put in a single sentence, it would be this: an existence apart from the temple — that is partharo. Whatever Jivanji Maharaj has said is itself the speech of Namdev-Kabirji, whose sakhi [couplet] is given here:

_Guru Ramanand prataapte | grahi Kabire dheer || man laayaa aakinsu | miti sab tanki peer ||4||_
_Ramanande je kahi | so suni daas Raghuvir || so sadguru kahi Jivanaa | bhajan Sitaapati Raghuvir ||5||_
_Teen lokmen tatvathaa | so sadguru diyaa bataay || kund addaavis Jivanaa | je jan ke diyaa chhodaay ||6||_
_Raamaavataare vraksh nipanyo | Krishnaavataare saphal falyo || so fal Julaahe chaakhiyo | tahaan naam boond Jivan jadyo ||7||_

Kabirji says that whatever Sadguru Ramanand told him, he bore with patience, and, having fixed his mind on it, the suffering of his body — that is, of worldly existence — was removed. By the strength of Ramanand's grace, Kabir was saved; when told to take up the name of Ram, Ramanand, as his guru, gave him this very name of God — and it gave him such courage that, holding faith in his heart, he took up the name of Ram. Then the suffering of having to be born and reborn through 8.4 million species of life was removed. ||1||

Jivanji Maharaj also says: what Ramanand said, Baba Kabirji heard; and that same teaching I received, through successive generations of disciples, from my own sadguru Gopaldasji — and that very thing I now tell you: worship Sitapati Raghuvir, Ram. ||2||

The essence, in the form of the name of Ram, that existed throughout the three worlds, was shown to me by the sadguru; by that essence King Janak delivered souls suffering in the state of hell — I too have obtained this supreme essence, the drop [bund] of the name "Ram." ||3||

Jivanji Maharaj says that the most essential element within the essence of devotion is love — without it, devotion cannot become pure. Ram, who appeared in the form of the tree of that incarnation, was, so to speak, love and compassion incarnate; while Krishna himself was love itself. That essence, which was love in its fullest culmination, was tasted — that is, made known — by Kabirji, the crown-jewel of the weaver's family. There Jivanji Maharaj obtained three essential elements: love, devotion, and light [prakash].

That is to say, whatever speech, name, and so on has come to us today came to Jivanji Maharaj by the grace of Guru Gopaldasji — and in this, the greatest share belongs to Baba Kabirji. Because it was Kabirji who gave the "Name," "Ram"; and for this very reason, Jivanji Maharaj gave Kabirji the name "Namdev" — the one who grants the vision [of God] called by that name. It is for this reason that we call it "the Partharo of Namdev-Kabir."

Thus, having had this much satsang conversation, Jivandasji acknowledged and accepted Gopaldas as his Sadguru. But it still seemed as though something remained incomplete. The guru had given a great deal, but had not given what every guru-maharaj gives — the secret mantra whispered into the disciple's ear. How can one manage without the guru's mantra? For every guru gives a secret mantra into the ear — but here, nothing of this kind had been given. The scriptures direct that certain things be kept secret: for instance, in giving charity, secret charity [gupt-daan] is held to be the finest; the practice [sadhana] of tantra ought to be carried out in secrecy. Moreover, gurus have given each of their disciples a mantra in private. Here, Gopaldasji had given teaching, but had given no mantra — and so Jivanji Maharaj asked for the guru's own utterance [guru vani].

_Sarasvati sanjog aave | to laave Shyaamalo || Raadhaa raas vilaas | rakhe man raakhe aamalo ||8||_

Kabirji, in a rameni, says —

_Vrindaavan Hari vipin vilaasi || tahaan khelat Kabir bhaye avinaashi ||_

Sakhi:

_Avigat agam apaar hai | koi virlaa chinhe sant || sadguru vachane paaiye | keval Kamalaakanth ||14||_

The Lord is sporting in the forest of Vrindavan; playing there, Kabir too became immortal.

Sakhi: such a Lord — who is ever beyond the reach of the senses, without limit, whom none can fathom — only some rare, capable saint can know Him; and so it is only through the sadguru's own teaching that we can attain such a Lord.

The whole world believes that once union with Saraswati [learning, knowledge] is attained — that is, once a mantra is received from a guru and worshipped through chanting — one attains the dark one, Shyam-Krishna. But do not be misled into believing this: the Shyam one to be attained is He who delights together with Radha, not with Saraswati. So do not fall into this false illusion; that is to say, Parbrahm cannot be attained through mere [worldly] knowledge — He cannot be recognized that way. Guru-vani — the guru's own utterance, the guru's word, the guru's mantra — by worshipping and revering which a disciple can gain a very great deal in this world — the disciple's [longing to ask for the guru's utterance was]...

...is a right; without the guru's own words (guru-vani) the guru-disciple bond remains incomplete. Gopaldasji had openly explained a great deal, but in the end he did not give the secret mantra. Because of this, Jivandasji's uncertainty grew, and he asked for the guru-vani (mantra). Jivanji Maharaj was a new entrant into Baba Kabirji's spiritual lineage (parthara), who had not yet studied Kabirji's teachings, and so he made this request. Kabirji says:

_Kabir pragat Ram kahe, chhana Ram na gay | phusak joda dur kari, jyun bahuri na lage lay ||15||_ (Kabir says: speak of Ram openly, do not sing of Ram in secret; cast off every false attachment, so that its fire never touches you again.)

Pipaji likewise says:

_Jyan pado tyan paap, paap vana pado nahi | nahi pado nahi paap, Pipo varnave aapo aap ||16||_ (Where there is a veil there is sin; without sin there is no veil. Where there is no veil there is no sin — Pipa describes this from his own experience.)

Carrying the same point forward, Gnaniji Maharaj says:

_Chhani chhani batadi, na kije khune peth | Gnani pargat Ram he, gaiye chaude beth ||17||_ (Do not whisper secret little talk hidden away in a corner; O wise one, Ram is manifest — sing of Him seated openly in the public square.)

It is through the guru lineage itself that the manifest Ram has been shown to us, because devotion (bhakti) is neither theft nor sin that we should have to go looking for a corner to hide in — it is Gnaniji's view that devotion should be done sitting right in the middle of the public square. Kabirji himself went among the pandits of Kashi and there challenged society and the hypocrites who, blinded, carried on their pretense in the name of scriptural doctrine. He sang in one bhajan:

_Rup arup khojkar dekho, tako karo viveka ho | pragat yog hai gaurav gosanhi, gupat yog hai chori ho ||1|| yahi yogte param pad pave, kahe Kabir mat mori ho ||_ (Search out and see both the formed and the formless, and use discernment about it. The open path is glorious and worthy, O Lord; the secret path is as good as theft. Kabir says it is only through this open path that the supreme state is attained — this is my own teaching.)

God's own form is formless; seek it out with the discernment that comes from the guru's grace, for it is admirable to keep one's inner state open and declared. Whereas to keep it hidden and secret in the mind amounts to deceit and theft — so Kabirji's teaching is that only through an open state of mind can the supreme state be reached.

According to the tradition of devotion, devotees never need to do anything in secret. That would be like going to fetch buttermilk while hiding the very pot meant to carry it — an absurd contradiction. The work of devotion is the noblest of works; moreover, devotees must chant the divine Name (namsankirtan) in order to attain the Supreme Being (Parbrahm). And what does a devotee need for that? Only cymbals and a mridang drum, and a public platform or veranda to sit on — then the mind becomes absorbed of itself.

_Shri Krishna Govind Hare Murare, He Nath Narayan Vasudev._ (A kirtan invoking the Lord's names — Krishna, Govind, Hari, Murari, Lord Narayan, Vasudev.)

And what shame is there in singing this? This is simply the holy madness (pagalpanu) of devotees — they do not care for the opinion of the world, for dancing openly and veiling one's face at the same time cannot go together. Thus, once he had known the manifest "Name" and all his doubts had been destroyed, Jivanji Maharaj spoke words of gift (a sakhi) to his guru. Here there is something worth understanding: once someone is made one's guru and the guru gives the disciple the mantra in the ear, the rite between guru and disciple is complete. But before taking leave of the guru, one must offer in return a gift called guru-dakshina — one must give the guru wealth as an offering. Yet the very guru who calls wealth — money, currency — an illusion (maya) and tells the disciple to renounce possessions is the same guru who then asks the disciple for guru-dakshina: what a strange and self-serving thing this is! Here, however, Jivanji Maharaj offers as his gift not rupees or money, not wealth or riches, but obedience to his guru's own word. And as to what one ought truly to give the guru, what does Kabirji say?

_Kabir guruku ek shir kaha dijiye, hoye to dije chaar | dash mastak to Ravan diya, kaaj birani naar ||18|| Guru to aisa chahiye, shishso kachhu na ley | shish to aisa chahiye, guru ko sab kachhu dey ||19||_ (Kabir says: why offer the guru merely a single head — if you must give, give four. Ravan gave ten heads for the sake of another man's wife. The guru should be such that he takes nothing at all from the disciple; the disciple should be such that he gives the guru everything.)

Why bow before the guru with an empty head alone? If your mind is filled with such conceit and pride, then lay before the guru these four kinds of pride as well: pride of body, pride of wealth, pride of lineage, and pride of learning. Ravan gave up his ten heads for another man's wife; so for the sake of the world beyond, you too must give up these four "heads" — only then will you attain the supreme state.

The guru should be so free of greed that he takes nothing whatsoever from the disciple, and the disciple should be such that he offers body, mind, and wealth — everything — to the guru. Only then are they to be counted a true guru and a true disciple.

In other words, the thread joining guru and disciple must be one of love, not of wealth. And as for what should be given to the guru, Kabirji has made that entirely clear. So, once Jivanji Maharaj had grasped this true teaching, he offered his guru a sakhi (couplet) as a gift — that is, giving his assent to his guru's words, he honored him with an offering of words, as follows:

_Sarasvati bichari kaha kare, jo nahi guru vachan pramaan | Sitapati bin Jivana, bhatke chare khaan ||9|| To vani dhunki Jivana, sant samagam manhi | mohe Sitapatiko aasro, ke Girdhariki chhanhi ||10|| Vani sab vyabhichaarini, jahan nahi guru vachan pramaan | guru mukh vani Jivana, so kalyane kalyan ||11||_ (What can poor Sarasvati — mere learning — do, where the guru's own word carries no authority? Without the Lord of Sita, O Jivan, one wanders lost among the four kinds of birth. Then I found my true voice, O Jivan, within the company of saints; there I found refuge in Sita's Lord, and the shade of Girdhari [Krishna]. Every word is unchaste where the guru's word carries no authority; but the word that comes from the guru's own mouth, O Jivan, is that which brings true well-being.)

Sarasvati means knowledge itself: even if one has gained any amount of learning by studying the scriptures, the Vedas, the Puranas and so on, it is of no use at all if one has not taken a guru — that learning goes to waste, uselessly (worth seeing here is the example of Naradji). ||1||

"I found my voice" means: the voice — the guru's own words — came to me; from where did it come? Within the company of saints my own voice became visible to me — that is, within the very satsang now being carried on among twenty-four lakh souls, it was there that Sadguru Gopaldasji had spoken it in manifest form, and it has now begun to be heard clearly by me. I understand it now, and moreover I have gained the refuge of Sitapati Ram and the shade — the grace — of Girdhari Shri Krishna. ||3||

Words that have not come from the mouth of the sadguru — that is, that have not been received through the sadguru — are unchaste words; they have received no confirmation (acceptance) from a guru. Therefore they cause suffering and induce delusion. But the word received from the guru's own mouth is that which brings true well-being. ||5||

The joyous flood of the sadguru's grace is like a great swell rising up in an ocean of milk, full of intoxicating delight — such is the grace of the guru that has come to me. Just as milk poured into a salty, brine-filled ocean cleanses away its bitterness, so this grace has washed away the bitterness of the salt sea of suffering in this ocean of worldly existence and made it all as sweet as milk — in this way my sorrows in this ocean of birth and death have been washed away. ||5||

Revered Yadunathji Maharaj writes: "Moj (joyous surge) means the surge of God's own will. Meherman means the ocean — the ocean of the Lord's will (the guru's grace) has overflowed. This ocean is not a salty one, but one of milk, and so the salty water has been washed away" — that is, it is not humanity's own dirty desires but God's own will that is fulfilled. Raskhan has given expression to the very form of love in his own poetry — see it for yourself in Raskhan's own book. There is a great work on love written by Viyogi Hari, in which Raskhan's own words on the path of love (prem-yog) are collected; it is composition number 48 in the index, on page 5.

_Premko hum kis rasme len, kis bhavme ginen? Jaise samudrame lahren uthti aur usime laya ho jati hai, vaise hi premme sarv ras tatha sarv bhav tarangit hote rahte hain._ (In what savor should we take love, under what sentiment should we reckon it? Just as waves rise in the ocean and merge back into it, so in love every savor and every sentiment keeps rising and falling like waves.)

_Sarva rasashcha bhavashcha taranga eva varidhau, unmajjanti nimajjanti yatra sa premasangyakah ||5||_ (All savors and all sentiments rise and sink like waves in the sea — that in which they rise and sink is what is called love.)

Meaning: all savors and sentiments rise and fall like the waves of the ocean — such is the very mark of love.

_Kuchh samajhme nahi aata, ki is avyakt ras-bhav kallolko kya naam diya jaay. Premka samudra kaisa agadh kaisa asim aur kaisa anupameya hai._ (It is impossible to know what name to give this unspoken swell of savor and sentiment. How fathomless, how boundless, how incomparable is the ocean of love!)

_Prem agam, anupam, sagar saris bakhaan, jo aavat yahi dhig lahuri jaat nahi Raskhan ||20||_ (Love is beyond reach, incomparable, praised as being like the ocean; those who once come near it, says Raskhan, never turn back small again.)

_Prem-payodhise lautna kaisa! Yahanke dube hue yahin uchhal kud karte rahenge._ (How can one return from the ocean of love? Those who have drowned here will only go on leaping and playing here.)

Meaning: love is beyond the senses, incomparable, praiseworthy like a boundless ocean; those who come near it, Raskhan says, never turn back elsewhere again.

Here too just such a state has come about. In the guru's company our own voice has been transformed, and its mighty swell is now, as it were, straining to burst forth, as in:

"It cannot be held back" — this guru-given voice can no longer be restrained; it comes rushing forth in wave after wave of eagerness. Because of the voice I received through the guru, I sing the praises of the pure Name of Raghunath that I obtained, which is Ramkabir. Bearing witness to Kabirji's own word, he says: ||6||

Kabirji says the voice has changed, that is, the voice has now been transformed. In this very land that is the human body, and in this very country that is the realm of death (that is, time), the voice that a little while ago was "vaikhari" (unrefined speech — speech without a guru is reckoned as vaikhari) has now become "gurumukhi" (guru-uttered). Though it is the very same human body and mortality, the voice and conduct have changed. ||7||

Moreover, my very reckoning has changed: a little while ago I was a lowly soul of this world; now I have gone beyond "that other land" — reckoned the rank of the saints — beyond caste (Hindu, Muslim, and so on), beyond varna (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra), and beyond lineage (gotra).

Kabirji says that in the Supreme Abode all these have gathered together, united in a single view formed only through the words of the sadguru's teaching; but through their bodies, minds, castes, and varnas they remain distinct from one another. No such distinction is to be seen there. ||8||

Continuing the same point further, he says that where form and varnashram, or color — black, white, and so on — are not even looked at, at that level of sanctity all that is looked for is whether everyone shares the same principle and worship of the sadguru; but no attention or glance is paid to which of the four varnas someone belongs, or what kind of devotion they are steeped in — because so-called scriptural pedants are eloquent of tongue, not endowed with true discernment (viveka). ||9||

_Ishta mile aru man milai, milai bhajan ras riti, miliyai tahan nihshank hai, kije tinso preeti ||21||_ (Where one's chosen deity matches, and minds meet, and the manner of savoring devotional singing matches, there one should meet without any doubt or hesitation, and form love with them.)

Where people's chosen deities (ishtadev) match, where their way of thinking matches, and where the manner of their devotional practice matches, one should meet such people without any doubt or hesitation, and hold love for them.

Just as it will not do if blood groups do not match, so people of various differing opinions and sects cannot truly mix with one another; hence those who match the sadguru's way of thinking — be they a tanner (chamar) like Rohidas or a Muslim like Kabir — are not looked at by varna or religion by those walking the path of devotion.

The "speech of the ancient land" is a speech laden with hidden, secret meaning; "that other land" refers to the Supreme Abode, in the sense of Mathura, where Krishna's cowherds were of Brahmin, Vaishya, Kshatriya, or Shudra caste or varna, yet in meeting with them — that is, in devotion to Krishna or Ram — no attention is paid to the caste or varna of any embodied devotee; what is looked at is only whether there is a shared, unified meeting of the words of devotion to Ram-Krishna and the sentiment of devotion within them; no attention at all is paid to whether they are of the same varna or caste.

Mathura has been called "the home from before" (purva ka ghar); those devotees who remain untouched and unaffected by the illusion of this world are the only ones who will understand Jivanji and Jivanji's true nature. Only such accomplished devotees will know that Jivanji Maharaj has come for the meeting and gathering of saints.

Kabirji says the speech is "ours from before" — that is, do not mock these words spoken today as merely of the present; they belong to earlier births upon births, and are not to be understood by just anyone; by following them one may cross this ocean of birth and death. But our word will be understood only by one who is a soul of merit from a former birth. Otherwise he will remain fallen in the sorrows of this ocean of existence. ||10||

In his sakhis, Jivanji Maharaj says a great deal about Mathura:

_Mahi mandal Mathura nahi, adhar nirantar khel, dhara kahat hai Jivana, taki sangat mel ||22||_ (Agadh) (Mathura is not upon the surface of the earth; it is a ceaseless, unsupported play; whoever says it rests on some earthly support, O Jivan — do not keep the company of such a one.)

Jivanji Maharaj says that Mathura is not on the surface of the earth; rather, it is the place where God's unbroken, constant divine play (lila) occurs, existing without any support in that inner sky. But whoever claims that it is founded on some earthly support is a fool devoid of true devotion — do not keep company with such a person.

God and the place of His divine play do not exist within the world of form and attribute (sagun sakar). Yet if any guru-less person or non-devotee claims that God's play is centered in an image or a place of pilgrimage within the realm of form and attribute, that is not acceptable. Kabirji too lends support to this same point in another way:

_Kabir mahimandal Mathura puri, teen lokme nahi, sada akhandit Ramji, bansivatki chhanhi ||23||_ (Agadh) (Kabir says: the true city of Mathura is not found on this earth nor in any of the three worlds; it lies in the shade of the banyan of the flute, where Ramji dwells forever unbroken.)

Kabirji says that the original city of Mathura is not to be found upon this earth or even within the three worlds; rather, that Mathura exists in the region of the Bansivat (the banyan of the flute), where the unbroken divine play of Krishna and Ram forever unfolds.

_Ghar adhar sab vraj jana, adhare dhar ramaye, e nirgun sargun Jivana, sadguru bhed bataay ||24||_ (Agadh) (The home is unsupported, yet all the people of Vraj are made to dwell within that unsupported support — O Jivan, the sadguru has revealed this secret of the formless and the formed.)

Jivanji Maharaj says that God cannot be held or grasped by anyone; He sports in the shade of the Bansivat, He who cannot be held or grasped, He who is beyond both form and formlessness — and as such, dwelling in the form of the people of Vraj, He, whether called the unsupported formless or the supported formed, abides within the people of Vraj. It is this mystery of God's formless and formed natures that the sadguru has revealed.

_Ras mandal Girdhar rachyo, tahan dharo kyun samaay, dharo kahat hai Jivana, jahan sadguru nahi sahaay ||25||_ (Agadh) (Girdhar, the Holder of the Mountain, fashioned the whole cosmic dance circle — how then could He be confined within a single earthly support? O Jivan, only those without the sadguru's help would say that He is.)

Jivanji Maharaj says that the Lord who bore up Govardhan has fashioned the entire universe as one great circle of divine dance; how then could He be confined and contained solely within the realm of form and attribute? Therefore, those who claim that God exists solely within form and attribute are only those who have not received the help of the sadguru's grace.

Kabir says in a rameni:

_Chaud lokthe Mathura nyari, sada akhand Hari ras vihari ||6||_ (Mathura, where Hari forever sports unbroken in divine play, is set apart from all fourteen worlds.)

That Mathura where God forever sports in unbroken divine play (ras) is set apart from even the fourteen worlds.

_Janam bhom Mathura taji, nayo kiyo pravesh, deve vasi Dwarka, uttam jaani desh ||26||_ (Leaving Mathura, His birthplace, He made a fresh entry; the Lord settled in Dwarka, having known it to be the finest land.)

Recognizing it as the finest of lands, God settled Dwarka. Jivanji Maharaj too, coming down from the peaks of the Himalayas, chose the land of Gujarat.

The witness of Mathura, that "home of before," has been borne out. Just as Kabirji's sakhi bears this out today, so too, confirming it, Jivanji Maharaj speaks a doha:

_Mathura mahalo desh, Kathiyawade katamb vase, aayo Gurjar khand, santo tane melavade ||18||_ (Mathura is the palace-land, but now the family dwells in Kathiawad; I have come to the land of Gujarat for the gathering of saints.)

Mathura — that is, the one who dwelt in Mathura — having destroyed Kansa, freed the city of Mathura and came to dwell in Dwarka-Kathiawad — this speaks of Krishna. Jivanji Maharaj says that he has come to Gujarat for the deliverance of the saints, to meet with the saints. ||1||

So it was that this meeting (samagam) between the Vaishnav Gopaldasji and Jivandasji took place on the thirteenth day of the bright half of Aso in Vikram Samvat 1683; they met having established it in accordance with dharma, that is, according to proper, ordained rule. In other words, as already said, learning — Sarasvati — is useless without a guru, and so too a guru is needed for the practice of devotion. A person without a guru can never become a true, excellent devotee. Thus Jivanji Maharaj takes Gopaldasji as his sadguru, and it is confirmed that the truths spoken of the Supreme Being (Parbrahm) in the Vedas concerning the enchanting flute-player, and those spoken in the Bhagavad Gita, and the praises of the Parbrahm's virtues sung in the Bhagavat too, described under a thousand names — these belong truly to the very Supreme Lord of Namdev and Kabirji.

In other words, Jivanji Maharaj shows here that one should follow only what Kabirji has said — that alone is the highest truth; the rest, the visible world, is illusory, and so one must not lose one's way. For why has this entire universe gone astray? Kabirji's sakhi has spoken of it:

_Kabir jaanta mila nahi, puchh na kiya gavan, bhulekun bhula milya, to panth batave kavan ||19||_ (Kabir says: I never met one who truly knew, nor did I ask before setting out on my journey; when the lost meet the lost, who then shall show the way?)

The meaning of this sakhi is indeed quite simple, though its layered sense runs deep in many places; but the meaning is one and the same — that without a true sadguru, who shall show the path? In this world, merely seeing ochre robes, one should not take just anyone as guru — gurus are found aplenty, but among them a true sadguru is rare indeed, found only once in a great while. So one must not assume that devotion's true teaching may be had from just anyone. Take, for example, Jivanji Maharaj: at the tender, unknowing age of eleven he renounced the world, yet he did not find a true sadguru until he reached the age of thirty-two, when he met Gopaldasji, who gave him the vision (darshan) of God. The very same thing happened to Gnaniji Maharaj: he stepped away right from his own wedding ceremony and took Khojiji Maharaj as his guru, yet his doubt did not vanish.

It was only when he met Kabirji that his doubt was resolved. Thus one must never go anywhere without due consideration; and this is why Jivanji Maharaj has said:

_Guru kije vichaarke, jehi batave Ram, saryu teere Jivana, je nagar Ayodhya gaam ||27||_ (Take a guru only after careful thought — one who can show you the Ram of the town of Ayodhya on the banks of the Sarayu, O Jivan.)

And so Jivanji Maharaj says that Seniji, Dhanaji, Pipaji, Rohidasji, Jaidevji, Mirabai, Premanandji, Narsinh Mehta, Adhyaruji, and countless other Vaishnav saints besides — they too sang of that same enchanting flute-player, the true Supreme Lord, whom Namdev and Kabirji sang of.

This meeting took place in Gujarat, in the village of Choranda, at the dwelling of guru Gopaldas, and there Jivanji Maharaj stayed for four years. Having considered the matter of Mathura, let us now turn to the discussion of the city of Ayodhya, and take darshan of Ayodhya.
