Jivanji Maharaj says that one must choose, after due thought, a guru who can reveal the Ram of Ayodhya — Ram of what kind? The Ram who is on the banks of the Sarayu at Ayodhya, the son of Dasharath, whose brothers are Bharat, Shatrughna, and Lakshman. The water is the Sarayu's; the place is Ayodhya. It is a union of the formless (nirgun) and the formed (sagun) aspects of the divine reality. Ayodhya has two forms: one eternal, the other of divine play (lila). In its lila-form it dwells within the realm of material nature, and yet is untouched by the defects of material nature.

Rather, it removes the defects of material nature in others and bestows upon them its own eternal nature.

According to one view, Ayodhya is twofold: one upon the earth and another in the wider cosmos; yet both are one and the same, unbroken, of a single essence. The only difference is between its sweetness (madhurya) and its majesty (aishwarya) aspects of divine play. The Shiv Samhita says:

_Bhogasthanam parayodhya lilasthanamtviyam bhuvi, bhogalilaawati Ramo nirankush vibhutika ||6||_ (The Ayodhya of enjoyment is beyond the cosmos; this earthly one is the place of divine play. Ram, possessed of both enjoyment and play, is of unfettered, sovereign glory.)

The Ayodhya of enjoyment lies beyond the cosmos, and the Ayodhya of divine play lies here on this earth. Ram, who partakes of both enjoyment and play, is of unrestrained majesty.

At the request of King Ikshvaku, Vashishthaji brought the Sarayu to Ayodhya; the story of the Sarayu's birth is found in the thirty-seventh chapter of the Satyopakhyan. The mind itself is Ikshvaku, longing itself is Vashishtha, and it was they who brought kirtan itself, in the form of the Sarayu, into the Ayodhya that is the community of saints. The Sarayu arose from God's own tears, and bears Ram within her womb. The Ganga, on the other hand, arose when God's foot struck against and spilled the sweat of the sons of Sanaka [the Sanakadi sages], which Brahmaji had collected in his water-pot. God has never even so much as touched the leftover, sweat-born Ganga. In the Das Ang, Kabir says:

_Kabir Thakur hamara Ram hai, jaka Dasharath baap, duniyaku dojakh diya, hamku apna jaap ||28||_ (Das) (Kabir says: my Lord is Ram, whose father is Dasharath; to the world He has given hell, but to me He has given remembrance of His own Name.)

My worshipped Lord is Ram, whose father is Dasharath; but He has kept worldly people in a wretched place, entangled in the illusion of sense-objects, while to me He has given the remembrance of His Name.

_Kabir nugra nar sanshe padya, suni nahi guru mukh baat, trigun ateet nirdhaar hai, so Dasharath sut Raghunath ||29||_ (Guru-less people have fallen into doubt, for they have not heard the true matter from the guru's mouth — that steadfast, immovable Raghunath, beyond the three gunas, is the same son of Dasharath.)

Guru-less people have fallen into doubt regarding Ram, for they could not learn the true matter about Ram from a guru's mouth: that Ram, who is beyond the three gunas, ever fixed and unmoving, is that very same son of Dasharath.

_Kabir sabka baap hai, beta kisika naahi, beta hoke avatare, so to sahib naahi ||30||_ (God is the father of all; He is son to no one. Whoever is born as somebody's son is not truly the Lord.)

God is the one who creates, and benefits, everyone; He is the father of all, and son of no one. If one who is born as a son is called an incarnation, such a one cannot rightly be called God.

_Kabir Ram Ram sab ko kahai, kahan Ramka thaam, Ramchandra guru Vashishth kiye, kya sunaayo naam ||31||_ (Everyone says "Ram, Ram" — but where is Ram's true abode? Consider what name it was that Vashishtha, whom Ramchandra took as guru, spoke into his ear.)

Everyone goes about saying "Ram, Ram," but consider carefully where Ram's true place is. When Ram took Vashishthaji as his guru, consider what name Vashishtha then made him hear. Vashishtha made Ram hear the very name "Ram" itself — so Ram is none other than that very Ram, and it was his own name that was made to be heard by him.

_Kabir nagar Ayodhya raay tum, bhaye anek hi baar, apni aadi bhulaaviya, tum kaise kirtaar ||32||_ (You have been proclaimed king of the city of Ayodhya many times over, yet you have made everyone forget your own true origin — what kind of creator of this world are you, then?)

You have been proclaimed, again and again, king of the city of Ayodhya, and in this way you have caused everyone to forget your own true nature — so it is not understood what kind of creator of this universe you truly are.

_Kabir Ram naam sab kahat hai, so to naam ameer, ajar amar ek naam hai, vaku japai Kabir ||33||_ (Everyone speaks the name "Ram" — that is the common, majestic name. But there is one name, ageless and deathless, and it is that name which Kabir repeats.)

Everyone speaks the name of Ram; that name refers to the common, ordinary Ram, endowed with the powers, authority, and sovereignty of the three gunas, in both form and formlessness. But there is one, single name of Ram that is ageless and immortal, beyond the three gunas, all-powerful — and it is that name which Kabirji repeats.

Jivanji Maharaj as well as Kabir make mention of Dasharath — so let us consider Dasharath.

_Ambarish gohaare aaviyo, sundar shyam swaroop, so Nand dware Jivana, je Dasharath kul bad bhoop ||34||_ (Prabodh) (In a beautiful dark form He came to Ambarish's rescue; it is that same God, O Jivan, who was born at Nand's door — He who was the great king of Dasharath's own line.)

In a beautiful dark form, the Supreme Being came to the aid of King Ambarish; it was that very God who was born at Nand's doorstep, in Nand's own home, He who was the great king Ram, of Dasharath's lineage.

_Pita hamara Ramji, mata Satvanti naar, jug jug maagun Jivana, ghar manav avataar ||35||_ (Das) (Ramji is my father, and the virtuous woman [Sita] is my mother; age after age, O Jivan, I ask only that you take human birth in my home.)

Jivanji Maharaj says: my father is God Ram, and my mother is His chaste, virtuous wife, Sita. Therefore, age after age, I make only this one plea — that you continue to take human incarnation in this same way.

_Mata hamare Janaki, pita hamare Ram, jug jug maagun Jivana, sant sangat vishram ||36||_ (Das) (Janaki is my mother, Ram is my father; age after age, O Jivan, I ask only for rest in the company of saints.)

My mother is Janaki — Sita — and my father is Ram. Jivanji Maharaj says: age after age I ask only this of you, that I may find my resting place in the company of saints who abide in your very form.

_Mata pita hamare Jivana, sadhu sadguru Ram, aur kachhu maagun nahi, do charankamal vishram ||37||_ (Das) (O Jivan, my mother and father are the sadhu-sadguru Ram; I ask for nothing else, only rest at his two lotus feet.)

Jivanji Maharaj says: my mother and father are none other than that Ram in the form of the sadhu-sadguru, and I ask for nothing else but to remain forever devoted in service to his lotus feet.

_Kabir saacha sadguru jab mile, to sat batave Ram, sarju teere khelke, aayo Gokul gaam ||38||_ (Krishnadas Parchari) (When one meets a true sadguru, then he reveals the true Ram — the one who, after His play on the banks of the Sarayu, came to the village of Gokul.)

When one meets a true sadguru, only then is one shown true devotion to the real, original Ram — that Ram who, having sported on the banks of the Sarayu, came in the form of Krishna to Gokul; the sadguru gives one true understanding of Ram's original nature.

In the Uda Dharma Panch Ratnamala, 4th edition, page 350, in a Prabhat (dawn hymn), Kabirji says:

_Avadh nagar chalo dekho meri sajani, raja Dasharathjike Ramji bhaye, kaun ghari Bharat bhaye sajani, kaun ghari raja Ramji bhaye || avadh || 1|| Chaitra maas naumiki puja, sukhe sarovar neer bhare, kahet Kabir daya sadguruki, ghar ghar mangal chaar bhaye ||4||_ (Come, my friend, let us go and see the city of Avadh — Raja Dasharath's Ramji has been born! At what hour was Bharat born, friend, and at what hour was King Ram born? On the ninth day of Chaitra, in worship, even the dry lake filled with water. Kabir says: through the sadguru's grace, in every home there arose auspicious festivity.)

In Avadh, the city of Ayodhya, Kabirji calls to his companions: "Come to King Dasharath's house — Ram has appeared! At what hour did Bharatji appear, and at what hour did King Ram appear?" On the ninth day (the Ram-navami) of the month of Chaitra, through worship and devotion, even a dry lake filled up with water. Kabirji says that through the sadguru's grace, in this way auspicious festivities and sacred rites began to take place in every single home.

_Kabir Ram pitaku chhandke, kare aan devko jaap, gunka kera poot jyaun, kahai kaunku baap ||39||_ (Anandev) (Kabir says: one who forsakes Ram, his true father, to worship some other god, is like the son of a courtesan, unable to say who his own father truly is.)

Whoever forsakes Ram, who is our true father, and worships and takes the name of some other deity, is like the son of a courtesan who cannot say who his real father is — likewise, whoever worships another deity will never truly know the real God.

Kabirji and Gnaniji have spoken many sakhis about how to take a true sadguru:

_Kabir bandheku bandhe milyo, to kyon kar utre paar, sangat kar nirbandhaki, palme lehi chhudaay ||40||_ (Kabir: if one who is already bound meets another who is likewise bound, how then shall he cross over? Keep company instead with one who is unbound, and in an instant he will set you free.)

If one who is bound in the fetters of maya seeks to be freed from bondage but instead finds a guru who is himself entangled in maya, how can such a guru help him cross the ocean of existence? Therefore, if one keeps the company of one who is not so entangled, that person will free him from maya in an instant.

Even to buy something as small as a toothstick (datan) we examine it carefully first; we choose grain only after inspecting it; we handle food in our hand and examine it; and we even taste it by putting it in our mouth — so too a guru ought to be chosen only after due examination.

Jivanji Maharaj took Gopaldasji as his guru not in his boyhood but in mature adulthood, after twenty-four hours of continuous satsang, and having determined, with regard to the enchanting cowherd of Gokul, both His formed and formless nature — He whose form is the Ram of Ayodhya on the banks of the Sarayu, whose brothers are Bharat, Shatrughna, and Lakshman, and whose wife is Janaki — it was after determining this that he accepted Gopaldasji as his guru.

Worldly people who believe in ritual observance regard all rivers as impure during the monsoon, attributing to a mere river, in accordance with human custom, the impurity of menstruation. And yet even these ritualists do not consider a young girl or an elderly woman to be impure through menstruation in the same way; likewise, they consider the river Sarayu to be free of menstrual impurity, because the Sarayu river carries Ram within her own womb, and is thus free from this defect. In the same way, Jivanji Maharaj has taken up the true understanding of the true Ram of Ayodhya on the banks of the Sarayu. He has shown that within the wombs of the women of our own society, saintly, devoted children — devotees like Ram — may dwell, and has thereby made them worthy of such a status, and thus has freed our own sisters from the taint of menstrual impurity. In Chapter (Vishram) 13 of Jivandasji's Parchari, the true nature of Ram has been established.

_Kabir agam agochar gam nahi, jahan jhalmale jot, tahan Kabira bandagi, paap punya nahi chhot ||41||_ (Parbrahm is unreachable, imperceptible, beyond the senses; there where the light forever shimmers, there Kabir offers his devotion — a place untouched by either sin or merit.)

The Parbrahm is unreachable, imperceptible, beyond the senses — it cannot be grasped or recognized. There, where light forever shimmers, its nature cannot be known; there Kabir, a soul among the saints, offers his praise and devotion — in that abode, neither sin nor merit ever touches or clings.

Chaupai:

_Inte bhaye dash hi avatara, inhika hain sakal pasara, soi kheer samudrka vaasi, soi jano vaikunth vilaasi ||6||_ (From Him came the ten incarnations; from Him alone this entire universe has spread out. He alone dwells in the Ocean of Milk, and know that He alone takes His pleasure in Vaikunth.)

From Him the ten incarnations came, and this whole spread of the universe has come from Him alone. He it is who reposes in the Ocean of Milk, and He it is who also takes His delight in Vaikunth.

_Satpuri aadi hai sakal asthaana, jahan tahan roop dhari hai sujaana, nij dhamten tarat na taarai, soi keval Ram hamare ||7||_ (The Saptapuri and all other places are His abodes; the All-Knowing One has taken form here and there. Yet even if one tried, He could never be dislodged from His own eternal abode — He alone, in His pure form, is our Ram.)

The Saptapuri and all the other holy places, wherever they are, are places where this all-knowing Supreme Being has taken form. But even if one wished to remove Him from His own eternal abode, He would not budge — He does not waver or move. Such a pure and stainless Ram alone is our chosen deity.

Vyasji's sakhi:

_Dinkar tare shashiyar tare, tare trigun vistaar, dradhvrat hit Harivansh ras, tare na nitya vihaar ||42||_ (Though the sun should move from its place, and the moon from its place, and though the three gunas should shift from their expanse, the eternal play in which steadfast Harivansh delights with loving devotion never departs.)

Even if the sun or the moon should move from its own place, or even if the three gunas should shift from their own expanse, still that Krishna in whom Hit Harivansh delights with loving devotion never departs from the place of his own eternal play.

_Kabir jaanita jab puchhia, paida diya bataay, chalta chalta tahan gaya, jahan alakh niranjan raay ||43||_ (Kabir: when I asked one who truly knew, he showed me the path; walking on and on, step by step, I reached that place where the imperceptible, stainless Lord dwells.)

When he asked a guru who truly knew of real devotion, that guru showed him the path of loving devotion. Following that path, devoting himself step by step and walking on gradually, he arrived at that place — the abode of the Supreme Being, Parbrahm, that cannot be known — where He resides.

Jivanji Maharaj did not merely ask; he also took this very same knowing guru along with him, and together they set out upon the path of devotion and the path to God's own abode, and thereby attained God.

It is heard only that in Samvat 1687, Jivanji Maharaj set out from Choranda for Malwa together with his guru Gopaldas — that much alone has been recorded. But it is not written that a famine had struck that year, which is why they had to go to Malwa; we must understand that for ourselves. For the circumstances of Gopaldasji's household at that time were such that they could not sustain Jivanji Maharaj and Gopaldasji even there. Moreover, there is also another reason given for going toward Malwa: that in Malwa, in Ujjain, there is always greenery. Ujjain is the capital of Malwa, and it is Mahadevji's city, called Avantipuri. In the Ramayan, Tulsidas writes that Kakbhushandi, in an earlier birth, was born a Shudra in Ayodhya, and he too, when a famine struck, went to Ujjain, where in a short time he gained wealth and prosperity. Whatever one may believe, popular tradition trusts folk sayings — and so too it is said of our own Gujarat, that some saint's blessing protects it, so that between the Mahisagar and the Narmada rivers famine never strikes; and yet even so, the great famine of Chhappaniyo did strike, and in the same way a famine struck also in Samvat 1687 — and hence there arose the saying, "Has a Satyashiyo [an '87 famine] struck your house, that you act so miserly?" Revered Lakshmiba too used to use this very saying, remarking, "Has a Satyashiyo struck his house?"

In this very difficult situation that had arisen, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj set out with Gopaldasji on a pilgrimage to the Char Dham [the four sacred abodes] on the thirteenth day of the bright half of Ashadh in Samvat 1687 — so it is recorded in the account-books of the vahivancha [the genealogist record-keepers]. It is written there: "Having stayed four years in the village of Choranda, he set out on pilgrimage to the Char Dham. In Samvat 1687, on the tenth of the bright half of Ashadh, a feast was held in the kitchen-hall; a mare, 51 rupees, and a silken cloth (pitambar) were given."

If a famine strikes for one year, it is called an akal; if it lasts two years, it is called a dukal. The reckoning of famine years, along with mention of the Satyashiyo, is given in the Bhagavad Gomandal as follows — famine years are traditionally named, in Gujarati custom, after the last two digits of their Vikram Samvat year:

1615 — Panrotaro; 1847 — Sudtalo
1687 — Satyashiyo; 1869 — Aganotaro
1775 — Panchotaro; 1934 — Chotriso
1787 — Lilo Satyashiyo; 1956 — Chhappaniyo

In Akhand Anand magazine, Year 5, Issue 1, page 173, there is an article on the famines that struck Gujarat. It is written there that in the meeting-account (samagam), Jivanji Maharaj went on pilgrimage on the tenth of the bright half of Aso, Samvat 1687. Whereas the vahivancha's account-book records the tenth of the bright half of Ashadh. But the month of Aso is likely to be the correct date.

sections.title_en: Journey to Malwa and Separation from the Guru
sections.translation:
Thereafter, on the tenth day of the bright half of Ashwin in Samvat 1687 — Vijaya Dashami — Vaishnav Gopaldasji and Vaishnav Jivandasji set out together from Choranda for Malwa (a region of Madhya Pradesh near Bhopal). In Malwa, Gopaldasji had a fellow devotee, a friend. They arrived at his temple, his home. He showed them great respect. Vaishnav Jivanji cooked the meal, and they took the offering — guru and disciple, Gopaldasji and Jivanji Maharaj, eating together. That night they held satsang (holy company), and unbroken hari-kirtan (devotional hymn-singing) took place. When they thought of staying a second day, the devotee said to his wife that between them they would not be able to provide meals for both guests. Vaishnav Jivandasji overheard this. Then Gopaldasji too gave his consent: "Jivan, you go on to Ujjain; I shall stay here." No sooner had this been decided than midday arrived. Jivandasji pressed to set out at once, so the woman of the house brought a plate of shyam bhoji.

(From the behaviour of this friend's wife it appears that Gopaldasji's fellow devotee in Malwa, too, must have held the same lofty outlook as our own Uda devotees — for even though she could not feed two visiting guests, she still lovingly served Jivanji Maharaj a plate of shyam bhoji as he departed. "Shyam bhoji" is the elevated term our Uda devotees adopted for boiled toor dal, ordinarily called bakra.)

In the world people call boiled toor-dal grains "bakra" and regard it as a poor, coarse food fit for people of low, base station — hence the saying "even a ghost is pleased with bakra," meaning a person of low caste is pleased even by such a trifling meal. But our community of devotees holds to the same love-devotion as Lord Krishna, and so, just as the simple folk of Vraj were delighted with a bakra-like food for their midday snack — the very food Shri Krishna himself used to eat — we address it by the sacred name "shyam bhoji." Not only that, but in Puniyad in earlier times only the offering of shyam bhoji was served; no khichdi or any other dish was cooked. That offering of shyam bhoji continued in Puniyad down to recent times, and to eat it the devotees would lovingly make plates from banyan leaves gathered in the courtyard — until once a devotee fell from the banyan tree, after which the revered Lakshmiba began preparing khichdi instead. Even so, from this incident of the Malwa woman's offering of shyam bhoji, one can see what an influence the mighty guru Gopaldasji must have had even upon his fellow devotees.

Loving devotees fondly called shyam bhoji by the name "jalpan" (light refreshment). Taking this offering, they got ready to leave. Then Jivandasji said to Gopaldasji: "O Gopaldasji! When we set out from Gujarat, you asked whether devotees of Vishnu should not keep maya (worldly wealth) at all." That is, when the journey began from Choranda, Jivandasji had said they should carry some money with them, and Gopaldasji had replied that Vaishnav devotees have no need of maya, since he had many friends in Malwa where they could stay comfortably. But now separation had come to stand between guru and disciple. At this Jivanji Maharaj said: "Had we kept maya, the two of us could have stayed together and worshipped the Lord together; this separation that has befallen us is the doing of maya. So maya, too, has its place in the devotion of Vishnu." Saying this, he recited a sakhi (couplet).

_Maya hamari atma, deh kriyake kaj. Parmatma hamare Jivana, Sitapati Bijraj. ||1||_ (Maya — wealth — is extremely necessary for the upkeep of our body, but our highest goal, the true bent of our mind, we shall keep fixed on devotion to Sitapati Ram and to Krishna, the king of Vraj.)

_Maya sathe Jivana, milkar kije bat. Harijankun Hari melve, aurankun lagave lat. ||2||_ (One should deal with maya, O Jivan, thoughtfully and with understanding, for it can even help Hari's devotees attain God. But those who fall into infatuation with wealth are kicked away by it and cast into the cycle of birth and death.)

_Kabir maya mohani, mange mile na hath. Manse utari jab hi, tab dolan lagi sath. ||3||_ (Kabir says: maya is enchanting; even striving to obtain it, it does not come into our hands. But the moment we turn our mind away from it, it starts walking along beside us, pleading.)

_Kabir maya dakani, sab kahun kun khaye. Dant upadu papani, jo santa nedi jaye. ||4||_ (Kabir says: maya is a witch-demoness who kills and devours everyone. But if she goes near the saints, Kabir will strike her so hard that her wicked teeth are torn out.)

_Kabir kar jodi maya khadi, thadhi det asis. Bilsi aur latan chhadi, samar samar Jagdish. ||5||_ (Kabir says: maya now stands with joined hands, giving blessings — she has abandoned her wanton ways and her kicking, and stands remembering the Lord of the world again and again.)

Kabirji speaks another sakhi of this same sentiment: _Kabir bhoot pret aru dakani, chetak aru jamkal, jo harijan dware avahi, tab Harji kadhe khal. ||1||_ (Ghost, spirit, witch, black magic, and the messenger of death — should any of these come to a devotee's door, Hari himself strips off its skin.)

Here again comes up, once more, the very matter Jivanji Maharaj had raised at the start of the Samagam: that for a devotee of Vishnu, maya is a great veil cast over Brahma, and the whole universe is covered by that veil — so how, then, does the soul cross over? The very question on which this scripture was composed appears again here. This is an extremely difficult and knotty question, and along with it "maya" is the obstacle. Yet here it is precisely the absence of maya that has brought separation between guru and disciple — so its true cause is maya itself. Both of them were free of worldly desire; both had set out for the spread of devotion and for meeting with saints. Jivanji Maharaj further says that had they kept maya (wealth) with them, the two of them could have stayed together and carried on their devotional work; but since separation has now come between them, the question arises: what is this "maya"? What is its true nature?

Various schools of philosophy and various commentators have viewed and evaluated the word "maya" in different ways. The first world-teacher, Adi Shankaracharya, called maya "mithya" (illusory). Declaring "Brahma is real, the world is illusory," he held that the world — all things moving and unmoving that can be seen, heard, or experienced, this whole world perceptible to the senses — is itself "maya," and is unreal.

Here "maya" has been used in two senses: (1) maya as wealth, property, riches, money; and (2) maya as desire, craving, and attachment toward the material — in short, one sense is spiritual and the other material. Even so, maya remains a wondrous thing.

Looking at the views of other commentators on Vedanta philosophy: Shankaracharya describes maya as the unknown, the unreal. Bhaskaracharya calls it ignorance without actual substance. Ramanujacharya, Shrikhand, Nimbarkacharya, and Shekhar all view it in the sense of "wondrous." Madhvacharya holds it to be the mind's affliction of the soul, brought about through the Supreme's primal power. Vishesha Bhikshu calls it divine power. Vallabhacharya calls it the power, the influence, of the Supreme Lord. Pandit Aryamuni calls it the power of knowledge.

In the Vedas, maya-avidya is used in the sense of "error" or "delusion." In the Isha Upanishad it is said that truth is covered by a golden vessel — hiranyamaya (a kind of white cloth, like madharpat, once worn in ancient times; Omkara too is of this nature, for it stands before Brahma like a veil of white cloth) — this covering is called Brahma, and in the Samagam, Om itself has been called a golden vessel. In the Katha Upanishad, darkness is spoken of: the blind lead the blind; take refuge in knowledge and ignorance departs; this ignorance-darkness is called maya. Jivanji Maharaj has spoken of this "blind pursuit."

_Ram Krishna je Jivana, do sagun avatar. Andh dhandh kaha bhaju, je Ved na pave par. ||2||_ (Prabodh) (Ram and Krishna, O Jivan, are the two manifest incarnations of God. So why keep chasing some blind pursuit — holding the false delusion of being unable to grasp whether God is formless and attributeless, or what he truly is — instead of simply worshipping Ram and Krishna? Even Brahma himself could not settle that question.)

_Andh dhandh vede tajyo, aaye Jamna kool. Jahan Brahma sanatan Jivana, Ramkrishna nij mool. ||3||_ (Prabodh) (Having tired of saying "not this, not this" — that God is neither with attributes nor without — Brahma gave up all such efforts and came to the bank of the Yamuna, to Krishna; for it is there, O Jivan, in Ram and Krishna, that the eternal Brahma truly, originally abides.)

The Mundaka Upanishad calls the very "knot of ignorance" itself maya. The Brahmakaranya says, "asato ma sadgamaya, tamaso ma jyotirgamaya" (lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light) — meaning the unreal, or tamas (darkness), is itself maya. The Rigveda uses it in the sense of "appearance," abhas.

The Shvetashvatara Upanishad calls it Prakriti (Nature), and calls the wielder of maya "Maheshwar." Other Upanishads use it in the sense of "mithya" (unreal). Later, maya also came to be understood as the Vaishnavi "leela" (divine play). Ramanujacharya also gives "maya" the meaning "wondrous."

In the Atma Purana: (1) that which does not occur in any of the three times — past, present, future; (2) that which is the cause of the world in its causal form; (3) that which veils the true self-nature of all beings; (4) that which is destroyed by right knowledge.

In the Padma Purana: "ma" means Lakshmi, or else it means liberation. Thus maya herself has fallen into the web of maya — in the present age maya, as Lakshmi, has drawn the world to her, and it is she who is worshipped there.

In truth maya and Brahma are not separate, but since the Vedantins regard Brahma alone as real, the various Vedas and Upanishads have given differing definitions of it. The revered Yadunath Maharaj, comparing the outlooks of the jnanis (men of knowledge) and the saints, observed that the difference between them is as vast as that between sky and netherworld. He writes that, set beside the explanatory style of the philosophical schools — through the great Vedic sayings such as "Prajnanam Brahma," and statements like (1) Tattvamasi, (2) Ayamatma Brahma, (3) Aham Brahmasmi, and so on — the style of the saints is altogether distinctive. Showing the difference between the devotee and God, Adhyaruji says in Vadu Ghol:

_Avigat dev anant niranjan, bhavbhay bhanjan Shri Vasudev. Jag ghade bhaje jeh, nav lahe kon per teh._ (God is unmanifest, endless, and stainless, the destroyer of worldly fear, Shri Vasudev; it is he who fashions and dissolves the world, and no one can grasp in what manner he does so.)

This is the nature and function of God — creation and destruction are God's own work. Then, showing the work of the devotee, it is said: _bhav narak tale bhakt_ (the devotee wards off the fear of the world and the hell that follows from the sin born of one's own wrongdoing); freeing others from fear is itself the devotees' vow. Merely by the sight of saints, all three kinds of affliction are removed — just as approaching a fire removes cold at once, needing no further proof. Baba Kabir shows the sequence of steps for attaining Brahma, and through it the greatness of saints becomes apparent as well.

This, then, is the style of the scriptures and of the saints. Sadguru Baba Kabir has set out below the sequence for reaching the state of Brahma, and it must be reflected on and practised repeatedly — anushilan meaning to study the very same thing again and again. To instil fear in others is the work of wicked people. _Manushyanam sahastreshu kaschidyatati siddhaye_ (among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection). Among these, the style of the Gita is celebrated the world over, yet the style of the saints is distinctive from it. The revered Yadunath Maharaj has put this beautifully: the devotee joins with maya and strives to attain God, and yet is not entangled by it. This much concerns the tradition of the acharyas; let us now look at it according to the tradition of the saints.

Gyaniji Maharaj calls maya "kanak-kamini" (gold and woman). Kuba Bhagat says "maya dindash jasi" — maya is nothing but a passing, momentary impulse. Kabirji calls it ego, ahankar; he calls maya the black serpent-queen, the serpent being a symbol of ego. Vedanta calls knowledge Brahma, but for devotees knowledge is not what matters — knowledge brings ego, and that is a sign of downfall, so devotees do not accept mere knowledge.

Besides these, saints such as Narsinh Mehta, Mirabai, Tukaram, Pipaji, Rohidas, and Surdas have described worldly attachment and infatuation itself as maya. Saints live in the world and yet perform bhakti (devotion); maya does not hinder them, because no infatuation or attachment to the world remains in them — they remain like the lotus leaf on water, engaged only in devotion. There is a difference between the devotee's maya and the world's maya; whoever understands this difference can conquer the world — for one man turns a palace into a wilderness in his mind, while another builds a palace in the wilderness. Let us look at the words King Janak once uttered in ancient times.

_Anantamiva me vittam yasya me nasti kinchichan, Mithilayam pradiptayam na me dahyati kinchan. ||1||_ (Mahabharat, Shanti Parva 178-2) (Janak says: though I possess boundless wealth and splendour, none of it is truly mine; if Mithilapuri were to catch fire, nothing of mine would burn — for whatever burns, I have no attachment to it.)

This is the true greatness: whoever lives detached never comes to grief. But here a real predicament falls upon guru and disciple, and no way out can be found. Whatever remedy exists is only a way of letting the time pass. Here even the principles and reasoning of the scriptures prove false, for reality speaks otherwise — a scripture that seemed reasonable to the mind yesterday breeds only confusion today. No one truly accepts maya, and yet today maya is showing its full power: separation has fallen between guru and disciple. Kabirji has said — whom has this maya not troubled? It troubled Indra, Narad, at every turn even Shiva, and Kans, Shishupal, Gorakhnath; it has troubled even the greatest of warriors — only poor Kabirji alone has it not troubled.

A dialogue took place between Kapil and Syumarashmi. Caught in the confusion of maya's bondage of action, Syumarashmi asks Kapil Muni thus: _Naiva tyagi na santushto nashoki na niramayah, na nirvidhitso navritto napavritto'sti kaschan. ||2||_ (Mahabharat, Shanti Parva 269-46) (In truth, in this world no one is wholly a renunciant, nor wholly content; no one is free of grief, nor free of disease; no one is wholly without the desire to act, nor wholly free of attachment, nor wholly a renouncer of action.)

That is: even one who outwardly renounces wealth and splendour, in truth attains all comfort and splendour in some other form, and suffers no real hardship. Thus even such a "renunciant" is, in reality, neither happy nor content, and his craving and indulgence go on increasing day by day; he can neither carry out his tasks fully nor withdraw from them completely. (Here "karma" does not mean ritual acts, sacrifices, and the like, but simply the work one must do to live one's life.) Thus man is in every way sorrowful and afflicted. What, then, is the release from his sorrow? How is one to become free from suffering?

At the very beginning of this Samagam, Jivanji Maharaj himself asked: how does the soul cross over? In answer, he answers this question for us step by step throughout: even a sannyasi is not happy, even a renunciant-yogi is not happy. But here the answer is given for how one may become happy while living in the world — namely, without becoming wholly attached to it, and without turning away from the Supreme Brahma. That is why it is said: maya is necessary for our livelihood; we shall live amid it, mixing with it, and yet we shall not be blinded by infatuation with it, and shall continue to follow the Supreme Brahma — this indeed is the devotee's task. Kabirji, for his livelihood, kept weaving cloth his whole life long. Pipaji, though a king enjoying boundless splendour, kept himself turned away from the desire for pleasure even while managing his kingdom's affairs, and still advanced on the path to attaining the Supreme Brahma. Narsinh Mehta never once cared about his own poverty, and yet he attained not merely happiness but the very rank of a supreme devotee — his life is like an open book.

This incident at Malwa is, for Jivanji Maharaj, merely the first chapter of the book of life's struggle. Here we are given direct, living proof of exactly what his aged guru wished to demonstrate. It is from here that Jivanji Maharaj's true life-journey truly begins. The four years of rest at Choranda had been only a battle of words, a study of books; but today its living, tangible experience stands directly before him. Man's real test lies precisely in this: it is only when reality comes and stands directly before him that his patience is truly tested. Today both of them are distraught. Jivanji Maharaj has been placed in a state of utter helplessness — one cannot simply leave one's aged guru and go on alone, and yet there is no other way. Jivanji Maharaj sought permission with just a glance, and Gopaldasji watched him leaving; he could say nothing. He understood that this was their last meeting — that he would never again meet his beloved disciple. Thus separation came between the two.

The following day the Malwa devotee gave Gopaldasji leave to move on as well, and so, setting out from there, he too went on to Ujjain. It was in Gopaldasji's mind that he would meet Jivanji there — Jivanji Maharaj had said, on leaving, that they would meet at Ujjain. Bidding a final "Ram Ram" to Vaishnav Gopaldas, Jivanji Maharaj had gone on ahead. Gopaldasji, in separation from Jivanji Maharaj, departed for his heavenly abode on the fourth day at Ujjain. Thus, after parting at Malwa, he stayed four days at Ujjain and then went to his own heavenly abode. Even today there stands in Ujjain a Gopal temple; it is possible that it was at this very spot that Gopaldasji left his body, though we have no certain information of this.

Having taken leave of Gopaldasji, Jivanji Maharaj walked through the forest for four days and nights. On the fourth day, overcome with hunger, he sat beneath a behedaa (myrobalan) tree and ate its fruit. After eating it, he lay unconscious beneath that tree for a full day and night, with no awareness of his body at all.

In the world, fear and superstition have grown enormously. Great scholars, instead of dispelling such superstition, have gone on increasing it among the timid and weak — it would not be wrong to call such scholars fools. Consider: for women we accept that there is such a thing as ritual impurity during menses, but what can we say of those who ascribe this same fault of impurity even to water, earth, and trees? Such scholars have planted in people's minds the superstition that if you sit under a behedaa tree, you will end up in hell (Bhagavati Katha, part 40, page 7).

Ayurveda, in fact, makes very good use of behedaa in medicine, and there is a saying that beheda, hirda, and amla together make triphala churna. The kernel of the behedaa fruit is poisonous, but its bark is useful; behedaa causes constipation and induces sleep. It is likely, then, that Jivanji Maharaj, distressed by famine, ate behedaa fruit, and that this is why he remained unconscious for four days. In tantra practice there is a rite in which one goes naked under a particular constellation, brings back sticks of behedaa wood, fashions a peg from that wood, recites a banishing mantra, and drives it into the ground at a place — whereupon the residents of that place flee, and the place is left desolate.

In the Atharvaveda, in the "Abhichara Kalpasutra," the details of such abhichara (black-magic) rites are recorded. Harmful tantric rites of sacrifice mention six kinds of abhichara: marana (killing), mohana (bewitching), stambhana (paralysing), vidveshana (causing enmity), uchchatana (banishing), and vashikarana (subjugating). Those who perform these abhichara rites are held to be punishable. (Registration no. 448, page 984.)

Jivanji Maharaj was not one to be frightened by superstition and fear, and he did not wish to look upon the behedaa tree with contempt. Compelled by the helplessness of the famine, he must have had to eat the kernels of the behedaa fruit — those kernels are tasty, and eating too many of them must have brought on his intoxicated, unconscious state.

On his return journey, after some days, he arrived at Jagannath. There he had the direct darshan of Lord Jagannath, and stayed there for several days. During this stay, one evening at dusk, Vaishnav Jivandasji was sitting leaning against a pillar when he entered a state of bhava-samadhi (devotional trance), and no outward consciousness remained in him. As night fell, the temple priests closed the doors and went away, and Jivanji Maharaj was left behind inside the temple. It is said that no one is permitted to stay overnight inside this temple — folk belief holds that anyone who spends the night in the temple either comes out dead in the morning or goes mad. Even today, for this reason, no one is allowed to spend the night there.

All the temple attendants closed the doors and left; Jivanji Maharaj remained inside. At midnight, an endless resounding began — endless instruments playing and singing was heard. Jivanji Maharaj heard this sound directly, and yet no one was to be seen; no one had entered the temple, nor was anyone outside, and yet the sound went on. (A more detailed account of this incident is given in Jivandasji's Parchari, composed by Shyamdasji — see Uda Dharma Panchratnamala, page 241.)

In this temple, Ekadashi is said to be hung upside down, and so no fast is observed there on the day of Ekadashi. Moreover, people of all eighteen varnas eat together there, seated in a single row.

Thus the night passed, and in the morning, when the attendants opened the doors, they saw Jivanji Maharaj seated inside in bhava-samadhi. They were struck with great astonishment — for no one is supposed to be able to remain inside — and when they saw this rare and exceptional saintly man seated in the temple in devotional trance, everyone bowed with devotion at his feet.

Thus, after staying here some time, Jivanji Maharaj came to Ayodhya seven days later. There he had darshan of the ancient Ayodhya. It is said, according to the view of the Puranas, that this is the place where King Ram ruled for eleven thousand years — that is, after Ram departed for his heavenly abode, Ram-rajya continued for eleven thousand years, meaning the kingdom went on being governed according to Ram's own righteous principle. The extent of this Ayodhya was sixteen yojanas (a yojana being an old measure equal to about four gaus, or eight miles, roughly thirteen kilometres — by this reckoning the kingdom's extent would come to about two hundred and eight square kilometres). When Raghunathji (Ram) departed for his heavenly abode, all the inhabitants of Ayodhya prepared to go along with him. Maharshi Valmiki writes:

_Tatah sarva prakritayo Ramam vachanamabruvan, gacchantam anugacchamo yatra Ram gamishyasi. ||3||_ (Ramayan, Uttarkand 107-12) (Then all the people said to Ram: "O Ram! Wherever you go, we shall all follow you there.")

The Adhyatma Ramayan, in the ninth chapter of the Uttarkand, verse 66, also says: _Tato vimagra sarayujaleshu nara parityajya manushyadeham, aruhya divyabharana vimanam prapushcha te santanikakhyalokan. ||4||_ (As soon as all those people plunged into the Sarayu and gave up their human bodies, they at once received divinely adorned bodies and a celestial chariot, and, seated in that chariot, went to the realm called Santanik.)

Besides human beings, God also took with him the souls born in tiryak yoni, the animal kingdom. "Tiryak" refers to living creatures other than humans — animals, birds, and the like — for when such a creature stands up, its head does not rise straight up as a human's does but stays horizontal, and its food, too, does not travel straight down into the stomach but goes in sideways; hence "tiryak" carries the meaning "crooked, horizontal."

Seeing the love of all the townsfolk, Ram gave everyone leave to come along with him. Of this it is said: _Brahmadikanam sannidhye sanathikritya devatah, brahmalokadhva chandala asheshaprani sanhitah. ||30||_ (In the presence of Brahma and the other gods, having brought the deities under his protection, Lord Ramchandra took with him to heaven every being, from the outcaste to the Brahmin, and all the Gandharvas — and so Ayodhya became a wilderness.)

That is, on going to Vaikuntha, knowing the heart's wish of all his people, he took with him every inhabitant of Ayodhya, from the poorest outcaste to the wealthiest, and all the animals, birds, and insects; all who bathed together with him in the Sarayu went along to Vaikuntha.

_Svanitah sarvagandharvastenayodhya vanikrita, Ramenoktau sutau satyarajyartha salakshmanih. ||31||_ (All the Gandharvas were led away with him, and by this Ayodhya was turned to forest; Ram, together with Lakshman, instructed his two sons Lav and Kush to rule the kingdom righteously.)

In this verse, in place of the words "tenayodhya vanikrita," there is a variant reading "chira-ayodhya"; hence the commentary within the Samagam explains it as "Chira Jodhya van keta-i." "Chira Jodhya" means the old Ayodhya, and the word "ketai-van" is a corruption of "kantar-van." "Kantar-van" means a forest of kovidar trees, or else a great, dense, uninhabited forest; "kantar" can also mean sugarcane or bamboo. One might say that trees like the kovidar must have grown up in the old, desolate Ayodhya. Further, if we take the sense of "ketai," it may also be a corruption of "kataka," meaning the kataka fruit — that is, nirmali — the powder of which, when put into dirty water, makes the water clear. So it may be said that the animals, birds, and other creatures of the tiryak yoni who dwelt in Ram's Ayodhya, by the power of Ramchandra's glance, gave up their bodies as they plunged into the water and went along with Ram. Thus Ram made Ayodhya like a nirmali-kataka fruit that cleanses even sinners.

The verse showing that Ram gave Lav and Kush the command to rule the mortal world appears as the sixteenth verse of the ninth canto of the Uttarkand in the Adhyatma Ramayan: _Prasthapayamasa cha tau Ramabhadrah kushilavau, ashtau rathasahasrani sahasram chaiva dantinam. ||5||_ (That night, having made this resolve, he sent Kush and Lav each to his own kingdom, giving each of them eight thousand chariots, one thousand elephants, and eight thousand horses.)

That is, before taking away everyone — Gandharvas and all — from Ayodhya, Ram first enthroned his two sons: he crowned Kush over the kingdom of Kosala and Lav over the region of North Kosala, handing separate kingdoms to the two brothers. Then Lord Ramchandra withdrew his divine play. Thus Ayodhya became desolate; no one remained there. Jivanji Maharaj came to this original Ayodhya and had darshan of all its sites — the site of Ramchandraji's palace, and the ground where Sitaji and Lakshman had dwelt. He saw the site of Bharatji's dwelling, bathed in the river Sarayu, and recited a sakhi.

_Main Ayodhyame Jivana, man mero Gokul manhi. Rishi patnisu kol hai, ve birad visrat nahi. ||6||_ (Meaning: Lord Ramchandra speaks to himself, saying: O Jivan, my mind is not truly attached to this play I am now enacting in Ayodhya; rather, my mind is fixed on the age to come, in which I am to take the Krishna avatar. I long for the moment when I shall assume the form of Krishna and fulfil the promise I gave to the sages' wives, letting them perform devotion to me — for, despite performing yajnas and other ritual acts, the sages themselves attained nothing, but their wives, through devotion, recognised Lord Ram and pleaded with him, "Grant us the opportunity to serve you." Ram promised he would grant them this opportunity at his birth as Krishna. It is in keeping with this episode that Jivanji Maharaj recites this sakhi at Ayodhya.)

Thus, staying in Ayodhya, Jivanji Maharaj remembers the life of Gokul; the memory of this leela of Shri Krishna comes back to him, and so he recites this sakhi. Our Jivanji Maharaj himself was one of the sixteen companions (sakhas) of Shri Krishna, and so it is only natural, and fitting to the place, that this memory should come to him here.

sections.title_en: A Petition to the Merciful Lord at the Himalaya
sections.translation:
Having stayed seven days in Ayodhya, Jivanji Maharaj went from there to Naimisharanya. He stayed here four days and wandered to various places. Naimisharanya is also known as Nimkhar or Nimsar. This is a very ancient place of pilgrimage, and it is also the birthplace of all the Puranas. At this place the sage Romaharshan recited all the Puranas and told them to everyone — such an account is found in many Puranas and in the Mahabharata. (In the month of Fagan a circumambulation fair is held here, and many devout people gather; also, on every amavasya, large numbers of people come and bathe in Chakratirth.)

Now, in our sampraday, places of pilgrimage hold no importance; but Jivanji Maharaj's purpose in wandering to these places was different. Jivanji Maharaj had set out to study the life of the people of India — that is why he went to many places. The purpose of giving further information about this particular place here is only for the sake of information.

Naimisharanya — After Ramchandraji slew Ravana, in order to be freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatya), he bathed in the Hatyaharan Tirth located within Naimisharanya and removed the sin; and he removed the brahmahatya under the name of Shiv Nirmalya. Jivanji Maharaj has spoken of Shiv Nirmalya:

_Ramnam bhaj Jivana, je Anjanisutke ish,_
_hatya utari Lankeshki, je Shiv Nirmalya shish ||1||_ — Pramodh 142

(Chant the name of Ram, the worshipped Lord of Anjani's son [Hanuman] — this Ram, who bore the sin of killing Lanka's king, had it removed from his head under the name of Shiv Nirmalya.)

Chant the name of that Ram who is worshipped by Hanuman. This Ram, who incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin by slaying Ravana, the lord of Lanka — that sin was removed from his head (that is, attributed to him) under the name Shiv Nirmalya; that is, the offering made to Shiva, which could otherwise be accepted as prasad, was declared unacceptable under the name Shiv Nirmalya, and by this Ram removed the sin of brahmahatya that had attached to him for [killing] the king of Lanka.

_Deh barabar kot ber, hem tol jo det,_
_so Shiv Nirmalya Jivana, jo Harijan su nahi het ||2||_ — Prabodh 143

(Even were you to give in charity gold weighed equal to your own body's weight, crores of times over — O Jivan, that too becomes like Shiv Nirmalya if you have no love for the Harijans.)

Even if you weigh out gold equal to your body's weight and give it as charity (tuladan), crores of times over, still — just as a thing offered to Shiva cannot be accepted by anyone — in the same way, that meritorious gift too, if you have no love and devotion for the devotees of God (Harijans), will be counted as unacceptable, like Shiv Nirmalya, and you will not obtain the fruit of that merit.

In the Padma Purana it is said regarding Shiv Nirmalya —

_Nirmalya Shankaradinam sa chandalo bhaved dhruvam,_
_kalpa koti sahasrani pachyate narakagnina ||1||_ — Padma Purana

(If a Brahmin, or the like, eats even once what has been offered to Shiva, he surely becomes like an outcaste, and burns for thousands of crores of kalpas in the fire of hell.)

If a Brahmin or others eat even once the substance offered to Shiva, they certainly become like an outcaste (chandal), and burn in hellfire for thousands of crores of kalpas. It is also said that one should not eat what is offered in a temple, nor should even the priest be fed anything from it.

_Patram pushpam phalam toyam dravyam anna mathasyacha,_
_vashrati narakan ghoran seveta chaika vishanti ||2||_ — (Purana)

(Whoever partakes of the leaf, flower, fruit, water, wealth, or food of a temple, dwells in twenty-one terrible hells.)

A person who eats the leaf, flower, fruit, water, or wealth belonging to a temple goes to hell twenty-one times.

_Narakaya matiste, chetyaurohityam samachar,_
_varsha yavaktimanyena mathchintam dinatrayam ||3||_ — Panchatantra, Mitra Sampraapti, 69

(If your mind is set on going to hell, then act as a priest for a year — or, if that is too much, simply attend to a monastery's affairs for three days.)

If you wish to go to hell, act as a priest for a year; or else — what more need be done? — merely look after the affairs of a monastery for three days (even just taking care of the monastery's work is enough).

On the subject of the Mahant, register no. 321, page 123, writes:

_Ab bhi log mahantoko pranam nahi karte, balki namo-narayan karte hain. Jiska arth hai ki 'He Bhagwan, inhe dekhnese jo kuch paap hua woh maaf kijiye.'_

(Even today people do not bow before mahants with a full pranam, but instead say "Namo Narayan" — meaning: "O Lord, whatever sin has been incurred merely by looking at them, please forgive it.")

Ram enacted the play (lila) of Shiv Nirmalya only so as to be called Maryada Purushottam [the ideal man who upholds all propriety]; the fault of brahmahatya could never actually attach to him.

The main point — the essence of Shiv Nirmalya — Jivanji Maharaj applied to freedom from addiction (vyasan mukti). He freed us from the addiction to bhang and tobacco, and gave the instruction to serve the Harijans and to chant the name of Ram. Having observed the site of Naimisharanya, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj regarded this very freedom from addiction as equal to Shiv Nirmalya. The inspiration to give up addiction and take up devotion to Ram was received from the sight (darshan) of Naimisharanya.

Badrinarayan: it is 13,200 feet high. The mountains to its east and west are called Jay and Vijay. The image of Badrinarayan is seated cross-legged; because of this China believes it to be an image of the Buddha. This site of Badrinath is called Mandarachal and Badrikashram. There is a saying —

_Jagannathama naat nahi, Badrima sonar,_
_Vaikunthma brahman nahi, Bhrigue lagavi laat ||3||_

(At Jagannath there is no caste; at Badri, no goldsmith; at Vaikunth, no Brahmin — for Bhrigu once struck [Vishnu] with his foot.)

At Jagannathji, people of eighteen castes eat together in a single row — there is no distinction of caste or community there. Also, at Badrinath, goldsmiths do not have the right to darshan. And because sage Bhrigu once kicked Vishnu in the chest, Brahmins are not permitted to enter Vaikunth.

Just as at Jagannathji, so too at Badrinath, there is no discrimination among the eighteen castes. Even so, Raghavdasji Maharaj had a separate cooking-pot (handi, an earthen vessel for cooking rice) set up at Jagannathji, so as to keep our place distinct, and had this recorded on a copper plate. The king of Jagannathji holds many such copper-plate records. The reason we need a separate handi is that among people of the eighteen castes there is no exclusive, single-minded devotion (ananya bhakti). Since they follow the path of Vedic ritual (karmakand), in our view they fall into the category of impure or mixed observance [sakut salil]. It is for this reason that Jivanji Maharaj instructed us to keep away from their company. For this reason we cannot accept another's garland or offered prasad — only if we ourselves offer the garland to the prasad can that prasad then be taken by us.

This Jagannathji, admitting his own weakness before Jivanji Maharaj, said: just as you have manifested from your own abode by the command of Purnabrahma Ram, in the same way I too wish to enact that same lila which that same Lord once performed — and how the trial of love is undergone, you yourself know; it was with that very intention of performing that lila that I played, sounding instruments and so on, and thereby increased the flush of love, and let you hear those instruments.

Going onward from Badrinath, one reaches the border of the country called Aryavart-Bharat. The boundary of Aryavarta is as follows: the region lying between the Vindhyachal and the Himalaya, and between the eastern sea and the western sea, is called Aryavarta. There, one came across the Ekpaag people. Regarding these people, "Hindustan ni Tirthyatra," register no. 283, page 397, writes that just as the parikrama of Vrajdham is of eighty-four kos, so the parikrama of Kashi is the Panchkoshi (five-kos) parikrama. From Kashi, the Panchkoshi parikrama is forty-seven miles. It begins at Manikarnika Ghat; along the way of this parikrama comes Bhimchandi, where one has the darshan of Gandharvasar, Bhimchandi Devi, Bhimchandvinayak, Raviraktaksh Gandharva, Narkarnavtarak Shiv, and the Ekpad-gana. It is said that the soil of this Panchkoshi cannot be taken elsewhere. Toys made of this clay turn out well, but they are not permitted to be carried outside.

We see that in Patan there is a good population of potters (kumbhar), and they make beautiful clay toys. The toys made by these clay craftsmen can be taken elsewhere. Not only that, but devout people also take the dust of Padmavadi to remove the three-fold afflictions (tritap). Sarvarkhan, the ruler of Patan, had a boil that had broken out on his back, and it was cured by this soil. Thus there is this much difference between Lord Padmanabh, considered an incarnation of Vishnu, and Shiva, considered the presiding deity of death: devotees of Vishnu are fearless, whereas devotees of Shiva walk about fearful in every matter. One must take special care regarding Shiv Nirmalya, and yet addicted people behave as though they have no regard for Shiva at all — and so that people would give up intoxicants such as bhang, tobacco, and dhatura, the scripture-writers made efforts, in the name of Shiv Nirmalya, to get people to abandon addiction; yet the slaves of addiction, acting on their own willfulness, have spread the belief that the nirmalya (leftover offering) of the twelve Jyotirlingas may indeed be taken. Thus, those who eat Shiv Nirmalya while considering themselves fearless still cannot escape the ill effects of bhang, tobacco, and dhatura — whereas, though Padmavadi in Patan is a cremation ground, the devotees of Vishnu who take home its dust remain entirely fearless and secure.

In the Himalaya, in the region of Shiva's Ekpad-gana (one of Shiva's names — that is, a class or group of people devoted to Shiva), Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, a great and capable man, went. Having set out to search for and look after his own people (nij jan), Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj investigated even as far as this abode of Shiva, and saw that those who practice devotion to Vishnu have no need to come to such an abode. So, crying out to God, he utters the words, "He Maharaj, ko nahi jato" [O Lord, no one is truly mine]. He roamed through the ranges of a hundred and twenty-five thousand mountains, yet found no place suited to devotion to Vishnu, nor any company of saints through which fitting devotion could be practiced. Even a meeting with the Ekpad Shiv-ganas, this great traveling Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj did not leave undone; and going on into these mountain ranges, he reached as far as Dantnagar, a town spread across sixteen yojans, and then — considering that Padmanabh Adhyaruji and others like him, who bestow devotion in Gujarat, and where the company of saints is readily available, and where he had the longing to look after his own people — Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj resolved to return to Gujarat, the land of places such as Dwarka and Patan. He climbed Kaleshwar mountain, went to Kailash — went there with the intention of settling and resolving afflictions (kalesh) — and looking, as it were, through a telescope, he judged it fitting to come to the land of Gujarat. He petitioned Kripanath: "O Maharaj! In all that I have seen thus far, there is no place elsewhere worthy of your trust, other than Gujarat."

Having stayed four days in Naimisharanya, Jivanji Maharaj set out on his journey toward Badrinarayan.

He began his journey there. Having arrived, he rested four days. From there, going further, he came to the country called Aryavart (within the borders of the nation of India), where he encountered the Ekpad people. Going on further from here, he came, upon the Himalaya, to a village named Dantnagar. After that, walking on for four continuous days, taking in natural beauty, viewing God's creation, going on and on, he reached one of the high mountain ranges of the Himalaya bearing thousands upon thousands of mountain hillocks. There he sat, leaning against a high mountain range. And at the end of such a long journey, sitting at this solitary place, he looks toward all four directions — that is, he surveys the activities then under way throughout the whole land of India. He finds the entire human community, as it were, wrapped in flames of a kind of fire. Let us see it in the words of "Samagam":

_"He Maharaj ko nahi jato," evo bol kahyo, vali uttar dakshin, purva pashchim disha char samu bhalyu (joyu)._

("O Maharaj, no one is [truly] mine," such words he spoke; and he looked toward the four directions — north, south, east, and west.)

That is: on the high mountain peak of the Himalaya, in a state of emotional absorption (bhav samadhi), Jivanji Maharaj hears the inward cry of the people of India — as if the world is crying out, "O Maharaj, no one is mine." These words are the sigh of the common people of India. All four corners of the world are ablaze. Through the many kinds of burning inflicted by ritualism (karmakand), homa, havan, yagna, yagadi, the sacred thread (yagyopavit), vows, fasts, pilgrimages, and so on, the mass of mankind is being burned. North, south, east, west — wherever you look, society is being scorched in these burning embers of Brahminism. And no one is willing to hear the plea of the common man. To twist the meaning of scripture to suit oneself, and to turn religion into sheer hypocrisy — in the name of religion, mere show, hypocrisy, and the sheer urge to plunder have become the root cause of this society's downfall. Jivanji Maharaj became grieved in the face of this suffering.

Amid the flames of fire in every direction, seeing coolness on one side, a silent peace arose within him. He sits leaning against a small mountain hillock. He has known great sorrow; there he petitioned Kripanath, and made a firm resolve: "O Maharaj! O Kripanath! Now I will go among the Vaishnavs and hold satsang [samagam] — fulfill my heart's wish."

That is: seeing society mired in Vedic ritual and karmakand, Jivanji Maharaj became sorrowful. So he resolves: "I will now rescue my own people from this suffering." In making this resolve, he uses two forms of address — "He Maharaj" and "He Kripanath." The first address, "He Maharaj," is directed to Guru Gopaldasji, because it was by the guru's blessing and inspiration that he had traveled to Malwa and other places. The reason behind this was that Gopaldasji had been able to recognize Jivanji Maharaj. He knew that in his disciple lay some wondrous power beyond his own; that if it were brought forth, everything would change in an instant, as if by an explosion — that in this way Jivanji Maharaj could transform society, or could kindle a fresh revolution within it. This is why, among Gopaldas's many disciples, his choice settled on Jivanji Maharaj alone.

Among Gopaldasji's other disciples may be counted Pandyaji of Kandari, and another, Jagaji Maharaj of Sokhda village. Today, the sites of their samadhi still exist in their respective places. Even so, through Pandyaji and Jagaji Maharaj, as much revolution could not be brought about in society as was needed. Anantdasji of Borbar too may have been as capable as Jivanji Maharaj, yet nothing remains today at his place. His family lives on in Borbar, but they know nothing of the Ramkabir tradition or of Guru Gopaldasji, nor do they follow this tradition. It falls to us to appreciate the devotion that dwelt within Anantdas — a recognition that Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj himself gave.

Anantdas wrote roughly nine parcharis [devotional accounts]. Jivanji Maharaj honored him by giving the important portions of these a place within Samagam. There is also a pad (hymn) he composed, found in Panchratnamala, 4th edition, page 396. Thus, although this disciple may have been an understanding man, still the light of devotion is not evident at his place. The work that Jivanji Maharaj carried out with full strength and dedication established a wholly new tradition; we shall discuss this at greater length further on. But here, the address "He Maharaj" was made in remembrance of the guru — in the guru's witness he is taking this vow to bring about revolution.

The second address, "He Kripanath," was made by invoking as witness the supremely merciful Lord. For just as the presence of the guru is essential, so too is the witness of the Supreme Being, Parabrahma, essential — because the devotee and God are never separate. God is bound up, joined, in every act of the devotee. This is why he calls to mind Kripanath here. We shall see further on, too, that in any undertaking of Jivanji Maharaj, God comes first of all. In any of our daily, routine, or social undertakings, the remembrance of God must surely come in. We should not begin any task without remembrance of God — this too he teaches us through this statement.

Thus, remembering both guru and God, Jivanji Maharaj, from the high peak of the Himalaya, forms the resolve to bring new awakening to society. Taking inspiration from this place, he turns back, carrying his resolve with him. Now the moments before the coming of new awakening and revival begin to be counted; that moment draws gradually nearer. Jivanji Maharaj, setting aside his sorrow, shaking off his weariness, readies himself for this new awakening. With firm stride he begins his return journey from the Himalaya. Now he has come to know the world thoroughly; he has seen, up close, the deceit and hypocrisy of man; he has come to understand the sophistry carried on in the name of religion. Whatever caste or community a person may belong to, he has seen very closely the self-seeking tendency at work in the mind of people everywhere.

Those upon whose shoulders rests the responsibility of upholding society and religion — the Brahmins — have become small-minded. In the name of scripture they have spread mere falsehood. So-called saints and elders too, in the name of various religions, have set up shops of religion and settled themselves in. It is against such elements that Jivanji Maharaj's indignation has flared. And now, whatever words issue from his mouth are the speech of his own direct experience. Jivanji Maharaj's sakhis were not composed leisurely, sitting in some corner, but were composed out of the experience of his life, and later, out of his relationship with his disciple Gopaldas at Shahpura. Thus this is the speech of direct experience — and it is for this reason he has said:

_Koi nahi tera Jivana, mein dekho des videsh,_
_Sitapatiko aasro, ke Sadguruko updesh ||1||_

(No one is yours, O Jivan — I have looked through country and foreign land; only the shelter of Sitapati [Ram], or the teaching of the Sadguru, is truly one's own.)

_Sab jag dhundhyo Jivana, tera koy nav hoy,_
_Apne apne padkun, laagi rahai sab koy ||2||_

(I searched the whole world, O Jivan — none was found to be truly yours; everyone remains attached only to their own position.)

_Kali darshan bohotu mile, Harijan mile na koi,_
_Harijan mile jo Jivana, to dukh mera kahu roy ||3||_

(In Kali Yuga many false devotees may be found, but no true Harijan [devotee of God] is found; if a Harijan is found, O Jivan, then I may weep out my sorrow before him.)

_Kabir des videsh main bhamyo, sumansa sugaal,_
_Jeh dithe man ulse, taka bada dakaal ||4||_

(Kabir says: I have wandered through country and foreign land; good people are not scarce, but those whose sight gladdens the mind are in great famine.)

_Mein pardeshi kahasu kahu, ihaan nahi koi mera,_
_E sansar sakal thag baji, ek bharosa tera ||5||_

(I am a stranger here — what shall I say? No one here is mine; this whole world is a game of deceit — my only trust is in You.)

_Kabir sab jag dhundhiya, dekha dodi joy,_
_Lahe parakh sukh paiye, aisa nav dekha koy ||6||_

(Kabir says: I searched the whole world, running about to look, but I never found anyone by knowing whom happiness could be found.)

_Kabir sant mile sukh upje, sant gaye dukh hoy,_
_Tathe dehi dubli, nayana het hai roye ||7||_

(Kabir says: when a saint is met, joy arises; when the saint departs, sorrow comes; from this my body has grown weak, and my eyes weep out of love.)

_Kabir te din gaye akaajthe, jahan sangat bhai nav sant,_
_Prem bina pashu jivano, bhagat bin bhagvant ||8||_

(Kabir says: that day is wasted in which no company of saints was had; life without love is like an animal's life, and God is as nothing without a devotee.)

Jivanji Maharaj says: I wandered much through country and foreign lands, but I did not find any person I could call my own — no one was found who was absorbed in Parabrahma. — 1

Wander the whole world over, and you will find everyone engrossed only in their own self-interest; selfishness has entered everywhere. Thus, to meet a truly genuine human being in this world is very difficult. — 2

In Kali Yuga many pretend-devotees will be found, but a Harijan — a true devotee of God — is hard to come by. If a devotee of God is found, sorrow can be shared with him; if a Harijan is found, one's inward pain can be spoken before him. — 3

Kabirji too says: I have wandered through country and foreign lands, but good people are not scarce — yet there is a great scarcity of those meeting whom my mind rejoices and blossoms.

Kabirji says: I have come into this world as a stranger, for my own country lies elsewhere; hence here there is no one who wishes me well or listens to me. What can I say of this world? For in this world, deception is everywhere at play. — 4

Moreover, today there are many who run after seeing outward show, and many who draw in those who come running like moths; but there are no such people whom, gaining as one's own, we could be happy, and whose company brings joy. O God, I have complete trust only in Your grace — surely You alone shall bring about my welfare. — 5

In the whole world, we searched frantically and in agitation for a well-wisher who might be truly our own, but nowhere did we find a person whose acquaintance and understanding would bring us the experience of peace and contentment. — 6

(There is a saying —

_Dhutta hoy sulakshana, veshya hoy sulaj,_
_khara paani nirmala, tino pahela parkhi taj ||4||_

(One who appears well-featured may be a cheat; a very bashful woman may be a prostitute; and salty water may look clear — all three should first be tested, then discarded.)

When someone with fine features appears, that person may be a cheat; a very bashful woman may in fact be a prostitute; and salty water may look clear — all three of these should be tested first, and then set aside.)

When a saint is met, joy arises for me, and when the saint departs, sorrow arises; and because of this sorrow, my body grows weak — otherwise I have no love or attachment for any other matter. For the sight of saints, my eyes weep and yearn out of the pain of my heart. — 7

That day is meaningless on which the company of saints does not occur; the day on which no saint comes is a wasted day. Just as animals lack love, so too there is no God without a devotee — in the same way, a true saint always remains in the company of saints. Without love and devotion, life is counted as that of an animal; likewise, without a devotee-saint, God too has no worth. — 8

Thus, having spoken this sakhi, Jivanji Maharaj, showing compassion upon Gujarat, resumed his journey. What was the nature of Jivanji Maharaj's kindness? It is like the kunj bird, which leaves its eggs on the seashore and goes all the way to Mansarovar to graze.

This is a folk belief, a legend from the Puranas. The kunj bird, though far away, still tends to its eggs. It undertakes a long journey to a distant land, yet it constantly remembers its eggs. In the same way, Jivanji Maharaj, from far atop the peak of the Himalaya, made his resolve for the deliverance of his own people, and also showed compassion. Thus, just as the kunj bird, wherever it may go to graze, keeps its gaze fixed on its eggs, so too, though Jivanji Maharaj may travel through country after country, his heart has now become bound to the cries of his own devotees, his own people — because —

Having endured hardship to travel as far as the Himalaya, Jivanji Maharaj became certain that the world has not fallen short of good, worthy people; everyone is respectful and welcoming. But there is a scarcity of those with whom our minds are in harmony, and whose company brings us contentment. Yet Jivanji Maharaj is indeed Kripanath — toward Gujarat he had devotees who were the recipients of his grace, and to look after them he returns from the Himalaya. Just as even a bird like the kunj does not delay in caring for its family, how then could Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, a Sadguru so full of love, ever forget his devotee?

_Kabir chuge chitare bhi chuge, chug chug hi chitare,_
_kunj laal bacha piu, haiya nahi bisaar ||9||_

(Kabir says: it grazes and grazes, thinking [of its young] all the while it grazes; O kunj, though far from your young ones, your heart never forgets them.)

That is: the bird called kunj leaves its eggs far away on the seashore and, grazing all the way, goes as far as Mansarovar. Yet, as evening falls, it comes back to its young. That bird never forgets its young from within its heart.

There are five sacred lakes in India: (1) Mansarovar, in the Himalaya; (2) Pushkar, in Ajmer; (3) Bindu Sarovar, in Siddhpur; (4) Pampa Sarovar, in Kishkindha; (5) Narayan Sarovar, in Kachchh. The kunj bird comes from Europe and North Asia to Kachchh, Gujarat, after the rainy season. Thus, though this bird undertakes a journey to far distant lands, it returns to its homeland. In the same way, Jivanji Maharaj returns from far away to Gujarat to look after his own people.

Such was his kindness. Beyond his own family, Jivanji Maharaj never regarded his own devotees as strangers. Jivanji Maharaj's devotees were as members of his own family, and he always held the same feeling toward everyone — which is why the word "family" has been used here. For just as the head of a joint family holds affection toward his family, that same affection Jivanji Maharaj held.

Thus, beginning his return journey from the Himalaya, he came to the region of Kashi. There, there was a Vairagi mathdhari [head of a hermitage]. Jivanji Maharaj asked him, "Where is Kabirji's temple (dwelling place)?" The mathdhari replied: In the middle of the Ganga, where a bright stream flows, that was the original site (dwelling place); but after Kabirji's departure to his own eternal abode, the Ganga took over this site. So, he had darshan of that place only from a distance, and offered his pranam. He stayed here four days and studied the life and works of Kabirji's lila [divine plays] (he called to mind Kabirji's word and speech). In Kashi there is Kabirji's site. The site where Jivanji had direct darshan of the Ekpad-ganas on Kailash mountain comes during the Panchkoshi parikrama of Kashi. Taking the karvat [ritual self-sawing] does not bring liberation — Jivanji says —

_Gulmalata ang modke, parasat kalindi nir,_
_akhil manav bhaye Jivana, sansaa mita sharir ||5||_ — Agadh 68

(Bending his body like a cluster of vines, when [Krishna] touched the waters of the Kalindi [Yamuna], for all mankind, O Jivan, the fear regarding the body was dispelled.)

When Lord Krishna bent his body like a cluster of vines and touched the waters of the Yamuna, the fear for the whole of mankind of having again and again to take on a body through the womb was removed.

Through the karvat of Kashi this fear is never removed; only by taking refuge in Krishna does the cycle of birth and death cease. During this time, he saw Kashi, saw Varanasi, and there spoke this sakhi.

_Sant darshankun Jivana, Kashi karvat le aap,_
_mukti kshetra vede kahi, mohi bado lagayo paap ||10||_

(For the sight of saints, O Jivan, people themselves take the karvat at Kashi — the Vedas call it a field of liberation, but a great sin has been laid upon me.)

_Karma hamaro katashi, koi Harijan aave manhi,_
_je kare hamari vasna, Jivan so to Harijan nahi ||11||_

(Whoever fulfills my [Kashi's] desire shall have my karma cut away, should any Harijan come within — but, O Jivan, one who acts on my desire is no Harijan at all.)

_Kashi nathi Jivana, nahi kalajug mero kaam,_
_mukti kshetra magahar bhayo, jahan Kabir kiyo vishram ||12||_

(Kashi has fled, O Jivan — in this Kali Yuga this is no work of mine; the true field of liberation has become Magahar, where Kabir took his final rest.)

People, believing that going to Kashi and undergoing the karvat brings the benefit of the darshan of saints, willingly take the karvat at Kashi; and, having been told that dying at Kashi in this way brings liberation, that Kashi is the abode of liberation, people are lured into taking the karvat, and are thereby led to their deaths — and this sin has been laid upon me [Kashi], so Kashi laments.

The power of Kashi has fled in fear — that is, the greatness of the abode of Kashi has departed. So Kashi says: in this fierce and terrible Kali Yuga, the work of delivering people is not within my power; hence my power to grant liberation has been destroyed. And it says: truly, the field of liberation that can actually grant liberation has become Magahar, the place where Kabirji shed his body.

_Pardar pardravya pardroh parangmukh,_
_Ganga bute kadaagatya maamayam pavayishyati ||4||_ — Skandapuran, Kashikhand

(When will there come one free of another's wife, another's wealth, and enmity toward others, to purify me? — thus speaks the Ganga.)

Like Kashi, the Ganga says: when will a man come, one free from [desire for] another's wife, another's wealth, and enmity toward others, who will purify me? (That is: I purify all beings, but it is such a man who burns away the sin that gathers within me.)

_Tan rahe sansarme, man harini paas,_
_tirath pan aasha rakhe, kyare aave harino das ||6||_

(Though the body may remain in the world, the mind stays close to Hari; even the pilgrimage site holds out hope, wondering when a devotee of Hari will come.)

Even if a person's body remains in the household and the world, if their mind stays close to devotion to Hari, then even the pilgrimage site holds hope for such a saint — hoping, when will such a devotee of God come to me?

_Dayala Kabir kala kartarki, jug jug rup akhand,_
_so Kashi manhe pragate, tode sab pakhand ||7||_

(Merciful Kabir is a manifestation of the Creator's own art, existing across ages in unbroken form; he it was who appeared within Kashi and broke through all hypocrisy.)

Dayaldas says that Kabirji is indeed one of the divine plays [kala/lila] among God's own incarnations; that Kabirji exists eternally, unbroken, across every age. Such a one as Kabirji appeared in Kashi and broke all forms of hypocrisy and pretense. In Kashi, renunciant sannyasis wander about, filled with expectation, roaming here and there; so it must be that Jivanji Maharaj too encountered some such Vairagi there.

_Naam vairagya dash viprayanam, karma vairagya shatani cha,_
_gyan vairagya mam dehi, tyag vairagya mam durlabh ||8||_

(Renunciation through the [divine] name may be found in perhaps ten Brahmins; renunciation through works, in hundreds; renunciation through knowledge exists in one free of body-consciousness; but true renunciation through relinquishment is rare indeed.)

Those absorbed in the divine name may perhaps number only ten. Those with renunciation through works [karma] may be in the hundreds. Those with the renunciation of knowledge would be free from attachment to the sense of the body — but true renunciation, through actual relinquishment, is rare indeed.

Jivanji Maharaj, striking at the pilgrimage site of "Kashi," says that, coming under the influence of scriptural claims, people come to Kashi hoping for the company of saints, and many even take the karvat here. In ancient times, Brahmins used to impress upon their patrons (yajmans) that death at Kashi is supreme — that one who dies there goes straight to dwell in Kailash. Because of this, many came here and had their bodies sawn upright with the very saw used for cutting wood. Jivanji Maharaj has called this episode extremely tragic and sorrowful. And it is precisely for this reason he has said that, seeing the place where the scriptures — the Vedas — had spoken this claim, and hearing the account, such a sin was attached to me — so speaks Kashi. For this is nothing but sheer blind faith and a wholly false belief; and it is this very belief that Jivanji Maharaj refutes here.

In this second sakhi, Jivanji Maharaj has presented a fine depiction. As if Kashi, seeing Jivanji Maharaj, cannot help but speak — as if, weeping in sorrowful lament, it is saying: this sinful play that goes on in my name causes karma [sin] to attach to me. If some saint were to come and put a stop to this sinful act, the stain attached to me would be removed. Ah, Kashi says, my desire — that is, the desire of anyone who comes wishing to take the karvat at Kashi — can never be that of a Harijan, a person of God.
