Such a one is nothing but purely blindly faithful, a hypocrite, engulfed in worldly desires, or else has come here having been led astray by false claims.

In the third sakhi as well, in the same way, as if Kashi, with its most sorrowful lament, says to Jivanji Maharaj (here two variant readings are found; in the sakhis of the 21 Angas, the reading is "Kashi kahe sun Jivana" [Kashi says, listen, O Jivan]) — "O Jivandasji! Listen to my words. What a terrible Kali Yuga this is! What a most fearsome sinfulness is this! How can I grant residence in Kailash to one who dies at this place? Ah, this is but a matter of ordinary common sense — just consider: if some terribly dreadful murderer, a killer, a sinner, comes here and dies, would all his deeds simply vanish? Could he become a holy, virtuous saint? Never." So, as it were, Kashi says that Kabirji truly did this world a great favor by breaking this very belief, and by going to Magahar — a region (village) that used to be reviled — and shedding his body there, he showed this world the sight of truth.

This itself is a great disgrace upon our country. The Brahmins, in writing the Puranas and scriptures, exercised no restraint whatsoever; and under the guise of "what's mine is yours, shared together," they began exaggerating everything they wrote, further and further. Moreover, instead of eradicating blind faith, they added to it. At places of pilgrimage, they sang the vast glory of charitable giving, and of religious rites such as shraddha [ancestral rites], and in this way they turned this very thing into their means of livelihood. Thus it was they themselves who spread more and more blind faith in society; and further, they themselves added self-serving statements into the scriptures, and thereby began leading the world astray. Today, in our language, there has even come about a forceful proverb built on this very belief: "Randh, saandh, sidhi, sanyasi — ehthi bache tab seve Kashi" [Widow, bull, staircase, renunciant — only one who escapes these should dwell in Kashi].

This proverb is a stain upon the nation's principal culture. Its meaning is that, after Kashi was declared a field of liberation, many families would leave their widowed women at Kashi to attain moksha there. Even today, in Kashi, there exist countless such monasteries, ashrams, and women's shelters, where widowed, helpless, and abandoned women of every condition live. Along with this, since Kashi is considered a city of learning and a place of worship, many sadhus, sannyasis, and tantriks too lie about and settle themselves here. Kashi is always crowded with pilgrims as well. Among these, hypocritical, deceitful sadhus and sannyasis and the like sexually exploit these helpless women. And many women, driven by helplessness, resort to wrongdoing merely to sustain their own livelihood.

Since Kashi is the land of Maheshwar Shankar, our Brahmins have also proclaimed a special glory in giving cows in charity here. Because of this, countless abandoned bulls and oxen roam this city, and they frequently knock people about as well.

The sannyasis here do nothing but dry Vedanta and scriptural debate. Mere disputation and argument have turned this pilgrimage site of Kashi into an arena of wrestling matches. And, most damning of all, it has been said that one must beware even of the "sannyasi." Here, a constant stream of pandas, priests, and tantric practitioners (ojhas) performing religious rites keeps growing. They have set up their base here and settled in. Often, at such pilgrimage sites, in the competition to perform such rites, fights even break out among the pandas; and such people also exploit the simple, innocent pilgrims. Thus, such degenerate people have established their dominance over this city — which is why a plain-spoken man like Jivanji Maharaj could never bear to tolerate this matter.

Jivanji Maharaj stayed in Kashi for four days, and from there went to Magahar, where Kabirji had resided in his final days. There he saw Baba Kabirji's crown (mugat); on his way back he came to the place called Kabirchaura. In the unseen presence of Kabirji, he attained great joy.

At the close of this review of Kashi and other places of pilgrimage running in the name of religion, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has expressed his own view regarding each of these places.

After resting four days in Kashi, Jivanji Maharaj set out again toward Mathura. Before reaching Mathura, the road passes through a village named Bareli. (Even today a district in this area is called Raibareli.) In this village of Bareli lived a Khatri family, and the householder was named Narandas Khatri. Narandas carried one great doubt in his mind. Let us go back a little for context. Narandas was a good soul devoted to holy company (satsang). He would serve any sadhu or saint who came to his door, and would always ask about the doubt that troubled him, but no one had ever been able to resolve it. Let us hear what his doubt was: "If some deceitful person puts on a tilak and a rosary, and comes to a Vaishnav with a deceitful heart, does that deceitful person attain God, or not?"

In other words: if a deceiver comes disguised as a sadhu or saint and meets a pure Vaishnav, and that Vaishnav serves and attends to the deceiver, does the deceitful person attain God or not? As for the deceiver himself, there is no question — he is deceitful, and is committing a sinful act. But what becomes of the genuine Vaishnav who served him? It was Vaishnav Jivandasji who resolved this doubt.

This Narandas Khatri would give a handful of grain to every sadhu and saint who came to his house and would bow to them. As Vaishnav Jivandasji was travelling from Kashi to Mathura, the village of Bareli came on the way, and Jivanji Maharaj arrived at Narandas's house. Since Narandas was a satsangi, sadhus and saints always stayed at his home, and a group of renunciate (vairagi) sadhus happened to be seated there; they too came and took their seats. Narandas Khatri brought the raw provisions for Jivanji Maharaj to cook, and Jivanji Maharaj cooked the meal himself and partook of the food as prasad.

Narandas Khatri put his question to the head (mahant) of the group of vairagi ascetics who had come and were staying there. On hearing this doubt, the mahant and all the vairagis with him began to offer their own opinions. Their own minds grew unsettled, for as soon as one doubt was raised, further doubts arose in its place, and none of them could give an answer. So the mahant pointed toward Jivandasji and said, "Ask this saint."

Narandas came, circled Jivanji Maharaj, prostrated fully before him, and spoke. What did he say?

"O Maharaj! If a deceiver deceitfully wears the tilak and the tulsi (basil bead necklace), and comes to meet Vaishnavs with a deceitful heart, does that deceitful person attain God, or not? Please resolve this doubt of mine — I long deeply for the answer." Jivanji Maharaj replied: "He does attain."

Then Narandas Khatri said, "Maharaj, show me some sign. Give me some testimony, some proof, then I will believe it."

In response, Jivanji Maharaj told the story of Pipaji. What story did he tell?

Four deceivers of the Mina caste (a Rajasthani community by this name) put on a deceitful disguise and came to Pipaji's house. Pipaji was not at home. Sitamata (Pipaji's wife), seeing that they wore the tilak and tulsi, took them to be Vaishnavs. She washed their feet, gave them seats, and cooked various dishes for them, satisfying the "Vaishnavs." After having them eat the food as prasad, she laid them on a bed to rest comfortably. In the middle of the night, they wounded Sitamata, took whatever wealth, gold and jewels there were, and fled.

The next day these same deceivers happened to meet Pipaji himself. Pipaji, taking them for Vaishnav saints, invited them along with him. The deceivers, not recognizing Pipaji, came along with him. But as they drew near Pipaji's house, they began to tremble, thinking to themselves, "Today our disguise will be exposed — we will be caught!" Meanwhile, seeing Pipaji arriving, Sitamata came out of the house.

Pipaji said to Sitamata, "O servant of Hari! Bring water, let us wash the feet of these devotees of Hari." Hearing this, Sitamata came out, bowed to Pipaji, and showed great respect to the deceivers, washing their feet and giving them seats. Then the deceivers spoke:

"Maharaj, we are four thieves of the Mina caste. We came to steal your wealth, and wearing this disguise we struck Sitamata, meaning to kill her. But the merciful Lord must have granted her a long life, for she survived."

Saying this, all four removed their rosaries and tilaks and laid them at Pipaji's feet, weeping bitterly in repentance. Moved by grace, Pipaji initiated them as Vaishnavs and made them Vaishnavs, and they spent the rest of their lives as true Vaishnavs. In this way all four attained God.

But why did this happen? Because Pipaji's own righteousness was genuine, and Sitamata's righteousness was genuine too — and so even the deceivers were carried across. This was the story Jivanji Maharaj told Narandas.

He also told a second story, of a king's daughter. The daughter of the king of a certain city wished to marry Shri Krishna; she had vowed that she would marry only God and no one else. A fisherman (Koli) came to know of this. A deceitful thought arose in his mind: to marry the king's daughter, he dressed himself up like the four-armed Lord Vishnu, and, riding a wooden Garuda he had made, began coming to meet the princess.

The princess could not tell that this was the fisherman; she truly took the fisherman himself to be Shri Krishna. One day the king came to know of this and, at the queen's word, decided the daughter should be married to Shri Krishna. Around this time, the king of another country came to attack. But this king stood firm, saying, "My daughter's bond is with Shri Krishna; he has become our son-in-law, so he will help us." He sent word by his servants to the Lord of Dwarka to resist the enemy army and defeat it. This news reached the fake, deceitful fisherman, and he panicked, for death faced him on both sides: if the king learned the truth he would have him impaled, and if he went to the battlefield the enemy would kill him. But there was no way out now — go he must. Thinking this, the fisherman prepared to go.

Meanwhile, the Lord of the Three Worlds came to know of this. He thought, "If the fisherman is defeated, it will disgrace my name — this stain will fall on me." Moreover, the princess's devotion to Shri Krishna was genuine. So Krishna commanded Garuda to prepare to go, saying, "We must live up to our title of being loving toward our devotees." Thus Krishna and Garuda arrived, killed and drove away the enemy, and set aside the fake fisherman who had posed as God — appearing in the fisherman's place as the true Lord Himself. Then the king said to Shri Krishna, "Let the marriage take place — now you must marry the princess yourself." Thus the Lord of Dwarka had to marry her, a fact to which Sadhanoji (Sadan the butcher) bears witness in his own hymn.

_Kapat bhekh koli kiyo, nrup kanyake kaaj ||
O naar bad bhaagini Jivana, je Shyame diyo sohaag ||1||_
(For the sake of the king's daughter, a fisherman took on a deceitful disguise as Vishnu. O Jivana, that woman was truly fortunate, for Shyam himself made her his bride.)

For the king's daughter, the fisherman deceitfully wore Vishnu's guise; but that woman is counted blessed, since God himself married her and made her a bride.

So Jivandasji said, "Brother, the gracious Lord had to go, and even had to marry the princess. But this happened because the princess's own righteousness was genuine — it was her truthfulness alone that bore fruit for her." Hearing these two answers, Narandas prostrated fully at the Lord's feet — like the chataka bird waiting eagerly for one who would end its thirst, so had Narandas waited for one who would end his doubt.

Narandas continued, "Maharaj, this village called Bareli lies on the main road. Everyone travelling to Jagannath, Badrikashram, Naimisharanya and other places, and to Ayodhya, Pushkar, Gaya, Kashi, and so on, passes through and stays in this village. Travelers come to my door because of the free meals and alms I give; Vaishnavs of all four sampradayas come, and countless ascetics of every order come too. But from none of these visitors could my doubt be resolved. Moreover, this place lies between the Ganga and the Yamuna — this region is known as Antarved, the sacred land between the Ganga and Yamuna stretching from Prayag to Haridwar. Around Mathura too there are many ascetics, sadhus, and pandits. Yet none of them could resolve this doubt. I have been asking every traveler this question for thirty-two years."

But who but Jagjivan (Jivanji Maharaj's original name) could dispel this doubt?

After this, he brought Jivanji Maharaj into his own house and served him greatly. Jivanji Maharaj stayed there two days. Narandas introduced Vaishnav Jivandasji to all the members of his family, presenting him to them as a true saint. This is the same Narandas who was the very first to become an "Udabhagat" (initiated devotee) and who, with his whole family and household, left Bareli and came to settle in Puniyad. It was this same Narandas who later influenced and astonished Krishnadasji, who had come from Agalod. After this Narandas had everyone else bow before Jivanji Maharaj, and then bowed to him himself.

This story appears as the fifth tale in the chapter on the "breaking of friends" (Mitrabheda) in the Panchatantra. Jivanji Maharaj presented this incident to make the point that when a devotee's faith is genuine, it bears fruit even for a deceiver. Narsinh Mehta too mentions this story in his morning hymns (Prabhatiya).

_Krishnajie Ajamil taryo, maha huto papi,
Ek Koliye kautuk kidhu, tene avichal padvi aapi._
(Lord Krishna redeemed Ajamil, who was a great sinner. Likewise, a fisherman performed a wondrous feat by taking on the form of Vishnu, yet the Lord granted him the imperishable abode.)

By "driving out" the fisherman, the Lord in fact delivered him to the highest abode, and then the Lord himself married the princess. Sadan the butcher was likewise a sinful man who became a supreme devotee; he sang this hymn:

_To gun kaha jagat guru, mera raag desaag karm naashe ||
Sangh sharan kit jaiye, jo pe jambuk graase ||tek||
Thokat thaakat kaahu bhavjal, kaahu paar na paad ||
Doob mooye nauka mile, kaho kaun chalaau ||1||
Swaati boondke kaarane, chaatak dukh paave ||
Praan gaye saagar mile, kaho kaun peeaavo ||2||
Nrup kanyake kaarane, bhayo bhekh dhaari ||
Kaamal bandh pakhand rachyo, vaaki pej samaari ||3||
Main kaami tum mitna, sab avgun mera ||
Koode kapate Keshava, Saghna jan tera ||4||_
(Sadan the butcher says: "O world Guru, what merit is there in me that could wash away my deeds? If jackals and the like devour us, then why should we need to take refuge in a lion? Struggling to swim across the ocean of worldly existence, I find no way to reach the far shore by myself. If I drown and die, and a boat comes afterward, tell me — who then will row it? Just as the chataka bird suffers for a drop of Swati rain, so, if its life departs, what use is even an ocean full of water — who would pour it into its beak? For the sake of a king's daughter, a fisherman, bound and tormented by desire, adopted a false, hypocritical guise — yet even so, his pledge and his faith were carried through to fulfilment. I too am full of lust and desire; only you can rid me of it. Otherwise I have nothing but faults — evil, corrupt, and deceitful as I am — yet, O Keshava, however unworthy, this Sadhna is your devotee.")

This story of the king's daughter is also mentioned in the 39th verse of the Arjuna Gita. Indeed, not every person wearing a saint's garb can be trusted.

_Vesham na vishvaset prajno, vesho doshaaya jaayate ||
Raavano bhikshu-roopena jahaara Janakaatmajaam ||1||_
(A wise person should never trust outward appearance alone, for a disguise can be worn with an evil intent — Ravana abducted Sitaji disguised in the form of a mendicant.)

In Narandas's case, the question was whether one who takes on a disguise out of a deceitful intention can still attain God. On this point, Jivanji Maharaj, by giving the examples of the thieves at Pipaji's house and of the fisherman, said that even one who assumes the guise of God attains liberation. Even though such a person may have put on the act out of deceit, by doing so under the name of God he has, indirectly if not directly, turned his gaze toward God — and therefore, it is held, he can certainly become deserving of God's grace.

Uday Mehta, minister of Siddharaj, followed the Jain faith. He was wounded on the battlefield, and, as he lay dying, expressed a final wish to have the darshan of a Jain ascetic (yati); but on the battlefield this was not possible. However, a soldier knew a folk-actor living in a nearby village, and had him put on the robes of a yati and brought him there. The "yati" greeted Uday Mehta with the blessing "Dharmalabh," and after having this darshan, Uday Mehta's soul departed his body. When the soldier later asked the actor to return the borrowed robes, the actor said, "These robes will not come off now" — for it had struck him that if even a false, imitation sadhu like himself could bring about someone's well-being, then surely he himself would attain well-being by truly wearing this garb in earnest. And so this folk-actor became, in truth, a real yati.

In the film "Gandhi," the actor who played Gandhiji's role is an Englishman. After playing the role of Gandhiji, Gandhiji's influence worked on him so much that this Englishman gave up alcohol and meat. So even when a role is played only in pretense, the character being portrayed leaves some impression, however small, on the one who plays it. This may not happen every time, but if such a pretense is enacted before a true devotee, it does not go to waste — God accepts it.

There is a hymn, "Bana ni pat rakh Prabhu tara banani" (Keep the honour of your pledge, Lord, for it is your own pledge). In this hymn, a hunter aims his arrow to kill a bird, and at the same moment a hawk circling in the tree above is also stalking the bird to kill it. So the bird faces death whether it stays put or flies away — and in this plight it cries out to God. Then God arranged that a scorpion stung the hunter, so that his arrow flew loose and struck the hawk instead, killing it. In this way God removed the danger from both the hunter and the hawk.

From Bareli he came on toward Gokul, Mathura and Vrindavan, and here Jivanji Maharaj is reminded of Vraj, Krishna's beloved land. He held Vraj to be dearer to Krishna even than Vaikunth, and to show how little regard God has for Vaikunth, he says that Lord Krishna left Vaikunth for good and came to Vraj. Therefore a devotee of God ought not to long for Vaikunth; one who clings to that desire and goes to Vaikunth will only find it empty of God, and his longing to attain God will remain unfulfilled — for God is simply not in Vaikunth. A true devotee prefers to bear hardship in Vraj rather than enjoy the comforts of Vaikunth. For—

_Baandar kaante dim dukh Vrajvaasi aru chor ||
Shat kales ya kunjmen, pai aasha Yugal Kishor ||2||_
(Monkeys, thorns, illusions, sorrows, wicked residents of Vraj, and thieves — despite these six kinds of affliction in Vraj, devotees choose to live there out of longing for the darshan of the divine pair, and have no desire for the barren happiness of Vaikunth.)

A devotee has sung this hymn:

_Mane Vraj vahalu re, mare Vaikunth nathi javu,
Tya mara vhala Nandakuvarne kyathi lavu._
(Vraj is dear to me; I do not wish to go to Vaikunth — for how could I bring my beloved Nandakuvar there?)

Setting out from Bareli, he came to Gokul, then went on to see the Banshivat ghat before proceeding to Vrindavan, where he stayed four days. A Vaishnav family lived there; he met them and there was a gostha, a satsang discussion, with them.

This Gokul-lila took place in the Dvapar Yuga; in the Satya and Treta Yugas the gracious Lord had been in Vaikunth. In the Dvapar Yuga he came to Gokul, and he came having locked the door of Vaikunth behind him. (We shall take up the subject of Vaikunth further ahead. Why this is mentioned here is itself a question — we ourselves do not hold Vaikunth to be real, but Jivanji Maharaj's intent here was probably this: not everyone at places of pilgrimage is a blind believer or one who exploits the faithful; among them too there can be a genuine Vaishnav who worships the Supreme Brahman with a simple, sincere heart. This Vaishnav also bears witness to the fact that the flute-playing, enchanting Lord is indeed the true God. It is to emphasize this point that he told this story here: Vaikunth was left empty, because the flute-playing, enchanting Lord is the real one — he never again leaves Vaikunth to come out — except that here he came for good.)

In Vrindavan he saw its glory, and saw what are called the twelve forests. He saw the spot where, during Krishna's leela, the kadamba tree stood from which Krishna used to dive into the Yamuna to bathe — though the kadamba tree standing there today is not the original one but a later planting, the original having long since washed away in the Yamuna. He also went to the spot where the gopis' clothes had been taken away. Having toured these and other places, he returned to Banshivat and spoke this sakhi:

_Aag jalo Vaikunthmen, jahan sant samagam naahi ||
Taathe neeki Jeevna, Shri Bansivatki chhanhi ||1||
Main balihari ta naarki, je bolayo Gokul manhi ||
Bansibat jyu Jeevna, tyu bat patra to nahi ||2||
Kotik Vaikunth upre, Shri Vrindavan sukh dham ||
Taathe neeki Jeevna, sant sangat vishram ||3||
Saptapuripe Jeevna, Vaikunth pe atisaar ||
Vrindavan sohamanu, jahan Radhe sang vihaar ||4||
Taha Ayodhya jahan Raghupati, kaahana taha Gokul gaam ||
Saptapuri taha Jeevna, jahan santsangat Harinaam ||5||_

1. Jivanji Maharaj says: even if Vaikunth were to burn and perish, it would cause no grief — for there the company of saints is not to be had. Better by far, then, than Vaikunth, is dwelling within Banshivat; living under the shelter of Banshivat is superior to Vaikunth.

2. I offer myself again and again to the loving devotion of those women — the wives of the sages, who came from Janakpur, Ayodhya and other places — who called me into Gokul to fulfil their heartfelt longing; for the supreme joy I find in Banshivat is not to be found even at Akshay Vat.

3. Vrindavan Dham is filled with more happiness than could be found in crores of Vaikunths put together; and higher still than even that supreme joy is the joy of dwelling in the company of saints — that is the highest happiness of all.

4. Vrindavan surpasses even the seven sacred cities (Saptapuri) and Vaikunth in excellence — it is a bright and glorious place, where the Lord sports together with Radha.

5. Wherever Ram is present, that place is itself Ayodhya; wherever Krishna is present, that place is itself Gokul; and in the same way, wherever there is the company of saints and the taking of Hari's name, that place is like the Saptapuri, as if all seven holy cities were present together in that one supreme place.

Having come here, Jivanji Maharaj speaks this sakhi; being originally a resident of Banshivat, its attachment does not leave him. For here it was that, day after day, the child Krishna's playful pastimes unfolded as he grazed the cows in the forest, and the intoxication of that saintly company was something else altogether. What is there in Vaikunth? There is no happiness there — only a kind of dryness. And compared to every other place on this earth, Vrindavan and Banshivat are exceedingly delightful. This is why Jivanji Maharaj says: wherever Ram is, there is Ayodhya, and wherever Krishna is, there is the village of Gokul.

Recalling these memories, Jivanji Maharaj views the Yamuna ghat and arrives at Mathura. The resolve he had made atop the high peak of Kailash in the Himalayas also comes back to his mind. Now an eagerness has awakened in him to be among the saints; he wants to keep the vow he made. And so he sets out in haste toward Gujarat.

On the road he came to a certain village (unnamed), where a very devout and pious family lived — but husband and wife had a serious ongoing dispute between them. The elder man of the household, the husband, was a staunch Ramanandi, while his wife was a staunch Radhavallabhi; over this difference in religious belief a dispute went on between them constantly. The husband's religious feeling and devotion ran very deep, and one day he had a premonition that some day a Ramanandi saint would certainly come and put an end to this suffering of his. Neither of them knew Jivanji Maharaj, nor did they know that he was coming.

As if by some prior sign, Jivanji Maharaj happened to be passing through this very village. The man recognized him as a Ramanandi saint and understood that this must be the very saint of whom he had had the premonition a few days earlier. Certain that the most merciful Lord had sent this saint for his own sake, he brought him home. He said to his wife, "Look, a Ramanandi saint has come."

The wife of the household came out and saw Jivanji Maharaj; but as she never bowed to any saint outside the Radhavallabhi tradition, she had come out only to honor her husband. A long discussion on matters of Hari took place between Jivanji Maharaj and the wife, in which he explained Ramanand's teaching to her. The wife was very knowledgeable and discerning, and her mind was in the end won over — she came to agree with what Jivanji Maharaj said, and both husband and wife then bowed to him, accepting him as their sadguru. In this way, on the road, he brought a happy resolution to the dispute within one family; both were filled with joy, and both accepted Jivanji Maharaj as their sadguru. Thus the resolve he had made on the way to Gujarat — that he would keep the company of saints and go to meet Vaishnavs — began to be fulfilled right there on the road.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, having seen the Gokul-Banshivat ghat, came to Vrindavan and stayed there four days. There he met a Vaishnav, and a discussion took place between them. In that discussion it was said that God performed the Gokul-lila in the Dvapar Yuga, but in the Satya and Treta Yugas the gracious Lord had been in Vaikunth; he came to Gokul in the Dvapar Yuga, and came there for good, having made a firm decision never to return to Vaikunth — coming, so to speak, having locked the doors of Vaikunth and shut up that abode. Such a one — the flute-playing, enchanting Lord Krishna — is himself the very Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Soul, God. He alone is the ruler of the entire universe, and he alone is real: this was concluded at the end of this discussion, and the words used in this meeting are very pointed and call for reflection.

_Te maate Morli Manohar Parmeshwar te khara,
tehe pan Vaikunthne mele paarangat nisro nahi, taanha khalaayu._
("For that reason the flute-playing, enchanting Lord is the real one; even his form as Lord of Vaikunth could not come forth as perfect and complete beside it — it remained held back there.")

In other words, in the final judgment, the flute-playing, enchanting Lord of the Gokul-lila of the Dvapar Yuga proved supreme in every respect — so much so that when his majesty as Lord of Vaikunth was set beside this enchanting form, that form of Vaikunth could not prove itself full and complete before the enchanting flute-player; and so his Vaikunth form as Narayan remained held back, stopped, right there in Vaikunth itself. This four-armed Narayan form was unable to enter into the Gokul-lila.

During the four days he stayed in Vrindavan and held this discussion with a Vaishnav, the conclusion that emerged matched exactly the conclusion Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj himself had reached during the twenty-four-hour discussion he once had with his own guru Gopaldas. Not only did their views agree; though this Vaishnav is not named here, he is named in Jivanji Maharaj's Parchari (biographical account) — that Vaishnav was Hariram Vyasji. This Vyasji had, at one time, felt an aversion toward Sadguru Kabir as a worshipper of nirgun (attributeless) devotion; because of this fault of aversion toward Kabir, God had once withdrawn from his meditation, and when it was pointed out to him that this had happened because Hit Harivansh had once wronged Kabir, Vyasji then sang a hymn in praise of Kabir as a true devotee, and came to honor Kabir's devotion. Thus Vyasji's views agreed with Jivanji's in every respect: both held Kabir to be a true sadguru, and both held the flute-playing, enchanting Lord to be God. Because these two points matched between the two saints, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj came to hold Vyasji in the highest regard, and said in a sakhi—

_Doo barabar Jeevna, das Kabir aur Vyas ||
O samre Sitapatiko, ye Radhakunj vilaas ||3||
Sab sakhiyanmen Radhika, sakhanme Balvir ||
Vyas viveki Jeevna, Kalindiki teer ||4||_
(Vyas and Kabir, servant-devotees both, are equal, O Jivana. One worships Sitapati, the other delights in Radha's groves. Among all the sakhis Radhika was the very best, and among all the male companions Balvir was the best — in just this way, among all the Lord's devotees, the very best is Vyas, who dwells, discerning and wise, on the bank of the Kalindi in Vrindavan.)

Vyas and Kabir are both devotees who worship God with equal devotion. Kabirji worships Sitapati, Ram the Lord of Sita, while Vyasji worships Krishna, who sports with Radha in the groves. Among all the sakhis, Radhika herself was the best sakhi, and among all the male companions, Balvir (Balaram) was the best companion; in the same way, among all the devotees of God, the very best devotee was Vyasji, who lived on the bank of the Yamuna in Vrindavan.

This Vyasji was a disciple of Hit Harivansh, who had founded the Radhavallabhiya sampraday in the year 1585 CE. The main temple of this sampraday is in Vrindavan — it is the temple of Krishna as the Vallabh, the beloved, of Radha. This sampraday does not hold with liberation as an aim, nor does it hold with the rules of prescribed injunction and prohibition. Nabhadas has written—

_Vidhi nishedh nahi das ananya utkat vratdhari ||_
(For the exclusive devotee there is neither injunction nor prohibition — he holds only to an intense, single-minded vow of devotion.)

According to Jivanji Maharaj's own understanding, this sampraday gives no place to rules of injunction and prohibition, and holds instead to a devotion of servitude together with an intense, exclusive devotion. Its followers apply an upright tilak running from the tip of the nose to the trikuti, with a black bindi placed in the middle; they take the vertical lines of the tilak to represent Krishna and the bindi to represent Radha, giving Radha a status even higher than Krishna's. Since Vyasji was a follower of such a sampraday, Jivanji Maharaj was extremely pleased with him. Vyasji did not even observe the Ekadashi fast, and had given up the sacred thread too, becoming what is called "Achyut-gotri," that is, a follower of Vaishnavi, Vishnu-devotion. Thus Jivanji Maharaj's meeting with this Vyasji, who fully supported his own way of thinking, gave him a complete understanding of the Radhavallabhiya sampraday as well. And as if that were not enough, he also came across a devout woman who followed the doctrine of exclusive devotion of the Radhavallabh sampraday — this was the same woman whose husband, Haridas, was a Ramanandi, so that there was constant friction between the two of them. But Jivanji Maharaj, having studied the teachings of the whole country, was able to resolve the mind of Haridas's wife with ease; not only that, but she too came to accept Jivanji Maharaj as her sadguru. Having had so many such experiences, a reflection of them can be seen in his sakhis. The mention of Radhavallabh appears in his sakhis too.

_Niranjani Niranjanku bhaje, Radha Vallabhi Kahaan ||
E birad hamare Jeevna, je Ramkrishna do naam ||6||_
(Followers of the Niranjan sampraday worship Niranjan, the Formless, while followers of the Radhavallabh sampraday worship Kahan, Krishna — but our own vow, O Jivana, is this: both names, Ram and Krishna, are worthy of worship.)

The Niranjan sampraday worships the nirgun, the attributeless — which is precisely why an aversion had arisen in the mind of Vyasji, a devotee steeped in the loving sentiment of divine play, toward Kabirji, whose hymns are marked chiefly by nirgun devotion; in the land of Vrindavan, so steeped in that sentiment of love, he had come to feel a distaste for anyone who sang Kabir's hymns. But Kabirji himself was in fact endowed with every virtue, and had fully absorbed and mastered that sentiment of love as well. This sampraday, along with the Radhaswami sampraday, holds Niranjan to be the Kalpurush, the being who governs time; for the remembrance of the Name, they say that the thread — the bond, the shelter of love — can be joined with Niranjan, whom they describe by various names for the Supreme Reality, such as Ram-Niranjan, Hari-Niranjan, or Alakh Niranjan, holding him to be without any form or feature. They do not, however, take a clear stand against worship with attributes or image worship.

In Krishnadas's Parchari, it is said of Niranjan:

_Kabir Aadya Purush ek vraksh hai, Niranjan vaki daar ||
Trigun roop hi shakha bhai, paat bhaye sansaar ||7||_
(Kabir, the Primal Being, is like a tree; Niranjan is but one branch of it, a mere portion. From that branch have spread the boughs made of the three gunas, and their leaves have unfolded in the form of this world.)

— Krishnadas's Parchari

Having studied the doctrines of the Niranjan sampraday, the Radhavallabh sampraday, and others, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj expressed his own view: that although the followers of the Niranjan sampraday hold to the nirgun, they do not oppose the sagun, and they follow the practice of remembering the divine Name; and that the Radhavallabh sampraday worships Radha and Krishna with an exclusive devotion. In the same way, he said, we too shall take our support from both Lords, Ram and Krishna, and practice our devotion accordingly — there is no need for anyone to raise objections or quarrels in anyone's mind over this.

His first meeting was with Narandas in Bareli; he and his whole family became devotees of Jivanji Maharaj, and husband and wife together accepted Jivanji Maharaj as their sadguru. (This family later came and settled in Gujarat, and as the family grew over time, their descendants live to this day not only in Puniyad but in many other villages as well.)

The compassion he had asked of God began to show itself along the way; and so, keeping the company of saints even as he traveled, Jivanji Maharaj at last drew near the borders of Gujarat.

sections.title_en: Mala and Tilak Given to Gopaldas and Santdas
sections.translation:
Gopaldas and Santdas, both Ramanandi in background, have now been given kanthi diksha (initiation with the sacred neck-thread). Earlier, when Jivanji Maharaj had left Gujarat together with Guru Gopaldas and gone to the house of an acquaintance (melapi) in Malwa, he has now returned to the home of that same close friend of Guru Gopaldas -- Gopaldas of the village of Khediya. Since this Gopaldas is older in age, he is known as elder (Motha) Gopaldas. Jivanji Maharaj, wandering from place to place, has come back here. Meanwhile, a very devout and pious relative of elder Gopaldas had earlier told him that if any true saint should come, he should be introduced. So elder Gopaldas had been waiting for Jivanji Maharaj's return, and today Jivanji Maharaj himself stood at his door. Remembering what his affectionate relative had said, elder Gopaldas takes Jivanji Maharaj along with him to a village named Chanderiya, to bestow grace upon his relative there.

If a true saint could be found in Chanderiya, one's life would be redeemed and one would attain the supreme state -- with this hope sat elder Gopaldas's dear relative, who is also named Gopaldas. Today his wish bore fruit: Jivanji Maharaj has come here. For one who had waited for a true saint the way the chatak bird waits for rain, it felt today as though the first shower of the Shravan monsoon was about to fall. Seeing Jivanji Maharaj, Gopaldas of Chanderiya -- steeped in the flavour of devotion, who had waited with true, heartfelt longing -- says:

_Chanderiye vaase vasu, Jivan pragate aay,
Sitapati Raghunathko, deeno naam bataay ||1||_ (I was residing in the village of Chanderiya when Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj appeared and came to me; he gave me initiation and bestowed on me devotion to the Name of Sitapati Ram. -- 1)

_Takiya teenu bahra, jahaan Sitapatike sant,
Sadguru mile Gopalku, tab paaya naam anant ||2||_ (Takiya = a fixed seat/resolve, beyond the three [worldly attachments], held only toward a true saint devoted to Sitapati Ram, who is beyond the three gunas. Fixing my gaze on such a one alone and settling my resolve there, Gopaldas says that when he met Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj he thereby attained the infinite Name. -- 2)

_Sadguru Jivan umage, shyaam ghata ghan ghor,
Ajhar jhare ras peejiye, so nirakhat jugal kishor ||3||_ (Just as a mass of dark clouds gathers and surges forth joyfully, so has Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj come surging upon me with great love; and now, just as yogis on the path of yoga drink the ajhar-ras -- the nectar that, at a certain advanced stage, flows down from the crown of the head into the mouth, and which they drink with great love -- so I too, gazing upon the Divine Youthful Pair [Radha-Krishna], shall drink a love-devotion nectar even finer than ajhar-ras. -- 3. [Shankarbhai Patel, a farmer of Puniyad village, who himself drank such ajhar-ras, told me of this experience of his. We, however, are capable of experiencing an even finer nectar of love. -- 3.])

_Jab the Jivan pragate, tab the bhayo kalyan,
Raksha bhai Gopalku, ab chumbego jamraan ||4||_ (From the moment Jivanji Maharaj appeared, our welfare has been secured; and now someone like me, Gopaldas, has been given protection from the ocean of worldly existence [bhavsagar]. So the messengers of Yama's abode will strike out in vain -- that is, they will not be able to do anything to me -- and this will vex and grieve them. -- 4)

_Madan jagaayo maanani, saame ven bajaay,
Aise Sadguru Jivana, ham sute liye jagaay ||5||_ (Just as Lord Krishna once played his flute among the honoured, beautiful gopis and awakened Kamdev, the god of love, within them, giving them the nectar of love to drink, so too has Jivanji Maharaj awakened us, who lay asleep in the sleep of delusion [moh-nidra] -- he roused us out of worldly illusion and taught us the path of loving devotion. -- 5)

In Rajasthan, forty kilometres from Bhilwara, there is a railway station on the main road. Next to it is the village of Medi Kheda, one kilometre from the station. Two kilometres further, on the road, is Hajuriya Kheda; and four kilometres from Hajuriya Kheda is the place known as Ramdevji's Chanderiya, or Old (Purana) Chanderiya. Its population is five to seven thousand, made up mainly of Rajput, Jat and other communities. Within three or four kilometres around Chanderiya lie three more villages: Mugaka Kheda, Khir Kheda, and Dagara Kheda. It was into this land that Jivanji Maharaj went to awaken his own devotees (nij-jans), and thereby sanctified this ground.

Having had darshan of Jivanji Maharaj, Gopaldas becomes overjoyed and speaks the sakhis above, in which the feeling of his heart is expressed: that though he dwells in Chanderiya, Jivandasji has come and appeared for his redemption; that the Guru has given him the infinite Name, Ramkabir; and that he is drinking the ajhar-ras of the Guru's word that flows on, and thereby his welfare has been accomplished.

Jivanji Maharaj then answers Gopaldas, in a sakhi, saying --

_Jap tap teerath Jivana, pooja paati prem,
Sant sangat Hari bhajan bin, aur na doojo nem ||6||_ (Jivanji Maharaj says: not japa [mantra repetition], not tapa [austerity], not tirtha [pilgrimage] -- my message and command is this: our worship is not of the vedic ritual kind but pure prem-lakshana [love-natured] devotion; besides keeping the company of saints [satsang] and singing the praises of Hari, we know nothing else, nor do we wish to know anything else -- such is our fixed resolve [tek]. We hold no attachment to reciting mantras, performing austerities, going on pilgrimage, or worshipping with leaves and flowers; the company of saints and devotion to Hari alone is, for us, the rule -- the resolve -- of devotion. -- 6)

In the Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, chapter 196, verses 6-7, it is said that the Vedanta scriptures speak of abandoning the practice of japa, because all their statements are chiefly oriented toward renunciation and the establishment of peace, and culminate only in Brahman -- that is, since japa is itself a form of active engagement (pravritti), it is not the principal means to liberation.

Chapter 197, verse 2, says: men who perform japa (owing to the many distinctions of intellect) fall even into various hells.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has given mala and tilak to the devotees of Malwa. It is necessary for us to accept the tulsi kanthi (neck-beads of tulsi wood) and the tilak. Tulsi has eight names:

_Vrinda vrindaavani vishnupoojita vishvapaavani,
Pushpasaara nandini tulasi shreekrishna jeevani ||1||_ (The eight names of Tulsi: Vrinda, Vrindavani, worshipped by Vishnu, purifier of the universe, essence of flowers, Nandini, Tulsi, and the life of Shri Krishna.)

Before making Gopaldas his disciple, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj had discussed with him the question of Akar-Nirakar (form and formlessness). During that discussion, Gopaldas had, through his own words, explained certain things to Jivanji Maharaj. Now Jivanji Maharaj, in turn, passes on that same teaching, giving mala and tilak to Gopaldas and Santdas of Chanderiya and making them devotees. In doing so he presented again the teaching he himself had received from his own Guru -- and in that teaching came this sakhi of Ranka and Vanka [a devotee couple]. It is presented here once more, so let us understand it again.

Here, mala and tilak were bestowed on both Gopaldas and Santdas, and they accepted Jivanji Maharaj as their Sadguru. Thus Jivanji Maharaj gave mala and tilak to Gopaldas and Santdas; it was through the grace (prataap) of elder Gopaldas (of Khediya) that both of them received the mala and tilak. (7)

Further, through elder Gopaldas, Jivanji Maharaj also gave mala and tilak to Devdas, and spoke this sakhi --

_Dheereku dheeju nahi, aisa paaya naaka,
Aakaar niraakaar vivarjit, taaka sevak Raaka ||7||_ (Ranka Bhagat says: the with-form [sakar] is a worldly, illusory thing, and it is perishable, so I place no trust in it. This is the secret key [naaka -- the device, the insight] my Guru has shown me through his teaching: that the Supreme is the support of all, one who has neither the notion of having form nor of being formless -- I, Ranka Bhagat, am his servant.)

_Dhireku dhiju sahi, rahu adharake maanhi,
Vaanka tahaan vilaambiyaan, jahaan dhoop nahi chhaanya ||2||_ (His wife Vankaji says: this perishable, worldly, with-form body cannot be entirely done away with, for devotion, understanding, spiritual practice, and action all require a body; so I hold to the body only to the extent necessary, but I fix my mind upon the Supreme, who is himself without support yet is the support of all -- my mind has become steady in that. And what is that Supreme like? A place where there is neither the shade nor the sun of the three gunas, no joy, no sorrow, no threefold affliction -- only the very form of supreme bliss.)

While expounding on form and formlessness, [Jivanji Maharaj] gives the example of God assuming the form of Narsingh to protect Prahlad, in order to show God's utterly fierce power. God is all-powerful; were he to will it, he could bring about even the great deluge (mahapralay) -- and the example of God taking the form of Narsingh is given to show this. God's might is shown here through verses of the Narsingh Purana.

Bhairav -- God's Bhairav-like form appeared. Bhairav is a fearsome name of Shiva, of which there are eight or twelve kinds, the chief among them being Kalbhairav. God took on just such a form, described here: at the time of the great deluge, God destroyed -- beginning with Brahma -- the Sun, Indra, the Moon, Kuber, Varun, the wind-god, Mahadev, the fifty-six crore yoginis, sixty-four crore Chamundas, nine crore Katyayanis, endless crores of attendant spirits, and Bhairav and the other forms of Time (Kaal) itself. He seized and drank up that Kaal, and it is for this that Krupanath [the Merciful Lord] bears the name Mahakaal.

The "nine crore Katyayanis" refers to the nine crore forms of Durga, namely: 1. Shailaputri, 2. Brahmacharini, 3. Chandraghanta, 4. Kushmang, 5. Skandhaman, 6. Katyayani, 7. Ratrikal, 8. Mahagauri, and 9. Siddhidatri.

The twelve suns of the twelve months are listed in the Kurma Purana:

Twelve months -- Sun (deity)
Madhu-maas = Chaitra maas -- Dhata
Madhav-maas = Vaishakh maas -- Aryama
Shukra-maas = Jeth maas -- Mitra
Shuchi-maas = Ashadh maas -- Varun
Nabho-maas = Shravan maas -- Indra
Nabhasakhya = Bhadarva maas -- Vishvavan
Tapo-maas = Magh maas -- Pusha
Tapasakhya = Fagan maas -- Parjanya
Saho-maas = Margashirsh -- Anshu
Pushya-maas = Posh maas -- Bhaga
Ishambhara = Aashvin -- Tvashta

There are sixty-four yoginis, who are the attendants of Parvati, and they too have sixty-four names.
There are eight Bhairavs: Asitang, Ruru, Chand, Krodh, Unmatt, Kupati (or Rupali), Bhishan, and Sanhar.

Kabir has sung in the Maru raga --

_(Maru)
Avadhu naade vaade gagan gaajai, sabad anaahad bolai,
Antargate to naahi na dekhai, dhoondhat ban ban dolai. (tek)_ (O renunciant, the sky resounds with sound and music, and the anahad shabd -- the unstruck sound -- keeps sounding on; yet you do not see it within your own inner self, and you wander, searching, from forest to forest.)

_Shaligraam taju Shiv pooja, sir Brahmaka kaatu,
Saayar phodi nirmukta laau, kuvaa sel de paatu ||1||_ (I will give up even the worship of Shaligram and of Shiva; I will cut off the very head of Brahma -- that is, I will not let him go on creating a world of birth and death; I will destroy and do away with the ocean of worldly existence and bring about liberation from bondage.)

_Chandra sooraj doy toobaa kari hai, chit chetanaki daandi,
Sukhamanaa taanti baajan laagi, ih vidh trishnaa khaandi ||2||_ (Into the well of amrit-ras [nectar of immortality] I will lower, with a stroke of love, the rope of my inner awareness [surta]; of that rope I will make the sun and moon its two gourd-floats, and mind and consciousness its crossbar. Thus the strings of the sushumna channel will begin to sound, and in this way I shall quench my thirst for drinking the water of love's nectar.)

_Param tatva aadhaar merai, Shiv nagari ghar meraa,
Kaal hi khaadau michaavi heendun, bahuri na kari hu pheraa ||3||_ (The Supreme Reality, the Paramatma, is my only support, and the city of Shiva is my home, my dwelling place. I shall shatter Time [Kaal] itself and move about fearlessly; no longer shall I go round and round through the cycle of the womb.)

_Japau na jaap hato nahi gugal, pustak lei na padhaau,
Kahai Kabir param pad paayaa, nahi aau nahi jaau ||4||_ (I do not chant japa, nor light incense [gugal], nor take up a book to read. Kabir says: I have attained the supreme state; now I shall neither come nor go -- neither be born nor die.)

Jivanji Maharaj presents this account of Prahlad to show that such fearlessness dwells within a true devotee. Our protector, the Paramatma, is an all-capable being, so there is no need to fear death (Kaal), for our Sadguru has taken us under his shelter, giving us mala, tilak, the company of saints, and the Name of Hari.

Jivanji Maharaj speaks this sakhi and explains the nature of form and formlessness. (We have already seen the exposition of this sakhi earlier, in the chapter on "Morli Manohar Parmeshwar," so it is not repeated here again.) The confusion about form and formlessness is dispelled here as he goes on to explain, giving as evidence the manner in which Prahlad was protected -- God appearing out of a pillar. What kind of pillar was this? The Narsingh Purana describes what form emerged from the burning, red-hot pillar --

_Atiraudram mahaakaayam daanavaanaam bhayankaram,
Mahaanetram mahaavaktram mahaadanshtram mahaabhujam ||32||_ (Extremely terrifying, of huge body, striking fear into the demons; with vast eyes, a vast mouth, vast fangs, and vast arms. -- 32)

_Mahaanakham mahaapaadam kaalaagnisadrishaananam,
Karnaantakritavistaravadanam chaatibheeshanam ||33||_ (With vast claws, vast feet, a face like the fire of universal destruction, eyes stretching to his ears -- utterly dreadful. -- 33)

_Kritvetthan naarasinham tu yayau Vishnustrivikramah,
Narasinha stambhamadhyaad nirgatya prananaad cha ||34||_ (Taking on this terrifying form of Narsingh, Lord Vishnu Trivikram set forth; and this Narsingh, emerging from the middle of the pillar, began to roar fearsomely. -- 34)

(Commentary) The fearsome, Bhairav-like form that appeared from the pillar had endless arms, endless eyes, endless inner faculties, and endless weapons; crores upon crores of flames of fire blazed forth, and one vast, cosmic form (virat swaroop) manifested.

_Kalpaante srishtim sanhatya utkeerya Brahmanonakhaat,
Tvacham shikhaaparyanta abadhnaat mukute prabhuh ||35||_ (At the end of the kalpa [cosmic cycle], having destroyed creation, the Lord flayed the skin of Brahma from his nails to the crown of his head, and bound it into his own crown. -- 35)

_Dvaadashaarkashirohaar Indraadikashirodaamaa,
Yoginichakrabaahookrit traataa Bhairavakaalajit ||36||_ (He wore a garland of the heads of the twelve suns; he made a cord of the heads of Indra and the others; he fashioned arms from the circle of yoginis; and he conquered Bhairav and the other forms of Time. -- 36)

That is: at the end of the deluge he severed (destroyed) the heads of the twelve suns; he destroyed Indra, Som, Kuber, Vayu, and others; he cut off Mahadev's head and bound it to his left foot; the yoginis and others were destroyed; and, having devoured all of these, Krupanath drank up Time (Kaal) itself -- for which he is called Mahakaal. Adhyaruji Maharaj says --

_Kaal tano Mahakaal, Swami paap dahan Gopal,
Tulasi vallabhu e, Hari te surnar durlabh e ||4||_ (Adhyaru 2-10-4-4-4) (He [Parbrahma] is the Kaal of Kaal, that is, Mahakaal; moreover he has the power to burn away anything in the universe, sin included. He is the beloved husband of Tulsi [Vrinda], and he is exceedingly difficult for gods and men alike to understand, know, or attain.)

_Shoorame shooro Shaamalo, Govaale Goval,
Leelaa saluno Jivanaa, Kaal maanhi Mahakaal ||8||_ (Among the brave and mighty, he is the mightiest; among cowherds, he is the finest cowherd; and in his divine play [leela] he is beautiful. Such is Parbrahma -- Mahakaal even among Kaal itself.)

So then -- a thing with form would burn; how then can it be said that he appeared out of that pillar? For the pillar was ablaze, burning red-hot with flames of fire; if he had form he could not have survived, that is, he would have burned. Yet here we say he "appeared" -- so how did he survive? He must, then, be the formless Parbrahma. And if he is formless, then he is as described earlier: he can have no upadhi (identifying attribute) at all -- no great eyes, no great, fearsome teeth, claws, and so on.

We have discussed this subject at length earlier, so there is no need to go over it again here. But after bestowing kanthi-diksha, Jivanji Maharaj carries on this discussion in order to remove the confused illusion about form and formlessness from the minds of devotees such as Gopaldas, Santdas, and Devdas. To make this clear to these devotees of Malwa, Jivanji Maharaj also recites a few shlokas --

_Sthaanam na yaanam na cha bindunaadam, roopam na rekhaa na cha dhaatuvargam,
Pushpam na gandham na phalam na chhaayaa, tasmai namo brahmaniranjanaay ||37||_ (To him who has no place and no going [no means of travel], no bindu, no naad, no form, no line, no group of elements, no flower, no scent, no fruit, and no shadow -- to that Niranjan Brahma, my salutations. -- 37)

_Adho na chodhvam na Shivo na Shakti, na naari pumaannaiva cha lingamoortih,
Kaalo na jeevo na guru na shishyah, tasmai namo brahmaniranjanaay ||38||_ (To him who is neither above nor below, neither Shiva nor Shakti, neither woman nor man, neither linga nor image, neither Time nor an individual soul, neither guru nor disciple -- to that Niranjan Brahma, my salutations. -- 38)

_Na paanchabhootam na cha saptasaagaram disho, na patraani na Meru-Mandaram,
Brahmaa na Rudro na cha Vishnuroopam, tasmai namo brahmaniranjanaay ||39||_ (To him who is not the five elements, not the seven seas, not the directions, not the leaves, not Mount Meru or Mandar, not Brahma, not Rudra, and not even Vishnu -- to that Niranjan Brahma, my salutations. -- 39)

What, then, are these teachings about the formless (nirakar) nature? The attributes of Parbrahma are: he is not white, not yellow, not dark, not blue, not red -- he has no colour at all; he is colourless. He is not Brahma, not Rudra, not Vishnu, not Indra, nor any god; not any rishi or sage; not a demon; not a country or a region; not the sky, not the earth, not the netherworld; he is no one's enemy nor anyone's friend; he has no joy and no grief; he is not born, nor does he pass through any other state (youth, middle age, or old age), nor does he die. Such a Parbrahma is known by the name Vasudev alone. He has no form; he is Niranjan (unstained) and Nirakar (formless). Then a natural question arises: what, then, is this "place" from which he is said to have appeared? To this we answer: whatever the mental disposition (vasana) of each devotee who worshipped Parbrahma at the time, such was the description they gave; each one saw Parbrahma according to whatever inclination (mansa -- wish or belief) was in their own mind.

What Jivanji Maharaj means to say here is this: without falling into confusion over questions like "What is Parbrahma like? To whom does he appear? What worship should be done? What mantra should be chanted?", and without getting entangled in the dispute over form and formlessness, one should, through pure character, constantly remember, contemplate, and meditate upon that all-powerful, glorious power which pervades the whole universe. His own devotees have only to sing his own qualities -- they should not fall into argument and debate.

Here, in one pada from Narsinh Mehta's "Haarmala" (the Garland), he sang --

_Sanyaasi vairaagi vismay paamyaa, vartyo jai jaikaar sarva dekhataan_ (Sannyasis and vairagis were struck with wonder; cries of victory rang out, in full view of all --)

When God gave the garland to Narsinh in front of all the devotees, seventeen sannyasis and vairagis (renunciants) were struck with amazement, and cries of jai-jaikar (victory) rang out, for it was in full view of everyone that God placed the garland around Narsinh Mehta's neck. And whatever devotion was in each one's heart, that is the form in which the compassionate Lord, kind to the humble, appeared to them. To Narsinh Mehta himself, God -- Madan Gopal -- came and embraced him again and again. At the Mukund ashram they saw God as Mukund; at the Keshav ashram, as Keshav; at the Narsingh ashram, as Narsingh; at the Madhav ashram, as Madhav; at the Brahma ashram, as Brahma-form; Shridhar saw him as a brahmachari; at the Vasudev ashram, as Vasudev; at the Shiva ashram, as Tripurari; at the Achyut ashram, as Achyut; at the Vishveshwar ashram, as Vishvambhar; at the Narayan ashram, as Narayan; at the Damodar ashram, as Damodar; Prasad Puri saw him in the form of Niranjan; Bhim saw him as Ram; the king's mother saw him as Chaturbhuj (four-armed); the queen saw him as beautiful, dark Shyam; the princess (Kunvar Bai) saw him as her grandfather; the protector of the world saw him as compassionate to the humble; the minister saw him in the form of universal dissolution; the king saw him in the form of Time (Kaal); the man of Brahma-knowledge saw him as the all-pervading form -- and thus everyone's doubt was dispelled, and that playful, charming, plume-crowned God embraced Narsinh Mehta by the neck.

In this pada, Narsinh Mehta shows that regarding Parbrahma Parmeshwar, one should stay above argument and above the question of form versus formlessness -- let anyone speak of whatever form they wish -- but in one's own personal life, one should worship according to whatever belief one holds faith in, or according to what a true Sadguru instructs (there are more false gurus in this world than true ones). On the matter of Parbrahma, Narsinh Mehta is entirely clear.

Jivanji Maharaj too says: this benevolent nature of Parbrahma is unlike anything else. Jivanji Maharaj says he is formless -- how, then, can the supreme Govind be said to have form? From the mythological story in which he took Hiranyakashipu onto his lap and tore him apart with his claws, he came to be given the name Narsingh -- but this cannot mean that the Supreme Lord actually possesses a form.

Here Jivanji Maharaj has explained one point with great depth and subtlety of meaning. The way the incarnations of Parbrahma and their deeds are outlined in the mythological narratives should not be used merely on the surface to judge or evaluate Parbrahma's deeds or life. We are not really concerned with either Hiranyakashipu or the Narsingh avatar as such -- rather, the lesson is to be drawn from the life of the devotee Prahlad. And, just as we have said earlier that God is affectionate toward his devotees (bhakta-vatsal), so was the devotee Prahlad protected -- this indeed is a source of great joy for devotees. Yet the lesson or essence that ought to be drawn from this episode has today been set aside, and the world has turned onto a wayward path. No one wishes to follow the path of the devotee-king Prahlad, or to give any real thought to anything at all. When we have become followers of a self-interested world, good thoughts simply do not arise in the mind; and even when good thoughts do come from outside, they are stopped right at the threshold of our own ears.

Just how much study the revered Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj must have made of the Niranjan Purana becomes apparent from these shlokas, 37 to 39, presented here. We cannot even imagine the depth with which the revered Jivanji Maharaj must have tried to understand the manner and practice of the followers of so many scriptures -- the Vedas, the Puranas, the Sahasranama, the Gita, the Bhagavat, the Ramayana, and so on. If so, we do not even have the capacity to understand all that he must have looked into. Let us, then, reflect a little with a truly far-reaching vision on these shlokas from the Niranjan Purana that this great Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has presented, and let us appreciate the graciousness Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has showered upon us. Shloka 37 states how far beyond the illusion (maya) of this world that Niranjan Brahma is: that Niranjan Brahma needs no place, and no vehicle for going anywhere, nor does he have any nada-bindu (sound-point). Let us here discuss nada-bindu. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, through very deep investigation, having, at the end of all kinds of striving, experienced the complete truth in which God's true essence resides, granted us the devotion of ratankaar [the constant inner repetition of the Name] and thereby brought about our welfare -- let us remember this kindness.

The Nadabindu Upanishad is an Upanishad of that name belonging to the Rig Veda branch. Nadabindu means the syllable Om. Nadabindu is the point (bindu) at which one fixes one's attention on the inner sound (nada). This Upanishad follows the model of the Chulika Upanishad. The Nadabindu Upanishad is one of the Upanishads of the Yoga group; it is composed in verse. Sadguru Kabirji, too, dismissed the nada-bindu [as insufficient by itself]. He has a pada on this in the Kalyan raga.

(Raga Kalyan, Granth 79, page 117.)

_Tum niranjan tum niranjan, tum niranjan raaya,
Taheru roop naanhi rekh naanhi, mudraa naanhi na maayaa. (tek)_

_Taahe naad naanhi bund naanhi, kaal naanhi kaayaa,
Ravi shashi doou eke naanhi, taa dan na Raam Raaya ||1||_

_Taa din samudra naanhi ne shikhar naanhi, dharani naanhi naan gaganaa,
Chaar jug brahmaand naanhi, paavak naanhi na pavanaa ||2||_

_Taa din devata naanhi ne dev naanhi, paanti naanhi ne poojaa naanhi,
Abe tabe tumhi ho swami, aur naanhi naa doojaa koi ||3||_

_Rig jajur aur saam atharved, bidyaa naanhi ne vaakun karani,
Teri teri gat tuhi jaane, daas Kabir tum sharan ||4||_

(O Lord, you are niranjan -- free of any stain or illusion -- you are the King of Niranjan itself. You have no form, no outline or shape or kind whatsoever; no facial form and no attachment to maya. You have no nada, nor any bindu that fixes upon the nada, nor any Om-ness; nor do you have Time or a body. On that day neither the sun nor the moon existed, nor did King Ram exist on that day; there was neither ocean nor mountain, neither earth nor sky. The four yugas and the cosmos itself did not exist; there was no fire, no wind; there was no deity and no god; there was no leaf, no flower, no worship or discussion of worship. In that time, and in this present time too, O Lord, you alone are the master -- there is no other besides you. There was no learning of the Rig, Yajur, Sama, or Atharva Vedas, nor any of the ritual acts prescribed in those Vedas. Only you yourself can know your own way and manner. Kabir, your servant, has come to your shelter.)

The sense contained in the words "nad" and "bund" is not something ordinarily understood, and so the common mass of people fall into error over it. They take the deeper meaning of "nad" to refer to the sentiment of Hari-kirtan (singing God's praise); or they take "nad" to mean divine inspiration, the voice of the inner self; or they understand it as the Guru's teaching. A similar confusion arises with the word "bund" as well -- it is taken to mean the hereditary son and successor of the Guru. We ourselves have held this same misunderstanding. The Vaishnav Nana Parekh, in writing anew an account of the departure to the divine abode -- in order to supply the burnt-away latter portion of the Samagam -- wrote, in the Udadharma-Panchratnamala, third edition, page 329, that Vaishnav Jivandasji said, "Dharma belongs to nad." Here he used this word "nad" because he was drawn to it. The intent behind using this word "nad" was that the basis for carrying dharma forward lies with one who properly understands the Guru's teaching -- such a person is fit to carry dharma forward. Further, people also take the meaning of "bund" to be that dharma does not belong by bund -- that is, it should not be understood that only the Guru's literal son can carry dharma forward. But nad-bund is, in fact, an entirely different matter. The word "bund" is a corrupted form of "bindu" -- "bund" is a word used, mistakenly, in place of "bindu." Nad-bund is, in fact, a term from the path of yoga, referring to Omkar. So it is not possible that Jivanji Maharaj -- who had made a complete study of all the paths of the world -- would use such a word as "nad" [in that confused, lineage-related sense] at his final hour. He himself has said in his own sakhi --

_Garbhadhyaan chinho nahi, kare Harijansun vivaad,
Ant bhaandivaado Jivana, kaha raachyo anahad naad ||4||_ (Garbhavali -- 44) (One who follows the path of yoga, but fails to understand the innermost meaning of the ratankaar of Ram's Name -- the divine essence dwelling within one's own soul -- and instead picks a quarrel, clutching at the tail-end of Omkar as a yogi, with devotees who practise devotion through the constant repetition [ratankaar] of Ram's Name: your fate in the end will be like that of a potter in a potter's quarter, firing pots in his kiln -- you too will have to be roasted in the fire of the womb, through the eighty-four lakh species of birth. So why do you climb onto the addiction of the unstruck sound [anahad nad] and remain absorbed in it? Better, instead, to follow the constant repetition of Ram's Name; walking the path of devotion will bring about your welfare.)

A great soul who was giving us such understanding would himself never use the word "nad" in that mistaken sense; but because we failed to grasp the true meaning of the word "nad," we -- from Nana Parekh down to the present day -- have been caught in a major error. Yet, from the moment we come to true understanding, we ought to correct our mistake. The devotees of Surat district had printed a book, for singing bhajan-kirtan just as we do, under the title "Ramkabir." But when a second edition was to be printed, a certain gentleman -- who, like us, had fallen into misunderstanding -- insisted on changing this title to "Nad Brahma" instead. This gentleman, who insisted on the change, once met me at Puniyad and told me that he had made a point of having the name "Nad Brahma" given to the book. I did not argue with him. But the kirtan-bhakti we perform, and the sound we raise in our kirtans through kaansi, mridang and narghan (cymbals, drum, and small kettledrums) -- that sound should not be called "nad." It is, rather, the voice of loving devotion born of the ceaseless repetition (ratankaar) of Ram's Name, rising up from within the soul. That sound is not nad; it is the resounding voice (nirghosh) that arises from the sound of the kaansi, mridang and so on, produced by a loving devotee wholly absorbed in devotion to Hari. We sing thus --

_Nand aangane nirghosh vaage, paanch shabdano poore naad._ (In the courtyard of Nand [Krishna's father], the sacred sound resounds -- the fullness of the five-fold sound.)

Thus, in this context, the word "nad" applies to our kirtan-bhakti; in that kirtan, as many as five kinds of sound come together, and so in this sense we do accept the word "nad." But not "Nad Brahma" -- rather, a word like "nad-bhakti" or "nad-kirtan" would be fitting for us; but for our faith, the word "nad-dharma" is not acceptable. In the five-fold sound, all five senses become immersed and drenched, absorbed in one single love.

God possesses the quality of niranjan-ness (being free of any stain); yet in Vraj Bhoomi there is the garden of Vrishbhanuji [Radha's father]. There is a village there named after a sakhi (companion) called Kamai; Shri Radha-Krishna used to visit her home. Near there is Ajnokhri, where there is Anjankund -- a pond where Shri Krishna applied anjan (kohl) to Radhaji's eyes. Referring to this, someone has written --

_Dhanyaa Gokulakanyaa vayamiha manyaamahe jagati,
Yaasaam nayanasaroje ajjaneebhooto niranjano vasati,
Suranjano'bhoot niranjanah saakshaat ||2||_ (I consider the gopa-maidens blessed in this world, in whose lotus eyes the very Niranjan [Krishna, the unstained one] himself has become anjan [the mark] and dwells as Suranjan -- that is, in whose eyes Shri Krishna resides, day and night. -- 2)

Such was the prem-lakshana bhakti (devotion characterised by pure love) of the gopis, that even one who is anjan-rahit (free of any mark) could become anjan-vaalo (bearing the mark). Adhyaruji, too, says --

_Khele khele jo rang Gopal niranjan anjanvaan shareero._ (Even though God is niranjan and nirakar [formless], for the sake of the gopis he became a body bearing form and plays with them -- such is that Gopal Krishna.)

Thus Jivanji Maharaj inspires us to practise this same kind of prem-lakshana devotion that the gopis had. "If one has form, fire cannot save him" -- this eternal, true statement Jivanji Maharaj repeated many times in the Samagam, and its meaning is very deep. Even if you reflect and meditate on this small sentence, a great deal of truth will become clear. In India the festival of Holi is celebrated, but we have killed the greatness that lies behind this festival.

According to one Puranic story, a demon named Hiranyakashipu became king, and, intoxicated by power, began to work destruction instead of the welfare of his subjects. Once he gained power, he began to fly high with pride, as though no one else could be more powerful than he; he even proclaimed himself to be God, and commanded his subjects to praise and worship him. But his son, though only a small child in years, turned out to be wise and just. The people could not oppose Hiranyakashipu's command, and, with heavy hearts, submitted to him, each thinking only of their own safety; out of a craving for momentary pleasure, they accepted the falsehood. Only his own son opposed his father's command. Sufferings came upon him, and he had to pass through many trials; a reign of threat and intimidation began, but still he would not yield. In the end, it was decided that he should be burned to death, to remove the threat once and for all. His beloved, favoured sister, Holika, had received a boon that she could never be burned, however fierce the fire; so it was arranged that she would sit with Prahlad on her lap while a fire was lit -- but Prahlad survived.

There are many festivals celebrated, of which four are principal: Shravan-Rakshabandhan for Brahmins; second, Dashera for Kshatriyas; third, Deepavali for Vaishyas; and fourth, Holi for Shudras.

It was necessary for Prahlad to say this — he could not tell the true fact, that he had cleverly escaped from the funeral pyre and so remained alive, because the cruel father would have caused further trouble. But the father accepted this account. He also expressed grief over Holika's death, shedding crocodile tears.

As if this were not enough, the world too came to accept this account. Many came to believe that Holika had received a boon — how then could she have died? She could not possibly burn! Even today this belief has taken root among us to such an extent that, considering it a miracle, many walk on the burning embers of Holi. Their claim is that all this is Holika's own glory, and many have come to regard her as a goddess — that though one walks on the Holi fire one is not burnt. But no one is willing to understand the true fact; everyone has been led along by religious superstition, everyone has become blind to this. No one wants to open their eyes and look — a herd mentality has taken hold.

It is true that walking momentarily on burning embers causes no injury. But this is because, after years of practice, the skin on the soles of the feet becomes thick and the nerve-endings of the sensory system get deadened, so that no sensation of heat is felt. But no human being can stand still on such embers for hours — this is a scientific law: fire is capable of burning anything, and its touch causes injury. But through practice and repeated effort it becomes possible to walk on it for a few moments; there is no miracle in this. But why the world, having lost its senses in religious superstition, is not willing to understand such a plain truth — that itself is the big question.

Jivanji Maharaj explained, giving a solid scientific reason, that fire burns any object that has form. Nothing escapes it — even if it be the Supreme Being (Parbrahm) come in an incarnation, or, in doubt, merely a human being, it will still burn. This is an eternal law, unalterable at any time or age. Therefore sensible people, upon reading and hearing the many mythological tales, should reflect that a scientific law never changes. If Prahlad had touched a hot, burning spot, he would surely have been burnt. Further, as we have already said, if the Supreme Being too takes incarnation in the world in doubtful bodily form, then the law that governs the world must certainly apply to him as well. Then why was Lord Narsinh not burnt? We do not wish to go into the depths of the mythological facts — Jivanji Maharaj too, having pointed to the scientific fact, has stepped aside from the matter, because engaging in debate is not the devotees' task. We only believe and know this much: that the devotee Prahlad was saved, and that divine power triumphed over demonic power. The victory of truth over untruth is our only aim.

Moreover, since devotee Prahlad was rescued and delivered from calamity, then whoever saved him is our Lord (Parmeshwar); we do not wish to enter into any debate about it — the world may consider the one who protected Prahlad to be the incarnation of Narsinh or anyone else, but for us the one formless, unmanifest Supreme Being (Niranjan Nirakar Parbrahm) alone is sufficient. We do not wish to enter into debates over incarnations, nor do we wish to worship or venerate any incarnations. Through a verse from the Niranjan Purana the form of God has been described, and, presenting an alternative view, it is said: if God has no form, then what is one to make of his manifesting from the pillar for Prahlad's sake? For this, the Haarmala (Garland) hymn has been presented. That hymn corresponds to the Bhagavat, Canto 10, Chapter 43, verse 17:

_Mallanam ashani nrinam natvarah, strinam smaro murtiman |
Gopanam svajano-satam kshitibhujam shasta svapitroh shishuh ||
Mrityur bhojapater virat cha vidusham tattvam param yoginam |
Vrishninam paradevateti vidito rangam gatah sagrajah ||3||_
(At the time when Lord Shri Krishna, together with Balram, entered the wrestling arena, he appeared to the wrestlers as one with a body hard as a thunderbolt, to ordinary men as the finest of men, to women as Kamadev — the god of love — in bodily form, to the cowherds as their own kinsman, to the wicked kings as the ruler who metes out punishment, to the elders, as venerable as their own parents, as a mere child, to Kansa as death itself, to the ignorant as the cosmic form (Virat), to the yogis as the Supreme Reality, and to the Vrishni clan, foremost among devotees, as their own chosen deity. Each experienced, according to his own disposition, the rasa — the aesthetic sentiment — of terror, wonder, romance, laughter, heroism, parental affection, fear, disgust, peace, or loving devotion.)

It is stated in Registration No. 846, page 41, that this Damodarashram was an ascetic Vedantic poet. He was a resident of Siddhpur and lived by Bindu Sarovar; he lived fifty years after Bhalan. Another view holds that he lived about five hundred to five hundred twenty-five years ago near Karnali by Chandod, and that he was a follower of the Shankar school. Ra' Mangalik, the king of Junagadh, at the instigation of these ascetic renunciants, persecuted Narsinh Mehta over the garland of Lord Damodar; because of this, Narsinh Mehta went to live with his daughter in Una, and passed away there. But the king was held at fault for wronging this devotee, and so Mahmud Begada forcibly converted this king and made him a Muslim; that king's grave was in Manek Chowk in Ahmedabad. Because Mahmud Begada conquered two forts, he came to be called "Begado" (the one of two forts); he had also conquered the second fort, Pavagadh.

_Samvat 1572 na Magsar Sud-7 Bhomvare, Shri Damodarji e apyo Mehtaji ne haar re_
(In Samvat 1572, on Tuesday, the seventh day of the bright half of Magsar, Shri Damodarji gave Mehtaji the garland) — this is one line from the Haarmala hymn. By offering this composition of Narsinh Mehta, Jivanji Maharaj sought to explain what would come of quarreling over whether God has form or is formless, and what he is truly like. God appears to each person according to that person's own disposition; God takes on the form suited to each one's taste and nature. God is the Lord of all — so how could he be said to have a fixed form? And yet he took Hiranyakashyapu onto his lap and tore him apart — so how could he be called formless either? Moreover, that which has form cannot survive fire. So, explaining and establishing the truth of form and formlessness to devotees such as Devdas, Kalyandas, Haridas, and Ramdas, Jivanji Maharaj said that the God who protected Prahlad is the very God we worship. Sakhi (couplet) —

1. When the demon Hiranyakashyapu became terrifying, God assumed the form of Narsinh and protected the devotee Prahlad, and there was rejoicing and cries of victory throughout the world over his triumph.

2. Ram is truly and verily God, and he is capable of shattering the heads of all and keeping everyone under his control; therefore worship that very God who was the protector of Prahlad.

3. Ramchandra is truly God — he who held up Mount Govardhan upon his hand, and he who went to Janakpuri, broke the bow, and married Sitaji.

_Naamroop dou Jivana, Sadguru kahe samajhai |
Prahlad kaso aparadh, je roope raha bandhai ||5||_
(Regarding both the Name and the Form of God, the true guru explains: Prahlad had to endure hardship because of one flaw in him — he was attached only to the Form of God, without having understood, through a true guru, the union of Name and Form. God takes whatever form the devotee holds in mind; but one who understands the intricacy of Name and Form attains God with ease.)

_Prahlad bichara kaha kare, kaman ki ghundi nahi |
Naame baho Jivana, chhodo Vaikunth mahi ||6||_
(What could poor Prahlad do — he was helpless. In his heart he held no knot of ill-will toward anyone, whether father or God; he simply clung to the Name alone. Therefore God sent him into his own abode, Vaikunth.)

The exposition of form and formlessness that the true guru Gopaldas had once given to Jivanji Maharaj — in that same manner, briefly, Jivanji Maharaj here explained it to Devidas and others: that God is beyond both form and formlessness. This sentiment has been shown. _Yadrishi bhavana yasya, siddhir bhavati tadrishi_ — (As is one's devotion, so is the fruit one attains.) Adhyaruji says: bhakt jya jevu man dhare taha teve pind — (wherever the devotee holds whatever disposition of mind, there does God take on that corresponding form). Devotees find God in the form corresponding to the devotion with which they worship him.

In the first chapter of the Sushruti Samhita, there is a statement of Lord Shivji:

_Karanam pranavasyapi Ramanaam jagadguruh ||
Tasmad dhyeyam sada chaitad yatibhih shuddha chetasa ||4||_
(Ramanandacharya, page 360)
(Shri Ram, the teacher of the universe, is the very cause even of the Om-kar; therefore let even the ascetic, with a pure mind, ever meditate upon and remember the Name of Shri Ram.)

For us, for the purpose of worship, only a Name that serves as the identifying mark of the Supreme Being is needed, and we worship the Name — let the world identify it however it may.

That is to say, having demonstrated the primacy of the Name, Jivanji Maharaj bestowed the mala and tilak upon Devdas and Ramdas; he gave mala and tilak to Haridas; he gave mala and tilak to Kalyandas and Ramdas. All these Vaishnavs had met Jivanji Maharaj in Malwa; he bestowed mala and tilak upon all of them.

In Jivandasji's Parchari (hagiographic account), Shyamdasji has given the list of Malwa's devotees as follows:

Gopaldas — Malibai
Gopaldas — Panabai
Santdas — Kaibai
Surajji Bhagat — Sahajibai
Haridas — Jivibahen
Ramdas — Panabai
Kalyandas — Baiyabai
Devdas — Jivibai
Ramdas — Jaytibai

Thus a list of these nine sant-devotees of Malwa has been given. The names of the women listed against the devotees' names are the names of their wives, who were themselves also devoted disciples of Jivanji Maharaj.
