Wearing a fringed skirt, the fool keeps vigil all night; but when calamity strikes she sells it all and eats — where then has all your fine skill gone? On the eighth and fourteenth days she cooks sweet lapsi and offers it to these deities, and stays awake all night singing worldly songs. She who was devoted to one alone has become devoted to many, like a courtesan with many husbands; Kabir says: with which one, then, will she go in the end, she who is wife to so many men?)

The people of the world remain caught up, dangling in a meaningless, worthless swing — that is, they remain occupied in wandering about — but devotion to Rajaram does not occur to them. Bhairav demands oil and grains of gram, and they offer him a goat by cutting its neck. The offering made to Bhairav is carried off by the shaman (bhuvo); and the blood that clings to Bhairav's stone is licked by dogs. Women go to the goddess's shrine carrying a burning brazier upon their heads; giving up all food and drink there, they sit as though placing hell itself, in the form of flesh, beside them. They ask Kshetrapal, the guardian deity of the field, for the gift of a son in exchange for the sacrifice of a goat. They wish to save the life of their own dear son, yet they cut down and kill the dear kid of a goat. In the presence of her father-in-law or brother-in-law, she rushes off swiftly to such a place; she covers her face with a veil out of modesty before them, yet feels ashamed to bow in respect when she sees devotees of Hari. Thus, among those who practise the impure devotion she has set going, causing pure devotion to be broken, and before whom devotees feel embarrassed even to greet with respect — some among these will turn out to be worshippers of one goddess, some of one god, and some of Chamunda. So if a courtesan's house has a son born to it, whom can he call his father? She keeps the eighth-day fast, worships the smallpox goddess, and to ward off obstruction and possession and their attendant troubles she ties charm-threads — and this becomes a laughable disgrace, because one such goddess's mount is a donkey while another's is a bull or lion. Furthermore, she wears a garment that flaps about at its hem; and fools have spent the whole night in loud vigil for her worship, and when misfortune actually struck, they abandoned it all and let it go — where then did all your fine skills go? On the eighth and fourteenth days and other such occasions, she prepares sweet lapsi and offers this to these goddesses, and thus she awakens her infatuated devotees and sings beautiful, sensuous songs. She was once the devoted worshipper of only one Husband, the Supreme Lord, but now has become the worshipper of many — she has become a courtesan with many husbands; so then, in the end, with which one of her many husbands will she burn? Therefore Kabir resolved—

_ab mai jana he mere bhai, bhuli duniya kal gher jai |tek|_
_nahi ma puju devadevi, nahi me pushp chadhavu_
_nahi me singhasan murati dharu, nahi me ghant bajavu ||1||_
_jo e murati jutha jame, khara mora kahi jane_
_pani mag pie apane mukh hase, to mera man man ||2||_
_jo e murat mukhse bole, to kar jodi shish namavu_
_char paisa le sonar ghar javu, me bi ek gadhau ||3||_
_tank tank kar gadhi re sonare, ber ber tapae_
_e muratke bharuse rahave, to agale janamki kamai ||4||_
_gyan kare hardai nache te, grahame rahe udasi_
_satanam the duna jage, kahe kabir avinashi ||5||_
(Now, my brother, I have understood: the deluded world goes into the clutches of death. Now I will worship no god or goddess, nor offer flowers to any; I will not install any idol on a throne, nor ring any temple bell. If this idol could know stale, impure food and salty water for what it is, if it could ask for water and drink it, and smile with its own mouth — then my mind would believe. If this idol could speak with its own mouth, I would fold my hands and bow my head to it; I would take my four coins — my little wealth — and go to a goldsmith's house, and have one cast for myself too. Beaten and beaten into shape, heated again and again by the goldsmith — if one could rely upon such an image, it would be the fruit of merit earned in a former birth! One who takes up true knowledge dances with joy in the heart, and remains detached even while living in the household; through the True Name he awakens doubly, says Kabir, the Name which is imperishable.)

O my brother, now I have realised that the whole world, having lost its way, is heading into the house of death. Now I shall no longer worship any god or goddess nor offer them flowers. I shall not enshrine any idol upon a throne nor ring any temple bell. If this idol could know that it has become stale, impure, or salty water, and if it could ask for water and drink it, or laugh with its mouth, then indeed I would come to believe. If that idol could speak with its mouth, I would bow my head to it; moreover, whatever four or five paise — that is, whatever wealth — I possess, I would take that money to a goldsmith and have an idol cast for myself as well. If the goldsmith, by hammering it again and again and heating it repeatedly, has fashioned it, then to be able to rely on such an image would be reckoned the fruit of merit from a past birth. Those who grasp true knowledge and remain joyful and content at heart, remaining equally detached in happiness and sorrow, experience double happiness through the Name of God — so speaks the soul of the devotee Kabir.

Kabirji says that just as "I too used to worship stones" — the wild deer of the forest are of no use to human beings at all, and moreover they cause damage to the standing crops of farmers; had I been as devoid of intelligence as they, I too would have worshipped stone. In the same way, such stone deities are useless. On this path of devotion, when I — that is, this body of mine — found the true Sadguru, he freed me from the burden upon my head, that is, from the act of worshipping various stones. —3.

O foolish one! Every day the people of this world get up in the morning and go to worship stones in temples; there they go and bow head upon head. But you are unable to recognise that Hari dwells within this very body, within the heart; fix your mind there — upon that inner being of yours where Hari dwells. —4.

Why should stone be worshipped, when it is not living and cannot give birth? Yet people call it their Supreme Father, the Lord! Because blind people are hungry for hope, for gain, they thus waste their own lives wherever it pleases them. —5.

_baitha so bole nahi, ubha kahe na av_
_suta so jage nahi, kisku lagu pay_
(Seated, it does not speak; standing, it does not say "come"; lying down, it does not wake — then to whom shall I bow my feet?)

The idol that is seated does not speak; the idol that stands does not say "come"; the idol that lies asleep does not wake — then at whose feet shall I bow?

If one could obtain the Supreme Brahman by worshipping stones, then I, Kabirji, would be ready to go and worship an entire mountain; but that is not how it happens. Alas, people worship a stone called Shaligram, taking it to be Vishnu and Shiva, but that is of no use at all, because the millstone used for grinding grain is more useful than the Shaligram; through it the worldly soul grinds grain daily and eats bread, whereas the stones of temples are of no use whatsoever. —6.

In a dark chamber of ignorance and nescience, people have imprisoned God and set out to search for Hari in a temple built of four walls. So-called pious men and pandits have set up this strange and false path. The whole world in this way has lost its way, running after stones. —7.

In books written with black ink, binding these teachings into fixed form and spreading them across the earth, and by building temples of stone across the earth, sowing the seed of scripture in people's minds, the pandits have laid down a set custom for people to follow accordingly.

After this utterance of Kabirji, Jivanji Maharaj says that bells are rung in temples, and the stone idol is bathed and anointed with water and so forth just as one would treat a living human being, and all manner of ceremonial dealing is carried out with it as though it were alive; but the eyes of the pandits and priests who perform this worship are fixed not on devotion but on the donations of the assembled devotees. Thus they are like hunters, and they draw us into the net of ritual action. —8.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, on the basis of the Bijak, Shabda 11, has called the pandit a hunter.

Shabda 11:

_santo pande nipun kasai_
_bakara mari bhainsa par ghave, dilme dard na ai ||tek||_
_kari asnan tilak dai baithe, bidhise devi pujai_
_atamram palakme binashe, rudhir ki nadi bahai ||1||_
_ati punit unche kul kahiye, sabha mahi adhikai_
_inhate diksha sab koi mange, hansi ave mohi bhai ||2||_
_pap katanko katha sunave, karma karave nicha_
_ham to dou paraspar dekha, yam laye hai dhokha ||3||_
_gay badhe te turuk kahiye, inhate vai kya chhote_
_kahihi kabir suno ho santo, kali me brahman khote ||4||_
(O saints, the pandit is a skilled butcher: he kills goats and strikes down buffaloes, and feels not the least pain of it in his heart. After bathing, he sits down having applied his tilak, and worships the goddess with proper ritual; in a moment he destroys the indwelling soul and makes a river of blood flow. Yet these are called of most holy, high lineage, and are given the highest place in assemblies; everyone begs initiation from them — it makes me, brother, want to laugh. They recite tales meant to remove sin, yet cause the lowest deeds to be done; I have watched the two of them side by side — Yama has fashioned them as one deception. He who kills a cow is called a Turk — how are these Brahmins any less than him? Kabir says: listen, O saints, in the Kali Yuga the Brahmins have become corrupted.)

O saints, the pandit is a cunning butcher, because he rushes to kill goats and buffaloes and feels not the slightest pain in his heart at slaughtering creatures small or great. Having bathed, he sits down after applying his tilak. He performs and has others perform the worship of the goddess by tantric ritual. Then, after killing an animal, he offers it as sacrifice to the goddess. In doing so he kills, in an instant, the very indwelling Self within that creature, and makes a river of blood flow. These people bearing the name of "Pandey" commit such violent, vile deeds, and yet call themselves the most exalted, of the highest and purest lineage; and in assemblies and gatherings they are praised. People take guru-diksha, the initiation mantra, from these very gurus — seeing this whole tradition of the ignorant makes me want to laugh, and I grow troubled. These priests named Pandey recite religious discourses to free their patrons from sin, while themselves causing the base act of violence to be committed. I have watched both Hindu and Turk (Muslim) alike commit the killing of living beings; Yama has fashioned instruments to lead both of them to hell. One who kills a cow is called a Turk; but Brahmins who kill goats and buffaloes are no less sinful than him — both are equally sinful. In the Kali Yuga, both the Brahmins and the Muslims who cause the killing of living beings are sinners. In the Hindi Collection (H. Li. Granth) No. 8, page 62, in the Asavari raga, Kabir says—

_ape betha loh nav par, orakun ehi dadhai_
_kahat kabir kashithe kadho, brahman jo hai kasai_
(He himself sits on an iron boat, urging others to place this very confidence in it; Kabir says: throw out of Kashi that Brahmin who is a butcher.)

_rakshasah kalimashritya jayate brahmayonishu_
(In the Kali Yuga, demons will take birth in the wombs of Brahmins.)

That is, when the Kali Yuga arrives, demons will be born upon this earth in the form of Brahmins. "If we were asked to give the definition of a devotee in a single word, we would place before it the word 'lokbahya' [beyond ordinary worldly convention]. In this single word alone the entire definition of the devotee's life, of the traveller on the sacred path of devotion, is expressed. All the deeds of devotees are wondrous indeed; they have no concern for what people think." — Prabhudutt Brahmachari, Shri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, page 534.

Wherever the pandits go — that is, wherever pandits enter, or whatever matter they meddle in — there they look only to their own self-interest; therefore for such people only exploitation remains, that is, death! But wherever the feet of a saint fall, there the Supreme Brahman comes to dwell. —9.

The bards and minstrels who entertain people while also instructing them through tales and stories, though these tale-telling bhats or Brahmins may appear innocent on the surface, are in truth the very chiefs of the faithless (sakut). Under their innocent-sounding words, the world is unknowingly led astray. Thus they are well capable of leading society down the wrong path.

_kabir panditki katha, jaisi chorank nav_
_sunkar baithe andhala, bhave taha le jay_
(Kabir says: the discourse of the pandit is like the boat of thieves — the blind sit and listen to it, and it takes them wherever it pleases.)

The discourses of Brahmins are like the boat of thieves. Those ignorant ones who are lured in by listening to such discourses are taken by the Brahmins wherever they please, and are robbed after being set down there.

_ishta bina bhajan kesu, jyu khevat bin nav_
_moji pari parabhayome, jit bhave tit jay_
(Without one's chosen deity, worship of another is like a boat without a boatman — carried by the current wherever it happens to go, into difficulty.)

Moji Bhagat says: how can one be called a devotee who, without an Ishtadev, one's own chosen deity, worships another deity instead? It is like a boat without a boatman, which, once cast adrift in the current, goes wherever it happens to go.

_kabir brahman guru jagatka, santanka guru nahi_
_lot potke dubiya, charo vedo mahi_
(Kabir says: the Brahmin is guru to the world, but he is no guru to the saints; rolling about, they drown, the four Vedas notwithstanding.)

The Veda-reciting, ritualistic Brahmins are gurus who lead worldly people, entangled in the wheel of the material world, along the path of ritual action; but saints are free from hope of illusory fruit, and therefore these Brahmins are not their gurus. So, entangled in the four Vedas, floundering and struggling, they — the people of the world as well as the Brahmins — sink lower and lower, drowning again and again in the net of illusion (maya).

This teaching above has been spoken by Sadguru Kabirji and Jivanji Maharaj, and the Purana bears witness to this very teaching. Shloka:

_tvam gantarah prapadyante vina bhaktya na chantimam_
_shastrani vedamarganam deva vishnorbahirmukhah ||44||_
(Those who go toward You cannot attain that ultimate goal without devotion; the gods who are turned away from Vishnu, as well as the paths of the Vedas and the scriptures, cannot attain You either.)

Without devotion, people travelling toward that supreme abode which is You cannot attain You. The gods who are turned away from Vishnu, and the path of the Vedas and the scriptures, cannot attain You.

Now the commentary (tika): Mahadev spoke, saying, "O beloved! That state which is of the nature of bliss, which is the supreme Vishnu — that supreme Vishnu is our very protector." Agradas likewise says—

_trata to tin lokme, jit dekho tit soi_
_santanka veri koi nahi, hoi to brahman hoi_
(Our protector, wherever you look in all three worlds, is that very one; the saints have no enemy at all — if they have any, it is only the Brahmin.)

Agradas says: in all three worlds, wherever we look, it is that same protector who is present to save us, the saints and devotees; but if the saints have any enemy at all in this world, it is only the Brahmin.

_nalam dvijatvam devatvam rishitvam vasuratmajah_
_prananatha mukundasya na vrittam na bahujnata_
_na danam na tapo nejya na shaucham na vratani cha_
_priyate'amalaya bhaktya harliranyad vidambana_
(Bhagavata, Skandha 7, Adhyaya 7 — O son of the demon! Brahminhood, godhood, or sagehood, good conduct, vast learning, charity, austerity, sacrifice, purity, or great vows — none of these are able to please Mukunda, the Lord of life; He is pleased only by pure, desireless devotion — all else is mere pretence.)

Brahminhood, godhood, or the state of a sage, good conduct, deep scriptural learning, and also charity, austerity, sacrifice, physical and mental purity, and even great vows — none of these are capable of pleasing God. God is pleased only by pure, desireless (nishkam) devotion. Everything else is mere theatrical show.

_brahmanke man bhakti na ave, bhule ap sabani samujhave_
_aurani thagi-thagi apun thagave, apun sove sabani jagave_
_ved-puran bechi dhan lyave, satya taji hatyadi milave_
_hari haridas na dekhyau bhave, bhuta, pitar, devata pujave_
_apun narak pari kulahi bulave, vyas bhakti binu ko gati pavau_
(233; Bhaktakavi Vyas, page 245 — Devotion never enters the Brahmin's mind — himself astray, he goes about instructing everyone else. Cheating others again and again, he ends up cheating himself; asleep himself, he wakes everyone else. Selling the Vedas and Puranas, he makes his money; abandoning truth, he takes up violence and the like. He has no love for seeing Hari or Hari's devotees, yet he makes people worship ghosts, ancestors, and lesser deities. He drags his own family down into hell with himself — says Vyas, without devotion who can attain true liberation?)

The thought of devotion to Vishnu never even enters the mind of Brahmins; they themselves are lost in the worship of Anadev, other deities, yet they instruct everyone else to practise devotion to Vishnu and to Anadev alike. Cheating others again and again, they end up cheating themselves, thereby becoming bound for hell. They themselves practise neither devotion to Vishnu nor any other true devotion, yet they warn everyone else to do so. They sell the Vedas and Puranas and earn money by it, and abandoning the true they pursue the false; they have no love at all for the sight of God or of God's devotees, and instead make people worship ghosts, ancestral spirits, and lesser deities. Thus they themselves fall into hell along with their whole lineage. And how can one attain any good state at all, without devotion?

The revered Yadunath Maharaj has written in Litiyu No. 74, page 1, that no living being can remain in this world without practising some form of devotion — this is beyond dispute. It is said in the Gita: _na hi kashchitkshanamapi jatu tishthatyakarmakrit_ (Chapter 3, verse 5) — no person can ever remain even for an instant without performing action. In the same way, everyone practises some devotion, but only devotion to the Supremely Merciful One is truly glorious; anything else is merely a burden, like forced labour —

therefore it is most beneficial to worship the Supreme Lord of all through this human body. Hence, even the ascetics who renounce all attachment, the sages who keep perpetual silence, and gods such as Narada, Sanaka, Sanandana and the rest, who without devotion still fear birth and death — the recurring cycle of birth and death and rebirth, that is, the fear of death — that fear does not remain if one practises devotion. Therefore it is essential that anyone who takes a human body must certainly practise devotion. The reason is that the wisdom to practise devotion is not even possessed by the gods and great sages — that is, by Indra and the like — because to practise devotion, it is first necessary to take refuge (sharanagati); refuge alone is the key to victory. The Supremely Merciful One, along with His compassion, is the giver of the imperishable state; Dhruva and Prahlad stand as the very examples, the proof, of that imperishable state and of firm resolve — therefore it is necessary to take refuge in the Lord of all. For taking refuge, do not forget Vibhishan.

This has been described as the dharma of the Treta Yuga, and called the Pravah-Margi Vaishnava dharma. The devotion to Vishnu practised in the Satya, Treta, and Dvapar Yugas has been discussed here; that path of devotion has been called the Pravah Marg. Now let us speak of the glory of the Pushti Marg: Rudra spoke to Parvati, describing the dharma of the Dvapar Yuga. The Pushti Marg is one of devotion to Krishna, and for this reason this path has been placed within the dharma of the Dvapar Yuga. Shloka:

_navaishnavaya datavyam vikalpaya hatatmane_
_bhaktishraddhavihinaya vishnunamadruhe na cha ||45||_
(This should not be given to one who is not a Vaishnava, who is caught in doubt and vacillation, who is spiritually ruined, who is devoid of devotion and faith, or who bears hostility toward the Name of Vishnu.)

This — the Ram Name — should not be given to one who is not a Vaishnava, who is caught up in doubt and vacillation, who is spiritually ruined, who is devoid of devotion and faith, and who bears enmity toward the Name of Vishnu. It has been said in shloka 45 —

_bhakti shraddhavihinaya_ — that is, to one who is devoid of devotion and faith, who has no faith for devotion, the Ram Name should not be given; regarding this it has been said —

_ashraddhane vimukhe'pyashrunvanti yashchopadeshah shivanamaparadhah_
(To teach the divine name to those who are faithless, turned away, and unwilling to listen — that itself is an offence against the sacred Name.)

Those who are faithless and turned away — that is, who direct their senses toward worldly objects — if the teaching of God is spoken to such people, it becomes an offence against the divine Name.

Kabirji made efforts to teach people devotion to God; even after being explained to once, twice, three times, when such shakta-worshipping, faithless people did not accept it, Kabirji, growing weary, called such people "sakut" (the faithless), and gave the injunction not to keep company with them, because upon persons of such varied and contrary nature no good effect is produced — rather, the opposite effect results, and they turn against us instead.

_kabir kalika ramjan, mata jaisa dhing_
_keval gyan dradhavate, sahama mande sing_
(Kabir says: in the Kali Yuga, some so-called devotees of Ram are like a mad, intoxicated animal; when one tries firmly to instill true knowledge in them, they lower their horns to charge.)

Kabirji says that in the Kali Yuga there are people, like mourners at a cremation ground, who behave like an intoxicated bull; when one goes to impress the true teaching upon them, they instead pick a quarrel with us.

_khalah sakriyamanopi dadati kalaham satam_
_dugdha dyotopi kim yati vayasah kalahamsatam_
(Even when good is done to him, the wicked man repays the virtuous with strife; even if bathed in milk, does a crow ever become a swan?)

Even if you do good to a wicked man, he will still do evil to the virtuous. Even if you bathe a crow in milk, it will never become a swan.

Vasant (raga):

_harirasa ajar mahara vahala, jirave virala koi_
_mand agni mishthanna na jirave, vaman kare taha soi_
_paro bhogave te bhogi kahiye, man bhogave te jogi_
_jaha lagi man paro nahi bhogave, taha lagi e bhayrogi ||1||_
_gay sikhe ne mota bole, em mota nav thaiye_
_moti dasha mota anubhav vina, parangat nav thaiye ||2||_
_megh vrishti kare nirantar, jal jai thambhe khame_
_sathu solu sovarnanu patra, tame sinhaninu dudh jame ||3||_
_svant tana meh saghale vutha, sip tharya te moti_
_kone kadhya kashta karine, pahere te panoti ||4||_
_shura je ranthi pachha na bhage, pura padma sahamai_
_sati bhando sanche nahi koi, pith na puthe palai ||5||_
_pandit te je sada sam drashti, vaid te je arogi_
_shubh ashubh jehane nahi sambhave, so nar sudha jogi ||6||_
_man pasarya hoy te pachha sankeli, niralamb thai rahiye_
_kahe kabir prem jal parasata, sada anand sukh paiye ||7||_
(The rasa of devotion to Hari is imperishable, my dear one, but only a rare few can digest it; one of weak digestion cannot digest sweets, and if he eats them he vomits at once. He who can digest raw mercury is the true "enjoyer"; he whose mind does not become attached to enjoyment is the true "yogi." So long as the mind has not, of its own accord, digested and conquered the mercury of illusion, one remains diseased with worldly desire. One who merely learns to sing like a cow and calls himself great does not thereby become great; without deep experience of the great state, one does not become perfect. The cloud rains ceaselessly, yet that water only collects and stops in a pit; only in a vessel of sixteen-anna pure gold can the milk of a lioness be kept without spoiling. When the rain of the Svati star falls, all showers fall alike, but only in an oyster-shell does it become a pearl; only a fortunate soul, after great labour, can pull that pearl out of the sea and wear it. The brave warrior does not flee from the battlefield, but faces it with full strength; the chaste woman never harbours another man in truth, and never turns her back to flee. The true pandit is one who always looks upon all with equal vision, and the true physician is the one who himself remains free of disease. He for whom good and bad fortune no longer arise is the true, nectar-drinking yogi. If the mind has strayed outward, one should draw it back inward again, and remain independent of all external support; Kabir says, by touching the water of divine love, one attains everlasting bliss and joy.)

Beloved ones, the rasa (essence) of devotion to Hari is such that it never spoils, yet only a rare few are able to digest it. Those of weak digestive power cannot digest sweets — if they eat them, they immediately vomit. Those who have such a strong digestive fire that they can digest even raw mercury, and who are able likewise to digest illusion (maya), are the true "bhogis," enjoyers; in the same way, those whose mind does not attach itself to maya are called "yogis." So long as the mind has not, through its own will, released and thus digested the mercury-like maya, such people remain afflicted with the disease of worldly desire. Those who, after learning to sing beautifully and gaining some knowledge, declare themselves to have become great, do not thereby become truly great; without deep, profound experience they fall into great calamity, and one who is incomplete cannot become a perfect scholar. Even if rain falls continuously, that water only collects and stays in a hollow; only in a vessel of sixteen-anna pure gold can the milk of a lioness be kept — in any other vessel it curdles and spoils.

When the water of the Svati constellation falls and lands in an oyster shell, it becomes a pearl; and that pearl is brought up from the sea by some diver who endures great hardship to fetch it, and whoever wears it must be a person of great merit. One who does not flee from the battlefield is called a hero; he charges forward with full strength and power to face the enemy. A chaste woman (sati) never keeps company with another man, and in remaining true to her chastity she never turns her back and runs away. The true pandit is one who always looks with an equal eye upon all, and the true physician is one who himself remains free of disease. Only those men in whom no distinction of good fortune and bad fortune arises are the truly wise yogis. If the mind has wandered off into sensual desire, it should be drawn back from there, and one should remain independent, without relying upon anything else. Kabir says: experiencing thus the water of loving devotion, may we always attain the bliss of joy.

Ignorant, worldly people are one thing, but even great scholars regard Anadev and Ishtadev — other deities — as equal to Vasudev, the Supreme Lord — and this is worse still, for such scholars have left nothing undone in reducing Vasudev to the level of an ordinary human being. Not only this, but it is a matter of great regret that even the Vaishnava Acharyas, who insist on purity of conduct, lend great support to such a view. That regrettable attitude toward Ram and Krishna is this: that at the time of the birth of Ram and Krishna, a period of ritual impurity (sutak) is observed, and so people delay eating their meal after the birth of Ram and Krishna, as if it were an ordinary human birth involving pollution. In this way, they regard Ram and Krishna, who are the mighty Supreme Purushottam themselves, as being lower even than ordinary gods, as mere humans. Therefore devotion which behaves in this manner toward God is faulty, and those who hold such faulty devotion fall into the category of the faithless (sakut).

Rudra says to Parvati: O beloved! Those who are non-Vaishnava (sakut), devoid of devotion and faith, who regard Anadev as equal to Vasudev — such ignorant people should not be given the Ram Name.

Kabirji says—

_kabir sakutkun na sunaiye, gun gan aur git_
_tulsi manjar todke, kyu chadhaiye masit ||1||_
_ramabhaktima jivana, vali anadev upas_
_khir khanekihush hai, pan bhele dudh aur chhas ||2||_
_anadev barabar jivana, je samare sitaram_
_mugatphal ve det he, nahi charan kamal vishram ||3||_
_sitapati taj jivana, dhyan dhare akash_
_pragat godko chhandke, kare garbhaki ash ||4||_
_sitapati taj jivana, rahyo brahmasu lag_
_rui mandirme peth kar, dvare lagai ag ||5||_
(Kabir says: do not sing praises and songs of Hari to the faithless — plucking tulsi buds and offering them at a mosque, what purpose does that serve? O Jivan, in devotion to Ram, worship also of Anadev — it is as if one desires to eat kheer, yet mixes buttermilk into the milk. O Jivan, whoever ranks Anadev equal to Ram and yet remembers Sitaram — such worship grants only the four lesser liberations, not rest at those lotus feet. O Jivan, forsaking the Lord of Sita, some meditate gazing at the sky — it is like a mother, holding her manifest child already in her lap, instead longing for a child still in the womb. O Jivan, forsaking the Lord of Sita, remaining attached to abstract Brahman alone — it is like entering a house made of cotton and lighting a fire at its very door.)

That is, Kabirji says that to those who are "sakut," faithless, one should not recite the qualities or hymns of Shri Hari Bhagwan, or sing devotional songs, because they are not entitled to it. There is no purpose in plucking tulsi leaves and offering them at a mosque — it would only bring disrespect upon us. In the same way, there is no purpose in showing or reciting the Name of God to the faithless — they will only show disrespect to God. —1.

_mul dvare edi dai, pavan valove akash_
_sitapati bin jivana, svarg narak mahi vas ||6||_
_anahad shabda jaha unmuni, ravi shashi donu mel_
_ramnam bin jivana, jamsu karvo kel ||7||_
_ashtadal kamal je koi jape, koi dhyan dhare akash_
_bhaj sitapati jivana, lakshmi charan nivas ||8||_
(Placing the heel at the base and churning the sky with the breath — O Jivan, without the Lord of Sita, one dwells only between heaven and hell. Where the unstruck sound arises in the state beyond mind, where sun and moon are merged as one — O Jivan, without the Name of Ram, one must play games with Yama. Whether one meditates repeating the eight-petalled lotus, or fixes contemplation on the sky — O Jivan, worship the Lord of Sita instead, at whose feet Lakshmi herself dwells.)

Jivanji Maharaj says that in devotion to Ram, worship of Anadev — other gods and goddesses — cannot stand together with it. For just as one may wish to eat kheer, but if buttermilk gets mixed into the milk meant for making that kheer, the kheer of that milk cannot be made — in the same way, in the devotion of true, unique Vaishnavism, no worship of Anadev can stand alongside it. Moreover, in devotion to Sitaram, worship of Anadev, of other gods and goddesses, cannot stand; the faithless are worshippers of Anadev, and therefore, just as milk curdles and spoils when mixed with something else, Ram-bhakti mixed with worship of Anadev likewise becomes useless. —2.

Sakhi 3 follows on from Sakhi 2. In Sakhi 2 it is said that if one who practises devotion to Ram also worships Anadev, then, just as milk curdles, the devotion to Ram, though practised, becomes corrupted. So in Sakhi 3 it is said that those who worship Anadev while also practising remembrance-devotion to Ram — such devotion to Ram becomes just like devotion to Anadev; therefore, though they are indeed practising devotion to Ram as well, they obtain only the fruit of the four lesser liberations, but they cannot attain the supreme state of dwelling at the lotus feet of God. Anadev must never be compared with Ram, because Ram cannot be compared with other deities — He is the Supreme, the highest God, the Supreme Brahman. He is omniscient, all-pervading, all-powerful. Therefore Ram and Anadev must not be worshipped as though they were equal; otherwise, by doing so, the worshipper does indeed reap the fruit of that devotion, but he cannot find rest at the feet of Shri Hari. —3.

Forsaking the Lord of Sita, many people seek the Supreme Brahman by meditating and searching for it in the sky. But this is like a pregnant woman whose first child is already playing in her lap, yet who neglects that child and instead remains absorbed in thoughts about the child still...

...is like being lost. To abandon what is manifest and easily accessible, and to hold the vain hope of searching for something else, is exactly like that. –4.

Some people give up devotion to their beloved deity, Sitapati (Lord of Sita, Shri Ram), and instead strive to fix their mind on the knowledge of Brahm. This is like entering a room stuffed full of raw cotton and then setting fire to its own door — one is bound to die an unnecessary death by burning. In the same way, entering the futile path of knowledge — knowledge of Brahm being like a wad of raw cotton — and then, at whatever doorway of knowledge resembles "I am Brahm," setting alight the claim "I myself am Brahm," is fatal: since such people are never truly all-powerful like the Supreme Brahm itself, they will burn in the fire of the digestive flame through 84 lakh (8.4 million) kinds of birth — that is, they will have to wander through 84 lakh wombs. –5.

Indeed, there are many in this world who abandon Sitapati Shri Ram to go searching for Brahm instead. Such thoughtless devotees, by entering the temple (house) of ignorance and then setting fire to its very door, are doing exactly this kind of self-destructive act.

Some engage in the practices of the path of yoga: pressing the anal opening with the heel so that no wind may escape there, tucking the tongue back into the throat, and then striving — through pranayam (breath control) — to strike the serpent-power (kundalini) with the breath, wakening it, and driving it upward from the lower end of the subtle channel that runs through the spinal column, so as to unite it, in the head, with the principle of Shiv, and thereby attain the supreme state through this union of Shiv and Shakti. But even if they succeed in bringing about this union of Shiv and Shakti, since they do it without devotion to Ram's name, such yogic practice only earns them the pleasures of heaven for a time; and once that store of merit (punya) is exhausted, their turn comes to go straight to hell. –6.

Again, closing the root gate — that is, the anal opening — with the heel of the foot, and drawing back into the sky-like space of the body the wind that would otherwise be released as flatus, is one such yogic practice. But doing this will not turn death back in any way, for without Sitapati Shri Ram there is no one's deliverance.

When yogis reach the state of unmuni (transcendence of mind), the unstruck sound (anahad naad) is heard; in that state there is neither the light nor the shade of sun or moon. Yet even though they may attain that state in which all the qualities of both sun and moon dissolve, still, without Ram's name, all these practices of theirs amount to nothing but dealings with Yamraj in Yama's abode — a method that only makes one a candidate for hell. –7.

Jivanji Maharaj says that the "unstruck word" — the sound produced during the pranayam actions of kumbhak (holding/taking in the breath) and rechak (releasing the breath), that is, the sound of "soham, soham" heard during yogic practice — leads one from that sound into the unmuni state of yoga, that is, into the state of no-sound (anaad). But Vaishnavs, whose task is to make the impossible possible — to unite sun and moon, day and night, so to speak — should not fall into such matters. For doing so cannot ward off death; indeed, it is like inviting Yama himself to a contest. It is therefore fitting that good, righteous people follow Ram alone.

In the heart, the innermost seat, there is an eight-petaled lotus called the heart-lotus; some yogis meditate there upon the light of Brahm shaped like a thumb, while other yogis meditate on the Brahm pervading the sky. But Jivanji Maharaj says: good man, rather than all this, simply sing the praises and do the devotional singing (bhajan-kirtan) of Sitapati Ram alone, at whose lotus feet Lakshmanji dwells. –8.

Sakut — The word "sakut" is first found in Kabirji's sayings (sakhis). It is a word of very broad meaning. According to the Gujarati dictionary Bhagvad Gomandal, sakut carries the meanings: one who gossips or slanders, unrighteous, wicked, low, sinful, cunning, wretched, and so on. Besides this, the saints who came in the Kabir tradition have given various meanings and characteristics for the word sakut. Kabirji, Jivanji, Gnaniji and other saints have described three types of people from the point of view of devotion, that is, of spirituality, by which the whole of humankind can be divided into three categories, in descending order: (1) the anin-ananya (exclusively devoted) Vaishnav, (2) the sakut, and (3) the salil — each rank lower than the one before. Of these, the state of the anin-ananya Vaishnav is regarded as the finest form a person can take. This is discussed in Shyamdasji's composition, the Parchari of Krishnadasji (see Panchratnamala, pages 297 to 302), where Shyamdasji has given a particularly detailed account of the characteristics of all three types. In addition, Jivanji Maharaj and Kabirji have listed their characteristics through separate sakhis called the "Sakutko Ang." Jivanji Maharaj has also given a "Salilko Ang." Kabirji, defining sakut, has said —

_Kabir sakut sakut sabko kahe, kachu sakuta ye dhaan
Ninda karvakun shoorma, nahi guru vachan pramaan ||1||
Kabir katha na sune kirtan, mukh na jape hari naam
Te nar sada sutki, abhadaya sara gaam ||2||_
(Everyone calls out "sakut, sakut" — but here is the sign by which a true sakut is known: sakut people are champions at slandering devotees, and they do not accept the guru's own word of Ram-bhakti. Kabir says: sakuts never listen to discourse or kirtan, nor utter Hari's name with their mouth — such men are forever as impure as one in mourning-defilement, and they render the whole village impure along with them.)

Everyone says "sakut, sakut," but the sign by which one recognizes what a sakut truly is, is this: sakut people slander devotees, and they do not receive Ram-bhakti from the guru's own mouth. –1. Sakuts pay no heed whatsoever to devotion to Ram, nor do they practise it; nor do they even utter Ram's name with their mouth. Such people are as untouchable as one under ritual impurity (sutak), and they render the whole of society untouchable along with them. –2.

Bhagat Trikamdas Gordhandas, resident of Suryaghoda, who has made a sincere effort to interpret the meanings of Jivanji Maharaj's sakhis, has interpreted this sakhi as follows: Shri Jivanji Maharaj says that devotees who remember Sitaram alongside their devotion to an "aan-dev" (a lesser deity, not the Supreme) may attain liberation (mukti), but they will not attain the lotus feet of the Lord — that is, they will not attain surrender at His feet. Hence the Ram-bhakti they perform amounts to no more than worship of the aan-dev; there can be no peace of undivided, single-minded devotion between such a devotee and the Lord. He has also written a kundali (a linked quatrain form) on this sakhi.

_Aandev barabar Jeevana, je samare Sitaram
Mugat phal ve det he, nahi charan kamal vishram ||1||
Nahi charan kamal vishram, mugati chhe santni daasi
Mrugjal joeene dhaay, janam bhar rahe pyaasi ||2||
Ek nishthathi samro Ram, avar upaay su nahi kaam
Je samare Sitaram, aandev barabar Jeevana ||3||_
(Jivana says: one who remembers Sitaram alongside an aan-dev is, in effect, worshipping the aan-dev; such remembrance gives the fruit of liberation, but not rest at the Lord's lotus feet. Liberation is merely the maidservant of the saints; one who runs after it, mistaking it for water, is like one running after a mirage — thirsty one's whole life through. Remember Ram with single-minded devotion; no other means will serve. One who remembers Sitaram alongside an aan-dev is, Jivana says, worshipping the aan-dev.)

Those who remember Ram alongside devotion to an aan-dev — that remembrance too is counted the same as devotion to the aan-dev; so by the power of that devotion one may obtain the fruit of liberation, but one will not obtain a place at the Lord's lotus feet. Liberation is merely the servant-girl of the saints; through that liberation one does not gain a place at the Lord's lotus feet. So chasing after such alluring liberation is like chasing after a mirage — just as running after the water of a mirage never quenches one's thirst, since there is no real water there, so too such devotion yields no truly good result. Therefore remember Ram with single-minded, exclusive devotion; there is no other means for our true welfare. In this way, if you combine devotion to Sitaram with devotion to an aan-dev, it will be reckoned no better than mere devotion to the aan-dev.

Jivanji Maharaj has drawn a beautiful comparison between the sakut and the salil.

_Salil pe sakut bhalo, je kabahuk paave paar
Salil booda keechme, Jeevan jaisi jal bin naav ||1||
Sakutki sabha rachi, taha jan bethan jaay
Ek gohade kyon bane, rojh gadha aur gaay ||2||_
(Better a sakut than a salil, for the sakut may sometime cross over; the salil drowns in the mud, Jivana says, like a boat stuck fast without water. Where an assembly of sakuts alone has gathered, how can a devotee of Hari go and sit among them? Just as a wild ox, a donkey, and a cow cannot be kept together in a single stall, so too, how can unity be forged between such sakuts and the devotees of Hari?)

A salil devotee sometimes worships his chosen deity and at other times worships an aan-dev — there is no telling which. So even though a sakut may well be worshipping an aan-dev, compared to such a salil, the sakut may, like Krishnadas, sometime get a chance to cross the ocean of worldly existence. But the salil, being mired in many different forms of worship, will get stuck fast in the mud of that ocean, just as a boat without water sinks into the mire. –6.

Where only sakuts alone have gathered together, how can a devotee of Hari join them there? Just as wild oxen, donkeys, and cows cannot be kept together in a single stall, so how can unity be achieved between the devotees of Hari and such sakuts? –2.

Further still, Vyas goes even further and says —

_Vyas sakut naari chhandiye, gunka kije naar
Dasi hoy Hari bhaktki, to kul na aave gaar ||1||_
(Vyas says: give up a sakut woman as a wife, and make even a woman of low repute your wife if she becomes a servant of Hari's devotees — then no disgrace comes upon the family.)

Hariram Vyasji wrote this sakhi. When he left Odchha to come and settle in Vrindavan, he refused even to accept his own wife back, because he had by then given himself over to Vishnu-bhakti, and his wife, being still the daughter of a Brahmin household unconnected to that devotion, was not acceptable to him for as long as she had not accepted Vaishnavism. So when the wife agreed to serve the Vaishnavs, he accepted her again. Hence the meaning of "make even a woman of low repute your wife" is not that she serves only her husband, but that if a woman — even one of low repute — is ready to serve the Vaishnavs with the same love as she would her husband, one should make even such a woman one's wife. Vyasji says that because of such a wife, our Vaishnav lineage will never have to hear the reproach of harboring a wicked woman; rather, she will only make our Vaishnav standing shine the brighter. Hence the sense is that a sakut woman should never be accepted as a wife. Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj too has shown this same courage. –1.

_Naari rove Jeevana, sir par ghaale dhool
Khasam gayo ham haathse, jai pakdo nij mool ||118|| (Prabodh)_
(Jivana says: the wife weeps and throws dust upon her head — "My husband has slipped out of my grasp; go, hold on to your own root, your true self!")

When the husband accepted Vaishnavism, and since the wife was not yet a Vaishnavi, the husband forsook her; finding herself thus stripped of her honor, the woman began to lament and cry out that her husband had now slipped from her grip and had attached himself instead to the true and genuine means of his own real welfare.

Gnaniji Maharaj had, in a previous birth, belonged to the Gorakh sect (panth). Coming into his incarnation as Gnaniji, he wrote a scripture called the Gnanpanthi Paati, in which, describing this same process, he writes —

_Dhundhuka mahe dhoon oothe, anahad sabad akhand
Taha Gnani man gagan hai, garajat rahe Brahmand ||42||_
(In the midst of that whirling tumult of sounds a single unbroken unstruck word arises; there the knower's mind becomes the sky itself, in which the whole universe keeps rumbling.)

In the whirlwind of many kinds of sounds, a single unbroken sound of the unstruck word arises; in that state the mind becomes like the sky, and it keeps reverberating within the brain, in the Brahmarandhra (the crown aperture) that stands for the universe itself.

_Dhoop na chhaya dekhiye, piyu bina nahi bhesh
Gnani taha man unmuni, jaha kachu roop na rekh ||46||_
(There one sees neither sunlight nor shade; there is no form except that of the Beloved alone. There the knower's mind reaches the unmuni state, where there is neither shape nor outline.)

In such a state there is nothing like sunlight or shade; there is no form other than that of one's own Master, and the mind reaches this unmuni state in which there is neither shape nor kind.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, who peered into every branch and sub-branch everywhere and gained direct experience of them, left nothing unexamined regarding the ways such yogis or gnanis practise their devotion, and he came to the firm conclusion that Ram's name alone is the best of all these paths. Sadguru Kabirji, in his handwritten scripture No. 79, in the "Unmuni-desh-ka Ang" (the section on the state of transcendence), has spoken a sakhi.

_Kabir shoon amar ajapa amar, anahad amar apaar
Alakh jaane so nar amar, kahe Kabir vichaar ||21||_
(Kabir says, after careful reflection: the imperishable Supreme Brahm is immortal as the Void, immortal as the unspoken chant (ajapa jap), and the unstruck word too is immortal and without end. But the man who truly knows that unseeable Brahm — that man alone is truly immortal.)

The imperishable Supreme Brahm is immortal in the form of the Void, immortal too in the form of the ajapa jap (the unspoken repetition), and the unstruck word too is immortal and boundless. But the Supreme Brahm that is alakh — that is, that cannot come within anyone's aim or perception — the person who can truly understand That is the one who is truly immortal. Having deliberated and understood this fully, Kabirji says —

_Kabir shoon mare ajapa mare, anahad bi mar jaay
Alakh purush o ek he, virla sant samaay ||20||_
(Kabir says: the all-powerful Supreme Brahm can bring even the Void to its end, can silence even the ajapa jap, and can make even the unstruck sound cease. But that unseeable Being is One alone, and only a rare saint can merge into That.)

The all-powerful Supreme Brahm can bring even the Void to an end and can silence even the ajapa jap; but the very essence of that Supreme Brahm has a nature that cannot be pinned down as an object of aim — it is unseeable. It is not many different things but only One; only some truly great saint can understand it. In this teaching (unmuni-desh) it is spoken of as the "Ram-kar" (the sound-form of Ram); it is called one's own true name. It is said that "the corpse is eaten by Death (Kal)," meaning that one who is "dead while living" — that is, unattached — is beyond the reach of Kal (Time/Death). There is much subtlety in all this, but the chief point that has been aimed at is devotion to that Ram-kar. The Gita says, "na me bhaktah pranashyati" — "My devotee never perishes."

In this way the saints have spoken against maintaining any relation with sakut and salil people. Jivandasji has even said that one should not accept food or water from them. Such souls will keep undergoing heaven and hell purely on the strength of their sin and merit, that is, they will keep being ground down in the cycle of birth and death.

Sarang (a musical raga)

_Ramko nit kije re, samaran Ramko nit kije
Nirmal nirmal prem Hari ras, sant sangat mali pije ||teka||
Jhoothi maya moh vishay ras, e mante tyagije
Hirde kamal bich nishdin e hi vilamb na kije ||sama||
Tan man dhan sab mansa re vacha, Ram samarpan kije
Kahet Kabir me aur na maagu, charan kamal chit dije ||sama||_
(Always remember Ram, always remember Ram. Drink, gathered in the company of saints, the pure, pure sweetness of Hari's love. Give up from your mind the false maya and the sweetness of worldly attachment. Ram is chanted day and night within the lotus of the heart — do not delay in worshipping Him. With body, mind, wealth, thought, and speech, offer everything in surrender to Ram. Kabir says: I ask for nothing else — only grant that my heart stay fixed on Your lotus feet.)

Always remember Ram, and, joining the company of saints, drink the pure, pure sweetness of loving devotion to Hari. Give up from your mind the false illusion of the pleasures of this world's sense-objects. And do not delay in worshipping the Ram whose remembrance goes on ceaselessly, day and night, within the lotus of the heart. Offer your whole self — body, mind, wealth, will, and speech — in surrender to Ram. Kabirji says: I ask for nothing else; only grant me this, that my mind remain fixed upon Your lotus feet.

In the yogic path of the eight-petaled lotus, an effort is made through yoga to see the Supreme Soul in the form of a lotus within the heart; one enters samadhi and meditates on this eight-petaled lotus. In the human body, four such lotuses are spoken of above (the upper ones): (1) the head-lotus, (2) the eye-lotus, (3) the mouth-lotus, (4) the face-lotus. And four below: (5) the heart-lotus, (6) the navel-lotus, (7) the hand-lotus, (8) the foot-lotus. In this way they are all accounted for within the body. The entire being of righteous men is itself like a lotus made of good deeds.

Some chant and worship the eight-petaled lotus, that is, they cherish the desire to attain Lakshmi (wealth and prosperity). Others meditate upon the high sky above. But the exclusively-devoted (anin-ananya) Vaishnav ought to worship only Shri Parmeshwar Parabrahm — that is, Sitapati Shri Ram — at whose lotus feet Lakshmi eternally dwells.

At the start of this chapter we saw how idol-worship, temples, and other outward attractions stand as obstacles on the path of devotional worship. Now, through eight further sakhis, Jivanji Maharaj discusses the method (manner) of worship and the elements that obstruct it. He begins with a sakhi of Kabirji that divides the whole of humankind into three categories and identifies them, teaching us to keep aloof from the company of sakuts. He then goes on to show the identifying marks and characteristics of the sakut. The sakut represents the single greatest obstacle on the path of devotion, because he is the fiercest critic of that path; and if, out of fear of his criticism, devotees flee far from devotion, they will certainly lose their life's purpose. So if there is any single greatest challenge, it is the sakut — and one must resist and stand firm against him.

The second great obstacle of this kind is the "Aan-dev." Just as Kabirji is the one who gave us the word "sakut," the word "aan-dev" too is his gift; both of these are new words Kabirji coined, and so their interpretation is not to be found in ordinary dictionaries. We have now become familiar with "sakut"; here we shall examine the meaning of the word "aan-dev." Aan-dev (masc.) — aa-na-dev: (1) meaning "this is not a deva," not the Supreme Brahm, not something that can be called Ishwar/Parmatma — a being or deity of that kind; (2) a deity who is not all-powerful, not all-pervading, and not all-knowing — that is, one who has only limited soul-power, is not all-pervading, and possesses only limited knowledge; (3) one in whom devatva — that is, divine power — is lacking. In short, to understand the word "aan-dev," it is enough to know this: whomever we call a deva or devi, or recognize as such, can never rightly be called Parbrahm or Parmeshwar. Such beings are to be recognized precisely as "aan-dev," because no principle other than Parbrahm or Parmeshwar is complete or whole. Hanumandas Shatshastri, in the Aan-dev Ang, interprets aan-dev as meaning "other than Hari." Moreover, an aan-dev does not have the power to bring one to the supreme state; by worshipping such deities, the worshipper obtains a result only according to the power of that particular deity (not the supreme state). But this result is short-lived and only casts one further into the bondage of illusion (moha-maya). The finest example of this is none other than "Krishnadasji," who came from Agalod to obtain devotion from Jivanji Maharaj.

Krishnadas was the son of Damodar, a Mevadi Brahmin of Idar, of the Katyayani gotra, a strict follower of the Madhyandini branch of the Yajurveda. This son, possessing the same faith and refinement as his father and upholding his father's tradition, was himself an ardent devotee of Ganpati.

_Isht dev Ganpatikun maane, aur devkun chitt na aave
Ganpatiko maha dhyan hi kare, Ganpati naam mukhse ochare
Ek din aisi chittme aai, Harki bhakti puchhun man laai
Manme guni dhyan jab kino, Ganpati aay darshan tabahi deeno
Maag maag ichchha ka tere, jo maage so deu savere_
(He held Ganpati as his chosen deity; his mind turned to no other god. He performed deep meditation on Ganpati and constantly uttered Ganpati's name with his mouth. One day this thought arose within him: let me ask about devotion to Hari. When his mind meditated with sincerity, Ganpati at once appeared and gave him darshan, saying: ask, ask whatever you wish, and I shall grant it at once.)

That is to say: holding Ganpati as his chosen deity, he worshipped only him and believed in no other god. He performed great daily meditation on Ganpati and constantly repeated Ganpati's name with his mouth. One day, by a divine hint, a wish arose in his mind: "Let me ask Ganpati about devotion to the Lord." Thinking so, he meditated on Ganpati; at once Ganpati appeared before him and told him to ask for whatever boon he wished. Thereupon Krishnadas asked, as above, to be given devotion to the Lord. At this, Ganpati revealed his own inability to grant it.

Being a giver only of riddhi-siddhi (worldly prosperity and supernatural powers), Ganpati was unable to give anything besides that. Ganpati offered him wealth, kingship, and riddhi-siddhi instead, but by his good fortune, Krishnadas held firm to his one request alone. Knowing that riddhi-siddhi, being a bondage of maya, would only lead one into hell, he asked for devotion alone to be granted. At this, Ganpati told him —

_Riddhi siddhi tokun me deun, agam vastuko marm na laheun
Santko sang karo tum jaai, taate aava gavan nasaai
Kahanav mandal rahe sukhdaai, taha mil hi sant jan bhaai_
(I can give you riddhi-siddhi, but I do not grasp the secret of that unreachable thing. Go instead and keep the company of a saint — through that your coming and going, your cycle of rebirth, will be destroyed. In the Kanam region dwells one who brings happiness — go there, brother, and meet that saintly person.)

That is to say, Ganpati says: I am a giver of riddhi-siddhi, but the unfathomable thing called "bhakti" cannot be granted by me. For that you must take refuge with a saint; only a saint can show the path of devotion and bring you out of the cycle of birth and death. So go to a saint. In the Kanam region there is a saint named "Jivandasji" who will give you devotion — go and take refuge with him.

On Ganpati saying this, Krishnadasji came to Puniyad, and we are all witnesses to whatever he received there from Jivanji Maharaj; the whole community of devotees, especially of the Kantha region, remains grateful to him for it. The point being made is this: whoever has a certain limit can act only within that limit, and cannot give what lies beyond it — though, yes, he can point a finger towards it, which is exactly what Ganpati did. For this the Kantha-region community, and Krishnadasji and his family, remain deeply grateful to Ganpati. But that does not mean Ganpati ought therefore to be worshipped. Now we must move forward on our own path — the very path Krishnadas himself wished to travel, but which he himself was unable to find. Ganpati played the role of a guide who showed him that path; as a guide he is fine, but he cannot be an object of worship. The same understanding applies to any other minor deities, or pirs, and so on. Today there are many who, driven by momentary greed or delusion, waste lakhs of rupees and precious time chasing after such deities; they ought to walk this path with proper understanding and thought.

Here, in the first sakhi, we were told to remain aloof from and watchful of the company of sakuts. In the next two, we were told not to worship or venerate an aan-dev. Devotees should worship only Ram and Krishna, and that too according to the path shown by Jivanji Maharaj, otherwise even here one may go astray. The remaining four sakhis concern the path of yoga, whose meaning we have already examined earlier. But some technical terms are not easy to understand; once we know and understand the meaning of those terms, we shall then determine why Jivanji Maharaj is unwilling to accept even this path of yoga.

Yoga Shastra is one of the six schools of philosophy (darshan shastras), as we have already seen earlier. Muni Patanjali is regarded as the original founder of Yoga Shastra. But as accomplished (siddha) yogis, the Navnath — nine individuals renowned as great masters of yoga — are spoken of: Adinath, Matsyendranath, Gorakshanath, Jalandharnath, Bhartruhari Nath, Gopichand, Meennath, Nityanath, and Bindunath are the principal Naths. The main basis of this path of yoga is pranayam, asana, dhyan (meditation), and so on. Matsyendranath and Gorakshanath made an especially great contribution to spreading this path. But this path also includes certain crude and unspeakable practices, which scholars try to explain by giving them a spiritual gloss. Practices such as vajroli, sahajoli, and amanoli, however, are genuinely such that they cannot be properly described. Later, spiritual interpretations were given to such practices, but even today there are those who follow these practices quite literally. Furthermore, the tantric texts associated with yoga are, for an ordinary person, thoroughly repulsive and crude. So long as the matter concerns bodily health alone, pranayam and asanas are perfectly fine — but one should not go further than that. As for health, our community, from the earliest times, has come from a hardworking farming class; in those days the farmer who laboured with his own hands remained naturally healthy. Today that same class has moved to the cities for employment or business, and so, to maintain fitness, it has become necessary to do physical exercises. For this reason, practising up to asana and pranayam is fine, but beyond this, this path is of no use for attaining liberation in this life (jivan-mukti).

As for the further practices that have been described, a plain, ordinary person should not fall into them. As the saying goes: "One who copies others and practises yoga just by seeing it done neither dies nor is cured — his disease only worsens." Just so, one who is attracted merely by watching others and imitates them lands in a wretched state. Rather than mechanical yoga, this natural (sahaj) yoga happens by itself, along with true devotion. Lovers are not taught how to love — it simply happens by itself. In the same way, anger too need not be taught — it too arises by itself. But manufactured love or manufactured anger is mere pretence; it is not true love or true anger. In just this way, the senses that God has given us do their own work by themselves; but to make them do more than their natural capacity, one has to resort to artificial instruments — a telescope to see far, a telephone and the like to hear far off — because the power of the senses given by nature is limited. The divine principle, however, is beyond the reach of the senses altogether, so the senses are not capable of attaining it. Yet by making good use of these five senses one can attain the supreme state, while by misusing them one meets with ruin — one neither dies nor is cured, one falls ill, and one must suffer bad consequences. God is not attained through mere technique (sadhan); He is attained only through grace (kripa). God, who sent the soul alone into the cage of karma, gave it five sense-organs of knowledge and five organs of action, and said: "Make good use of these, or else you will suffer." The soul caught in delusion and illusion thus falls into birth and death; therefore one should perform devotion according to one's capacity. When the merciful Lord bestows His grace, He makes no distinction of woman or man, of loved or unloved — therefore one should practise desireless (nishkam) devotion. Adhyaruji says: _geete naade shrute jeh nav rije, e te kem kije vash aap_ (one whom song, sound, and sacred hearing themselves fail to please — how, then, can such a one be brought under one's own control?).

When, according to one's karma, the soul comes into a body that is blind, deaf, crippled or lame, the power of the senses does not function. And even when the senses are sound, they are still not of full power — the senses are gained only through passing through the womb and being born. Even when one has the senses, the outer environment can act as an obstruction to them; to block that out, one has to shut the eyes and ears and apply one's inner strength. The blind and the deaf, however, do not need to shut their eyes and ears.

One blind from birth has no idea what light is like; the same holds for one deaf from birth — he can know nothing at all about language or sound. But for one who deliberately shuts his eyes and strives for the inner divine light or sound, outer light or sound too can begin to feel like an obstruction. The sight of the figure of Time (Kal Purush), or the sound of Kal Purush, is reckoned a sign of misfortune. The Supreme Principle is beyond words and beyond the senses altogether. Yet, compared to the all-powerful Supreme Principle, sound and the objects of the senses remain subordinate to that Supreme Principle; the workings of word-meaning or of the senses do not possess any independent existence apart from the divine principle. But though sound or the senses cannot bring the Supreme Principle under their own sway, they themselves remain subject to that Supreme Principle. The Supreme Principle is all-powerful; but it cannot be said that the Supreme Principle — which is "smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest" — consists merely of sound.

Further, some, by means of yogic practice, perform a discipline (sadhana) of sound. It is said that through this sadhana one first hears sounds like the roar of the ocean, drums, kettle-drums, and cymbals, as well as conch, bell, and battle-trumpet sounds. Finally one hears sounds like a small bell, a flute, or a veena. In this way, listening to such sounds is shown as a path to the attainment of Brahm. Kabirji and Jivanji have already said much about this earlier, and a wise person should not fall into this, because —

_Naado'ntarang, saarang bandhane vaaguyaraate
Antarang kurangasya vadhe vyaadhayaate'pi cha ||1|| (Hathayoga Pradipika 4-94)_
(The unstruck sound itself becomes a snare, binding the deer-like mind; and it is that same snare that becomes the hunter who slays that deer-like mind.)

The unstruck sound itself becomes the snare that binds the deer-like mind, and that very same sound becomes the hunter who slays that deer-like mind.

That is to say, the discipline of nad-yoga can itself become an obstacle on the path of worship. As stated above, worshippers of this yoga stop their ears with their fingers, close their eyes, and try to listen for that sound. There is much deception hidden within this, and there is no instrument or means to measure that sound or to test its genuineness. This is why Jivanji Maharaj says —

_Aankh michine aandhalo, dhyan dhare aakash
Sitapati bhootal Jeevana, jaha sant sangat nivaas ||1||_
(Jivana says: one who closes his eyes and meditates on the sky is only making himself blind. Sitapati dwells here on this very earth, in the place where the company of saints resides.)

Kabirji goes even further and says —

_Kabir aasan maare kaha bhaye, mooi ne manki aash
Teli kera bel jyon, gharahi kosh pachaas ||2||_
(What does it profit to sit fixed in an asana, when the desires of the mind have not died? Like the oil-presser's bullock, one goes round and round, staying within the confines of home, covering fifty kos yet never moving from the spot.)

_Kabir indri eko bas nahi, chhod chala parvaar
Parja pichhe yon phire, jese chaak kumbhaar ||3||_
(Kabir says: not one sense-organ has come under control, yet he abandons his family and departs; behind him his kin whirl about just as a potter's wheel spins.)

_Kabir indri eko bas nahi, bhagva kari kopeen
Baahir bag dhyaavi bhaye, machhlisu man leen ||4||_
(Kabir says: not one sense-organ has come under control, though he wears saffron robes and a loincloth; outwardly he appears absorbed in meditation like a heron standing still, but his mind is fixed on the fish.)

The meaning is quite simple: closing the eyes does not, by itself, bring about meditation or samadhi, for merely closing the eyes outwardly accomplishes nothing when, inside, all the passions still rage in full force and the mind wanders here, there, and everywhere. Thus not a single sense is truly under control, and it becomes mere hypocrisy, like the pretence of a heron. Kabirji goes further still and says that when a person whose senses are not even slightly under control abandons home and family to become a yogi, the family left behind is thrown into a state like a potter's spinning wheel. In fact, the world (sansar) is itself the best place for practising devotion — one can perform devotion while remaining right here in it. The direct proof of this is Narsinh Mehta, Mirabai, Kabirji, and others. Tulsidas says —

_Tulsi gharke gher me, ghadi ghadi tan chheen
Kabahu van van na phire, kar karva kopeen ||5||_
(Tulsi says: caught up in the entanglements of household life, his body grows thinner moment by moment — yet never does he wander from forest to forest, staff and loincloth in hand.)

For one who is caught up in the entanglements of household life, when the attachment to the body keeps growing weaker moment by moment, such a person never needs to go wandering from forest to forest, gourd-bowl in hand and loincloth on the body.

_Tulsi badhat kachhu badh gai, ghatat ghatat bhai chheen
Banat banat kachhu ban gai, kar karva kopeen_
(Tulsi says: as worldly desire kept growing and growing, it reached its peak; then, as it kept diminishing and diminishing, it grew thin — and so, gradually taking shape, it finally took the form of the staff and loincloth in hand.)

In the mind, when worldly desires kept increasing and increasing until they reached their extreme peak, and then, growing weary of them, the attachment to them kept diminishing and diminishing until an intense dispassion (vairagya) arose — then, transforming step by step out of that dispassion, one arrived at last at taking up a gourd-bowl in hand and a loincloth on the body. Advancing step by step from the stage of celibate discipline (brahmacharya) up to the stage of renunciation (sannyas), and reducing worldly desires bit by bit, in the end, carried along by that emotional transformation, the practice took an outward form as well: taking up a gourd-bowl in hand and wearing a loincloth on the body became the outward custom that resulted from it.

_Gharahi maahi ban kare, Hari charane laulin
Tulsi aise santkun, kaha karva kopeen_
(Tulsi says: for such a saint, who turns his own home into the forest and remains wholly absorbed in Hari's feet, what need has he of the gourd-bowl or the loincloth?)

Tulsidas says that for a saintly person whose heart has truly, through detachment, become wholly absorbed in devotion to Hari, what need does he have for outward trappings such as the gourd-bowl or the loincloth? Those who are hypocrites may well wear the gourd-bowl or the loincloth, yet their attachment to sense-pleasures does not leave them.

In this way, Jivanji Maharaj has not accepted the path of yoga as a means for Vishnu-bhakti, nor has he accepted the siddhi (attainment) of this path, that is, the fruit obtained after such practice. For this reason, through the sakhi "Anahad shabda jaha" (12-7), he has refuted the highest attainment of the path of yoga. Contrary to what was said earlier about listening to nad, the yogi gradually reaches, through the hearing of that sound, the state of anahat nad. That is to say, the sound of conch, kettle-drum and so on is only the first stage; one must reach beyond it to that further state. This state is called the unmuni state.

_Unmanyavasthapraptasya mune: varnanam
Shankhadundubhinadam cha na shrunoti kadachana
Kashthavajjnayate deha unmanyaavasthaya dhruvam ||106|| (Hathayoga Pradipika 4-106)_
("A description of the sage who has attained the unmuni state: he never again hears the sound of conch or kettle-drum, and in the unmuni state his body surely becomes as still and lifeless as wood.")

In truth, all such talk is nothing but empty, deluded speech (mithya pralap). As we have already said, so long as it concerns the body alone — that is, up to the level of asanas (physical exercises) — the matter is indeed sound. But one should not go back into its deeper spiritual entanglements, where certain crude and forcibly-performed postures are also to be found. For Prajapati Daksha composed a scripture of dharma called a smriti under his own name, in which he says —

_Naranyasevanaadyogo naanek grantha chintanaat
Vratairyastapobhirva na yoga: kasyachidbhavet ||1||
Na cha pathyaashanaadyogo na naashaagrinirikshanaat
Na mantramaun kuhakairaneke, sukrutai stathaa
Lokayatraaniyuktasya yogo bhavati kasyachit ||3|| (Daksh Smriti 7-4,5,6)_
(By dwelling in the forest, by reflecting on many scriptures, by vows, sacrifice, and austerity, no yoga of any kind is accomplished. Nor is yoga accomplished through wholesome eating, gazing at the tip of one's nose, excessive scriptural study, or the practice of restraining excretion. Nor is yoga attained through mantra, silence, deception, various acts of merit, or diligence in worldly dealings.)

Dwelling in the forest, various kinds of sacrifices, various kinds of rigorous yoga, postures, fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose, various rules for bodily purification, the practice of silence, the repetition of many kinds of mantras, and the performance of meritorious acts — none of these bring about the attainment of yoga.

That is to say, one does not become an accomplished (siddha) yogi merely by acquiring various kinds of riddhi-siddhi. All such things bring only sorrow and are perishable. It is for this very reason that Guru Nanak Sahib, an exclusive devotee in Kabir's own tradition, says —

_Je yug chaare aarja hor dasuni hoi
Nava khanda vichi jaaniye naali chalai sabhu koi
Changa naad rakhaai kai jasu kirati jani lei
Je tisu nadari na aavare ta vaat na puchhe ke (Guru Granth Sahib)_
(Even if one's lifespan should equal the four ages, and grow tenfold more still; even if one becomes known throughout the nine continents and everyone comes along with one; even if one keeps a good name and wins fame and praise — yet if one does not come within the Lord's gracious glance, then no one will care to ask after one at all.)

Even if a person's lifespan should become equal to four ages of the world (even if such practices as yoga were to extend one's life that far) — indeed, even if it were to become ten times more still — even if he gained fame across the nine continents and all fourteen realms, even if the whole world came to follow his command, even if his reputation spread from land to land and everyone sang his praises — still, if the gracious glance of the Supreme Soul does not fall upon him, he will find no refuge anywhere. In other words, one can truly never draw near to God by means of material power or attainment alone.

In short, what Yoga Shastra calls ashtayoga (the eight limbs of yoga) — namely yam, niyam, asana, pranayam, pratyahar, dharana, dhyan, and samadhi (yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi being the eight limbs of yoga) — and, in addition, what is called chaturyoga (the four yogas): mantrayoga, hathayoga, layayoga, and rajayoga — all of these are outward means. They bring about a development of material well-being (including bodily matters), but by means of them one cannot come to recognize the supreme state of the world, that is, true glory (aishvarya). Forms such as dhyan, dharana, and samadhi hold the mind back from outward wandering only for a brief while, but they cannot make it eternally absorbed. History gives examples of sages like Vishwamitra, who performed austerities (tapas) for thousands of years, only to fall later into the snare of apsaras such as Menaka.

Devotion (bhakti) alone is that means by which pride never arises; a devotee never needs to put on a show, nor does he ever need to acquire perishable things such as riddhi-siddhi. Bhakti alone is "avyabhicharini" — that is, unwavering and never unfaithful. The reason it is known by this name is precisely that it never gives rise to any corrupting passion.

In the end, all these are simply various paths by which the individual soul longs to attain both material and spiritual happiness. Those who lose their way on these paths become unhappy. Jivanji Maharaj has no interest in outward show or display, and it is for this very reason that he has forbidden outward practices such as idol worship, yoga, and meditation-for-display. Let us now go on and see what he says next.
